items.question: What If the Mongol Empire had gone to Western Europe instead of the Levant?
human_answers: You are thinking of the Mongol's as a unified force which by this time is not exactly correct. Hulegu and the Ilkhanate were based in Iran (mostly) so the OTL force would not be interested in expanding in Eastern Europe. Batu / Berke and the Golden Horde started their drift towards Islam in this period but their control over the European fringe via their vassals in Kiev and Muscovy wasn't absolute and relied on the tolerance of their Orthodox faith. Any attack on Europe may well become religious in nature (which by itself is an interesting counterfactual) and I suspect any support from the Russian principalities would be lukewarm perhaps even moving towards outright rebellion. It would also be short lived given that the Mongol Civil War is coming. Biggest outcome if the Russian principalities do revolt could be a more Islamised Russia which would be a huge change for world history.

Is there any reason to assume that the forests of western europe were somehow “denser” than those of the eastern? Specifically, those of the Central Russia? BTW, it is not like the Mongols uniformly came from the open steppe: IIRC, Subotai came from Uryankay area which, AFAIK, mostly forests and mountains and he was doing quite well in the Russian forests and pretty much everywhere else. Of course, the Southern direction was much richer than the western one but #1 was the eastern one - China. AFAIK, the South ended up being problematic due to a limited feeding base for the horses but all theories about Mongolian conquest of the west are seemingly ignoring allocation of the resources. The western campaign (including Russia) presumably started with a big force but its second stage, Hungary and Poland, was on a much lesser scale. The map on the OP has “Ulus Jochi” and “Ulus Batu” as separate entities but this was not the case: Batu was a titular head of the Ulus of Jochi. Was there an interest in Mongolia in expanding Ulus Jochi even further at the expense of other endeavors (and other family members)? IMO, this is unlikely because China remained the main theater (BTW, Subotai was sent there after the european campaigns). Were there unlimited human resources? Hardly: part of Hulagu’s force were troops “lended” by Batu. So, with what would Batu conduct his european conquest and why would the Great Khan be interested in its continuation? Formally, the task as formulated by Genghis was fulfilled: the Kipchaks punished and subdued and “the last sea” (Adriatics would do) reached. Was Batu too interested? It does not look like this was a case because he had to create a brand new state from the scratch with the very limited resources (something like 5,000 Mongols).
items.original_question: What if the Mongol Empire had gone to Western Europe instead of the Levant? https://www.reddit.com/r/imaginarymaps/comments/pkb97x/what_if_the_mongols_invaded_europe_the_old_world A sudden interesting thought came to mind. What if, unlike in OTL, the Mongol Empire had not expanded into the Levant and had instead resumed its campaign into Europe? In this TL, during the reign of Möngke Khan, the Mongol Empire invaded Europe again instead of attacking the Abbasid Caliphate. Assume that, starting with the Kingdom of Hungary, they continue pushing westward into the Holy Roman Empire, France, and beyond Western Europe for as long as they keep winning. What I’m curious about is this: 1. What kind of POD would be needed for this to be possible? 2. To what extent would this actually be feasible? - Could the Mongol Empire conquer Western Europe as well, just as it did in Eastern Europe? - Or, unlike in Eastern Europe, would it struggle in Western Europe? 3. If this did happen, what changes would follow? - The Mongol Empire’s advance into Western Europe. - The survival of the Abbasid Caliphate.

items.model_answer:
If the Mongol Empire had launched a sustained, full-scale invasion of Western Europe instead of halting after the 1241 campaigns in Hungary and Poland (and turning back due to Ögedei Khan’s death), it likely would have overwhelmed the fragmented and militarily inferior European states of the mid-13th century. Western Europe lacked centralized command, professional standing armies, or effective defenses against the Mongols’ superior mobility, discipline, and siege tactics. Major centers like Vienna, Paris, or even Rome could have fallen, leading to widespread devastation, population displacement, and the collapse of several kingdoms.

However, long-term Mongol rule over Western Europe was unlikely. The empire struggled with governance beyond steppe-style administration, and Western Europe’s dense forests, wet climate, and urbanized landscape were ill-suited to nomadic cavalry dominance. More plausibly, the Mongols would have extracted tribute, installed puppet rulers, or established a short-lived khanate before internal succession disputes or local resistance eroded control—similar to how their hold weakened in Persia and Russia over time. Culturally, such an invasion might have accelerated technological and intellectual exchanges earlier than the Renaissance, but it also could have delayed or altered the development of European nation-states, the Catholic Church’s authority, and later colonial expansion.

items.question: What If Americans capture Quebec in 1775. How does Quebec's culture & society develop?
human_answers: I can easily see Quebec not wanting to be part of either France, or USA. So they'll opt for independence. France never really wanted it back, so they won't get into their own American Revolution. Even if they did, it is the cost that will impact the French Revolution. The cost will add to French woes. This notion that France will rise up in revolution because Quebec wants independence is erroneous. France wanted regime/gov't change, which is not at all what Quebec wants (independence). France will add Quebec to the list of grievances. That does NOT make Quebec the birthplace of this alt FR. There were various causes of the ARW. One of them was putting Ohio under Canadian jurisdiction. Plus the French and Indian War was fought over the Ohio Valley, and led to a lot of the grievances leading to ARW. No one considers Ohio the birthplace of the AR. Semantics? maybe, but I don't think so.

It is difficult to ascertain how the French in Canada felt, as they lived in a quasi-medieval subsistence economy. Although not under full-blown feudalism, their society was paternalistic, hierarchical, and agrarian. The Church and the seigneurs (many of the seigneuries were owned by religious orders) were the pillars of authority. This is crucial in explaining the lack of widespread revolutionary fervour. However, in the late eighteenth century, there remained a cultural and sentimental connection to France, particularly to the Ancien Régime and the monarchy. After the executions of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, masses were said for them, and the French press in Quebec noted this. They were mourning the grandson of their last French sovereign, not celebrating the secular republic that executed him. In December 1778, from Boston, French Admiral d’Estaing called on the Canadiens to rise and rejoin their motherland, but this was difficult as Canada was where most British forces were stationed. It is unclear whether they wished to return to France, but the Continental Congress felt uneasy about the French returning to North America. Because the Canadiens were largely illiterate (literacy was still below 40% in 1850), it is difficult to say whether they were politically sophisticated, as the colony had been largely marginal and lacked a large merchant class under French rule. Education was not widespread and was largely controlled by seminaries or convents. It was even less politically sophisticated than the Spanish colonies in the Americas. My guess is that independence would have been the least likely of options, unless the Bishop of Quebec assumed the role of head of government.

Then the place will find a way to get out of American control ASAP. Mismatched expectations and all that because of a fundamental misreading by the Continental Army/Congress of the situation, particularly WRT the Quebec Act. The French never wanted to retain Canada après la Conquête because the sugar colonies in the Caribbean were far more valuable, plus lots of bad blood between the Canadiens and Versailles about which direction their part of New France should go. You'd basically be accelerating the French Revolution's TL but with a Canadien cause - and this time the British would come off as the good guys by allying with the habitants, whether or not it takes it back under its wing or accepts it as an independent country but under the British sphere of influence. And it finds a way to get out of the US ASAP, particularly if the initial military occupation goes as OTL and they basically alienated everyone. More probable than getting annexed by the US. Considering Quebec in this case would be a direct cause for the French Revolution ITTL, that's easy to remark on. While still predominantly Francophone (albeit with Canadian French given the same recognition as, say, Brazilian Portuguese), society and culture would take a more, say, Argentine or Uruguayan-like direction but w/ its own quirks (including probably far more indigenous influence) and probably different relationships among groups that would be relatively more egalitarian and opposed to reinstating the colonial relationship. Considering the British would still be next door viz. Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, as well as the HBC doing its thing, British influence would remain strong and that would include the cultural sphere, too.

It depends on how the Americans treat the Canadiens, and how they handle the Iroquois. If the Americans can't keep the Iroquois mostly neutral, and if they prevent them from trading with the Canadiens, then Quebec will want want to leave in a hurry. If the Americans could be deft in the administration of Quebec, better in battle, luckier with allied victories, and more skillful in peace negotiation I think there is a good chance that the Canadiens would want to be in a confederacy, or a customs union with a mutual defense pact. The centralizing reforms of the Constitution would likely have been opposed by the Canadiens as antifederalism, which brings me to the next point, though it is possible they could remain in the union if it transitions from Articles of Confederation to Constitution. While the Canadiens would most likely have forbade slavery, that doesn't mean they would have been abolitionists in the vein of the northeastern Calvinists and Quakers. While they could have been like the 1840s and 1850s Free Soilers, their antifederalism and relative lack of industrialization might have moved them into common cause with Southern states. The Canadiens also could have been aligned with the "Westerners" in looking for federally funded internal developments to help with their access to Atlantic ports, and their access to settling Upper Canada and Indiana/Illinois Territory. Being so close to Nova Scotia and Newfoundland the Canadiens could also be interested in a strong navy. So perhaps an American Quebec could be allied with someone like Calhoun. As for the issue of Loyalist Migration, their emigration would likely have been reduced if they didn't have British Upper Canada as a destination. Many of the Loyalists would have resigned themselves to life in the new government. There still would have been Loyalist emigration from both America and Lower Canada, and there would still be a movement of Loyalists to Upper Canada and other territories despite them being no longer British Empire owned. So those populations would have thrown a new political impulse into the country later especially after the Constitution is ratified.

I'd assume a French route with independence after the French revolution. Maybe some nobility or rich flee to Quebec during the revolution. I'd think US keeps what it would get otl plus Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward island. Ontario might go to the U.S. While Newfoundland and Labrador goes to Quebec. The American loyalists could be moved into western Canada to try to colonize Western Canada. England might be more harsh in dealing with the Oregon territory. You could see a war over it with Quebec siding with a side. Should U.S. Win they might get British Columbia in the treaty. Quebec might get islands in Nunavut. Russia in this timeline would probably favor selling Alaska to England. With more northern territory. I can see the South looking for more Mexican territory. There's a possibility the slave and free state addition could continue on longer. This causes a delay of the civil war potentially.
items.original_question: What if Americans capture Quebec in 1775. How does Quebec's culture & society develop? So having just watched a new video from Blue, it gave me an idea of dusting off an old topic I used to talk about In 1775, the Continental Army under Generals, Richard Montgomery, Daniel Morgan, James Livingston, and Benedict Arnold (Yes, that Benedict Arnold) marched north into Canada in an attempt to capture Quebec from the British and persuade the French Canadians in joining the revolution. It went well for part of the expedition at first, with Montgomery nearly capturing British Govenor Guy Carleton in Montreal. Meanwhile Arnold's part journeyed through the wilderness to get to Quebec City, which was very difficult. However, by the time the Americans gotten to Quebec, a snowstorm occurred and the battle turned into an utter disaster. Montgomery got killed, Arnold was wounded, smallpox plagued the Americans, the British suffered few causalities, and the Americans managed to alienate the Canadians. Meanwhile, Carleton received reinforcements and made a counter offensive that drove the Americans back to Fort Ticonderoga. For context, what if the Americans captured Quebec? Say Montgomery captured Govenor Guy Carleton and the Americans managed to catch Quebec City by surprise. In my previous thread about the fate of Quebec (Roughly around Lower Canada; Upper Canada is a whole other can of worms), there were four possibilities I gave, but we're going to talk about three: A) French route- The Americans offer Quebec back to France for support in their war, meaning France regains Quebec by the end of the war B) American route- The Americans annex Quebec, making Quebec part of the USA. C) Independent route- The Americans make Quebec into a sister republic, making Quebec independent by the end of the war. (There's no British route since that OTL) Now, I want to focus on one particular aspect of the fate of Quebec: Culture. If Quebec wasn't under the British/TTL Canada, what would culture be like for the French Canadians. Depending on the route we take, how would culture, society, art, cuisine, fashion, etc, develop for the French Canadians? In the French route, how would Quebec be affected by the French Revolution? In the American route, how would Quebec develop under the USA? In the Independent route, how would Quebec develop stuck between the British and Americans while having access to the St Lawrence?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise and Immediate Post-1775 Political Settlement
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly builds from the premise that American forces capture Quebec in 1775 and plausibly handles the immediate governance problem: Continental occupation, local Canadien reactions, the Quebec Act context, Catholic rights, seigneurial society, and whether Quebec is annexed, autonomous, restored to Britain, or moves toward independence.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or mishandles the 1775 premise; treats Quebec as simply becoming modern U.S. territory without explaining occupation, consent, or resistance.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges American capture but gives a shallow or deterministic political outcome with little attention to Canadien attitudes or wartime constraints.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible immediate settlement and notes some friction between American republican aims and Quebec's Catholic, Francophone, hierarchical society.
criteria.7-8: Explains multiple plausible settlement paths and ties them to Continental policy, military occupation, Catholic rights, local elites, and British counterpressure.
criteria.9-10: Carefully models the contested post-capture situation, including occupation legitimacy, Congress's limited capacity, Quebec Act expectations, clergy/seigneur roles, and why annexation, autonomy, British restoration, or independence would follow.

criteria.name: Mechanisms of Quebec Cultural and Social Development
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the depth and plausibility of mechanisms shaping Quebec's later culture and society: language retention or erosion, Catholic Church power, seigneurial landholding, education, literacy, legal institutions, migration, class structure, and relations between habitants, merchants, clergy, Indigenous peoples, and Anglophone settlers.
criteria.1-2: Offers vague cultural claims with no mechanisms; ignores language, religion, institutions, and social hierarchy.
criteria.3-4: Mentions French language or Catholicism but treats them as static traits rather than institutions affected by politics and migration.
criteria.5-6: Explains some mechanisms such as church influence, Americanization pressure, land tenure reform, or Anglophone immigration.
criteria.7-8: Connects political status to concrete cultural changes in language policy, religious authority, education, law, elite formation, and demographic shifts.
criteria.9-10: Gives a nuanced account of how Quebec's Francophone Catholic society might persist, adapt, liberalize, or hybridize through institutions, schooling, land reform, commerce, migration, and elite negotiation over generations.

criteria.name: External Power Dynamics and Regional Context
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses how well the answer incorporates the surrounding strategic context: British Canada and Atlantic colonies, France's limited interest in Canada versus Caribbean priorities, Revolutionary War diplomacy, possible French Revolution effects, U.S. expansion, Indigenous diplomacy, the fur trade, Hudson's Bay Company, and neighboring colonies such as Nova Scotia and Newfoundland.
criteria.1-2: Treats Quebec in isolation and ignores Britain, France, the United States, and Indigenous or regional actors.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one or two outside powers but uses them simplistically or anachronistically.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that Britain, France, and the U.S. would shape Quebec's options, though some mechanisms remain underdeveloped.
criteria.7-8: Plausibly integrates external pressures, including British military return, French priorities, U.S. weakness, Atlantic trade, Indigenous alliances, and regional Anglophone influence.
criteria.9-10: Provides a rich geopolitical chain showing how Quebec's culture and society are shaped by competing American, British, French, Indigenous, commercial, and imperial pressures across the late 18th and 19th centuries.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Coherence and Downstream Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer carries consequences forward coherently beyond the initial capture, including effects on Quebec's nationalism, church-state relations, legal culture, economic modernization, relations with the U.S. or Britain, possible independence, and comparisons to later Latin American, Canadian, or American trajectories where appropriate.
criteria.1-2: Jumps from 1775 to modern outcomes with no causal chain or relies on unsupported assertions.
criteria.3-4: Provides a basic timeline but major transitions are unexplained or implausible.
criteria.5-6: Develops a mostly coherent chain from military capture to political status and some later cultural or social outcomes.
criteria.7-8: Shows clear multi-stage causation across decades, linking early settlement choices to institutions, identity, demography, and modernization.
criteria.9-10: Constructs a robust long-range trajectory with credible turning points, feedback loops, and second-order effects on nationalism, religion, law, class, language, economy, and regional identity.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration, Plausibility, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Judges whether the answer avoids overclaiming, distinguishes likely from speculative outcomes, respects known historical constraints, and avoids contradictions such as assuming simultaneous deep Americanization and unchanged ancien-régime society without explanation.
criteria.1-2: Highly deterministic, contradictory, or historically careless; makes sweeping claims without evidence or caveats.
criteria.3-4: Some plausible points but frequent overconfidence, internal tension, or unsupported causal leaps.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible and mostly consistent, with some uncertainty acknowledged but limited alternative-path reasoning.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates likely, possible, and unlikely outcomes; handles ambiguity in Canadien preferences and external reactions without major contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrated and internally consistent; presents alternatives where evidence is thin, weighs probabilities, and controls for tensions among occupation, identity, religion, language, and geopolitical pressures.

items.model_answer:
If American forces had successfully captured and held Quebec during the 1775 invasion in the early stages of the American Revolutionary War, Quebec’s cultural and societal development would likely have diverged significantly from its actual historical trajectory. Instead of remaining under British control—and later becoming a foundational part of Canada with strong protections for French language, civil law, and Catholic institutions—Quebec would have been absorbed into the nascent United States as one of its northern territories or states.

Under American governance, Quebec would have faced strong pressures toward assimilation into Anglo-American Protestant norms. The U.S. revolutionary ethos emphasized republicanism, individual rights, and disestablishment of state religion—all of which would have clashed with Quebec’s hierarchical, Catholic, and French civil tradition. Over time, this could have led to the erosion of French-language institutions, the marginalization of the Catholic Church’s public role, and the imposition of common law. Immigration from the U.S. and Europe might have further diluted the French-Canadian demographic majority, especially if land policies encouraged English-speaking settlement.

However, resistance to assimilation might still have persisted, potentially fostering a distinct ethno-cultural minority within the U.S., akin to Acadians or Cajuns but on a larger scale. Alternatively, persistent tensions could have fueled separatist movements or regional autonomy demands. In either case, the unique bicultural foundation of modern Canada—rooted in the British accommodation of French Canada through the Quebec Act (1774) and later Confederation—would not have emerged, fundamentally altering North American political geography and identity.

items.question: Administration of British colonies in North America if the USA would have never existed?
human_answers: With this POD, Spain and, especially, France may have a very different trajectory from 1776. Both have been looking for a way to get back at Britain for the disastrous 7YW. ARW provided that way, OTL. That involvement did 2 things (more than that, but)...it waylaid the slow progress Spain was making up the Pacific Coast, and most importantly, helped set the stage for the French Revolution. There will be another war. Maybe the WoBavarian Succession spins out of control. Maybe Britain decides to assist Portugal in its struggles against Spain in mid-late 1770s, and this spins out of control. Maybe one or the other leaves the path to the French Revolution still on track. Or, maybe the wars are delayed, and FR as we know it is butterflied. That is beyond BIG. And, this all assumes that the colonies remain at peace, not rising up for round 2, or 3. During the Nootka Crisis, Spain looked to France for assistance, which it didn't get because of the FR. Plus, throughout the 18th century, France didn't go to Spain's aid, but, rather, expected it to be the other way around. I wouldn't count on France backing Spain in the Nootka Crisis, even if there was no FR. If left by its lonesome, Spain likely backs down as OTL. Or maybe Spain has used the decade or 2 of peace to continue settling the Pacific north coast.

I guess if England would have kept the economically important and more or less developed 13C it would have a smaller interest in Notka/Oregon/access to the pacific. If the ARW ends in 1775/1776 then yes, Spain would have had more time and resources to actually colonize Notka. To be honest, I never understood why so many people believe that with a failed ARW, the French R. simply never happens. France was still economically and politically and socially in a bad situation. So yeah, I think the FR still would have happened. Maybe sooner or later (most likely a bit later) and maybe less bloody, but IMO it still would have happened nonetheless. And yeah, France and Spain still would have tried to get revenge on England. How realistic is that if the ARW ends in 1775/1776? I mean the whole American mythos of Americans rising up against the british crown is not that true. A lot of American colonists were loyal to the crown. Its not that every peasant in the 13C rose up against George III and with that rebellion or uprising put down quickly, I think the motivation for another rebellion would be low. How realistic is a peaceful solution to the pacific question? So England keeps the 13C and let's say that that James Cook dies earlier so there is no English expedition at the pacific coast and England has less information and is less interested in these regions. And if Spain has more time, money to colonize Notka could England have decided to just let Spain have it?
items.original_question: Administration of British colonies in North America if the USA would have never existed? I have seen several maps of North America in alternate history scenarios where the 13 colonies lost in 1775/1776. IF England would have won, how would they have administered their colonies in North America afterwards in the late 18th, the 19th, and the 20th century? Would they have administered their colonies separately (Pensilvania, Massachusetts, Newfoundland, Quebec, "Canada?", Florida, Louisiana, Oregon etc.) or would they have united them sooner or later in a big north american british dominion? Also, would they have eventually taken oregon/nootka? what about louisiana and alaska from france and russia respectively? PS: Yes I know there are a lot of "What if the US lost the war of 1776..." threads here but this is mostly about the administration of these colonies

items.model_answer: If the United States had never existed—meaning the American colonies did not declare independence in 1776—the British Crown would have continued to administer its North American colonies as part of the British Empire. Governance would likely have evolved along lines similar to other settler colonies like Canada or Australia. Over time, Britain might have granted increasing self-government through colonial legislatures while retaining control over foreign policy, defense, and trade. The absence of a revolutionary break could have led to a more gradual path toward autonomy, possibly resulting in a federated dominion within the empire by the late 19th or early 20th century. Slavery, westward expansion, Indigenous displacement, and relations with French Canada would still have posed major challenges, but without the unifying rupture of revolution, political development would have remained tied to imperial structures longer, potentially altering the pace and nature of democratic reforms, economic integration, and national identity formation.

items.question: What If the Southern Ming had survived?
human_answers: I foresee a successful Chinese expedition to retake the North within a decade or two. Sichuan was perhaps ironically where the most effective anti-Qing forces were based in OTL. Remnants of Zhang Xianzhong and Li Zicheng’s forces continued fighting there for decades until well into Kangxi’s reign IOTL. The site saw repeated struggles between different forces for many decades. It’s actually the reason for the significant decline in the population of Sichuan IOTL, not Zhang Xianzhong’s Sichuan massacre. Population wise, the Qing Dynasty would have difficulty regrowing the population of the north due to lack of food. The North has always been a basket case since the end of the Northern Song Dynasty. During the Ming Dynasty, Southern China had at least two times the population of the North. And that is before the collapse of the Ming Dynasty Which saw massive fighting. You see plenty of areas throughout Northern China eating rice as staples today, but the truth was that this is evidence for how much northerners have come to rely on Southern grain. Rice does not grow in the North, and has to be imported from the South. Before the Sui-Tang Dynasties when the Grand Canal was not built, Northern diet was based on wheat. Still is to a lesser extent today. After this period, they became increasingly reliant on Southern crops until from the Ming Dynasty onwards, they became entirely reliant on it. Northern Qing can’t just regrow when they don’t even have the rice to feed the people. As time goes on, even by the 17th century, warfare is gonna increasingly dependant upon firearms, meaning population,technology and economy is gonna become decisive in eventual Southern victory. Individual prowess of the troops that the Manchus relied heavily on will become less relevant,especially as the Qing simply does not have Manchu population to supply large armies to both stamp out rebellions or to fight the Southern dynasty. The Manchus iotl exploited a critical window before that was gonna be a problem to conquer the South.

This is what I have in mind: 1. In OTL, as I understand it, by this point the Ming dynasty’s North China had been devastated, the population had grown unevenly, and the state had come to depend heavily on Jiangnan’s grain resources. In that situation, if the Qing were to occupy only North China while the Ming retained control of Jiangnan, the Qing would likely suffer from serious food shortages. Under such conditions, I think it is highly likely that the Qing would resort to massacres in North China similar to the Yangzhou massacre seen in OTL. However, in the end, the Qing might later face the problem of overpopulation once again. Personally, when it comes to the Malthusian trap, I think the Northern Qing would suffer from it more severely than the Southern Ming. What do you think? 2. In OTL, the Dzungars were destroyed by Qing expeditions. However, in this timeline, the Dzungars would likely expand their power significantly across Mongolia and Tibet. Unlike in OTL, the Qing would probably remain largely on the defensive. As a result, the Dzungars would not be destroyed and would likely enjoy a substantial imperial existence until they were eventually conquered by the Russian Empire. Russia, too, would likely push into Manchuria more frequently and more deeply than it did in OTL. The Qing would have a much harder time containing them and would probably have to request military assistance from Joseon more often than in OTL . It is even possible that, unlike the Treaty of Nerchinsk, Russia might succeed in extracting territorial gains much deeper inside the region. And here is the next question. In your view, assuming that the Southern Ming and the Northern Qing both survived until the mid-18th century, which state do you think would collapse first? And in what ways do you think each polity would face its respective crises? First of all, in OTL, the course of the Yellow River changed in the 1850s. This could also have significant effects on China.

Why do you say they will sinicise faster? By contrast, I think they’d sinicise even slower, as they can’t hope to match the southern Ming in chineseness and so would have to rely on other pillars of legitimacy to prop up their rule, perhaps leaning further into Tibetan Buddhism. Edit- looking more into how Tibetan Buddhism had spread so deeply into Mongol society in the late 16th century, people seem to say that the Qing need to appeal to Taoist and Confucian ideologies meant they could not be called a primarily Buddhist state. Ittl, I think the Qing would lean much more heavily into buddhist kingship, and this might also make their policy towards Han people less racist- there would be a way for Han people to politically abandon the Confucian-Taoist kingship embodied by the Ming, by adopting Tibetan Buddhism, which would make them part of the ruling group without becoming Manchu. Why do you say it didn’t happen in India? As an aside, there was a mid 17th century equivalent to the treaty of Westphalia in Central Asia, the Great Code of 1640, by which various Oirat and Mongol clans agreed to act as a collective body to uphold general peace and a universal legal code, while upholding the sovereignty of the individual tribes. Otl, it became irrelevant once the Qing got rid of any form of Mongol sovereignty by defeating the Dzunghars and winning the Khalkha Mongols to their cause, but in a world where the Qing aren’t so powerful, the “Holy Mongol Empire” likely maintains its constitutional structure for longer. Instead of a Dzunghar khanate, we’d therefore talk Ming China allying with the Western Yuan Dynasty to hold back the Qing, and perhaps the federal Yuan would be more successful than the Dzunghar were otl in their wars against the Kazakhs/the Khanates of Bukhara. Or perhaps, the Qing end up functioning as the Austria analogue- personally controlling by far the most land and people, but still unable to strip away the autonomy of the various Mongol and oirat ulus’, who regularly meet and would all revolt against imperial overreach.
items.original_question: If the Southern Ming had survived? Thread 'Perpetual Brightness: Surviving Southern Ming' Apr 12, 2006 Once, the Confucian school outside Quanzhou had bustled with students and scholars. Some of China’s greatest administrators had come from there, and in its day the school had been a center of learning. But since the famines, and the Manchu invasion, the school had grown quiet. The buildings were dilapidated, with peeling paint and rotten timber. There was only one man there, in the dark of night, standing by a fire. The man watched as the flames cast a red glow over the temple, as it consumed the robes of a scholar. An Empire was collapsing outside its walls, but inside the silence was... Faeelin Replies: 168 Forum: Alternate History Discussion: Before 1900 In OTL, after an empire collapsed in China, there were many cases where it was not completely destroyed and replaced by another empire, but instead split into northern and southern regimes. Even before the Qing dynasty, the Jurchen states themselves formed a northern empire, while the Southern Song continued to exist in the south. In the 17th century, the Ming dynasty, like the Song before it, also established the Southern Ming. However, it ultimately fell after only twenty years. Was there no way for the Southern Ming to survive? The problems of the Southern Ming, as I see them, are as follows. 1. In the case of the Southern Song, all other imperial claimants were captured by the Jurchens, and as a result, a person low in the line of succession became the only remaining claimant. This, paradoxically, allowed him to secure a certain degree of legitimacy and take power. By contrast, the Southern Ming began in a situation where the legitimate imperial princes had largely been captured from the outset, while there were still too many lower-ranking imperial relatives remaining. This excess of potential claimants triggered disputes over the imperial succession. 2. In the case of the Jin dynasty, it had not yet fully subdued the Western Xia or the Mongols. In particular, the Mongols were later unified by Genghis Khan, who went on to establish the most powerful nomadic empire in history. At the time, the Goryeo dynasty was nominally a tributary state of the Jin, but it had not been decisively subdued through war. The Jin lacked the capacity to invade Goryeo and had no choice but to settle for maintaining relatively moderate relations. In other words, the Jin dynasty could not devote all of its national strength to the conquest of the Southern Song. By contrast, the Qing dynasty had already conquered the Chahar Mongols and had invaded the capital of the Joseon dynasty, forcing it into clear submission. Although the Dzungars and Russia would later enter the Chinese arena, this occurred only after the game had effectively already been decided. 3. The Southern Song was able to survive thanks to outstanding generals such as Yue Fei and Han Shizhong, who successfully defeated the Jurchen armies. By contrast, on the eve of the Ming dynasty’s collapse, Wu Sangui’s forces—virtually the only remaining elite army—defected outright to the Qing side. As a result, the Southern Ming was forced to struggle on with inadequate military strength, trapped in a situation where incompetent warlords fought among themselves in constant internal conflict. Taking these factors into account, I think that for the Southern Ming to have survived for a long time, things would have had to be different from the very beginning. “Before the fall of Beijing, the Chongzhen Emperor decides to transfer the capital to Nanjing. Abandoning Beijing, he withdraws south, and Wu Sangui’s army joins the emperor’s entourage and moves to Nanjing as well.” In effect, this would mean that the Chongzhen Emperor is “ceding North China to the Jurchens,” but even so, the southern regions would be far more securely preserved. However, he did not do so. The reasons lie here. In short, he was an “indecisive and irresolute emperor,” and as a result, instead of taking responsibility for such a momentous decision, he merely kept postponing it. What I am curious about is this: 1. If the Chongzhen Emperor were to decide on relocating the capital, what kind of POD (point of divergence) would need to occur? 2. If the Southern Ming had survived at least until the 19th century, how would East Asian history from the 17th to the 19th centuries have changed? Assuming the Southern Ming succeeded in repelling the initial Qing offensives, who would be in the more advantageous position thereafter? If the Southern Ming were to endure, how would Western powers in the 19th century approach China?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Fidelity and Initial Conditions
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer anchors its reasoning in a plausible survival scenario for the Southern Ming and correctly handles the 1640s balance among Southern Ming, Qing, Ming loyalists, rebels, Jiangnan, Sichuan, Manchuria, Mongolia, and frontier actors.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or distorts the premise; treats the Ming as simply restored everywhere or the Qing as absent without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges a surviving Southern Ming but gives vague or historically weak starting conditions with major omissions.
criteria.5-6: Establishes a plausible north-south division but only partially accounts for regional military, fiscal, and demographic realities.
criteria.7-8: Grounds the scenario in credible 1640s conditions, including Jiangnan resources, Qing northern control, loyalist forces, and rebel remnants.
criteria.9-10: Defines a highly plausible survival path and carefully preserves the altered-but-recognizable constraints facing Southern Ming, Qing, rebels, Mongols, Joseon, Russia, and inland provinces.

criteria.name: Causal Mechanism Depth: Demography, Food, Fiscal Capacity, and Military Change
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer explains the material mechanisms that would shape Southern Ming survival, especially southern grain, northern devastation, Grand Canal dependence, taxation, manpower, firearms, logistics, and Qing limitations.
criteria.1-2: Relies on unsupported claims of inevitable victory or collapse with little mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Mentions factors such as population or food but does not connect them convincingly to state capacity or military outcomes.
criteria.5-6: Explains some key mechanisms, such as Jiangnan wealth or northern shortages, but leaves major causal links underdeveloped.
criteria.7-8: Shows how grain flows, taxation, manpower, firearms, logistics, and Manchu demographic limits would affect the Ming-Qing struggle over decades.
criteria.9-10: Integrates economic, demographic, ecological, fiscal, and military mechanisms into a coherent explanation of why either Southern Ming recovery, Qing entrenchment, or durable partition is plausible.

criteria.name: Long-Range Geopolitical and Cultural Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of downstream effects beyond the immediate Ming-Qing conflict, including Mongolia, Tibet, Dzungars/Oirats, Russia, Joseon, Manchuria, legitimacy strategies, Sinicization, Buddhist kingship, and possible treaty/frontier changes.
criteria.1-2: Discusses only a short civil-war outcome and ignores wider Eurasian and cultural consequences.
criteria.3-4: Adds a few external actors but treats them as disconnected side notes.
criteria.5-6: Covers several downstream effects, such as Dzungar survival or Russian pressure, but with limited causal integration.
criteria.7-8: Connects Southern Ming survival to Qing frontier weakness, Mongol/Oirat politics, Tibetan Buddhism, Joseon, Russia, and altered legitimacy strategies.
criteria.9-10: Provides a broad, well-linked long-range map of East and Inner Asian consequences, including frontier diplomacy, religious-political identity, Mongol autonomy, Russian expansion, and altered Qing or Ming state formation.

criteria.name: Temporal Chain Coherence and Path Dependence
criteria.criteria_description: Judges whether the answer builds a plausible sequence from the 1640s through later crises instead of jumping to conclusions, while accounting for feedback loops, windows of opportunity, and changing constraints over time.
criteria.1-2: Presents an arbitrary endpoint with no chronological chain.
criteria.3-4: Uses a loose timeline but with large unexplained leaps or reversed causality.
criteria.5-6: Gives a broadly sequential account but misses important feedbacks between war, taxation, famine, legitimacy, and frontier pressure.
criteria.7-8: Develops a credible multi-decade chain showing how early survival changes later military, fiscal, demographic, and diplomatic options.
criteria.9-10: Constructs a rigorous long-range trajectory with path-dependent turning points, plausible contingency, and changing incentives for Ming, Qing, rebels, and frontier states.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration, Plausibility, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer avoids deterministic overreach, acknowledges competing plausible outcomes, and remains internally consistent about Southern Ming strength, Qing weakness, Sinicization, legitimacy, and external pressures.
criteria.1-2: Makes absolute claims, contradicts itself, or asserts implausible outcomes without caveats.
criteria.3-4: Shows some uncertainty but still contains major contradictions or one-sided determinism.
criteria.5-6: Offers plausible outcomes with limited caveats, though some tensions or unsupported assumptions remain.
criteria.7-8: Balances several plausible trajectories, flags uncertainties, and maintains consistency across military, cultural, and geopolitical claims.
criteria.9-10: Carefully distinguishes likely, possible, and speculative outcomes; tests counterarguments; and avoids contradictions while preserving a nuanced open-ended forecast.

items.model_answer:
If the Southern Ming had survived, China’s political, cultural, and geopolitical trajectory would have diverged significantly from the historical Qing-dominated path. The continuation of a Ming loyalist regime—likely based in southern China or possibly Taiwan—would have preserved Han Chinese imperial institutions, Confucian orthodoxy, and Ming-era administrative practices, resisting Manchu rule and its associated policies like the queue order. This could have prevented or delayed the full integration of frontier regions such as Mongolia, Xinjiang, and Tibet into a centralized Chinese state, as Qing expansionism was instrumental in consolidating those territories.

Internally, a surviving Southern Ming might have faced chronic instability due to factionalism, financial strain, and military vulnerability, potentially leading to fragmentation or reliance on foreign aid—perhaps from European powers or maritime allies like Zheng Chenggong’s (Koxinga’s) network. Such alliances might have accelerated Western influence in China earlier than historically occurred. Externally, a divided China—with a Manchu north and Ming south—could have altered East Asian power dynamics, affecting Korea, Japan, and Southeast Asia, and possibly inviting greater colonial intervention during the 18th and 19th centuries.

Culturally, the survival of the Ming court might have reinforced classical Confucianism and Ming artistic traditions, potentially slowing the syncretic developments fostered under the Qing. However, prolonged conflict and division could also have weakened China’s ability to respond cohesively to internal rebellions or external pressures, possibly hastening decline rather than ensuring resilience. Ultimately, a surviving Southern Ming would likely have resulted in a more fragmented, less territorially expansive China, with profound implications for modern Chinese identity and statehood.

items.question: What If the British won the 1812 War?
human_answers: As far as the political landscape is concerned, I think the Federalists are routed as per OTL. They'll be blamed for losing the war, even if theyre ultimately vindicated over the long haul about being right about how the war would go. The whole post-war love affair that existed OTL is going to be gone, and I think the eight years following the war are going to be politically toxic. Depending on the border shuffling, the US might lose multiple free states which will affect the long term sectional rivalry already in development. Illinois might flip to a slave state due to butterflies if the slavers back a single candidate upon the state's formation. The Virginian dynasty probably crumbles and Monroe probably stays put as Secretary of State instead of seeking the presidency. If the Battle of New Orleans doeant take place Jackson's path to power is much longer and more arduous, if he even seeks the office at all. Theres a not unreasonable chance that the capital moves to Philadelphia and stays there. America may seek to purchase Texas around the time they signed the Adams-Onis Treaty of OTL, they could afford it, and if Monroe is still Secretary of State they're probably dabbling more in that area as it was already a pet project of his. If Texas isn't purchased, I think there's going to be a greater push against annexation by the Whigs given the greater disparity between free and slave states. A lot depends on the peace treaty, though.

I would consider OTL to be a tie, and I think spin city can depict it as such at the time. I've seen threads arguing it was a USAmerican victory because Britain wasn't able to conquer them. What does winning look like? Typically, it means taking something from the loser. Since USA never gained anything during the war, there's nothing they can be forced to give back. So, it would have to be something they held prior (or had claim to). Retaking control of any of the lost colonies is largely devoid of reality. Border adjustments in Maine/Vermont/New York are on the table. Making the old Northwest part of Canada, perhaps as a Native Reserve, is a possibility. Would Britain keep New Orleans if they had taken it prior to truce and/or the rest of Louisiana? Give it back to Spain? Trade it for full control of the NW, if they haven't secured control of that already? Realistically, how much could Britain gain? But, I think OP wants to discuss political ramifications if the war ends with there being zero doubt which side won. There could be a major territorial concession which is bound to completely change the USA even if it rebounds spectacularly (such as loss of New Orleans/Louisiana), in which case political ramifications are a secondary concern. Or, territorial concessions are more limited, leaving things a bit more recognizable. A lot of things left unsettled by the ARW, are going to be settled in Britain's favor. Trade agreements may emerge also favoring Britain. Depending on the severity of the peace, politics will also be severely affected far beyond a 'USA lost, unequivocally, but otherwise everything is the same' . So, yeah, we need to know the scope of the peace. The OP needs to be fleshed out more.

items.model_answer: If the British had won the War of 1812 decisively, the consequences for North America would have been significant. The United States might have lost substantial territory, particularly in the Northwest (modern-day Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, and Wisconsin), which Britain could have ceded to its Native American allies as a buffer zone—fulfilling one of its wartime goals. Additionally, Britain might have retained or re-established control over parts of Maine or imposed stricter limits on U.S. westward expansion. American sovereignty and national confidence, already fragile in the early republic, could have suffered a major setback, potentially delaying or altering the course of Manifest Destiny. However, it is unlikely Britain would have sought to reabsorb the U.S. as a colony; instead, it would likely have aimed to contain American power and secure its Canadian holdings. The war’s outcome also shaped Canadian identity—British victory might have reinforced loyalty to the Crown and accelerated the development of a distinct Canadian nation separate from the U.S.

items.question: What If the English Armada of 1589 had succeeded in destroying Spain's remaining Atlantic fleet and triggering a Portuguese revolt?
human_answers: Actually, I think one could argue the opposite: that it's magically deterministic to assume that, in some unspecified way, this crisis will send the whole country into a downward spiral that will lead to its implosion. I mean, once you go over the list of changes, there isn't too much difference: yes, the Spanish Navy has been severely damaged; yes, Portugal has become independent; yes, Spain has lost all its possessions in Europe that are outside the Iberian Peninsula... but really the only significant difference from OTL is that Portugal became independent earlier, the burden that the Netherlands represented is now "someone else's problem," the remaining Spanish Navy is much smaller, and now Portugal has very serious reasons to hate England for keeping the Azores "because we can." The American Empire remains intact, it is doubtful that the English will be more successful in appropriating anything than in OTL, and they are possibly too busy antagonizing someone else once they see that the possibility of another Invincible Armada is not going to happen in the near future. OTL Spain recovered from that, even if 200 years later they declined for other reasons, but this alone should not condemn them to failure.

Spanish resilience at the time was incredible, considering how Philip II expended so many resources on fronts that ultimately yielded no tangible gains beyond preserving his honor (which was the sole reason he remained in the Flanders War). Even if England were to seize the Azores, I do not believe this would satisfy the Portuguese nobility and bourgeoisie—the main factions Antonio, Prior of Crato, would need in order to legitimize his rule. Furthermore, if Spain was able to rebuild a second fleet within two or three years—not as large as the first, but still significant—we must not forget that while the English might capture a treasure fleet, they could not always be expected to capture all of them. If there was one defining trait of Spanish admirals regarding their treasure fleets, it was their elusiveness. Even so, a Spain under Philip II, burdened by numerous problems, could compel Philip III to reconsider his policies and explore the possibility of a genuine peace with the Dutch Republic—something that could ultimately benefit Spain in the long run.

While I agree the OP is going way too far and too fast, I'd say 1589 had the potential to screw Spain over far worse than it did in OTL. I'd say your best POD is probably for Antonio to die on the way to the Iberian Peninsula, but too late for the fleet to turn back. To get out of that pickle, Drake and Norris opt to just try to do as much damage to Spain's fleet and resources as they can. In that they proved far more successful than in OTL, even temporarily occupying some of the Azores and capturing the treasure fleet. Spain has even more money problems than in OTL. The rebuilding of the Spanish fleet is an even bigger task than in OTL, and the Royal Navy does start to gain a reputation for invincibility. In France, Henri III's OTL assassin made his attempt when the Royalists celebrated the English successes, and the butterflies ensured Henri III survived ITTL. Henri III retakes Paris, and the wheel starts to come off the Catholic League significantly earlier than OTL, especially since the retaking of the capital is quickly followed by Henri of Navarre also winning the ITTL version of the battle of Arques. Spain is stuck providing far more resources to sustain the elements of the Catholic League than it had to in OTL until significantly later, when it has less resources available in the first place. And all over the Western World, the Habsburgs' enemies are taking heart... Colapse might be too strong a word but the ruin of Philip II's continental ambitions would probably come earlier, and cost more to Spain in the long run, than in OTL.
items.original_question: What if Spanish "collapse" in 1589 One of the most famous failures in modern European history, the 1588 Spanish Armada destroyed a big part of the Spanish naval forces, and was a major humiliation for Philip II. Yet England, one year later, completely blew its chance to fully wreck the Spanish by launching the ill-fated English Armada, which sought three main objectives: 1) Destroy the remaining Atlantic fleet of Spain 2) Incite a rebellion in Portugal against Philip II 3) Seize the Azores and turn it into a permanent English possession It failed in all of these objectives. Yet, the POD is not a minor or major decision, it is simple: somehow England succeeds. The remaining fleet of Spain that survived the 1588 Armada is destroyed in a series of naval battles, a landing is made in Portugal and António Prior of Crato is installed King of Portugal, starting a Portuguese Restoration War 50 years before OTL, and finally England manages to seize the Azores from Philip II's forces. Say that the Spanish naval forces are completely obliterated by the English; Portugal gains independence from Spain in 1590 with heavy English backing; the Azores (through negotiation with Portugal) become a English territory. What would happen with England, Spain, Portugal and the rest of Europe? How might the colonization of the New World be altered by a successful English Armada? Let's not get into details on **how** this happens, but assuming that it just does happen

items.model_answer:
If the English Armada of 1589 had succeeded in destroying Spain’s remaining Atlantic fleet and triggering a successful Portuguese revolt, it would have dramatically altered the balance of power in late 16th-century Europe. Spain, already strained by the costs of empire and warfare, would have lost its naval supremacy in the Atlantic, severely weakening its ability to protect its overseas colonies and transport treasure from the Americas. A restored independent Portugal—freed from Spanish Habsburg rule since 1580—would likely have reasserted its own maritime empire, possibly aligning with England or other anti-Spanish powers like France or the Dutch Republic.

This outcome could have accelerated the decline of Spanish hegemony decades earlier than historically occurred, potentially shortening or reshaping the Eighty Years’ War and the Anglo-Spanish War. England, emboldened by such a victory, might have expanded its colonial and commercial ambitions more aggressively in the Atlantic and Americas. Moreover, without Spain’s naval capacity to project power, Catholic counter-reformation efforts in Western Europe could have faltered, strengthening Protestant states. However, such a success might also have provoked a more determined and unified Catholic response, possibly under papal or French leadership, leading to unpredictable realignments in European diplomacy and conflict.

items.question: What If Britain pursued a more hostile stance against the American Colonies following the Boston Tea Party, going on the offensive in 1774?
human_answers: This is why it might have been shortsighted for the British Empire to put so much investment in achieving the total conquest and liquidation of the French Colonial position in the Ohio Country and Canada in the 1754-1763 timeframe, to disproportionate benefit of their Colonial 'Fortunate Sons'. While for Britain, it had the side benefit of defeating French forces, which feels nice, and drawing French fleets out for fights they would lose, and capturing some value from the fur trade, Britain particularly "got over its skis" in providing all this support for the Colonies *without* first compelling the Colonies, then under some fears for their frontier populations, to revise their Charters to accept the principle and practice of taxation by the Westminster Parliament, as a regular, reliable contribution to common defense of the empire, its frontiers, and its trade-based prosperity. Instead, by 1763, Britain brought home French North America like Christmas toys and puppies on its own schilling (though Colonial Assemblies chipped in some from their allowance, but often got reimbursed). But then, late 1763 turned out to be a cold, cold, bitter post-Christmas January hangover, when London Parliament started to tell the Colonies, "now start paying tax for all your presents........oh and by the way, sorry, can't let you play with the new Christmas puppy (settle the new lands in the Ohio, west of the Alleghenies), because it turns out the puppy bites and scratches and we can't afford to keep going to the clinic." ---The Americans certainly were not going to react well to the new message of 'fun's over, time to pay up'. While Britain and the American colonies had certain minimum legal rights, even for tenant farmers (still far less than for small freeholders though) I certainly do not think the three protections you mentioned were observed universally, neither in Britain nor even in all the Colonies, in the 1700s pre and post independence. Making this assertion might be a bit of falling for and repeating English/British self-congratulatory propaganda. Evictions were a fact of life in the English-speaking world in the 1700s and all other centuries. The 1700s were known for the enclosure of common lands [yes, that by itself is not eviction but can lead to starvation-inducing poverty even if one is in a cottage, but it can also lead to failure to meet rent obligations and consequent eviction] and consequent driving of English peasants from the countryside to create an ever increasing town and urban laboring population for industry. White tenants on southern landholdings in the Colonies could be subject to evictions as could tenants in Hudson Valley patroonships. Yes, I'm thinking this is descriptive of the Scandinavian situation until after 1800, or nearly that late, which made it, legally speaking more like serfdom systems East of the Elbe than like tenancy systems in Britain or Western Europe. Serfs lacking really any rights of appeal or any rights at all, whereas tenants in England, parts of France, and I would think the Low Countries and Switzerland would have some rights of appeal, even though their landlords would have superior rights through the 1600s and 1700s.

If the British objective was to set off a full-scale war in every colony right off the bat in which they would lose that is exactly what they should do. The British had no means to do what you're suggesting. The incident that set off the fighting was the British trying to disarm the colonists. In the first year of the war the British lost control in all 13 Colonies. Britian had to spend a year mobilizing an army 1/3 of which were German mercenaries for the invasion of the New York. After winning a number of tactical victories they were unable to bring a single colony back under their control. At no time were they ever able to bring even 10% of the population under occupation. After 1777 all they could hold were coastal enclaves, although there was fratricidal warfare in Georgia & South Carolina. They could hold no territory without the Presence of British or Hessian regulars. Loyalist forces were weak everywhere. The coastal enclaves they held became shells eventually with most of the people leaving, and little trade with the interior. What had brought about the war were British policies to control American trade to force them to trade only with England. That alienated the merchant class. Planters had to sell into a closed market were the buyers set the price, and controlled credit terms. That alienated the planter class. They tried to strangle early industrialization so the colonies could only sell raw materials, and buy English finished goods. That alienated the rising manufacturing class. They blocked westward expansion beyond the Proclamation Line. That alienated the landed class. The overall effect was to squeeze specie out of the colonies creating a growing barter system which alienated everyone. Closing courts, and assemblies, and finally trying to disarm the militia left the colonies with the choice of ether abject surrender or rebellion. It wasn't easy but the British Crown went from being very popular in 1765 to every colony taking up arms against them in 1775.

There are tons of things they could do. They could dissolve the militias and ban the Americans from owning weapons. They could introduce an actual tax to fund a permanent military presence - the Americans paid no land rent, only tarriffs. They could abolished the American right to elect judges and sheriffs, instead appointing crown loyalists by decree. They could have given soldiers immunity from local prosecution and law enforcement, instead tasking their commanding officers (who would of course do pretty much nothing) with upholding the law for their soldiers. They could have created an American trading company owned by the crown and banned Americans from any imports and exports except through this company and cracked down on smuggling. The facts are that the Americans enjoyed the most liberal and democratic system in the world at the time of their revolt. They wanted something even more democratic and liberal. But to most people at the time, especially colonial subjects, they would seem like spoiled toddlers throwing a tantrum. Swedish peasants paid roughly 30-40% of the value of an average harvest in land rent at this time. Icelanders could only trade with the very corrupt royal Danish tradign company, which paid aroudn 5% of the value of their wool and forced the Icelanders to buy moldy flour in return. Austrian and Prussian peasants were banned from owning arms, and their courts were handled by government-appointed bailiffs, unless nobility had the right to neck and hand (to be police, prosecutor, judge and executioner all in one, Judge Dredd style) on their estate.

This is a quote from Wikipedia, as of January 20th, 2026: "With the ascension of peace in 1763 the army was dramatically reduced to a peacetime home establishment of just over 11,000 men, with a further 9,750 for the Irish establishment and 10,000 for the colonies. This meant 20 regiments of infantry totaling just over 11,000 men were stationed in Great Britain, 21 regiments were stationed in Ireland, 18 regiments were stationed in the Americas, and 7 regiments were stationed in Gibraltar. Alongside this, the army could call on 16 regiments of the cavalrymen and 2,712 men in the artillery. This gave a theoretical strength of just over 46,000 men exclusive of the artillery." Curtis, Ph.D. www.americanrevolution.org "The English establishment comprised 25,871 infantry organized into 46 regiments and 20 independent companies; 4,151 cavalry organized into 16 regiments; and 2,256 artillerymen organized into one regiment of 4 battalions." "Such were the numbers of the British army in 1775 and such they had approximately been ever since the close of the Seven Years’ War. "An examination of the location of the British army in 1775 reveals the fact that while small detachments of it were to be found in many distant quarters of the globe, the bulk of it was distributed unequally among three different countries. There were roughly speaking 15,000 men in England, 12,000 in Ireland, and 8,000 in America. The remaining 10,000 were distributed among the West Indies, Africa, Minorca, Gibraltar, and Scotland." Each regiment had a listed strength of 477 men. The British concentrated four of these, or just under 2,000 men, in Boston in 1773 to close the port and essentially establish martial law in Massachusetts. This was achieved by moving them New York City, where these regiments had been stationed. The other 6,000 to 8,000 men to cover Canada, Fort Ticonderoga, the forts around the Great Lakes, Florida, Jamaica, and the West Indies. After abandoning Boston, in 1776 the British increased the size of their army from roughly 45,000 to 60,000 troops, mainly be recruiting in Germany. Out of these, they were able to concentrate about 40,000 to take New York, including troops that had been sent to and which failed to take Charleston. Another 10,000 or so chased the Americans out of Canada. Peak strength of the Briitsh army during the American War of Independence was around 80,000. It was only in New England where the situation was turning violent, and it was only after the formation of the Continental Army, and armed clashes between British and American troops, that they declared all thirteen colonies to be in rebellion and started expanding the army. And they really had to wait for the situation to turn that bad to be able to do that.

items.original_question: What if Britain pursued a more hostile stance against the American Colonies following the Boston Tea Party, going on the offensive in 1774? As the title suggests, I've been trying to figure out what an earlier beginning to the American Revolutionary War might entail. As to how this happens specifically, military action was advocated as soon as news of the tea party reached London by some hard-line MPs such as Germain OTL. Some thoughts: - This happens before the Continental Congress even assembles, so everything might happen much more hastily. There probably is much less wrangling over things like sending an olive branch to the King and instead a more decisive stance taken on independence. - With the states forced to pick sides immediately, I think it's highly likely that Georgia remains decidedly loyalist, which has very interesting implications for the US post-independence Other than that, my knowledge on the American Revolutionary War is very much limited and it'd be great to have some input on this scenario. Cheers!

items.model_answer: If Britain had pursued a more hostile and offensive stance against the American Colonies immediately following the Boston Tea Party in 1774—rather than enacting the Coercive Acts and attempting to isolate Massachusetts—it likely would have accelerated the outbreak of armed conflict and unified colonial resistance sooner. A preemptive military crackdown or large-scale deployment of troops to enforce punitive measures could have been perceived across all thirteen colonies as an existential threat to their rights and self-governance, galvanizing moderate colonists who were previously hesitant about rebellion. This might have led to an earlier formation of a coordinated colonial military response, possibly even before the Second Continental Congress convened in 1775. However, such aggression could also have strained British logistical capabilities, as sustaining a large-scale offensive across the Atlantic would have been difficult without secure supply lines and local support. Ultimately, a more aggressive British posture in 1774 would likely have hastened the Revolutionary War’s onset and potentially strengthened colonial unity, making reconciliation less feasible and independence more inevitable.
