items.question: What If not Russia, which country could have become the Soviet Union?
human_answers: Also, with or without overseas colonies, Communist France / Germany would be in a relatively poor position to defend themselves, as their territory is relatively small, so they can't trade space for time, or evacuate their industry far behind the frontlines (the way Russia did), and most of their core industrial and agricultural are close to borders or to coasts. They also would also be outnumbered by their combined enemies (eg. Communist France having to fight an anti-communist coalition of Britain, Germany and other countries), while the USSR actually outnumbered the Axis in WWII (and always had more reserves). Communist France would be very vulnerable to an Anglo-German invasion, with the British blockading the country and possibly landing in Brittany, Normandy, Picardy and/or Nord-Pas-de-Calais, and the Germans invading from the east (possibly with Italians and Spaniards also attacking, and those attacks could probably be contained thanks to the Alps and Pyrenees, but would divert men away from the main fronts). Communist Germany would essentially be in the same position as OTL WWI Germany, stuck between the Anglo-French and Russians. Now, a Franco-German communist union already has more potential. In addition, if France and Germany become a communist state together, there's a strong possibility that other nations will join them. Belgium and Netherlands are quite likely give their position, and also Italy, Spain and Portugal, due to their economical conditions and political instability.

Leading up to WW1, moat of the communist parties of the great powers were following the line of the second international, and therefore we're unable to seize power, the exception being of course the Russians. Had lines equivalent to those of Lenin prospered in the communist parties of other great powers, it is likely that any number of them could have had a successful communist revolution during or immediately after WW1. Germany is the most obvious candidate, as they had a big revolution irl even though it failed. Italy is another candidate, and to a lesser extent France. However, any of these countries would have issues with surviving alone under siege socialism as the Russians did. It was assumed at the time that a revolutionary state could only survive with the export of the revolution, lest it be surrounded and defeated by hostile imperialist powers. Stalin proved this wrong, Russia did benefit from it's unique geography in this sense. Could greater German industrial power make a German Soviet Republic defensible? I'd argue yes. Whilst Russian geography helped defensible, it was the economic boom, industrialisation, and enthusiasm of the people that helped it survive imperialist intervention. History ahs shown how enthusiastic armies fighting for a cause can and do defeat foreign powers. France is far more vulnerable to attack than Russia, and yet the French revolutionary wars showed how successful a mobiles french populace could be against the powers of the day. Whilst Germany does not have all the strategic depth and resources of Russia, could Britain France and Russia really afford fulls cake invasions just after WW1? They would run the risk of Revolution spreading among their own tired soldiers. AS for exporting revolution, depending on timing, an established communist Germany could be in a good position to support revolutions in Hungary and Finland , to give a couple of examples.

I think the stickiest element here is the combo of ideology and great/superpower status necessary to mimic the Soviets. If all that was needed was a large and relatively undeveloped country, China or India are easy picks. The problem is ideology. China only went communist in OTL because of the Soviets. No Soviets, no communist China (or India). These places could hypothetically adopt some other far-left socialist ideology, but it probably wouldn't be identifiably Marxist. Meanwhile, if all that was needed was ideology, many other European countries could conceivably fulfill the role. But if, say, France and France alone went communist, they would be considered threatening, but their industry was already decently developed and central planning isn't exactly good at innovating. Their threat level would not be able to rise much compared to the Soviets who had the wiggle room of being able to look at more developed countries and copy their homework. The Soviets also had a massive pool of labor and natural resources that France would lack. A France that probably lost its colonies and has a lagging industry is a middling concern, ultimately. Ditto with Germany. What's really needed, IMO, for another communist entity to arise to pose a similar threat to the Soviets is a multinational revolution in places where Marxism had decent traction. This means multiple Western European countries experiencing revolution and then deciding to cooperate heavily. Alternatively, a multinational coalition of revolutionary socialist states in South America (which must include Brazil since it has the largest population) could potentially adopt a similar role to the Soviets, although they'd be working with both a somewhat smaller population than the Soviets and a less developed industry than Western Europe. As an outside bet, maybe a revolutionary Spain somehow inspires its former colonies to follow suit and they join hands? Wouldn't need Brazil if you could pick up most of Hispanic America.

I do agree to some extent. Germany and France, though geopolitically disadvantaged, both demonstrated explosive potential for modernization. France, during the Napoleonic Wars, nearly conquered Europe by maximizing the advantages of advanced military doctrines, exceptional leadership, and the power of the nation-state. It’s interesting to think, though, how things might have unfolded if Napoleon had pursued democratic ideals rather than imperial ambitions. What if, instead of installing his relatives as kings, he had focused on exporting republicanism to other nations? Germany also revived after its defeat in World War I, almost conquering Europe by defeating France in just six weeks. However, their ideology, which was not universal but rather intended for domestic consumption, was deeply flawed in terms of fairness and equality. However, there is an issue with the immediate post-World War I period. It was the time when Germany's political system was most vulnerable, yet it was also the period when Germany faced the greatest risk of invasion. If the Kiel mutiny had led to a communist regime in Germany, the Entente Powers would likely have continued the war, eventually attempting to capture Berlin. Indeed, the Soviet Union only became one of the dominant global powers after World War II. Before that, it primarily focused on spreading communism in its neighboring countries.

I think Tsarist Russia was the only country able to become a truly 'marxist' superpower. And even they immediately morphed into a 'Marxist-Leninist' and eventually 'Stalinist' one-party state. If for some reason the Russian Revolution never happened, failed, or never became 'Marxist', Marxism as we know it would remain a political philosophy rather than an ideology, although it would be embraced by various socialist or workers-right parties in the various European parliamentary systems. The closest to a 'soviet-style' communist state I can think of would be Mao's China in the 1940's/1950's where due to it effectively still being run by the last remaining pre-WWII era warlord, China would still be. One-party state with the one party adhering to Chinese-style communism. Before that, any country where the Socialist/communist parties gain a majority in the democratic parliament would be the 'communist' world leader, be it Labour Britain, France, Weimar Germany or even a USA with a pro-labour pro-social(ist) president.
items.original_question: If not Russia, which country could have become the Soviet Union? In OTL, the Soviet Union was essentially the leader of communism, the state that embodied and exported the ideology. In France, after the birth of the “first republic in Europe,” the country faced massive wars against the old Western monarchies. As a result, although Napoleon, an extraordinary hero, almost succeeded in conquering Europe, France ultimately fell. Soviet Russia also faced a similar crisis. After the October Revolution, the first communist state was born, and the great powers, much like the monarchies a century before, sought to destroy Soviet Russia. However, unlike France, Soviet Russia survived the Russian Civil War. Afterward, the Soviet Union was no longer simply "Communist State A." They developed the potential of the land that was Russia. They transformed the underdeveloped economy of the Russian Empire into one of growth. Using that newfound capability, they exported revolution to various countries around the world. From Eastern Europe to Asia, the surrounding countries of Russia were all affected by communism. Furthermore, after 1945, they became a superpower alongside the United States, exporting revolution globally. Let’s consider a historical counterfactual. After Alexander II, the imperial succession changed. Unlike in OTL, Tsarevich Nicholas survived, and instead of the reactionary Alexander III, he ascended the throne. This alternate Nicholas II continued the reforms initiated by Alexander II, complementing, improving, and strengthening them. Unlike in OTL, Russia underwent a different trajectory. The Russian Empire was preserved, and Soviet Russia never came into being. In this scenario, which country could have replaced the Soviet Union? Which nation would need to become communist in order to "survive against surrounding capitalist powers" and "become a great power capable of exporting revolution?" Sometimes, in alternate history works (especially in game mods by Paradox Interactive), there are many timelines where a socialist revolution occurs in a country other than Russia. However, in my view, it’s questionable how many countries could do what the Soviet Union did. France? Germany? They have many geopolitical enemies. Even if they were to become communist after World War I, could they, like the Soviet Union, export revolution worldwide and become a superpower? It seems more likely that they would struggle just to survive. Britain, the United States? In OTL, Marx argued that a sufficiently developed capitalist system was necessary for a communist revolution to occur, with Britain being his example. Britain was also the world’s leading superpower at the time. However, a communist revolution did not occur in Britain. Because capitalism was so advanced, ironically, the entrenched privileges of the system were also too strong. British socialists who advocated for a revolutionary overthrow of the system did not have the power to challenge the entrenched elites, while others accepted the system and sought reforms within it. Ultimately, the conditions I believe are necessary for a "Soviet candidate" are as follows: 1. Geopolitically, it must be easy to defend. The country should be able to secure its borders and have a strategic position that allows for long-term survival and expansion. 2. It must have the potential to become a great power. The country needs the necessary resources, population, and industrial capacity to rise as a major global player. 3. Capitalism cannot be overly developed, and the elites must be driven toward 'system overthrow' rather than 'system compliance.' There must be enough dissatisfaction with the existing system to foster a desire for revolution, not merely reforms within the system. These are the core elements for a country to replicate the role of the Soviet Union. Where, besides Russia, could there be a land or country that fits these conditions? As a side note, it doesn’t necessarily have to be pure communism in this alternative Soviet ideology. It could be something like Maoism, syndicalism, or a unique form of socialism tailored to the needs of that country.

items.model_answer: The Soviet Union was a political entity formed through the specific historical conditions of the Russian Empire’s collapse, the 1917 Bolshevik Revolution, and subsequent civil war. Its core was Russia, both geographically and demographically, and its leadership (including Lenin and later Stalin) emerged from the Russian revolutionary movement. While other parts of the former Russian Empire—such as Ukraine, Belarus, or the Caucasus—were incorporated into the USSR, none possessed the combination of industrial base, population size, administrative infrastructure, or revolutionary momentum to have spearheaded such a union independently. Therefore, it is highly unlikely that any country other than Russia could have become the nucleus of the Soviet Union; without Russia, the Soviet Union as we know it would not have existed.

items.question: What If the Alans had formed a lasting kingdom in Europe?
human_answers: Yeah, Medieval Europe in a lot of ways was already influenced by steppe culture like the Huns, Magyars, Avars. This is most obvious in the way these cultures introduced the stirrup and revolutionized cavalry warfare in the political and social structure. IMO knighthood would probably not have developed in its recognizable form without these cultures. I guess what I was thinking is that with the Alans, it wouldn’t just be inherited bits and pieces . A stable Alan kingdom could’ve institutionalized that heritage in law, military organization, and diplomacy in ways that a post-Hunnic and Avar kingdom probably wouldn’t. And yeah, I didn’t mean “Zoroastrian” in the sense of fire temples and Avesta orthodoxy. More like echoes of older Iranian cosmology or ritual that might’ve persisted under the surface alongside Christianity, at least in the early centuries. Basically, I think the difference is between having remnants of a steppe culture floating around versus having it as the living core of a political state right in the middle of medieval Western Europe. That alone could’ve made for a noticeably different flavor in the region’s history.

Looking at the map I wonder if we would see the Alans have their focus in what is Portugal especially when the Muslims go a-conquering. Also I wonder with this arrangement would we see a Alanic-Latinite language develop since it does seem that the elite would speak Alanic while the lower classes would speak some flavour of vulgar latin. A scenario where high register words that the ancestral Alans cared about, like rulership (leader, group meeting, horse, that kinda stuff) and normal stuff stays roughly Hispanic. It probably would have a reduced grammar too and be completely different from what we see in English, so that's fun to see. All the talk about knighthood also is highly ironic because it ultimately evolved into one of the best ways to defend against steppe raiders, and the diffuse way that every noble defended their lands via castle did stop steppe invasions alongside other factors.
items.original_question: What if the Alans had formed a lasting kingdom in Europe? Most people normally associate the Völkerwanderungen period with the mass migration of Germanic tribes into the Roman frontiers. But a large number of non-Germanic people also joined these groups. One of them were the Alans an Iranian people who crossed the Rhine in the winter of 406 along with the Vandals, Suebi, Goths Burgundians etc. and fanned out into Roman Gaul . They would eventually form a kingdom in North Africa alongside the Vandals. But what if Instead of getting absorbed by the Vandals and the Franks, and disappearing into history, they had actually carved out a stable kingdom, say in southwestern Gaul ? What would that look like? An equestrian -based kingdom with a mix of Iranian steppe traditions and local Roman and Germanic culture. Their language and customs might’ve stuck around longer, even mixing with early medieval Christianity or holding onto some older beliefs. I think that this Alan kingdom could’ve complicated Frankish expansion, maybe even keeping Charlemagne from totally dominating Western Europe or at least delaying it? Their military skills might have decided the outcome in battles and diplomacy, and their cultural blend could’ve made medieval Europe way more diverse , for example maybe in unique artistic terms, linguistic influence and traditions. They don't necessarily have to dominate Europe, but form a lasting kingdom long enough for their language, culture, military tradition, religion to make an impact. The whole medieval map could’ve looked very different, and who knows, maybe Zoroastrian-inspired beliefs and horse culture would still echo in some French villages today.

items.model_answer:
If the Alans had formed a lasting kingdom in Europe, it would likely have significantly altered the political and cultural landscape of late antiquity and the early Middle Ages. The Alans, an Iranian-speaking nomadic people who migrated into Europe during the Migration Period, were known for their skilled cavalry and initially settled in regions like Gaul (modern France) and Iberia (modern Spain and Portugal) alongside other groups such as the Vandals and Visigoths. Had they consolidated power—perhaps by establishing stable rule in Aquitaine or Lusitania—they might have created a syncretic Alan-Roman state that blended steppe military traditions with Roman administrative practices.

Such a kingdom could have acted as a buffer or rival to both the Visigoths and the Franks, potentially delaying or preventing Frankish dominance in Western Europe. It might also have preserved elements of Alanic language and culture longer than historically occurred, possibly influencing regional identities in southwestern Europe. Additionally, a stable Alan kingdom could have affected the course of Christianization in the region, especially if it adopted Arian Christianity (as many Alans did) or maintained religious pluralism. Over time, this polity might have evolved into a medieval kingdom comparable to those of the Ostrogoths or Burgundians, leaving a distinct legacy in European history—though its long-term survival would have depended on its ability to integrate local populations, resist external pressures, and adapt institutionally.

Spain is typically meh, while Austria typically needs propping up. I'm guessing Britain/France holds the upper hand in the finance department. Britain, although not yet the naval powerhouse of a century later, is undoubtedly the supreme naval power of these four countries. On land, Spain is rather meh. This partition plan (Stanhope and Townshend) would require worse Anglo-Austrian relations. Britain would have to be convinced that Austria is the biggest threat to the European balance of power and stability. So had Emperor Charles VI gone ahead to marry Maria Theresa to Don Carlos, then we would see a more solidified Anglo-French alliance as a counterweight. A Bourbon-Hapsburg alliance would reshuffle the post-Utrecht European order and a war could be a real possibility (Europe plunged into a wider war during the OTL Anglo-Spanish War of 1727). After the war, this partition plan could be the basis of peace negotiations (if the Anglo-French alliance gained the upper hand), and Austria could be compensated with Tuscany like in OTL. Personally, I am more interested in James Stanhope's first idea of giving Austrian Netherlands to Leopold or Francis of Lorraine. items.original_question: What if Partition of the Austrian Netherlands in the 18th Century? Hi, everyone. This is my second post sharing some lesser-known yet fascinating PoDs in European history. I stumbled upon a historical academic journal written by Frederik Dhondt, a history professor from the Ghent University in Belgium titled " So Great a Revolution’: Charles Townshend and the Partition of the Austrian Netherlands, September 1725 " (2012, Journal of Low Countries Studies). According to the article, Charles Townshend, the British Northern Secretary (equivalent to the Foreign Minister) and his predecessor James Stanhope (†. 1721) had proposed a partition of the Austrian Netherlands. The plan would see Austria surrendering its holdings in the Low Countries. The article summarised three possibilities. Some background before moving on. In the Nine Years' Year and the War of the Spanish Succession, Austria had allied with the Dutch Republic and Great Britain (or England-Scotland before 1707) to counter French ambitions in the Low Countries and the Rhineland. Towards the end of the Spanish Succession War, Britain became weary of increasing Austrian power. In 1716, it allied with France. The Austro-Spanish alliance confirmed by the Treaty of Vienna rang alarm bells in London. Not only did it reconcile the enmity between Emperor Charles XI and King Philip V, the combined power of Spain and Austria threatened the established balance of power. There were even talks to marry Maria Theresa to Don Carlos (future Charles III). Prime Minister Walpole and Townshend, therefore, desired to weaken the power of Austria. These plans were never made public, Townshend only discussed them with the ambassador in Paris, Horace Walpole. On page 56, Townshend suggested the partition plan could be implemented if the marriage between Maria Theresa and Don Carlos took place. James Stanhope first suggested that the Duke of Lorraine could receive Austria Netherlands. Alternatively, Stanhope suggested awarding it either to the Elector of Cologne or the Elector of Trier. The Electorate would be secularised. Townshend outright dismissed these ridiculous ideas, and offered his own solution. The Dutch will annex some territories including Antwerp. Ypres, Bruges, and Ostend would fall under joint Dutch-British control while the inland and southern portions of the Austrian Netherlands will go to France. What will be the geopolitical and diplomatic consequences of one of these plans was realised? Although I personally doubt the likelihood of this happening, nevertheless the ramifications will be interesting. You can access the article here through your university: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1179/0309656411Z.0000000002 .

items.model_answer: If the Austrian Netherlands had been partitioned in the 18th century—rather than remaining under Habsburg control until their annexation by revolutionary France in 1794—the geopolitical landscape of Western Europe might have shifted significantly. A likely scenario would involve neighboring powers such as France, Prussia, and possibly Britain or the Dutch Republic carving up the territory during a moment of Habsburg weakness, perhaps during the War of the Austrian Succession (1740–1748) or the Seven Years’ War (1756–1763). France, historically covetous of the region for strategic and economic reasons, might have seized key southern provinces like Hainaut or Luxembourg. The Dutch Republic could have expanded southward to secure buffer zones against French aggression, while Prussia—though geographically distant—might have demanded compensation elsewhere in the Holy Roman Empire. Such a partition could have preempted the later French Revolutionary Wars’ expansion into the Low Countries, altered the balance of power that led to the Congress of Vienna, and potentially prevented the formation of a unified Kingdom of the Netherlands after 1815. It might also have intensified Anglo-French rivalry earlier, reshaping colonial and continental conflicts throughout the late 18th century.

human_answers: It's very obscure and I couldn't track down the reference this morning, which I think came from some book on the First Serbian Uprising. The Turkish fortress on the island blocked easy communication between the Serbs and the Russian forces in Wallachia. Well, Russia sent an auxiliary force into Poland to aid Napoleon, as promised, and was rewarded with Tarnopol in the peace treaty. So it looks like a victory. But in reality as you say Russia did very little but go through the motions and Napoleon gave them the merest scrap of a reward. Despite the common view, I don't think Alexander ingratiated himself to Vienna by doing this and I don't think Austria would have been more active in 1812 had things been different in 1809. Fair enough. Austria was at least thought to be supplying weapons to the Sultan in 1829, though I don't know if that was confirmed to actually be true.

Why would Hapsburgs or Hohenzollerns circa 1803 care about the US? None of them had colonies in the Western hemisphere (or anywhere else) and, IIRC, at that time the former colonies were not ideologically, not to mention economically or militarily, of a any serious importance for the continental Europe. Which, putting aside Spain, leaves “certain trade arrangements” and the obvious question is what these arrangements would be? Would they hurt or benefit France? In OTL to a great degree the French bellicosity was supported by the strategic factor called “Bonaparte” who, besides military glory, provided looting (both on state and individual levels) on the “industrial” scale. It seems that ITTL French government behaves “Napoleonic” without Napoleon, which brings some obvious questions without clear answers to which episode with tearing the document looks as an act of imbecility. AFAIK, none of the OTL generals of that period were that good in both areas and without Bonaparte the war of 2nd coalition most probably would end due to the exhaustion of both sides without too much to show for it (in OTL in 1799 the French were kicked out of Italy and exercises on the Danube led to nowhere for either side so the only area of clear success was Switzerland). Which means that enthusiasm in France is unlikely and, in OTL the Directory was in almost permanent fiscal crisis. So, it would be quite interesting to find out in more details how the things were proceeding (including financial aspect) without Nappy? Were ITTL any indications of the Russian desire to conquer Hungary? Anyway, this was clearly not an consideration during the 2nd Coalition when Austria asked for the Russian help (at least in OTL). BTW, without Nappy, is Paul still on the throne? If yes, and if the 2nd Coalition ended along the OTL lines, the issue would be not Francis’ reluctance but Paul’s refusal to deal with a former ally who screwed him up. Alexander hated Napoleon on a personal level, which mostly defined his actions in the 3rd and 4th coalitions, but, while being pro-British, was not actively anti-French in general. Anyway, it does not look like he would be doing Francis’ bidding. Why not Greenland? The XVII - XVIII centuries coalition wars against the Ottomans demonstrated to the Russians that the Austrians are, at best, useless as the allies and impotent as the enemies. If Austria is at war with France, whoever is the Russian emperor, can start war with the OE without paying any attention to Vienna’s position. Besides, how would Russia simultaneously fight the French and the OE? Obviously, expecting that after the French war the Hapsburg emperor is going to honor his generous promise to grant Russia the Ottoman territories (how about the Ottoman consent?) assumes a rather unrealistic level of a naivety on the Russian side. Which is of no importance to Vienna and Berlin by the obvious reason: none of them has colonies in the Americas. Then, the US in the early 1800s as a serious military threat? In 1812 it had less than 10,000 troops when war started and its navy had 12 frigates. Yes, and the question is how an obvious idiot managed to become the head of the French government and how his actions got approval of the parliament?
items.original_question: My Alternative History Scenario: What if Napoleon couldn't make it to France at 1799? EPISODE THREE​ German Pact ​ ​ A sudden storm breaking out across Europe had created a massive shockwave. Austria, still struggling to recover from the economic and military wounds of the War of the Second Coalition, was deeply displeased by France’s abrupt rekindling of hostilities. Emperor Francis II had been expecting a long period of peace, one he intended to devote to revitalizing Germany. Unfortunately, history had once again disappointed him. His federalist ambitions had not yet completely faded, but this meant confronting French republicanism earlier than anticipated. Moreover, following the referendum held on 18 February 1803 and the subsequent election, the country transitioned into what was called a presidential system. As a result, Fourier—who came to power and was a prominent representative of socialist thought—began spreading his ideas more widely across Europe. This signified a gradual shift of the German peoples toward republicanism. Although the Kingdom of Prussia and the Habsburg Monarchy did not hold each other in high regard, they shared a common enemy: France and republicanism. Approximately one week had passed since the outbreak of the Franco-Spanish War. French armies advanced rapidly, exploiting the dire condition of the Spanish forces to seize Catalonia and push toward Eastern Aragon. The Basque region had also fallen. Emperor Francis convened his cabinet, and they debated at length what course of action should be taken. Johann Amadeus Franz, the Minister of Finance of the era, was firmly opposed to breaking the peace with France, as any potential war would further devastate Austria’s already fragile economy. József Alvinczi, the Chief of the General Staff, argued that this war represented an opportunity to eliminate both France and the spread of republican ideas on the European continent. He maintained that, as demonstrated in the previous conflict, the Austrian army was not in as poor a condition as believed and demanded that an open ultimatum be issued to France. However, the Emperor had a different plan in mind. Although there was no certainty it would succeed, he deemed it worth attempting. For this reason, he decided to send a delegate to the Kingdom of Prussia, carrying a note requesting a private meeting with the King. The delegation set out on 15 March 1803. Meanwhile, across Europe, no clear decision had yet emerged from the British Isles. Prime Minister Henry Addington had no desire to see Spain under French control, but he also believed that the British Army was not yet prepared. After lengthy discussions with other statesmen, he sent an envoy to the Kingdom of Portugal to further expand the Anglo-Portuguese Alliance and present several proposals. In the meantime, the delegation sent by Austria to Prussia returned two weeks later. The Emperor’s proposal to the King of Prussia was to intervene in the Franco-Spanish War by forming a German coalition. The Prussian King, eager to enhance his prestige among the German states, responded favorably and announced his acceptance. Thus, the German Pact was formed. Both sides began final preparations for their already mobilized armies, and within approximately two weeks, everything was ready. A note bearing the personal signatures of both the Emperor and the King was delivered to the French delegates by a joint Austro-Prussian mission. The note demanded that France sever its alliance with the United States, withdraw from Spain, and agree to certain trade arrangements. French President Charles Fourier tore the original document to pieces in parliament. This act provided the Habsburg Monarchy and the Kingdom of Prussia with sufficient legitimacy to launch a military intervention against France. Emperor Francis II was deeply uneasy about Russia’s ambiguous stance. He neither wanted Russia to emerge excessively strong nor excessively weak. Poland could be the first step, and the Russian flag might one day fly over Hungary or the borders of the Holy Roman Empire. Taking such a risk seemed irrational. Therefore, depending on the course of the war, he considered enticing Russia into joining their side by offering the Balkan territories of the already weakened Ottoman Empire—despite his preference for preserving the balance of power in the Balkans and Eastern Europe. The French threat, however, took precedence. Although the United States did not yet pose a direct threat to Europe, it continued to threaten the colonial powers in the Americas. While it had not yet entered the conflict, such an involvement was not impossible. On the other hand, the Emperor foresaw that the French government’s aggressive and overly idealistic actions would ultimately lead to its downfall. By initiating this war, France had effectively shot itself in the foot, and these events would pave the way for a rise in anti-French sentiment throughout Europe.

items.model_answer: If Napoleon Bonaparte had been unable to return to France in 1799—perhaps detained in Egypt or lost at sea—the Coup of 18 Brumaire (November 1799) would likely not have occurred as it did. Without Napoleon’s military prestige, political maneuvering, and alliance with key figures like Sieyès, the Directory might have persisted longer or collapsed under different leadership. A rival general, such as Jean-Baptiste Jourdan or Lazare Hoche (had he lived), or a civilian faction might have filled the power vacuum, but none possessed Napoleon’s combination of charisma, strategic acumen, and popular support. Consequently, France might have avoided the centralized authoritarian Consulate and later Empire, potentially leading to a more prolonged period of revolutionary instability, an earlier restoration of the monarchy, or a different trajectory for European wars—possibly delaying or altering the Napoleonic Wars and their transformative impact on Europe’s political map and legal systems.

items.question: What If the Greek 'Great Plan' had succeeded and the Greek War of Independence had triggered an early collapse of the Ottoman Empire?
human_answers: A more decisive Ottoman defeat against Greece can give birth to the "Megali Idea" before 1844. In such a scenario, a larger independent Greek state can invited Louis-Philippe d’Orléans to become its king, before 1830 of course. This arrangement can be supported by both France and its Bourbon king, who might want to sideline a troublesome cousin, and by the United Kingdom. For the British, the presence of a Great European power south of the Straits, one aligned with neither Austria nor Russia can further divide the continental great powers and serve British strategic interests. With France satisfied in Greece and Austria compensated with territories along the Adriatic coast, Britain can focus on securing Egypt for itself. Even if the Suez Canal is not even a dream, control of Egypt is already strategically valuable for strengthening connections with India. By 1829, railway projects are already under consideration, making overland transit increasingly plausible and reinforcing Egypt’s geopolitical importance. And if its happen after 1830, Louis-Philippe has enough sons (6 minus one who died in 1828) to send one to Greece.

Considering their interest is not even religious (GB: Protestant, France: Catholic, Russia: Orthodox) and that really none of these Great Powers saw the Greek War of Independence with positive eyes (to them it was no different than the revolutions in Spain, Portugal and Naples; which, btw, they sent huge armies to crush). There was later a British change, but even the Metternich, Alexander and so on weren't super happy about it. Remember: at this point, the memory of Napoleon is far fresher than that of the Ottoman invasions into the Balkans, so the concern, far above Islam, is revolutionary sentiment. What I do see happening is them deliberating and taking too long to make a decision that the situation ends up devolving on its own (it took them like 3 years to agree to send an invasion to Spain). Then again, the French were sympathetic to Muhammad Ali while the British aided Ali Pasha plenty of times (through Maitland, specifically). They will always prefer a rotting corpse of the Ottoman empire maintaining power over the ambitious and reformist Albanian Pashas in power, this is why they went out of their way to put them out IRL, but when shit hits the fan, they have to re-examine their approach of course.

Agreed that the Great Powers, including even Russia under Alexander, don't want a full Ottoman collapse. That's not the same as saying they would intervene to stop it. It's hard to conceive of a situation in which Great Britain, France, or Russia would go to war to suppress Christian rebels fighting against the Sultan, particularly after the various atrocities committed at Chios and other places. There were also similar atrocities committed by the Greeks against Muslims, but this did not register in the European consciousness of the time and would not be a factor. It's also not a given that any intervention would be successful at stopping chaos and preserving the Empire, even if it did somehow occur. This would be a formidable job if the situation became so extreme that the Ottomans asked for such support. More likely the intervention would be directed towards managing the collapse and achieving a partition either formally or in terms of spheres of influence.
items.original_question: What if 'Great Plan' more or fully successful - Greek War of Independence causes early Ottoman collapse? There have been many threads about the Greek War of Independence here, but one what if I haven't seen anyone talk about might be one of the most crazy ones. Mark Mazower states the following in his book on the Greek War of Indepdendence: Of course, aside from the revolt in the Peloponnese, none of these plans ever came close to succeeding. These plans were modified or abandoned entirely when the focus of the revolt shifted from the Peloponnese to the Danubian Principalities. There was a letter sent to cause terror in Constantinople, but the letter never made it and plans were changing so often that no action was taken. Now this seems like an insane scheme which would be insanely hard to pull off, even if all the circumstances were right, but let's hypothetically ask, what if some, or all of them did? Would this cause the Ottoman Empire to collapse entirely, or enter a prolonged period of unrest? A torching of the fleet, coordinated with the assassination of Mahmud II, coupled with all the other issues the empire was facing in the early 1820's seem like they would be a complete headache, who would even be Sultan had this happened, considering Abdulmecid wasn't even born yet and Mahmud II had no sons? Edit: Turns out Mahmud II had a single surviving son by this point, Abdulhamid. But he died in 1825 IOTL, which, if it still happens, might actually make things even worse if the revolt didn't fizzle out by then.

If the Greek “Great Plan” (Megali Idea) had succeeded in its most ambitious form during or immediately after the Greek War of Independence (1821–1830)—that is, if Greece had not only secured independence but also catalyzed the rapid and total collapse of the Ottoman Empire—the geopolitical landscape of southeastern Europe, the Balkans, and the Eastern Mediterranean would have been dramatically reshaped much earlier than it historically was.

First, the power vacuum left by an early Ottoman collapse in the 1820s or 1830s would likely have triggered intense competition among European powers—particularly Russia, Austria, Britain, and France—for influence over former Ottoman territories. Russia, already positioning itself as protector of Orthodox Christians under Ottoman rule, might have expanded deep into the Balkans and possibly seized Constantinople, fulfilling long-standing strategic ambitions. This could have provoked a major European war far earlier than the Crimean War (1853–1856), potentially altering the balance of power established by the Congress of Vienna (1815).

Second, the Balkan peoples—Serbs, Bulgarians, Romanians, Albanians, and others—might have achieved independence decades sooner, possibly leading to the emergence of nation-states along ethnic or religious lines well before the late 19th century. However, without the gradual administrative and nationalist developments that occurred later, these new states might have been more unstable, fragmented, or subject to direct great-power control.

Third, the absence of a lingering Ottoman presence in Europe could have prevented or significantly altered later conflicts such as the Balkan Wars (1912–1913) and even aspects of World War I, which was partly ignited by tensions in the declining Ottoman sphere. Additionally, the fate of minority populations—including Armenians, Jews, and various Muslim communities—might have diverged sharply, with uncertain consequences for demographic patterns and intercommunal relations.

Finally, Greece itself, had it absorbed large swathes of Anatolia and Constantinople early on, would have faced immense challenges governing a multiethnic empire far beyond its administrative capacity at the time. This could have led either to internal fragmentation or to a different trajectory of Greek state-building—one more imperial than national.

In sum, an early collapse of the Ottoman Empire triggered by a successful Greek War of Independence would have accelerated nationalist movements, intensified European rivalries, and potentially avoided some 19th-century conflicts while creating others, fundamentally reordering the modern history of southeastern Europe and the Near East.

items.question: What If the French become one of the largest communities in the US
human_answers: Hordes of Catholics, even if not all that devout, descending on the US will cause some tension. On the flip side, though, France is one of the civilized nations, and they're seen as more desirable shade of white. Timing matters, too. Napoleonic era, when immigration is still low, is a whole lot different than the final decades of the 19th century, when millions is a drop in the bucket. Location matters, too. Are the French hordes joining into the crowded East, where they likely assimilate? Or are they carving out a big chunk of the midwest/west as largely French? Reason for the diaspora might matter. If we mess with the Napoleonic era, especially if we butterfly it (not killing off a generation or two of males would be a good start in having excess population to export), the state of the world could affect the state of the USA (maybe even the size if no Mex-Am War/Texas). With such a generic What if, we can only talk in generics. If we stipulate a recognizable world, more or less the same, except a massive French diaspora for some reason that hasn't caused OTL to derail.... I would guess the French would be like any other large group. There'll be tension, but everyone will adapt. It's an age of racism, and French are in the top class, so I suspect they'll have an easier time of it. (caveat edit: In no way am I saying French are better than any other nation, but reality is that skin color mattered. My understanding is that not all whites were considered equal)

I would assume rather than staying in the east, the French would largely settle in former Louisiana- centring probably on New Orleans. Texas and Florida as well are likely spots for French settlement. Of the 13 colonies, I would guess it’s the southern ones which would be most amenable to French settlement- though how that affects racial dynamics in the south, and how that affects potential north south tensions is difficult to say. It’s difficult as well to say what the economic impact of French settlement would be- I’d say as a community they’d probably be more educated and thus better off than the Irish or Italians, perhaps more comparable to German or Swedish immigrants. Perhaps the planter class ends up going fully bilingual. Depending on how the 19th century goes you could end up with an Alt-confederacy that stays independent because it has so many French speakers and Catholics that the north simply isn’t interested in reintegrating them.
items.original_question: What if the French become one of the largest communities in the US Let’s suppose that millions of French flocked to the US in the 19th century for one reason or another—for example, because harsher Napoleonic Wars and a more severe Congress of Vienna plunged France into a deep economic crisis, while the Irish and Italians would be less numerous in the US, for example because the Irish Great Famine never happened and the Italian peninsula unified and modernized earlier. No PoD before 1780. How would the French be treated in the US? Would they face xenophobia and form a distinct community like the Irish and Italians, or would they be assimilated among the WASPs within one or two generations like the Germans did IOTL? French culture was admired, but I’m not sure that the arrival of millions of French people (with a Latin culture and Catholic religion) would be particularly well received.

items.question: Independent Naples: What If Catherine of Aragon marries Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria in 1505?
human_answers: I wouldn't say that Philip is foolish, simply naive, since it is impossible for him to imagine that Ferdinand II and Catherine are plotting against him, to shape Joanna and especially the little Charles into a figure totally different from his own ( so that he may become the perfect archetype of a Christian Monarch ), but in any case I am certain that Queen Isabella would never do anything wrong in compromising her nephew's chances of inheriting his father's possessions ( Burgundy and Austria ) or preventing him from aspiring to the imperial throne, after all doing this risks it compromise to the international prestige of his family ( the Trastamaras ) let's say that the Catholic Monarchs only want to make sure that the future King of Castile and Aragon is not too accommodating to French wishes, it is realistic to think that Charles was initially educated at his mother's court, and then, when he was sure he could face a sea voyage, he was transferred to his grandfather Maximilian

Oh, please… the POD is interesting but the development is full of things that are blatantly false. OTL Isabella and Ferdinand were the ones that wanted Catalina’s remarriage to the future Henry VIII, and insisted that her marriage with Arthur was not consummated. Henry VII OTL was bullied in accepting the engagement of his second son to Catalina as he believed she was too old for his son. He would have zero troubles in giving back the half of her dowry he had already received (for all that getting back her dowry meant that Catherine had no right to any English money or lands) and send Catherine back at home as he had no use for her. Catalina’s aunt, the Dowager Queen of Naples would first try to marry her own daughter to the new Ferdinand III of Naples, as Giovanna was still in her mid-20s (or she would expect to see another match arranged for her daughter before agreeing to support Catalina as future Queen of Naples. Sea journeys at the time were extremely dangerous (I don’t remember if Catalina got lucky, but both Joanna and Margaret got close to die in their respective wedding journeys) reason for which Philip used his friendship with the French King for securing a land passage into France for going to receive the investitures. Eleanor and Charles at the time were too little for making safely the long journey, for not talking about baby Isabella, and Philip would never agree to bring them in Castile in any case. And if she had been so inclined Catalina, being the youngest of her sisters, could very well be allowed to take the veil. In 1502 Juana had three children and Maria one and both were likely to have soon more…

The year 1502 starts very rough for Catalina of Aragon. She and her husband, Arthur , Prince of Wales had both fallen ill at the end of March and when she recovered, she discovered that her husband had died. She could not believe it. She was a widow after only five months of marriage. She knew that she was not pregnant, as her marriage was unconsummated. One month after she was made a widow, Catalina was moved to Durham House in London and was visited by King Henry VII and his wife, Queen Elizabeth of York. Catalina told them that she had bled already and there was no hope for an heir from their late son, so his younger brother, Prince Henry, Duke of York, was officially declared as the heir. When the news to Catalina's parents, King Fernando II of Aragon and Queen Isabella I of Castile, they were disappointed that the alliance seemed to have fallen through and that their daughter was widowed at only sixteen years old. This began a struggle over Catalina. Queen Isabella was adamant that her youngest child be returned to her, since there was not a hope of an English grandchild to seal the alliance with Spain and England. King Henry VII, however, did not want to lose her or her dowry. He offered to marry her to his younger son and she could still be Queen of England one day. Queen Isabella made up her mind and told her husband that she wanted their daughter to be returned home. King Ferdinand sent an ambassador to tell King Henry that the Princess would be returned to Spain, either with her entourage or by force. When King Henry VII heard this, he was furious, but also terrified. He needed this alliance with Spain and he did not want to let his daughter-in-law go. Finally, an agreement was finally reached. The Infanta would return to her parents and half her dowry would be returned with her and she would retain her status of Dowager Princess of Wales and would still receive her marriage jointure for the remainder of her life. Her English attendants, like Margaret Pole, would remain in England. When she was told Princess Catalina had a mix of grief and relief. She was happy to return home to her parents, especially since her older sister, Juana, who was now Princess of Asturias, was back home as well. On August 1, 1502, Princess Catalina and her entourage arrived at Dover, preparing to board the ship that will cross the sea once again. Prince Henry, the young Prince of Wales accompanied her, just like he escorted her down the aisle to marry his late older brother. The eleven year old, who was talkative and social, was unusually quiet through the journey. Princess Catalina gave him a little kiss on his forehead and told him that she will never forget him or her time in England and she knew that one day, he will be the greatest King that England ever had, before she boarded the ship. Thankfully, this journey was much easier than her original one taking her to England. She and her entourage arrived in Laredo on the 15th of August. Princess Catalina found herself smiling, as she saw the familiar Castilian villages and knew she was home. However, she then was wondering what would happen to her and her future. Due to the deaths of her older brother, sister and nephew, she knew that taking holy vows was not an option, as he parents only had three surviving daughters. Would she just remain a spinster? Would she be married off again to a foreign Kingdom, even France? Her father was definitely ambitious and was a shrewd ruler, so she knew that she would not remain unmarried for long, but she was still looking forward to just feeling her mother's embrace once more.
items.original_question: Independent Naples: What if Catherine of Aragon marries Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria in 1505? Hey all! This question has been on my mind a little too. What if instead of the long seven years in England in virtual poverty, Catherine of Aragon returns to her parents in the summer of 1502 and they arrange a marriage for the young King of Naples, which is still an independent Kingdom in this timeline? In this timeline, Henry VIII will instead marry Eleanor of Austria instead.

items.model_answer:
If Catherine of Aragon had married Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria (heir to the Kingdom of Naples) in 1505—instead of marrying Henry VIII of England—the geopolitical trajectory of southern Europe would have shifted significantly. At the time, Naples was contested between Spanish and French claims, and Ferdinand of Aragon (Catherine’s father) had recently secured control of the kingdom after defeating the French in 1504. Marrying Catherine to his Neapolitan namesake nephew (Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, son of Frederick IV of Naples) would have reinforced Aragonese legitimacy in Naples by uniting the royal houses more tightly.

This union could have stabilized Spanish rule in southern Italy earlier and more durably, potentially reducing French ambitions in the region during the Italian Wars. It might also have diminished the Habsburg-Valois rivalry’s intensity in Italy, as Charles V (Catherine’s nephew through her sister Joanna) already inherited vast territories; a stronger, consolidated Spanish Naples under a branch linked directly to Catherine could have acted as a loyal satellite rather than a contested frontier.

For England, the absence of Catherine’s marriage to Henry VIII would have removed the dynastic and religious crisis that led to the English Reformation. Henry might still have sought annulments or remarried for an heir, but without Catherine’s specific papal dispensation and subsequent refusal to concede, the break with Rome may not have occurred—or at least not in the same form or timeframe.

In this scenario, Naples might have retained greater autonomy under a cadet branch of the Trastámara dynasty, possibly delaying or altering its full integration into the Spanish Empire. However, given the overwhelming power of Ferdinand of Aragon and later Charles V, full independence for Naples would have remained unlikely; instead, it might have evolved as a semi-autonomous kingdom within the Spanish sphere, with Catherine acting as a cultural and political bridge between Iberia and southern Italy.

edus.text: If Catherine of Aragon had married Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria (heir to the Kingdom of Naples) in 1505—instead of marrying Henry VIII of England—
the geopolitical trajectory of southern Europe would have shifted significantly.
At the time, Naples was contested between Spanish and French claims,
and Ferdinand of Aragon (Catherine’s father) had recently secured control of the kingdom after defeating the French in 1504.
Marrying Catherine to his Neapolitan namesake nephew (Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, son of Frederick IV of Naples)
would have reinforced Aragonese legitimacy in Naples by uniting the royal houses more tightly.
This union could have stabilized Spanish rule in southern Italy earlier and more durably,
potentially reducing French ambitions in the region during the Italian Wars.
It might also have diminished the Habsburg-Valois rivalry’s intensity in Italy,
as Charles V (Catherine’s nephew through her sister Joanna) already inherited vast territories;
a stronger, consolidated Spanish Naples under a branch linked directly to Catherine could have acted as a loyal satellite rather than a contested frontier.
For England, the absence of Catherine’s marriage to Henry VIII would have removed the dynastic and religious crisis
that led to the English Reformation.
Henry might still have sought annulments or remarried for an heir,
but without Catherine’s specific papal dispensation and subsequent refusal to concede,
the break with Rome may not have occurred—or at least not in the same form or timeframe.
In this scenario, Naples might have retained greater autonomy under a cadet branch of the Trastámara dynasty,
possibly delaying or altering its full integration into the Spanish Empire.
However, given the overwhelming power of Ferdinand of Aragon and later Charles V,
full independence for Naples would have remained unlikely;
instead, it might have evolved as a semi-autonomous kingdom within the Spanish sphere,
with Catherine acting as a cultural and political bridge between Iberia and southern Italy.

items.question: What If Curb Global Warming after 1980
human_answers: India has only recently emerged as one of the world’s chief polluters; some two decades ago, Russia and Japan had a bigger mark, and in 1980 Canada was the bigger polluter. Depending on how decarbonized the economies of the First World are by 2000, India’s subsequent economic growth could be magnitudes cleaner than it was OTL. China you have a better point about, though first, their massive economic rise in the three decades after Mao’s death or so is pretty contingent, and second, they still only caught up to the already carbon stagnant EU in 2002. Imagine if the US was still comparable, as they were OTL until the mid 1980’s; now imagine, as China is getting ready to join the WTO in the late 90’s and early 2000’s, the west is also pushing a world climate treaty that (among other things) pushed these three major blocs (the US, Europe, and China) to curb their emissions going into the future. Even if India still sees their emissions rise, wouldn’t the fact that by far the largest producers are simultaneously cutting emissions lead to net reduction?

Well, is the point of your question, can we limit temperature rise by today , or in perpetuity? If the former, then greater adoption of nuclear energy in the West is probably a good enough answer; by the time Chinese and Indian energy use spikes, the resultant temperature spike won't come until after today. Maybe. But that seems like the wrong question, I interpret it as how to prevent such a spike from EVER occurring, rather than just occurring 10 years late. And for that, there's a big challenge. How do developing countries get off the ground? Hydrocarbons are great for that. If the big emitters of the 60s all switched to nuclear, that's fantastic--but China and India can't afford to START with nuclear, nobody can, which means a huge amount of hydrocarbons being burned when they start heavily industrializing. As a solution, perhaps their rise as industrial powers can be delayed a few decades? If they started industrializing in 2025 instead, they might use shale gas or solar, which are now the cheapest sources of power. But the production of those isn't domestic to China, which is a huge part of their use of coal--they don't have to import it. Tentatively, maybe the Soviet Union needs to have greater economic development and a softer landing when it falls? If they can be an industrial exporter while powered off domestic nuclear and natural gas, and remain so in the 1990s, then Chinese growth will be very different, and overall emissions will be lower. Cars and planes are obvious problems. I would also posit beef as a problem--methane is significantly more powerful than carbon in greenhouse effect, and is estimated as responsible for 20 to 30 percent of human-origin warming. Sixty percent of methane emissions are estimated as human-caused, with a big one being agriculture, and beef is responsible for a LOT of agriculture. So a poorer world, that eats less meat, would have lower methane emissions. So too would a world with fewer wetlands, so perhaps a little more paving of swamps would be good from the perspective of this question. Just thoughts. I'll be back for more, probably.

No, because they're already too anti-nuclear. The R&D and thus cost curves on silicon-based solar cell production, and on improved battery capacity, are both pushed pretty hard historically by electronics industry spinoffs. It's hard to see any sort of policy pushes for renewables accelerating those more than marginally, and dramatic acceleration is what you need to make them cost-viable decades ahead of schedule. On the other hand, nuclear was deliberately hobbled by US policy in the 1970s. People like to blame 1979's Three Mile Island, but (for a couple examples) the AEC to NRC switchover was passed by Congress and signed by Ford in 1974, while Carter's anti-reprocessing moratorium was in 1977. If you instead have the US adopt its own version of France's Messmer Plan in 1974 (which is tricky, because Messmer was able to simply ignore anti-nuclear sentiments due to government and economy structure in ways the US government couldn't), you get nuclear power economies of scale driven by the joint US-French demand that make it a more-attractive alternative throughout the rest of the industrialized world. Imagine Thatcher's government nuclearizing Britain in part to undercut the coal unions, for example. Then, if US electricity is something like 75% nuclear in 1990 (like France in 1990, instead of the historical 20%), with the UK fast-following? Now you have the necessary condition (it not hobbling the US) for international trade treaties and the like based on carbon emissions, after a decade of greenhouse effect publicity (since the 1979 NAS report), with the first IPCC report coming out. (Yes, sure, butterflies will scramble the details, but "coal is bad" science, if anything, will be better-funded if the US is transitioning from coal.) If Japan has (as is likely) lagged the US/France/UK in adoption of nuclear, this will be a particularly easy sell, since everybody in the West in 1990 is looking for an excuse to be protectionist against "Japan, Inc." And with that set up, you have the trick for going forward. If China (etc.) has to avoid coal power to export to Western markets, China either will figure out how to avoid coal, or it won't develop because it won't have markets to sell into.

I can give you two, PODs, One being no 3 Mile Island and the other being no John Sununu. So the real easy way to cut down on CO2 emissions is to cut down on coal use, and both PODs give easy ways to do just that. After the banning of CFCs in the late 80s, momentum existed for much harder caps on carbon than were discussed later. In particular, serious curtailment of coal as an energy source in the developed world was mooted. However, this momentum was handicapped with a lack of US Presidential support, with Bush Sr being advised against supporting these efforts by his Chief of Staff, John Sununu. Remove Sununu, and US support for carbon caps become more likely earlier. In addition with no 3MI incident, nuclear technology in the west could become less taboo, giving a viable alternative to coal fired power earlier. I could see a scenario where industry, much like CFCs, sees the financial opportunities in replacing coal with a nuclear/gas mix, and does not get in the way of any cuts to carbon emissions. A good book on the subject in your timeframe is Loosing Earth, by Nathanial Rich, which goes into detail about the drive to curtail emissions in the late 80s. would highly recommend giving it a read.
items.original_question:
AHC: Curb Global Warming after 1980

So you know how Global Surface Temperatures have increased 1.3°C over pre-industrial levels at present, and how a big part of the current Climate Movement is trying to limit further change as much as possible, 1.5°C being the best known* goal? Well, as recently as circa 1980, GST above PIL was only about 0.3°C, and had been hovering just below those levels for decades since the aftermath of WWII; in other words, a full degrees celsius of global warming only happened in the past 45 years alone. This is actually pretty astonishing when you realize how much of a turning point circa 1980 was to global carbon emissions -- both the biggest producers world-wide at the time, the US and Europe, initially saw their emissions peak, with Europe remaining controlled even as the US reversed course after a few years; Japan and Canada have a similar "false peaks" around the same time as the US; the USSR, of course, collapse circa 1990 and saw their emissions collapse thereafter, never to recover; and China was about to undergo a massive economic expansion that would see them become the world's largest emitters. So what I want to determine here is -- what is the latest PoD for avoiding this massive escalation of climate change, or of making it as small as possible? Could a PoD in the late 1970's (eg a continuation of Carter's energy policies in the US) have done the trick? If avoiding a full degrees celsius of warming wasn't seriously avertable by, say, 1975, how early do we need to go? 1960? The aftermath of WWII? In the event we can come to a consensus on the latest possible PoD and what would do the trick, we might also discuss how those changes to said countries' energy polices and to the global economy as a whole would have changed things overall. Thanks. *I'm really trying to avoid getting sidetracked in this discussion for the thread, so for anyone wanting to weigh in on whether its still feasible or how big of a deal missing that goal is, please take that to one of the Chat discussions -- much thanks!

criteria.name: 1980 Baseline and Emissions Chronology Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accurately anchors the counterfactual in the post-1980 emissions landscape, including which countries/blocs mattered when, and avoids anachronistic assumptions about China, India, the USSR/Russia, Japan, Canada, the EU, and the US.
criteria.1-2: Misstates the 1980 baseline or treats present-day emitters as if they had the same role in 1980; little connection to historical emissions timing.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes some major emitters but gives a shallow or partially anachronistic chronology of who drove emissions after 1980.
criteria.5-6: Mostly accurate on broad emissions timing, distinguishing early Western dominance from later Chinese and Indian growth, with minor omissions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly tracks major emitter shifts across the 1980s, 1990s, 2000s, and later, using this chronology to shape the counterfactual.
criteria.9-10: Precisely integrates historical emissions sequencing, industrialization timing, and bloc-level comparisons to evaluate whether post-1980 warming could plausibly be curbed.

criteria.name: Decarbonization Mechanism Plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the specificity and plausibility of proposed mechanisms for curbing warming after 1980, especially nuclear expansion, coal displacement, renewables cost curves, efficiency, carbon treaties, and fossil-fuel lock-in.
criteria.1-2: Offers vague claims such as 'use clean energy' without explaining feasible mechanisms or constraints.
criteria.3-4: Mentions plausible technologies or policies but ignores cost, deployment speed, political resistance, or energy-system inertia.
criteria.5-6: Provides one or two workable mechanisms, such as Western nuclear buildout or coal limits, with some attention to feasibility.
criteria.7-8: Explains multiple mechanisms and constraints, including nuclear politics, renewable timing, grid deployment, coal dependence, and international policy leverage.
criteria.9-10: Builds a highly plausible decarbonization pathway with detailed technological, economic, political, and institutional mechanisms appropriate to the 1980 onward timeline.

criteria.name: Developing-World Industrialization and Trade Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles the central downstream issue: how China, India, and other developing economies industrialize if the West curbs emissions, and whether trade, technology transfer, delayed growth, or carbon standards change their trajectories.
criteria.1-2: Ignores China, India, and developing-country growth or assumes they simply copy Western decarbonization without constraints.
criteria.3-4: Mentions China or India but gives little explanation of energy affordability, domestic coal, export markets, or development incentives.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that developing-country industrialization is a major challenge and links it to coal, trade, or technology access.
criteria.7-8: Analyzes how Western decarbonization, carbon tariffs, WTO-era trade, Soviet/Russian alternatives, or technology transfer could alter Chinese and Indian emissions.
criteria.9-10: Gives a nuanced account of developing-world growth paths, including affordability, domestic resources, export dependence, geopolitical contingencies, and whether global emissions fall despite later industrialization.

criteria.name: Climate Outcome Reasoning and Greenhouse-Gas Coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Measures how well the answer connects emissions changes to climate outcomes, including cumulative CO2, timing of warming, methane, land use, transport, agriculture, and the distinction between delaying warming and preventing it in the long run.
criteria.1-2: Conflates annual emissions with temperature outcomes or ignores cumulative emissions and climate lag.
criteria.3-4: Makes broad claims about reduced warming but gives little explanation of cumulative carbon, timing, or non-CO2 gases.
criteria.5-6: Correctly notes that lower emissions reduce warming and includes some discussion of climate lag or non-CO2 sources.
criteria.7-8: Distinguishes short-term delay from long-term prevention and covers major sectors such as electricity, transport, industry, agriculture, and methane.
criteria.9-10: Rigorously links sectoral emissions pathways to cumulative forcing and temperature outcomes, explicitly assessing whether warming is merely postponed or durably limited.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Coherence, Uncertainty, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses the overall counterfactual chain from post-1980 interventions to late-20th and 21st-century outcomes, including internal consistency, handling of contingencies, and calibrated confidence.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected claims, deterministic assertions, or contradictions that break the counterfactual chain.
criteria.3-4: Has a recognizable scenario but weak causal links, unsupported leaps, or unacknowledged conflicts between assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Maintains a mostly coherent chain with some uncertainty acknowledged, though parts remain underdeveloped or loosely connected.
criteria.7-8: Develops a consistent multi-decade causal pathway, flags key contingencies, and avoids major contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Provides a tightly reasoned long-range scenario with explicit causal dependencies, alternative branches, uncertainty calibration, and careful distinction between necessary and sufficient conditions.

items.model_answer: If global warming had been effectively curbed after 1980—through immediate, coordinated international action to drastically reduce greenhouse gas emissions—the world would likely have avoided many of the most severe climate impacts observed since then. Global average temperatures would have risen far less than the approximately 0.9°C actually seen between 1980 and 2023. This would have significantly reduced the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events (such as heatwaves, hurricanes, and droughts), slowed sea-level rise, preserved more Arctic sea ice and mountain glaciers, and lessened ocean acidification. Ecosystems and biodiversity would have faced lower stress, coral reefs might have largely avoided mass bleaching, and agricultural systems would have remained more stable. Human health, infrastructure, and economies—especially in vulnerable regions—would have been spared substantial costs and displacement. In essence, early mitigation after 1980 could have kept warming close to 1°C above pre-industrial levels, aligning with safer climate thresholds later enshrined in agreements like the Paris Accord.

items.original_question: What if No Seven Bishops' Death in 1558? Everyone knows about the death of Cardinal Pole, Archbishop of Canterbury shortly after Queen Mary in 1558. But less known- as in, not even listed when you google them- is that there were six other bishops who died around the same time (including Maurice Griffith, Bishop of Rochester). This led to the opening of several vacancies in the English Catholic Church at the start of Elizabeth I's reign. To the seven bishops who died, can be added Bishop Oglethorpe of Carlisle (who, while he crowned Elizabeth, was no fan of hers after she stormed out of his celebration of Christmas Mass in 1558 because he defied her) and Nicolas Heath, the archbishop of York, who, as the highest ranked cleric in England should've crowned Elizabeth, but declined the "honour". He lost his see in 1559. What would've happened to the Elizabethan Settlement if those seven (or nine) sees had not fallen vacant at exactly the same time (many remaining vacant until 1561). How much opposition would there be to Elizabeth TTL? And how would Elizabeth have dealt with the situation TTL? @BlueFlowwer @isabella @RedKing @HortenseMancini

items.model_answer:
If the Seven Bishops had not died in 1558—though historically, the "Seven Bishops" incident actually occurred in 1688 under James II, not in 1558—it appears there may be a conflation of events. In 1558, Queen Mary I (a Catholic) died and was succeeded by her Protestant half-sister Elizabeth I. During Mary’s reign (1553–1558), nearly 300 Protestants were executed, including prominent bishops like Thomas Cranmer, Hugh Latimer, and Nicholas Ridley—often referred to collectively as the "Oxford Martyrs," not the "Seven Bishops."

Assuming the question intends to ask: *What if the leading Protestant bishops martyred under Mary I had not died in 1558?*—then the answer is as follows:

Had these key Protestant leaders survived into Elizabeth I’s reign, the English Reformation might have proceeded with stronger theological continuity from the earlier Edwardian reforms. Their presence could have lent greater legitimacy and doctrinal cohesion to the Elizabethan Religious Settlement of 1559, potentially reducing internal tensions between Puritans and more conservative Anglicans. Surviving reformers like Cranmer might have shaped the Book of Common Prayer and the Thirty-Nine Articles more directly, possibly resulting in a more explicitly Protestant Church of England from the outset. Their martyrdom under Mary, however, already served as powerful propaganda for the Protestant cause; their survival might have altered both the symbolic narrative and practical governance of the early Elizabethan church.
