items.question: What If Almanzor had never risen to power in al-Andalus?
human_answers: I had to read about Ghalib because my knowledge of him is quite limited. Overall, he seems to be a competent Saqaliba (slave-soldier) leader and served three caliphs. I don't see why he would try to reshape the composition of the caliphate as Al-Mansur did when trying to use Berbers against the rest of Islamic Iberia. Ghālib's rise coincides with the retirement of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III from active military command following his defeat at the Battle of Simancas in 939. So he came to serve under the first caliph and had a life of distinguished service fighting against Vikings, Moroccans, Fatimids, and Christians from northern Iberia. Gaining his freedom and patronage from the Umayyad. Perhaps it will have a greater influence from the Saqaliba in general within the caliphate. But to be honest, overall, they were good slave soldiers, and in the OTL, when the caliphate began to collapse, they were the ones who desperately fought against the Berbers to try to keep the caliphate alive and prevent the sackings of the city of Córdoba. I think one factor that made them generally better managers than the Mamluks in Egypt was that the ṣaqāliba were much less institutionalized and more integrated into local society. This was largely because Andalusian power was always balanced by military pluralism. With Arabs, Berbers, local Andalusians (the Muwallads), Ṣaqāliba, and Christian mercenaries, this balance prevented a single military group from monopolizing the state, as the Mamluks had done. So a Mameluke is freed to never cease being a Mameluke, while a ṣaqāliba is freed to cease being a ṣaqāliba. I'd guess that overall, you have a continuation of the status quo of the period, with a normal caliph (not the puppets of the period). There will be ethnic tensions that rise and fall depending on the situation, disputes over spheres of influence, campaigns in North Africa against the Fatimids (and in the future the Berber caliphates if they rise to power), and campaigns against Christians in the north (Kingdom of Leon), which may or may not succeed depending on the general, as happened in the OTL. It's difficult to say whether this prevents the reconquest of Iberia, but it certainly prevents the implosion of the caliphate of OTL. I would say that what will have the greatest impact on the survival of the Caliphate is not the Christians in the north, but rather the possible rise of the Almoravids.

I think that after ibn Abi Amir is killed, Ghalib is hailed as a hero by the Arab ruling class. As hajib, the old general, committed to the survival of the Caliphate as an institution, would free Hisham II from his irrelevance and perhaps have advisors train the boy-Caliph for rule. Once he reaches the age of maturity, Hisham takes power, albeit he mostly delegates authority to capable bureaucrats. His rule might be an extension of his father’s, a time of peace and prosperity and a golden age of the arts and sciences. The Christians are still too disorganized and weak to push into al-Andalus. Sancho III of Navarre is likely never even born as a result of butterflies. So no Jimenez dynasty either. Christian Spain remains small and disunited while Cordoba remains quietly strong and prosperous. I agree, the real threat to Cordoba wouldn’t be from the north, but from the south. So Cordoba focuses on maintaining hegemonic control over Morocco for strategic purposes. And without the constant warfare against the Christians, I think this will create a favorable situation for the Umayyads in Morocco. So no Almoravids. Fanatical tribes from the desert are repelled by strong Umayyad clients. Once Hisham passes away, he likely leaves an heir. This heir would inherit a strong and stable state, one that is durable for the century to come…
items.original_question: What if No Almanzor Ibn Abi Amir ‘al-Mansur’, better known Latinized as Almanzor, was the Hajib (chamberlain) and de facto ruler of the Caliphate of Qurtubah (Córdoba) from 978 to 1002 AD. A highly ambitious man, ibn Abi Amir would rise through the collection of various powerful offices over the course of the 960s and 970s as an administrator. Through this and his alliance with Subh, mother of the Umayyad boy-caliph Hisham II, ibn Abi Amir would become the most powerful man in al-Andalus by 980. Except, he wasn’t alone. He shared this spotlight with Ghalib ibn Abd al-Rahman ‘al-Siqlabi’ (the Slav), a widely-respected octogenarian general who had served both of Hisham’s predecessors. The two men formed an alliance with one another following the death of Caliph al-Hakam II in 976, allowing for them to rise the ranks of the Caliphate. However by 980 the two men had fallen out, and were increasingly at odds. That year, while together on campaign against the Christians, Ghalib attempted to murder ibn Abi Amir during a feast. The injured ibn Abi Amir would escape with his life and then proceed to capture Ghalib’s fortress in Madinat Salim (Medinaceli). This would lead to a brief civil war between the two, culminating in 981 with the Battle of Torrevicente. There, Ghalib’s army of Andalusi soldiers and his Christian allies would initially rout the Berber troops of ibn Abi Amir. However, Ghalib would unexpectedly die of seemingly natural causes in the middle of the battle, allowing for ibn Abi Amir to claim victory and the mantle of ‘al-Mansur’. Al-Mansur would go on to rule al-Andalus with an iron fist for the next two decades, sidelining the Umayyads, Arab nobility, and Muwalladi (native Iberian Muslims) alike while utilizing increasing numbers of Berber troops to repeatedly devastate the Christian north. While al-Mansur would lead al-Andalus to its peak of dominance over the whole of Iberia, he would also destroy its literal and cultural wealth while gutting its institutions. Upon his death in 1002 the Caliphate was a house of cards waiting to collapse, which it did after Abd al-Rahman ‘Sanchol’, better known as Sanchuelo, attempted to directly usurp the Umayyads as Caliph himself in 1009. This led to the 22-year-long Fitna (unrest) of al-Andalus, ending with Córdoba in ruins and the Caliphate shattered into 30+ petty kingdoms known as Taifas . A situation that would enable the Reconquista to gain steam, culminating in the capture of Tulaytulah (Toledo) by the Christians in 1085. Had Ghalib succeeded in the attempt on his life, ibn Abi Amir would have never become al-Mansur. The Umayyads would have maintained control over their Caliphate. Al-Andalus wouldn’t come to be dominated by a single dictatorial ruler. And the seeds of the Fitna wouldn’t be planted. The Reconquista will unfold differently, or even not at all. What are your thoughts on this scenario? I’ve come to believe that it represents the best chance the Caliphate of Córdoba had at ensuring long-term survival. Averting Almanzor and his excesses would blunt the height of Andalusi authority, but paradoxically preserve the state itself. Of course, stability following his death wouldn’t be ensured, and Ghalib wouldn’t have much longer to live anyway. However, the two had taken care of most rivals, and Ghalib was in good standing with the old guard of al-Andalus. Caliph Hisham II can actually grow up and become a proper ruler, preserving the legitimacy of the Caliphate itself. And without Almanzor, you don’t see increasing numbers of Berber tribesmen relocated to Iberia, provoking ethnic strife.

items.model_answer: If Almanzor (Muhammad ibn Abi Amir) had never risen to power in al-Andalus, the political trajectory of the Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba would likely have been markedly different. Without his military dominance and de facto rule from the 970s until his death in 1002, the caliphate might have avoided the centralization of power around a single strongman, potentially preserving more institutional stability under the nominal authority of the caliphs. Almanzor’s relentless campaigns against Christian kingdoms in the north temporarily halted their expansion but also drained resources and fostered resentment among Andalusi elites. In his absence, internal factionalism might have intensified earlier, possibly accelerating the fragmentation of the caliphate—but without the destabilizing effect of his personalist regime and the militarization of politics, the collapse into the taifa kingdoms after 1031 could have been delayed or taken a different form. Additionally, Christian principalities like Castile and León might have gained territory sooner without Almanzor’s aggressive raids, altering the balance of power on the Iberian Peninsula during a critical period of state formation.

items.question: What If In 1972 have Nixon make America the definitive winners in Vietnam before his re-election
human_answers: No there was still a path to victory as late as Watergate. The ARVN with US air support and a shitload of supplies showed it didn't need US ground troops to win battles in 1972 and 1973, and sometimes won without US air support too, and still was winning battles into late 1974 before their supplies and manpower reserves gave out. The problem was Watergate meant Nixon did not have the political capital to prevent Congress from reducing supplies to the ARVN, and then Ford had the same problem, but also couldn't get airstrikes approved for Phouc Long (the lack of which explicitly accelerated the NVA's final offensive by a year). NVA planners actually considered 1976 to be their last shot at winning, as after that point the ARVN would have gotten over its teething troubles So extra US aid means the ARVN wins more of the smaller engagements and US air support smacks the first post cease fire NVA Corps level offensive. That buys another year without lots (possibly any) of American deaths and thus less resistance to having airpower smack the NVA again when they try their "do or die" offensive in late 1975-early 1976. If that gets fought off, that's probably the last chance as the Sino-Vietnamese border is heating up and the ARVN will have gotten over its teething troubles, while the Soviets had become increasingly unwilling to resupply the NVA after the ceasefire

Yes, if the US could have continued the war, then the war would have continued. That's axiomatic. But it couldn't, so it didn't. Remember your Clausewitz: if your armies in the field are still capable of fighting, but there is no political support for continuing the war, then the war is over. They couldn't muster the political capital because the US had already lost. South Vietnam hadn't been defeated yet, but the writing was on the wall in 1972. The major US operations of that year weren't about winning the war - they were about getting favourable conditions for US withdrawal. Arguably everything after Nixon took power was about getting favourable conditions for US withdrawal. You don't agree to withdraw your troops from a theatre of war while your opponent leaves 200,000 of theirs because you're winning. You don't sign a peace agreement that leaves your opponent in control of territory you were trying to defend because you're winning.

Without fundamental reforms, the South Vietnamese government could not achieve any tactical victories, let alone destroy most of the northern army. I believe OP refers to the US destroying most of the North Vietnamese army. However, I doubt the South Vietnamese government was so incompetent as to be destroyed by local warlords and rebellious peasants. And the more the Americans suppressed these local forces, the more they aligned themselves with the Northern government. Things there somehow like Afganistan. Either a fundamental reshaping of the South Vietnamese government is necessary (which I don't think could be achieved during Nixon's term) or complete military control. This would require a large number of troops stationed in every town to maintain order in place of the South Vietnamese government. Not American, so from some Asia ally, maybe South Korean? This could come at a significant political cost and carries the risk of war with China.

By 1972 there were only around 50,000 American soldiers in Vietnam, which means with a POD of January 1, 1972, any military victories would be by the South Vietnamese ground forces, supported by US air power. I feel that the incompetence of the South Vietnamese army is greatly overstated. They were reliant on American support, but with that support they were a fairly decent force. Edit: I mean to say that the ARVN could not achieve any tactical victories is ridiculous. Look at the actual 1972 offensive of OTL. What I’m saying is basically exactly what happened. South Vietnamese ground forces defeated a northern invasion with the help of American air power. The North Vietnamese suffered 100,000 casualties. Jungle is going to be a mess. This mess was somewhat avoided in WW2 because when fighting in that kind of area vs Japan both sides were “foreigners” and we had more support from the locals. But yo take the local? You need to stand on and hold the land. ALL the land, if you hold any hive area but large parts are not occupied by your troops then the other guys just slip away to areas your troops aren’t at. I never understood why this wasn’t pretty obvious. I can only think it WAS obvious but being as the U.S. didn’t what to commit that kind of level of force it was ignored in favor of the new high tech way of fighting. criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer defines a credible way Nixon could make the U.S./South Vietnam the 'definitive winners' before the 1972 re-election, while respecting the actual military, political, and diplomatic constraints of 1972.
criteria.1-2: Assumes instant victory or total North Vietnamese collapse with little explanation; ignores 1972 constraints.
criteria.3-4: Gives a vague path to victory but relies on implausible leaps, such as unlimited U.S. escalation without cost.
criteria.5-6: Identifies a plausible lever, such as heavier airpower or aid, but only partially defines what 'winning' means before November 1972.
criteria.7-8: Clearly specifies a feasible victory condition and ties it to 1972 realities such as the Easter Offensive, Linebacker, ARVN performance, and election timing.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual, distinguishes propaganda victory from durable strategic victory, and rigorously tests feasibility against military, domestic, and diplomatic limits.

criteria.name: Military Mechanism Coverage in Vietnam
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the depth and accuracy of the military causal chain, including ARVN capacity, U.S. airpower, logistics, North Vietnamese forces, and whether battlefield success could translate into durable victory.
criteria.1-2: Treats the war as winnable by simply bombing harder or sending more troops; omits ARVN, NVA, and battlefield realities.
criteria.3-4: Mentions military escalation but gives little detail on how it changes the Easter Offensive, supply lines, or South Vietnamese defenses.
criteria.5-6: Discusses some relevant mechanisms, such as Linebacker, Haiphong mining, U.S. supplies, or ARVN performance, but leaves major gaps.
criteria.7-8: Explains how U.S. airpower, aid, ARVN operations, and NVA logistics interact, and assesses whether these could prevent renewed offensives.
criteria.9-10: Provides a nuanced operational account linking 1972 combat outcomes to longer-term force sustainability, territorial control, morale, logistics, and NVA recovery capacity.

criteria.name: U.S. Domestic Politics and Policy Sustainability
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer accounts for Nixon's re-election incentives, antiwar opinion, congressional constraints, the draft, credibility politics, and the later effects of Watergate and aid cutbacks.
criteria.1-2: Ignores U.S. domestic politics or assumes Nixon could act without congressional, electoral, or public constraints.
criteria.3-4: Mentions public opinion or the election but does not connect it to military decisions or post-1972 sustainability.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that Nixon needed a politically saleable outcome, but gives limited treatment of Congress, antiwar pressure, or Watergate.
criteria.7-8: Connects battlefield choices to Nixon's re-election strategy, Vietnamization, Paris negotiations, and later congressional limits on bombing and aid.
criteria.9-10: Shows how domestic legitimacy determines whether tactical success becomes durable victory, including the interaction of re-election, Watergate, Ford, aid reductions, and the end of U.S. air support.

criteria.name: Long-Range Regional and Diplomatic Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer traces downstream effects beyond November 1972, including the Paris Peace Accords, North Vietnam's strategy, China and Soviet behavior, South Vietnamese governance, and regional stability.
criteria.1-2: Stops at the 1972 election or assumes the war simply ends after a U.S. battlefield success.
criteria.3-4: Offers a short aftermath but ignores major actors such as Hanoi, Saigon, Beijing, Moscow, or Congress.
criteria.5-6: Discusses some post-1972 consequences, such as a modified peace deal or continued fighting, but lacks a coherent long-range chain.
criteria.7-8: Traces several downstream effects, including ceasefire terms, NVA regrouping, South Vietnamese resilience, foreign aid flows, and renewed offensives.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent multi-year scenario showing how a 1972 'win' might endure, unravel, or transform the Cold War balance, regional conflicts, and South Vietnam's internal legitimacy.

criteria.name: Causal Coherence, Uncertainty Calibration, and Contradiction Control

criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, anachronisms, or unsupported certainty; confuses actual history with the counterfactual.
criteria.3-4: Has a basic scenario but includes inconsistent claims or overconfident conclusions about victory or defeat.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent and historically grounded, but some causal links are asserted rather than argued or uncertainty is weakly handled.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a consistent timeline, flags uncertainties, and compares plausible branches such as temporary U.S. victory versus durable South Vietnamese survival.
criteria.9-10: Offers a tightly reasoned, non-contradictory counterfactual with explicit contingency points, probability-sensitive judgments, and clear separation between tactical, political, and strategic victory.

items.model_answer:
If Nixon had made America the “definitive winners” in Vietnam before his 1972 re-election—meaning a clear military or political victory that ended the war decisively in U.S. favor—it would have required a dramatic departure from historical reality. By 1972, the U.S. was deeply committed to “Vietnamization,” withdrawing troops while bolstering South Vietnam’s military, and public and congressional opposition to the war had grown overwhelming. Achieving a definitive win would likely have necessitated massive escalation—such as renewed large-scale bombing, invasion of North Vietnam, or even use of nuclear threats—which risked direct confrontation with China or the Soviet Union and further domestic unrest.

Had Nixon somehow achieved such a victory, it might have secured him an even larger electoral mandate in 1972 than he historically received (he won 49 states). It could have temporarily restored national confidence and delayed or diminished the postwar “Vietnam Syndrome” that made Americans wary of foreign interventions. However, sustaining a pro-U.S. South Vietnam long-term would have remained unlikely without permanent U.S. military presence, given deep internal divisions in South Vietnam and persistent North Vietnamese resolve. Moreover, such a victory might have prolonged Cold War tensions, undermined détente, and possibly intensified anti-war movements or constitutional crises at home. Ultimately, while politically advantageous in the short term for Nixon, a “definitive win” would have contradicted the geopolitical and domestic realities that made U.S. withdrawal inevitable.

items.question: What If NACA had significantly improved the P-38 early in World War II?
human_answers: "All told, these NACA modifications solve three of the biggest issues with the early combat performance of the P-38 with the 8th Air Force: Limited Dive, Engine Cooling/Reliability, and Cockpit heating. In addition, the lack of the radiator ducts in the booms reduces drag and would likely result in a better level-flight top-speed (I would expect a gain of 10-20 mph from this) and improved/decreased fuel consumption. This leaves only two big problems to solve with later models. The first of these remaining problems was that the Fuel Mixture, Propeller RPM, and Throttle controls were independent and never had an implemented solution in OTL. For those not familiar with what those are, it means that to change from a “Cruising” condition to a “Combat” condition, the pilot needed to adjust three different levers for each engine (a total of six adjustments): Move Fuel Mixture from Auto-Lean to Auto-Rich; Increase Propeller RPMs; Increase manifold pressure (throttle). I have read some anecdotal evidence* that Lockheed had developed an “automatic manifold pressure regulator” which automated all of these adjustments into a single lever per engine but that the Air Force deemed it “unnecessary” and never authorized its implementation (Allison, the engine manufacturer, implemented this system on the post-war “G” series V-1710 engines). Supposing, with the “big three” problems solved due to the NACA redesign early in the combat life of the airplane the 8th AF decided to keep the P-38’s in primary service longer it is reasonable, I think, to assume this modification would become “necessary” and it could be implemented by late 1943/early 1944 models of the airplane (OTL P-38J, but in ATL, probably be considered second or third block P-38H). The second remaining issue was that the ailerons became heavy at high speeds and the so the airplane’s roll rate was quite slow, limiting its use as a dog-fighter. In OTL this was fixed in June 1944 with the P-38J-25-LO which introduced hydraulically boosted ailerons. These exponentially increased the force on the ailerons when turning the yoke and allowed the P-38 to flick-roll faster than most other fighters of the time. I am not certain how much more quickly these would be introduced in ATL vs. OTL as the slow-roll performance wouldn’t be altered by the NACA modifications nor was its solution delayed or prevented by AF brass. So, let’s say that this modification is introduced as it was in OTL, i.e. June 1944. Finally, with the 8th AF decision to keep the P-38 as the primary long-range escort fighter I believe it is reasonable to presume that they would have dedicated more time and resources to addressing the basic and tactical training for the pilots that was largely ignored in OTL, possibly even to the extant to sharing information with the P-38 FGs in the PTO—although that is uncertain. The result is, that when the 55th FG is transferred to the 8th AF with P-38H’s in September 1943 they have an aircraft capable of escorting bombers, at high-altitude, comfortably, reliably, and with significantly improved performance over most Axis fighters. This would reduce the demand for P-51’s and while I still expect them to come in theatre I would expect the P-38 Fighter Groups to keep the P-38’s rather than switching to P-47’s and P-51’s resulting in a near even three-way split between the fighter types by war’s end. I don’t know that this would have any significant impact on the eventual course or outcome of the war but improved long-range escort earlier in the war could have had a large positive impact on bomber-loss rates and morale. The reduction in bomber-losses in turn could mean a faster buildup of US Bomber forces and an earlier launch of major 1000+ raids perhaps even increasing the time-table for the Normandy Invasion, although other logistical problems likely lock that in no earlier than May ’44. The biggest difference would be in the reception and memory of the P-38 and its potential for a continued career post-war, similar to the P-51. The possibility of keeping them in service longer could also lead to the late-war approval for the adoption of the P-38K-1 with the F15 (Allison V-1710-75/77) engines and Hamilton-Standard Hydromatic high-activity propellers. In OTL only one of these was made using the large P-38J style chin and retaining the high-drag boom radiators. Even with all that drag it was able to achieve 432mph in level flight using Military Power and was expected to make 450mph with War Emergency Power with matching improvements in range and fuel consumption (about 10%). It also had a ceiling of 46,000 feet, a max climb of 4,800 ft/minute and could make it to 20,000 feet in only five minutes. Without the full coat of pain and with the reduced drag of the NACA design modification I can only image what its performance could be. In this case the P-38K would likely replace the F/P-82 Twin-Mustang of OTL and see continued service into the early 1950’s including limited combat in Korea as bomber-escorts and Close Air Support. So, any thoughts on this, its feasibility, and any effects I may have missed?" ----------------------- * http://www.ausairpower.net/P-38-Analysis.html (Pertinent section about 45% down in the italicized letter from Col. Harold J. Rau to “Commanding General, VIII Fighter Command, APO 637, U.S. Army”)[/QUOTE] Thank-you, I wasn't aware that this investigation into the P-38 compressibility problem had been conducted. It would have been a very productive and effective modification and I'm inclined to agree if the NACA mod had been developed earlier then it would have made it into production. After Pearl Harbor the pressure to produce what ever was available delayed OTL improvements to the P-38 like for example the high-activity propellers as you mentioned. I haven't finished reading the 1942 document yet so I have some questions for you. After the NACA mod had been developed the engineers still thought that dive recovery flaps would be required? Also with the relocation of the Prestone radiators and oil coolers to the new leading edge did the designers consider the Meredith effect when designing the new installation? Making the assumption they were aware of it at the time. The P-38's OTL canopy was one of its' poorer features. If they were redesigning the canopy contours could that also mean replacing it with a bubble type sliding canopy?

1) There is no explicit mention of the Dive Recovery Flaps in the NACA report, however the information about the airflow under the wing at different flap possitions is what ultimately led to their development so it is possible that they could have still been developed although they would have been by no means neccesary (assuming the NACA estimates are accurate). 2) I haven't read any specific refereces to it but it is possible they were aware of the Meredith effect. However, if memory serves, the radiator installations in the P-38 were not well suited or designed for it producing more drag than thrust. The NACA installation would likely also be poor canidatea for Meredith thrust so it is likely a dead end for the sake of this exploration. 3) Indeed the canopy was junk. While it never happened OTL I may explore better canopy options in the ATL. I think this is likely the direction I would go anyway. Some narrative, some ATL technical evaluation reports, maybe even some Encounter Reports when the shooting starts. Yeah, several of the British twin wing designs could be good but are beyond the scope of the PoD and this ATL. The issue with the dive flaps was that the first shipment in a C-54 was shot down by the British and they never bothered sending replacements. Then they didn't want to slow down production to integrate them into the line until all the planned blocks werw complete which meant they weren't factory installed until the P-38J-25 starting June 6, 1944...what a day! And yes, the treatment of the P-38 in the 8th AF was criminal because their disdain led directly to lost aircrew. Edit: sorry for all the typoes...I am on my phone instead computer at the moment.

As a lover of the P-38, a believer in its unrealized superior potential, a person saddened that it was not properly appreciated and thus its potential to escort early US bomber raids and save the lives of countless bomber crew members (not to mention recovering and reusing their OTL shot-down planes)--let me play a bit of Devil's Advocate here. I've seen some of the online wars between P-38 fans and their detractors, and come away more convinced by the former, especially after this most informative OP! But one simple point the naysayers have is clearly true...P-38 was a two-engine plane, while its eventual successor (if we assume the -38 were improved and permitted to do the escort mission) the P-51 was single engine. Thus Lightnings were inherently more costly than any single engine plane, good, bad or mediocre. If the choice was between an excellent two engine job and terrible to mediocre single engine, we just pay the higher price as part of the necessary cost of doing business with the best--except that in Jan 1942, the USAAF needed aircraft in numbers, and soon. If single engine alternatives existed that would be cost-effective, then clearly the Army would prefer that. I don't mean to mention this as some sort of trump card killing the -38's prospects, just as pointing out a factor that was relevant in decision making. The fact is I believe the P-38 was originally authorized under the impression it would be a superstar, just as the B-17 was hoped to be a super bomber the P-38 was to be the star fighter. But that was when war was hypothetical; once it started a panic for sheer numbers set in, and the question of whether one P-38 was worth 2 of another type--or less than 2, or more--was not transparent. One big advantage the P-38 offered, especially if it had indeed been modified to remove its worst drawbacks, and more appreciated hence ordered in more numbers, is that though it used twin engines, those engines were not Merlins! Not to say anything was wrong with Merlins, quite the contrary--though I do seem to recall some comparisons over ranges of altitude wherein the Allison engines, due to being turbosupercharged, had superior perfomance, while the Merlins had a mechanical supercharger. But the point here is, Merlins were good--but in severe demand therefore, so it was most excellent that the Lightning did not require them. I particularly like the way the twin engine layout leaves the central command nacelle to be loaded with heavy and reconfigurable arms.

TTL, it seems likely the dive-recovery spoiler (even assuming it takes OTL's duration to find the answer, which seems less probable; IMO, it'd be quicker TTL) would be on a different C-54, so not shot down. (Might be soon enough to get to production directly, in the *P-38E or -F TTL.) Other improvements? Turbos are hard, but without new materials, there's still reducing the rotating mass (drill the blades, so they look a bit like Swiss cheese), & (possibly) sizing issues (boost lag). Direct improvements to the aircraft itself? Cockpit heat is a must. Adding the wing leading-edge fuel tanks sooner would be good, but TTL, better fuel economy might butterfly them away... Flipside, tho: more P-38s means more headaches, with pilots who don't like twins & aren't trained in them correctly getting themselves in trouble. There was a myth going around England: if a P-38 lost an engine on takeoff, it'd kill you. It would--because the pilots weren't trained how to recover. Tony LeVier showed 'em: kill one engine, boot the rudder hard over against the dead one, crank on full power to the other & climb out to go around...

The 1944 Report clarifies some things I'd heard elsewhere. Thanks for that. All I have for the 1940-41 period is Dolittles commentary, but since he had worked some years as a aircraft engineer for a fuel manufactor his account has some small weight. The short version is through the 1930s commercially available gasoline fuels had a very low octane rating by post WWII standards. 65 Octane is the number I recall. Dolittle & his peers were trying to persuade the corporate suits to develop and market higher octane fuels, up into the 80 & possiblly 90 octane range. The refusal was based on the lack of market since the engine manufactors provided nothing that could use such fuels. To complete the circle the motors that could use high octane fuel were not built because the fuels were not being made. Dolittle did make clear that custom built engines were common for fuels in the 70 to 90 and higher octane ranges. Additives and custom fuel mixes were available in small batches to those who could pay. Dolittle like other knowledgeable pilots carried a witches brew of additives in his aircraft for boosting the commercial fuels of the aircraft he used. Later in 1940-41 Dolittle observed the same problem in plotting the development of the Army Air Corps engines beyond 41. At one point the head of the Quartermasters Corps informed the Air Corps that only 65 octane fuel would be provided across the board to simplify logisitcs. Fortunately the reorganization of early 1942 gave the Army Air force control of its own material supply & development went ahead.
items.original_question: What if NACA Modified P-38 What if NACA Modified P-38 fighter ------------------------------------------------------- Notice to Readers: This TL is still alive but only occasionally updated at this time (Summer 2021). Real life and the greatly expanded scope of detail required to continue advancing the TL at this point (including a fair share of original design and research) has kept me from more regular postings. But, Please, follow along and keep your eyes open for updates when they occur. I really value everyone's input and often the discussion around specific developments has been key to finalizing the next development. Cheers! E Jul. 2021 ------------------------------------------------------- (This was something I had planned to post after being on the board longer but a discussion in another thread prompted some discussion of P-38 development so I thought I would go ahead with this for the sake of discussion.) I know there have been several discussions over the years surrounding the Lockheed P-38 American Twin-Engine fighter/interceptor of WWII but one part of the equation that I have never heard discussed is the “What If…” the NACA recommended modifications to the airplane had been implemented, especially at or near the beginning of P-38 operations. OTL Background : Without re-hashing the origin and initial development history of the Lockheed Model 22 / P-38 (all of that information is readily available on numerous on-line sources) I will focus on what led to the NACA studies of the airframe, their proposed solution to the problems encountered, and why these solutions weren’t put in place. A record-breaking cross-country flight in early 1939 (which resulted in the loss of the only XP-38) garnered enough attention and excitement that the US Army Air Corp (USAAC) placed orders for pre-production (YP-38) and production (P-38) aircraft in numbers greater than Lockheed had anticipated for the entire Model 22 life. This necessitated a rushed production development and major reconfiguration to accommodate the unintended mass-production. Tests in early 1941 of the first pre-production YP-38’s quickly ran into issues when at high speed (around Mach 0.68), especially in dive, where the nose of the aircraft would drop--locking into an often un-recoverable dive accompanied by “buffeting.” The problems getting the production line up and fully operational prevented Lockheed from directing any engineering resources to these problems until November 1941, but they were unable to identify the cause or provide any solutions until Gen. Hap Arnold, head of the by then renamed Army Air Forces (USAAF), ordered the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA—predecessor of NASA) to analyze the YP-38 in their full-scale wind-tunnel in December 1941 – January 1942 which resulted in the report “ Full-Scale Wind-Tunnel Investigation of Buffeting and Diving Tendencies of the YP-38 Airplane .” [EDIT: NASA reorganized its online archives in 2020 so this link is no longer functioning. The upload size limitations on this site prevent me from dropping the file here, but you can find a copy I uploaded at another site, Here ] This report was finally able to identify that the control lock and diving difficulties were the result of a high-speed pressure wake developing over the wing and fuselage resulting is loss of lift to the central wing and buffeting of the tail as the turbulent wake passes over it, a phenomenon just recently discovered at the time which led the idea of the “sound barrier.” This is often referred to a “Compressibility” problem as it related the change of aerodynamics at high speed from a traditional non-compressible fluid to a compressible one. The specific behavior of the P-38 is now better known as “Mach Tuck.” NACA tested several solutions to the problem including wing filleting, partial flap deployment, three different inboard (between the engine booms and the center gondola) wing designs, two revised canopy designs, and an extension to the trailing edge of the gondola. They found the best performance gain (delay of up to 64 mph in the formation of the shock-wave) resulted from a simple 0.2c (20% of chord) leading edge extension to the center wing section and using their second canopy revision. They also noted that although the gondola extension did not increase the Critical Mach number, it did reduce the turbulence of the wake re-joining the airstream and smoothed out the air flow over the tail surfaces. One aspect which I find very interesting with these design modifications was that the extended leading edge moved the center of lift forward causing the plane to become unbalanced. They recommended moving the coolant radiators from the mid-boom into the extended leading edge of the wing to rebalance the aircraft with the added benefit of reducing drag and further streamlining the aircraft. I will address this again in the ATL discussion to follow. The problem is that the report wasn’t completed until March 31, 1942, by which time the US was at war and Lockheed was ramping up to start production on the combat-ready P-38F (beginning in April 1942) at war-time production rates. With the P-38 the most capable fighter then in inventory there simply was not the opportunity to re-design and re-tool for the modifications NACA recommended and the P-38 was sent into combat while still suffering numerous problems, not least of which was the issues with compressibility. The results are well known and documented: the P-38 in the ETO struggled the first 18 months of combat prompting 8th Fighter Command to pre-emptively phase them out in favor of the new P-51 as they became available at the end of 1943 and through the first half of 1944 which prevented Lockheed and the USAAF from implementing a number of fixes for the problems and delayed others until it was too late to have much impact in the reputation of the P-38 in Europe. It was not until the P-38J-25-LO and P-38L-5-LO/VN the airplane really came into its own and that was realized almost entirely in the Pacific. ATL Discussion : For this examination of a “What If…” I have decided to place the POD with the NACA study. Specifically, that Gen. Arnold did not wait for Lockheed to tackle the dive issues first and instead ordered the NACA study to take place in June-July of 1941 with the final report completed September 30, 1941 (six months earlier than OTL). This updated timeline would allow Lockheed engineers to immediately go to work implementing the NACA design changes in fall 1941 prior to US entry into the War and the corresponding production pressures which prevented it from happening in OTL. The first production P-38’s with the NACA modifications would then roll out either as late block P-38E’s in early ’42 or, more likely, as the finalized P-38F in April 1942. OTL, the P-38F/G/H continued to use the enclosed intercooler in the leading edge of the outboard wings, which provided adequate cooling for the early model engines and low-boost ratings but which, by the P-38G and even more so the P-38H, limited engine power to lower settings due to in-adequate cooling. This was a problem that was not anticipated so it wasn’t until the P-38J in August 1943 that the intercoolers were switched to the core-type, chin-mounted position—squeezed between and behind the oil radiators. However, in my ATL, with the oil radiators moved adjacent the coolant radiators in the leading edge extension the space in the chin of the nacelles is completely freed up which allows the core-type intercoolers to be installed in the space previously occupied by the oil radiators as soon as it becomes apparent it is needed without re-designing the nacelles themselves. This means that the engine power limitations of the G either never occurs (because the intercoolers have already been moved) or are quickly overcome by sending field modification kits in early 1943 with full integration on the assembly line taking place with the P-38H in the spring of 1943. Additionally, moving the intercoolers in these earlier models (G or H) would allow a matching earlier installation of the leading edge fuel tanks in the outer wings, increasing the range and combat radius in 1943 sufficient to provide full escort coverage to 8th AF Bombers even to deep penetration targets. Another advantage of moving the Prestone (engine coolant) radiators to the inboard position in the extended leading edge is that the heated coolant can be run through a heater core close to the cockpit cupola, increasing available cockpit heat as soon as it becomes apparent the existing heat is insufficient for high-altitude or cold weather operations. Again, this is something I expect would be utilized no later than early-mid 1943. One final advantage of this layout is that frees up a large amount of space in the tail booms which could be utilized in later production models. With engine weight increases in the F/G and again in the H/J models the Center of Gravity could potentially have been moved forward enough to justify installation of either additional small fuel tanks in the booms where the radiators used to be, or—perhaps a better option—small water/alcohol tanks which would permit the use the Water Injection under War Emergency Power, further increasing performances and reducing the risks of detonation under high manifold pressure (> 60 in/Hg). Even if pushing the ’51 to Mach 0.8 or beyond is considered acceptable these NACA estimates for the modified ’38 show a similar diving capability considering a margin for error of the conservative estimate, especially if using Dive Recovery Flaps in addition to the NACA modifications. In these cases the P-38 would be favorable because it can accelerate to max speed faster than the P-51 allowing to either pull-away faster or to gain faster on a diving E/A. Combine that with the faster climb of the P-38, higher peak turning rate, and—in later airplanes—faster roll, there would be nothing that the P-51 could do that the P-38 couldn’t do better. All while bringing a heavier weight of fire on target (128 oz/sec vs 111 oz/sec). I am not certain how much more quickly these would be introduced in ATL vs. OTL as the slow-roll performance wouldn’t be altered by the NACA modifications nor was its solution delayed or prevented by AF brass. So, let’s say that this modification is introduced as it was in OTL, i.e. June 1944. rubrics.question_focus: What If NACA had significantly improved the P-38 early in World War II?

criteria.name: Technical fidelity to the NACA-improved P-38 premise
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accurately reasons from the specific counterfactual: early NACA-driven fixes to the P-38's dive/compressibility behavior, cooling/reliability, cockpit heating, radiator/drag configuration, and related performance implications.
criteria.1-2: Misstates the premise or treats the P-38 as generically improved without identifying the relevant NACA-related fixes.
criteria.3-4: Mentions some P-38 improvements but confuses major technical issues or overstates effects without support.
criteria.5-6: Correctly covers the main fixes and gives plausible first-order effects on speed, reliability, altitude use, or pilot comfort.
criteria.7-8: Connects specific modifications to concrete performance changes while noting remaining issues such as controls, roll rate, or dive flaps.
criteria.9-10: Provides a technically grounded, nuanced account of the NACA changes, their limits, likely production incorporation, and interaction with later P-38 variants.

criteria.name: Operational and tactical causal chain in the European air war
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer traces effects from an improved early P-38 to 8th Air Force escort operations, bomber losses, fighter group retention, pilot training, Luftwaffe attrition, and escort doctrine.
criteria.1-2: Jumps directly to broad war outcomes with little or no operational reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Gives a simple claim such as 'better escorts reduce losses' without explaining timing, units, tactics, or opposition.
criteria.5-6: Explains plausible changes to bomber escort capability and loss rates, with some attention to 1943-44 conditions.
criteria.7-8: Builds a coherent chain involving P-38 deployment, high-altitude reliability, training, fighter mix, and Luftwaffe responses.
criteria.9-10: Integrates aircraft performance, 8th AF decisions, escort range, combat tactics, attrition dynamics, and timing into a convincing operational counterfactual.

criteria.name: Industrial, logistical, and procurement constraints
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accounts for wartime production pressures, Lockheed capacity, Allison engine supply, Merlin/P-51 competition, cost of twin-engine fighters, retrofit versus production-line changes, and USAAF procurement behavior.
criteria.1-2: Ignores production and procurement constraints or assumes unlimited rapid adoption.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges constraints vaguely but does not apply them to the P-38, P-51, or USAAF choices.
criteria.5-6: Discusses key constraints such as twin-engine cost, production disruption, or competing fighter programs.
criteria.7-8: Balances improved P-38 attractiveness against realistic factory, engine, logistics, and training limitations.
criteria.9-10: Shows detailed causal reasoning about how procurement, production blocks, spare parts, engines, and opportunity costs would shape the alternate fighter force.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream effects and proportionality
criteria.criteria_description: Measures whether the answer plausibly extends the counterfactual beyond immediate performance, including bomber campaign tempo, P-51 demand, Normandy timing, postwar reputation, P-38K or F-82 implications, and possible Korean War service, without exaggeration.
criteria.1-2: Presents implausible sweeping outcomes such as decisively changing the war with no chain of support.
criteria.3-4: Mentions downstream effects but treats them as automatic or disconnected from earlier mechanisms.
criteria.5-6: Identifies several plausible downstream consequences while keeping war-outcome claims moderate.
criteria.7-8: Explores second- and third-order effects with appropriate caveats about logistics, strategy, and competing bottlenecks.

The P-38 initially suffered from compressibility issues during high-speed dives, which caused loss of control and structural stress. NACA’s wind tunnel research and aerodynamic expertise could have led to earlier implementation of fixes such as dive flaps or refined wing and tail designs, mitigating these problems sooner.

This would have allowed the P-38 to fulfill its potential as a long-range, high-altitude escort fighter and interceptor more effectively during critical early war campaigns, such as in the Pacific and over Europe. Earlier reliability and superior performance might have increased Allied air superiority in 1942–1943, potentially accelerating strategic bombing effectiveness and reducing bomber losses. It could also have influenced tactical decisions, such as delaying or altering the development priorities of other fighters like the P-51 Mustang. Overall, an earlier-optimized P-38 could have shifted air combat dynamics in favor of the Allies during a pivotal phase of the war.

items.question: What If The Enterprise completes its five year mission (Star Trek survives for 5 seasons)
human_answers: The problem with keeping "TOS" on the air is its consistently poor ratings. In third season, it never got out of the bottom 50 (&, IIRC, was #52 when cancelled). NBC recognizing the better demos early enough might save it in spite of that, much the same way golf gets broadcast despite poor numbers: it attracts a desirable audience. They had two great opportunities to set up a continuing villain, undermined (I suspect) by inability to cast the same actor each time: "Tribbles" & "Day of the Dove". It would have taken more forethought about what Klingons would be like to achieve it, but I'd have loved "DotD" to end with Kirk saying, "Die well, Kang.", & a surprised Kang to say, "Die well, Kirk."--in essence, to be forced to acknowledge UFP as peers. (I know, I know, they didn't even have the concept for the bat'leth , yet...) Depressingly, the writing would have to get a lot better. Even if you take out "Spock's Brain", you've already been saddled with "Errand of Mercy" (the Organian Treaty) in S.1 & "Omega Glory" in S.2. About half of S.3 is pretty awful. Even Dorothy's "Enterprise Incident" has a major flaw, one that would recur for the rest of the franchise: doesn't Starfleet Intelligence have it's own f*ng operatives? You've also got two big issues: personality conflict between Shat's ego & just about everybody, & Leonard being really sick of playing Spock. That said, I'll be watching to see how you save the show, & what butterflies that has down the road.

NBC CONDUCTS STUDY ON TREK: NIELSEN RATINGS NOT FULLY ACCURATE? NBC is unsure of how to handle Star Trek, the big hit with younger American television viewers but a ratings laggard with the general public. The network conducted a study to determine exactly what it has with the science fiction series and its findings were surprising. They determined that younger Americans often watched Star Trek in groups, and it was one of the most popular shows among the age 20-30 and age 30-40 brackets. They also determined that Captain Kirk, Mr. Spock, and the rest of the characters were extremely popular with young kids, who often wanted to stay up past their bedtimes on Friday night to see where they and the Enterprise would go next. However, NBC found a significant decline in popularity among viewers older than 50. Due to this wide age disparity, NBC is mulling over whether they will place Star Trek on Mondays in The Man From U.N.C.L.E.'s old time slot at 8 PM; U.N.C.L.E. was pulled in January and is unlikely to return to television. The Monday 8 PM time slot is often popular with younger audiences, but comes with great competition as is well known in the industry. NBC contacted Gene Roddenberry, the show's creator, Herb Solow, the showrunner at Paramount, who recently acquired Desilu Studios, and Robert Justman, one of the show's producers, for a planning session to widen the show's popularity for a general audience. Roddenberry objected to NBC's proposal to make Star Trek a show with a more pragmatic, less optimistic future. He also objected to the idea that the show had to appeal to older audiences, arguing that the strength of the show was rooted in the creative storytelling that attracted younger adults and children. Solow and Justman also disagreed to an extent but determined that parts of the show had to be remodeled in order to make it a wider hit. Ideas for the third season were pitched to the network; one was rumored to involve Mr. Spock's brain being removed from his body, while another was rumored to have the Enterprise enter Romulan space unprovoked in order to spy on them, a major diversion from the normal behavior of the Enterprise crew.
items.original_question: What if The Enterprise completes its five year mission (Star Trek survives for 5 seasons) One of the worst decisions ever made by a television network was NBC's cancellation of Star Trek (the Original Series) after its third season in 1969. After two years of middling ratings placed Star Trek in the Friday Night death time slot, at 10:00 PM, so fewer fans would be able to watch the series. In our timeline, NBC killed off Star Trek, but it went to syndication where it became more popular than ever in the 1970s. NBC knew of the depth of Star Trek fandom but had no idea how deep it ran until they no longer made the show. So here we go...the divergence point. NBC REEVALUATING ITS PRIMETIME LINEUP March 1, 1968 NBC, having finished a distant second in the ratings battle with CBS, was forced to reevaluate its primetime lineup to see where they could find potential strength for the fall 1968 television season. Two shows which faced the chopping block this season were The Man From U.N.C.L.E., on Mondays from 8:00 to 9:00 PM, and Star Trek, on Fridays from 8:30 PM to 9:30 PM. The Man From U.N.C.L.E faced a lot of turbulence when showrunners decided to turn the spy show into a comedy. Its ratings, formerly very competitive with CBS, dropped dramatically in the 1967-68 season; NBC is pondering what direction the show can turn to next. Star Trek was rumored to be cancelled because it rated poorly with an audience of older Americans, but its largely young fanbase swarmed NBC with tens of thousands of letters demanding its renewal. NBC is undecided at this point about U.N.C.L.E.'s fate but is bringing Star Trek back for a third season. However, the suits at the Peacock Network are uncertain about which timeslot to place Star Trek in. Could it replace U.N.C.L.E. on Monday or will NBC try to move it later to Friday night, where its chances of survival are slim?

First, the expanded runtime would allow for deeper character development, more nuanced exploration of the Federation’s ideals, and richer world-building across the Star Trek universe. Episodes could delve further into political, philosophical, and social themes with greater continuity, potentially influencing 1970s science fiction television more profoundly. Additionally, the franchise might not have needed to rely on animated series or films to sustain its presence; instead, it could have evolved directly into sequels or spin-offs from a stronger network foothold. This continuity might accelerate the creation of *The Next Generation*-style successors or alter the trajectory of later Star Trek series, possibly resulting in a more cohesive canon earlier on. Ultimately, completing the five-year mission on-screen would reinforce the show’s core message—that exploration, diplomacy, and optimism can prevail—and cement its legacy even more firmly in popular culture during its original broadcast era.

items.question: What If Complicate the US Civil War
human_answers: No Free State even tried to secede, and 4 Slave States stayed in the Union. The Constitution conceives of no right of secession. The only theoretical way the Union can be dissolved is in a Convention of the States. Kentucky is the only State I can think of that might have decided to join the CSA. If the Union Army had invaded Kentucky at the onset of civil war she might have gone South. Most of the States population lived in or near the Ohio Valley and although Southern in culture they were economically tied more with the States north of the river. Kentucky was not so dependent on Slavery as to be willing to fight for it. Geography forced NC to join the CSA, and Delaware to stay in the USA. No Free State had any realistic chance or convincing reason to leave the Union. The economic, cultural, and political pull of the Union was too strong for the Free States to break away. The Free States held the majority of the population, industry, rail links, shipping, national finance, food production, international commerce, and sources of gold & silver. These factors are the ones that are usually discussed in assessing why the Union won the war and they are also the reasons the Union held together. There must be a compelling reason to break away from the center of national power. Slavery was the economic and emotional issue that could do it. No Free State had so strong a grievance to secede. Virginia was a State that stood on a knifes edge till Fort Sumpter forced the issue. If the Old Dominion stayed with the Union North Carolian might've stayed in to. In that scenario the ACW would last 2 years with half the death toll. However, this is really unlikely because Virginia was simply unwilling to fight against the rest of the South. The positions of the States were pretty fixed and only a much earlier POD would be needed to change the lineup of States.

This the top paragraph of my comment of that video: The 1792 Presidential Succession Act was for if BOTH the President and Vice President died or were unavailable to serve during their terms of office. Under a scenario in which President-Elect Lincoln is assassinated, then on March 4 Hannibal Hamblin takes the oath of office as Vice President then immediately takes the oath of office for President. Cody forgot that John Tyler was the first Vice President to become President, the second was Millard Fillmore in 1850 when Zachary Taylor died. So there were two examples of Vice Presidents becoming President before Lincoln's assassination (whenever it happens). And in case anyone wants to bring up the Electoral College, it was certified on February 13 so if Lincoln is shot February 23 which I assume the POD takes place on then Hamblin becomes President. So Cody's badly researched scenario for outgoing Vice President Breckinridge (who is NOT the President Pro Tempore) becoming President then getting kicked out for Seward is complete garbage.
items.original_question:
AHC: Complicate the US Civil War

Some time ago, somewhere, I stumbled upon some talk about the US Civil War - and of course, the good ol' debate what it was all about appeared - states rights, whatnot; but then, a single person rugged the whole debate with an argument that went something along these lines: The American Civil War was about states' rights, but not their rights to slavery - instead, it was about the states' rights to secede. This I found to be, pretty much, the final word on that whole argument - sure, slavery was the cause of the Civil War - but in the same manner tensions between Great Powers were the cause of WW1. Whereas the World War was triggered by the assassination of Franz Ferdinand, essentially making the war about it in the first place - the Civil War wasn't started by slavery merely existing or not existing, but instead by the Southern states seceding, making the entire war about secession in the first place. This also tracks with the fact that several states only seceded after the start of the war (such as Arkansas), after President Lincoln ordered all states to mobilize troops. Now, with that in mind, I have a challenge for the esteemed posters of this venerable Forum: without changing the cause, nor the trigger for the war (it has to be over slavery, and it must be triggered by secession), complicate the sides of the war. For example, a free state siding with the Confederacy counts as a complication, and so does a slave state siding with the Union. Note that the latter already happened, in the form of Delaware and Maryland - now let's be clear, I'm not talking about this being a "make Maryland secede" challenge: the weirder the pick, the better - I'm talking Confederate Michigan and Union Mississippi tier. You may, however, shift when the war occurs. Good luck, and happy imagining!

items.model_answer: If the U.S. Civil War had been further complicated—by factors such as foreign intervention, internal divisions within the Union or Confederacy, or prolonged guerrilla warfare—it likely would have lasted longer, caused even greater loss of life, and potentially resulted in a fragmented North American political landscape. For example, if Britain or France had formally recognized or militarily supported the Confederacy, the Union might have faced a protracted two-front conflict or been forced into a negotiated settlement that preserved some form of Southern independence. Alternatively, deeper internal dissent—such as widespread Northern opposition to the war or successful secessionist movements in border states—could have undermined the Union’s ability to sustain its war effort. Such complications might have delayed or prevented national reunification, altered the trajectory of emancipation, and reshaped the development of American democracy and federal authority.

items.question: What If Break the British-Russian Alliance
human_answers: A some things that could happen.: During the Russo-Japanese War you have: - the 2nd Pacific Sqn hit something with their guns in British waters - When they do get to Pacific the French assist them and they do a bit better - Russia as they did a bit better demand more and more from Japan - Japan moves closer to the UK sphere as they feel like both Russia and France is ganging up on them - Russia demands that UK to not get involved - the Royal Navy parks some ships just outside Port Arthur for "training" - Japanese diplomats don't make crazy demands and sour some of the Anglo-Japanese relationship. In Germany - The Kaiser see that they will not be able to out build the Royal Navy but sees that France and Russia are what they need to prepare for - The German navy decides that they need a pile of fast cruisers to protect any overseas holdings that they have and leaves the battleship race - As people suggested Kaiser Wilhelm II does not have a disability In the Middle East and Asia - Russia and Britain have even greater cold war on Persian control - Russia is found to be assisting the start of Indian independence groups (not 100% sure on time line with that ) - Russia is seen to be making demands on China and trade I am sure there are more PoD but this just popped in my head

Three major factors were at play in the Russo-British diplomatic relations at the turn of the century. 1. Generational change at the Foreign Office, with the rise of more eurocentric and anti-German key decisionmakers. 2. The failed French attempts to form an anti-British coalition during Second Boer War. This more or less forced Britain to come to terms with France, or accept the fact that von Holstein had been right, and that by merely waiting Germany could indeed ultimately dictate terms for her new treaties with Britain. 3. The Eastern Question and the Boxer war were drawing new powers in to the old Great Game in Asia, and Britain had to react to the rising power of Japan and their genuine attempts to strike a bargain with expansionist Russia that had just occupied northern Manchuria and was viewing the Korean peninsula as the logical next target. Combined with the determined naval buildup of Franco-Russian alliance and Germany, the international status quo of the late 1800s was becoming untenable. While France was fumbling, her governments were also pouring in vast amounts of money and building a naval force explicitly tailored to counter the Royal Navy. Russian naval buildup also seemed most formidable on paper before the Russo-Japanese war, and first and foremost her land armies seemed poised to sweep to northern India at any moment in the prewar fears of the Committee of Imperial Defence. Lansdowne tried to sort out this challenge out by solving all outstanding imperial disputes on a case-by-case basis, which led him to support both the Anglo-Japanese alliance and reconciliation with France. And after that, only Russia and Germany were left - and Russia seemed so weak after 1905 that Britain sought to strike a bargain with Nicholas II not out of fear of Russian power, but because it seemed like a real risk that humiliated Russia would reapproach Germany instead! Because of these decisions Sir Edward Grey inherited a much more fixed diplomatic board. He, in turn, fatally fumbled it all by trying to build a new balancing act to maintain some sort of strategic ambiguity, when pre-existing treaties and commitments meant that the only way to deter German expansionism and a new major war was through clear and determined military posture. But then again, such a commitment to building a large land army was outside of the realm of political possibilities in the pre-1914 British politics of the day. So, you'll need a really early POD, or alternatively a WW1-analogy has to be delayed long enough.

There are a multitude of butterflies that could prevent the July Crisis. The plan to assassinate Franz Ferdinand could have failed to materialize in the first place, it seems like at one point it was called off and then put back on. Maybe the "back on" message gets lost or delayed and it doesn't go forward, and Franz goes to Bosnia unimpeded. There would still be Black Hand terrorism against higher ranking members of the AH government, as their had been prior to the assassination IOTL, but it wouldn't be big enough to cause a July Crisis equivalent. Here's what I'm thinking: In 1915, Russia sours British opinion by demanding much, much more influence in Persia and makes it obvious that they want some sort of naval access in the Persian Gulf, but they aren't explicit about it and it's not part of the renegotiated treaty. It's enough to sour British opinion, but not make them rethink relations altogether. However, things get worse when Greece and the Ottomans escalate tensions over the Aegean islands (this was thought to be the realistic catalyst for a European conflict prior to the July Crisis) and Russia gives full throated support to Greece and observers know that Russia is clearly eyeing to firmly control the Dardanelles either directly or through a proxy like Greece or Bulgaria. Keeping the Ottomans around wasn't a key part of British policy, but the possibility of total Russian dominance in the Middle East is too much for Britain to bare. Finally, AH + Germany clearly favor the Ottomans right in time for the Home Rule Crisis to get even worse, forcing the British to keep more soldiers home. So here we have a Britain that's tied up at home and frazzled abroad. IOTL it was the Ottomans that declared war on Russia, which brought in France and Britain. But here, it's Russia declaring war on the Ottomans, meaning that Britain (and France) don't have a clear entry into this aggressive war.
items.original_question:
AHC: Break the British-Russian Alliance

Hello all. I've been reading up a lot on the buildup to WW1, and one of the more interesting aspects I found was the frayed relations between Russia and Britain. It seems like they were on another sort of collision course over Persia as their agreement over spheres of influence was up for renegotiation in 1915, and Russia was in a much better position to negotiate terms than it was in the aftermath of the Russo-Japanese War. Your challenge is to create a plausible scenario where Russia and Britain can no longer even pretend to be allies. For me, I think an overzealous Russia that asks for too much in 1915 Persia talks could torpedo the alliance, but Russian overreach with regards to the Straits of Constantinople could be another pain point for Britain. A scenario where Britain can't bring itself to support Russia, and Britain itself finds itself completely embroiled in the Home Rule Crisis, would make a very interesting TL.

items.model_answer:
There was no formal, enduring British–Russian alliance to “break” in the way the question implies. While Britain and Russia were allies during specific conflicts—most notably as part of the Grand Alliance against Napoleon (1805–1814) and later as co-belligerents in World War I (1914–1917)—they were more often rivals, especially during the 19th-century “Great Game” over Central Asia.  

If one imagines a counterfactual in which Britain and Russia failed to cooperate during World War I—say, if their 1907 Anglo-Russian Entente had never been formed—the consequences would have been significant. Without that agreement resolving colonial disputes in Persia, Afghanistan, and Tibet, mutual suspicion might have persisted, potentially keeping Russia isolated or pushing it toward other powers. Britain might have faced greater strategic uncertainty on its imperial frontiers, and the Triple Entente (Britain, France, Russia) might not have solidified, altering the balance of power before 1914. Germany could have exploited this disunity, possibly deterring Russian mobilization or encouraging earlier aggression. The war’s outbreak, scope, or outcome might thus have differed substantially.

human_answers: The Netherands was one of the first nations to declare full mobilisation. This resulted that the Dutch army was fully mobilized and on their positions. The field army, the mobile part, was for 1914 conditions, modern. The other half of the army, the older echelons, manned the forts. The chalange in August was to delay the Germans so the waterline inundations could be set. Considering the beautiful summer of 1914, resulting in low water levels of the rivers, this could be a chalange. The Germans probaly would use 3rd or 4rd welle, erzats units for attacking mid and north netherlands, same training level or below as the Dutch coscript soldiers. If troop movements will take place at the same time as the main attack south? Only 1st and 2nd welle of the 1st Army will cross Limburg and Brabant, which is in the path of advance for the main objective, Paris, France

Evacuation is an option. OTL the English evacuated all the children from London and other cities facing Blitz bombing to the countryside; the RN can well secure the crossing to England for a pretty large number of Dutch noncombatants who aren't deemed more useful staying in the bastion to sustain what production is possible in the circumstances. The only thing the Germans can do to interfere would be to attempt to place their U-boats to interdict, but I believe the subs would be terribly vulnerable to the most elementary ASW methods the RN is inventing on the fly in those narrow waters with their limited channels of access north and south. If this eventually amounts to evacuating half the population or more, it might be a problem to have that many refugees in Britain itself--but from there, there are more options for farther relocation. As far as moving people who otherwise would pose too much a logistic burden without being useful to the war economy even in Britain, Canada is not too far on; during WWII that is where German and other Axis POWs wound up being sent until the USA entered and more of them went to American camps where they generally were employed as farm labor. Free allies of the Commonwealth will be welcome enough, plus the Dutch have their own colonies as well. The Netherlands being all in as Entente allies pretty much from the get-go is bad news for Germany too as others noted. To add to such basic concerns as the Germans losing their major back door to try to circumvent the blockade OTL, not to mention losing such resources as the Fokker airplane works, I suppose the DEI forces, such as they are, will move immediately to attack nearby German colonies in their region, which means first of all German New Guinea; in the ATL Japan will acquire fewer of the German Pacific possessions as the Dutch will be taking some of them instead. Short run, the Entente will have little trouble rushing in food and other vital supplies, longer run they sort out the population in the bastion to maximize their effectiveness in holding and pushing back their siege while evacuating people less useful there, many of whom will be useful elsewhere such as in British war industries. None of them need be left to starve! Meanwhile the Entente has an excellent complex of ports and the Germans have another front to worry about. It is pretty obvious why the Germans had the wit not to open this door OTL, and if it was only a matter of chance they avoided it--well that was a lucky chance indeed. It seems pretty clear to me they just knew better and would avoid doing this unless handed an industrial strength Idiot Ball with a lead paint chaser.

Hmmm, I am curious as to if the Dutch are given a mandate over any bit of New Guinea at the end of this war. Maybe it is like with the French and British giving up claims of land in Egypt to Italy, with French and British Guiana having their borders changed in the interior in favor of Dutch claims? The British are going to be unable to get the Japanese to give up anything they get, and they believed IOTL that taking away areas from the Dominions to give back to the Germans would poison relations with them, and that they would need to find land elsewhere to pay off the Germans, if needed for a peace. The land wasn't exactly the most valuable anyways. The Dutch are unlikely to want colonies that are too out of the way of Indonesia that would make e them split their manpower in the future. Getting some land from Germany in Europe would be ideal, though the Germans had already Germanized the area a lot. How brutal the invasion is will have an effect.

items.original_question: What if Netherlands being invaded in WW1 Suppose the Netherlands is invaded in WW1, does the Netherlands stand a chance of withstanding such an attack? Most likely, the Dutch army will retreat behind the New Dutch Waterline ( Nieuwe Hollandse Waterlinie ). The fortresses are already obsolete, AFAIK. However, the inundation zones may still be an impassable obstacle.... Most obvious POD is that Molkte decides against a coup de main on Liege, but instead decides to bypass Liege to the north. This is consistent with Schlieffen's original "Schlieffen plan". The German army moves roughly between Maastricht and Roermond on its way to northern France.... Assuming that France is not defeated in this ATL either, will attention shift north? Will Germany want to occupy all of the Netherlands? Will the waterline hold? What does it mean for Germany's chances in WW1? It is also fine to discuss other POD's in which the Netherlands is invaded. The Dutch defenses are shown on this map I made:

items.model_answer:
If the Netherlands had been invaded during World War I, it would have significantly altered the course and dynamics of the conflict. In reality, the Netherlands maintained armed neutrality throughout the war, avoiding invasion by carefully balancing diplomatic relations with both the Allies and the Central Powers and maintaining a credible defensive posture.

Had Germany invaded the Netherlands—perhaps as part of an expanded Schlieffen Plan or to secure additional supply routes—it would likely have occurred early in the war, around 1914. Such an invasion would have violated Dutch neutrality, much like the German invasion of Belgium, and could have drawn stronger condemnation from neutral powers, potentially accelerating or altering U.S. involvement. The Netherlands’ strategic location, access to North Sea ports, and developed infrastructure would have offered Germany logistical advantages but at the cost of further international isolation.

Conversely, if the Allies had invaded (a far less likely scenario), it might have been to open a new front or disrupt German supply lines, but this would have risked alienating other neutral nations and stretched Allied resources thin.

Domestically, a Dutch invasion would have ended the country’s neutrality, likely triggering mass mobilization, economic disruption, and humanitarian crises. Post-war, the Netherlands might have emerged as a belligerent rather than a neutral host to exiled royals and refugees, possibly gaining a seat at the Versailles negotiations and altering its interwar foreign policy trajectory. Overall, an invasion would have intensified the war’s geographic scope and political complexity, with ripple effects on diplomacy, wartime economies, and postwar settlements.

edus.text: If the Netherlands had been invaded during World War I,
it would have significantly altered the course and dynamics of the conflict.
In reality, the Netherlands maintained armed neutrality throughout the war,
avoiding invasion by carefully balancing diplomatic relations with both the Allies and the Central Powers
and maintaining a credible defensive posture.
Had Germany invaded the Netherlands—perhaps as part of an expanded Schlieffen Plan or to secure additional supply routes—
it would likely have occurred early in the war, around 1914.
Such an invasion would have violated Dutch neutrality,
much like the German invasion of Belgium,
and could have drawn stronger condemnation from neutral powers,
potentially accelerating or altering U.S. involvement.
The Netherlands’ strategic location, access to North Sea ports, and developed infrastructure would have offered Germany logistical advantages
but at the cost of further international isolation.
Conversely, if the Allies had invaded (a far less likely scenario),
it might have been to open a new front or disrupt German supply lines,
but this would have risked alienating other neutral nations
and stretched Allied resources thin.
Domestically, a Dutch invasion would have ended the country’s neutrality,
likely triggering mass mobilization, economic disruption, and humanitarian crises.
Post-war, the Netherlands might have emerged as a belligerent rather than a neutral host to exiled royals and refugees,
possibly gaining a seat at the Versailles negotiations
and altering its interwar foreign policy trajectory.
Overall, an invasion would have intensified the war’s geographic scope and political complexity,
with ripple effects on diplomacy, wartime economies, and postwar settlements.
