items.question: What If the Haber process is never invented?
human_answers: there are very very very few inventions that are so dependent on one person or group or situation that they wont get invented without them. Frankly i am not sure i can think of any. Yes it may get delayed but never invented? seams doubtful Now this isn't my area of expertise but. Usually when it is time to railroad you can pretty much count n somene inventing and building a railroad. This is why we often get similar inventions in multiple locations. Even back in the day a lot of inventions that get credited to one country and that other counties then “stole them” probably had more then a few cases of contry B finally get to the same level of knowledge in that area and this leads to someone figuring it out. The differencecis that as we get to more modern times the knowledges of 1st world countries gets closer and closer and spreads thoughout . This is why things like nuclear science, jet engines and radar were all “sort of” being looked at in multiple countries with a relatively short time span. So unless there are some very unusual circumstances odds are someone will eventually figure it out.

Luigi Casale develops the Casale process after WWI. Italy had a deficit of fertilizers pre-war; it didn't have the trade networks or finances of other nations to purchase Chilean saltpeter in large amounts, and they invested heavily in nitrogen fixation as a result. WWI worsened that deficit, compounded by the loss of wheat imports from Russia, so Casale started work in 1917 on a more efficient method of nitrogen fixation. Said research continued in the postwar, because BASF refused to license the Haber-Bosch process elsewhere, and the Haber-Bosch process would have required modification anyways because Italy didn't have sufficient coal to use it to produce hydrogen gas in the original Haber-Bosch process. So Italy has the incentive to develop efficient nitrogen fixation processes for strategic autonomy, and Casale has the means to do so. Casale did postgraduate research in Berlin under Walter Nernst, whose research into physical chemistry mirrored that of Haber's, before returning to Italy. Casale then works near the Terni steelworks, which provided the steel to build pressure reactors able to stand pressures more than 3 times that of the Haber-Bosch process (notably by providing an unused battleship gun barrel). Even if we assume some sort of inexplicable theft or espionage on the part of Casale not mentioned in these histories and somehow nobody else thinks to apply Le Chatelier's Principle or try different catalysts, that just means the Frank-Caro process dominates. Sure, the 3x difference in energy usage is going to be difficult to bear, but between that and losing a total war/starving, people will just build more power plants and mine more fossil fuels or mineral nitrates/phosphates. Sources: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0920586121004831 (might be paywalled) https://riviste.fupress.net/index.php/subs/article/download/2809/2057/21510 The Social Side of a Scientific Breakthrough: Fritz Haber, Walther Nernst, and the Discovery of Ammonia Synthesis 1830–1930 | MPIWG Ammonia synthesis. Central to the mass production of fertilizer and explosives. It has been billed as the most consequential scientific breakthrough of the twentieth century. Arguably the only hard bit of the Haber process is the need for pressurisation to encourage the reaction to react in the right direction. The rest is more or less basic chemistry. So initially the other less efficient methods get adopted (because the nitrates are useful and profitable) and when suitable pressure vessels become available someone discovers the alt-Haber process. Unlike OTL, there will be more opportunity to refine and improve the other less efficient methods of manufacture. Pressure vessels themselves are relatively easy once you have late 19th century naval guns to adapt or inspire: durable pressure vessels are a bit harder [1], but any ferrous vessel will tend to provide iron catalyst even if nobody thought of using it beforehand. So in short, it's just delayed a few years - maybe up to a decade - and meanwhile other less efficient processes get used more than OTL. [1] As of about 20 years ago, the detailed mechanism of metal corrosion in high temperature reducing environments was still poorly understood and under investigation.

items.model_answer: If the Haber process had never been invented, the large-scale synthesis of ammonia from atmospheric nitrogen and hydrogen would not have become feasible in the early 20th century. This would have severely limited the production of synthetic nitrogen fertilizers, which are essential for modern intensive agriculture. As a result, global food production would have remained constrained by natural sources of fixed nitrogen—such as manure, guano, and nitrate deposits—leading to significantly lower crop yields. The world’s population, which grew dramatically in the 20th century partly due to increased agricultural output enabled by synthetic fertilizers, would likely have remained much smaller, possibly capped at around 2–3 billion people instead of exceeding 8 billion today. Additionally, without the Haber process, Germany’s ability to produce explosives during World War I would have been compromised, potentially altering the course and duration of the war. Overall, the absence of the Haber process would have profoundly reshaped demographic, geopolitical, and environmental trajectories of the modern era.

items.question: What If one people, two nation-states
human_answers: Italy would be easy to do, even with a recent-ish POD: there were proposals floating around in the mid-19th century, concerning Victor Emmanuel II crowning himself king of the Two Sicilies rather than annexing the place outright, while keeping the local government around; since Cavour himself was hesitant to annex the South, and only did so because Garibaldi was becoming too much of a loose cannon, if things had gone slightly differently, this could've happened, and since the South had its own distinct identity and history (even though it used Tuscan as its own official language, as every other state in the peninsula did), this could've stuck, with northern and southern Italy becoming kind of like Australia and New Zealand, independent countries closely tied to each other and under the same monarch. Ironically, the Third War of Independence could've gone better for northern Italy, since northern and southern troops couldn't integrate well IRL, and Italy could've gained Trento and Trieste before World War I, butterflying away the need for intervention; the Two Sicilies could have eventually gained a protectorate of sorts over Albania (history would rhyme there, since Skanderbeg had ties to the Neapolitan royals of his era and fled to Naples when his anti-Turkish uprising failed) and would've surely annexed the Papal enclaves once the north annexes Rome. Garibaldi's OTL expedition to Trento might instead take place in Pola or even Fiume but, as I stated earlier, northern Italy could be more willing to just accept territorial bribes from Austria here, since most of the Irredenta would've been gained already.

Faroese should linguistic be seen as a dialect of Western Norwegian. You could pretty much write Faroese with Nynorsk (the written standard the dialects in this region use) and vice versa. Where Faroese differ from Icelandic is that like Norwegian it have seen near complete replacement of vocabulary with Danish vocabulary thanks to the use of Danish Bibles, while on Iceland the Bible was translated into Icelandic early on and the Danish state supported the existence of a distinct Icelandic language for ideological reasons.. The main reason why Danes and Norwegians have trouble reading Faroese is because it use a it own variation of the Latin alphabet which is different from the one Danes and Norwegians use, while even if Icelandic was written using Danish or the different Norwegian written standards, it would be hard to understand it because of the difference in vocabulary. If the Danish-Norwegian Union had survived the Faroese Island would simply have been seen as part of Western Norway.

If the Prussians had done a better job containing the Great Northern War plague, then there might have been far more Prussian Lithuanians, who differ from Lithuanians in that they are Lutheran, strongly influenced by German culture, and speak a Germanized register of Lithuanian. While they kept the Lithuanian language alive during the Russian repression, the Prussian Lithuanians actually opposed Lithuaniation nationalism and explicitly refused to live in an independent Lithuanian state, accepting nothing else than German rule. Thus, when the Memel Territory was established, the Prussian Lithuanians declared themselves to be "Memellanders". Subsequently, after WW2, the Soviets saw them as Germans and expelled them from East Prussia. IOTL, the GNW plague absolutely decimated the Prussian Lithuanians, who comprised nearly 90% of its victims. Had it been contained effectively, and a butterfly net used afterwards, there would've been far more Prussian Lithuanians in East Prussia, perhaps enough to cause a national awakening. The Soviets likely would've propped up "Prussia" as a separate SSR from Lithuania while still expelling the Germans, and supported Prussian Lithuanian nationalism to divide and conquer (having just annexed resistive Lithuania). Basically Moldovenism, though in this case with genuine religious and cultural differences (plus a very different standard language).
items.original_question:
AHC: one people, two nation-states

There have been plenty of cases where one people with a common language and ancestry are separated into two nation-states. I'm not talking about ideological reasons like in the case of Germany and Korea, but in terms of centuries-long division of religion (Catholic Croats and Orthodox Serbs or Catholic Austrians and Protestant Germans) or geopolitics (Montenegro and Ottoman-dominated Serbia, Russia-dominated Moldova and Romania, Bulgaria and North Macedonia). And this explains why I specifically use the term "nation-state", as one people separated for long enough by the aforementioned factors would eventually evolve into different nation-states with their own ethnic identities. Is there any other scenario where this can happen?

items.model_answer: The phrase “one people, two nation-states” describes a situation where a single ethnic, cultural, or linguistic group is divided between two separate sovereign states. A prominent historical example is the division of Korea into North and South Korea after World War II. Despite sharing a common language, history, and ethnic identity, Koreans have lived under two distinct political systems—communist in the North and democratic-capitalist in the South—leading to divergent national identities over time. Similarly, the partition of Germany into East and West during the Cold War reflected a single German people split by ideology and geopolitics, though reunification later resolved that division. Such scenarios often arise from external intervention, ideological conflict, or geopolitical realignment rather than internal demands for separation, and they can foster complex dynamics of kin-state relations, diaspora politics, and contested sovereignty.

items.question: What If Reverse Cuba and the Philippines
human_answers: American interest in Cuban had been more or less secured after the Span-Am War, so it'll be difficult for them to justify annexation, which could earn the ire of the Cuban independentists and the Southern States. But the Philippines presented some once in a lifetime opportunity for the US to finally gain their own foothold in the China market, instead of lurking around ports under the jurisdiction of other great powers. In a relatively practical POV, the US didn't need to annex the whole islands. Why waste men and money against the people that's prepared to fight to the last man to preserve their freedom (some historians even claimed that the Fil-Am War was the US first taste of a Vietnam scenario)? They could just let them be, make some economic agreements with them, get some ports, etc. and voila, they've got themselves a permanent presence in the Pacific without too much blood. Heck they could even convince the Brits to recognize the Republic and establish relations hoping to have Germany (or Japan) to back down from doing anything funny (although that may be a long shot).

Well, these few regions can try to secede. The issue is if they can maintain status quo. Malolos Republic controlled the navy or whatsoever left of the Spanish Navy. The government also controlled majority of the population of the Philippines. The Malolos republic can raise 100k men while your local provinces seceding have that same or lower population than the opposing army with your army having no or minimal rifles whatsoever. Your opponents have also better and well educated generals compared to you. You got also the issue of loyalty of your populace if they are more loyal to your seceding province or Malolos Republic. It is simple reality of warfare, you can try but the question is if you can succeed. It is pure imagination that civil war is because some or one provinces seceded. The only way that Civil war will happen is if Luna or Aguinaldo or anyone in the army fights among themselves. Or if you got a PoD that will butterfly away anything the resembles OTL 1890s Philippines.

Not really. The mood in the US was generally fairly pro-Cuban, and many of the Yellow Journalists of the time were agitating for Cuban independence. Plus, the labor unions in the US were also tied pretty closely to the Cubans. The whole reason the Maine was in Cuba was because the US had much more vested in what happened there than in the Philippines, due to the proximity to Florida. They were very concerned that the violence in the island might damage US investments further, and they were determined that either Cuba would remain Spanish or that Cuba would be in the US sphere somehow. Given that 6 decades later, human civilization nearly ended with a foreign threat got a foothold on that island, that was a fairly prescient concern. The US didn't care much about the Philippines until they managed to sink the Spanish fleet and realized that nothing was stopping them from taking the islands, so they did. So, in summation, if you want the US to annex Cuba and liberate the Philippines, you'd have to change things much earlier than the war.

AHC: Reverse Cuba and the Philippines

Your mission is to reverse the fate of Cuba and the Philippines after the Spanish-American War. That means Cuba getting annexed and the Philippines being made a protectorate. Puerto Rico can be either.

items.model_answer:
If Cuba and the Philippines were “reversed”—meaning their geographic locations, historical trajectories, or geopolitical roles were swapped—the consequences would be profound due to their distinct colonial histories, cultural developments, and strategic positions.

Geographically swapping them (placing Cuba in Southeast Asia and the Philippines in the Caribbean) would drastically alter global trade, military strategy, and cultural exchange. The Philippines, as an archipelago near China and Southeast Asian trade routes, has historically been a crossroads of Asian, Islamic, and later Spanish and American influence. Cuba, situated at the entrance to the Gulf of Mexico, became a linchpin of Spanish colonial power in the Americas and later a focal point of U.S. foreign policy and Cold War tensions.

If their historical roles were reversed—say, if the Philippines had become a communist state aligned with the Soviet Union just 90 miles from the U.S. mainland, while Cuba remained a U.S.-aligned outpost in Asia—the Cold War would have unfolded very differently. A communist Philippines next to Florida could have triggered earlier and more intense U.S. containment efforts in the Western Hemisphere, possibly leading to direct conflict or even nuclear brinkmanship far sooner than the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis. Conversely, a pro-American Cuba in Southeast Asia might have altered U.S. involvement in Vietnam or shifted the balance of power during decolonization in Asia.

Culturally, such a reversal would also reshape national identities: Filipino society, shaped by centuries of Malay, Chinese, Islamic, Spanish, and American influences, would develop very differently in the Caribbean context, while Cuban culture—rooted in African, Spanish, and Caribbean traditions—would face entirely different pressures in maritime Southeast Asia.

In short, reversing Cuba and the Philippines—whether geographically or historically—would fundamentally reconfigure modern geopolitics, colonial legacies, and cultural landscapes in both regions and globally.

edus.text: If Cuba and the Philippines were “reversed”—
meaning their geographic locations, historical trajectories, or geopolitical roles were swapped—
the consequences would be profound
due to their distinct colonial histories, cultural developments, and strategic positions.
Geographically swapping them
placing Cuba in Southeast Asia and the Philippines in the Caribbean
would drastically alter global trade, military strategy, and cultural exchange.
The Philippines, as an archipelago near China and Southeast Asian trade routes, has historically been a crossroads of Asian, Islamic, and later Spanish and American influence.
Cuba, situated at the entrance to the Gulf of Mexico, became a linchpin of Spanish colonial power in the Americas
and later a focal point of U.S. foreign policy and Cold War tensions.
If their historical roles were reversed—
say, if the Philippines had become a communist state aligned with the Soviet Union just 90 miles from the U.S. mainland,
while Cuba remained a U.S.-aligned outpost in Asia—
the Cold War would have unfolded very differently.
A communist Philippines next to Florida could have triggered earlier and more intense U.S. containment efforts in the Western Hemisphere,
possibly leading to direct conflict or even nuclear brinkmanship far sooner than the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis.
Conversely, a pro-American Cuba in Southeast Asia might have altered U.S. involvement in Vietnam
or shifted the balance of power during decolonization in Asia.
Culturally, such a reversal would also reshape national identities:
Filipino society, shaped by centuries of Malay, Chinese, Islamic, Spanish, and American influences, would develop very differently in the Caribbean context,
while Cuban culture—rooted in African, Spanish, and Caribbean traditions—
would face entirely different pressures in maritime Southeast Asia.
In short, reversing Cuba and the Philippines—whether geographically or historically—
would fundamentally reconfigure modern geopolitics, colonial legacies, and cultural landscapes in both regions and globally.

items.question: What If West Germany and Italy had withdrawn from the PANAVIA Tornado program at the outset?
human_answers: That would fall under the bad economics heading. Germany and Italy might well have a good aircraft industry but for something of the Tornado's complexity and expense, they would need partners to spread the burden. Germany previously partnered with Fairchild-Hiller-Republic prior to Panavian efforts and as much as I like the G.91, it isn't really in the Tornado's league. In terms of a precedent for an Italian combat twin, the closest I can get is the PD.808GE which was of course originally a joint-venture between Piaggio and Douglas. If a number of nearby industrial/aerospace powerhouse nations have approximately compatible requirements, not to mention nations that you have other economic partnerships with in mind, why on earth wouldn't you consortium-up? Germany would not be so fiscally inept as to squander the opportunity and go it alone. Why would they choose to build an inferior type that their singular budget would necessitate? I know the popular narrative has Germany as the unwilling partner but much like the recent-ish Typhoon discussion, the narrative isn't bone out by the facts. The reality was Germany studied cheaper, less capable alternatives such as single-seat, fixed wing etc. and then ploughed right on with the full capability. Eminently logical and seemingly blown out of proportion by two generations of media. A simple question. If Germany were errmming and ahhhing so, why is it Panavia GmbH ? I realise that this thread is probably designed to engender responses like: RAF F-15Bs! Yeah, man, cool! Fine as far as it goes but not very probable. From my perspective, the premise is more like what if money, industry and defence stop mattering in Europe in the 1970s and my response is

The Marineflieger simply wanted a replacement for the F-104 but that doesn't matter because as OTL showed, whatever the airforce (both branches) wanted it didn't matter because the politicians decided. As an example of this look at the text below: Spoiler: text At least the VAK 191 would fulfill some of the requirements of the Luftwaffe and the Marineflieger. Both coming in single and two-seat variants, fighter/interceptor configuration and nuclear capable strike bomber. Supersonic and subsonic variants. And if the German aerospace industry lobbies enough, they might see one variant put into production as they actually have an existing product that consumed tons of R&D funds and ended up flying. Well, conventional wisdom showed that the single-seat, single-engine, fixed-wing design ended up outliving the variable-geometry twin-engined two-seater one. Yeah I doubt they were happy with their low-level supersonic strike F-104s and F-4s... The VAK 191 could fulfill the low-level supersonic strike-aircraft role.

IIRC the British Taxpayer paid 48% of the R&D cost of the Tornado IDS and I definitely remember that it paid 100% of the ADV's R&D cost. I don't know if HM Treasury could have paid the other 52% of the R&D cost of the IDS and that's the expensive one because it includes the cost of developing the engines and airframe. If that's correct which defence projects have to be cancelled to pay the difference? Then there's the cost of building them. My guess is that the assembly cost of the aircraft would be the same because they were made in three different factories and the same number of RAF aircraft are built in the same factory IOTL and ITTL. The British factory also built all the IDS and ADV that were exported too. However, the economies of scale for the engines, avionics and the "bits" of the airframe will be lost because the number built will be cut from nearly 1,000 to about 550. A lot fewer aircraft to support may put the operating cost up too by increasing the price of spares. Also the British defence industry may not have enough scientists and engineers to do the R&D on its own. Which may mean it takes longer and costs more. Or other defence projects have to be cancelled so the scientists and engineers can be concentrated on the Tornado IDS. OTOH I've heard people say that collaborative projects cost more and take longer than national projects. That's partially because of the extra layer of bureaucracy and mainly for political reasons. Each nation (naturally) wants its share of the work to be the same as the amount as it pays. That produces a less than optimal distribution of the R&D and production contracts. Or at least a worse distribution than a purely national distribution, as national politics means the best firm for the job doesn't necessarily get the contract either. Is there any truth to that? Or is it a false memory?

items.model_answer:
If West Germany and Italy had withdrawn from the PANAVIA Tornado program at the outset, the project would likely have collapsed or been drastically scaled back. The Tornado was a tri-national effort initiated in the late 1960s by the United Kingdom, West Germany, and Italy to develop a multirole combat aircraft capable of fulfilling varied national requirements—particularly low-level strike, reconnaissance, and air defense roles. The financial, technical, and operational burden was shared among the three partners; without West Germany and Italy, the UK alone would have faced significantly higher development costs and reduced economies of scale.

Given the UK’s constrained defense budget at the time, it is unlikely that it could have sustained the program independently without major redesigns or capability compromises. Alternatively, the UK might have pursued a less ambitious domestic aircraft or sought a different international partnership—possibly with France or the United States—but this would have delayed delivery and altered Cold War-era force structures. Moreover, the absence of a collaborative European fighter program might have weakened interoperability among NATO allies and potentially accelerated reliance on U.S.-built platforms like the F-111 or later the F-15 and F-16. In short, the Tornado as historically fielded would not have existed, and European air power development during the Cold War would have followed a markedly different trajectory.

edus.text: If West Germany and Italy had withdrawn from the PANAVIA Tornado program at the outset,
the project would likely have collapsed or been drastically scaled back.
The Tornado was a tri-national effort initiated in the late 1960s by the United Kingdom, West Germany, and Italy
to develop a multirole combat aircraft capable of fulfilling varied national requirements—particularly low-level strike, reconnaissance, and air defense roles.
The financial, technical, and operational burden was shared among the three partners;
without West Germany and Italy, the UK alone would have faced significantly higher development costs and reduced economies of scale.
Given the UK’s constrained defense budget at the time,
it is unlikely that it could have sustained the program independently without major redesigns or capability compromises.
Alternatively, the UK might have pursued a less ambitious domestic aircraft or sought a different international partnership—possibly with France or the United States—
but this would have delayed delivery and altered Cold War-era force structures.
Moreover, the absence of a collaborative European fighter program might have weakened interoperability among NATO allies
and potentially accelerated reliance on U.S.-built platforms like the F-111 or later the F-15 and F-16.
In short,
the Tornado as historically fielded would not have existed,
and European air power development during the Cold War would have followed a markedly different trajectory.

items.question: What If No nuclear weapons?
human_answers: As has been noted it is pretty much impossible to avoid having nuclear weapons ever being created. The science is pretty obvious. What CAN be altered, to a degree, is the "when". The U.S. threw a dramatic amount of funding at the effort, along with huge amounts of resources (Manhattan literally built the entire city of Oak Ridge TN to house the workers on the project. It was farmland, with about 3,000 people living in the area then in less than 2 years, it was a city with a population of 75,000. Government just walked in and "acquired" 59,000 acres, evicted everyone in the local farms and villages, and started building a fence (BIG ASS fence). The same thing happened in Washington with Hanford, except it was 500,000 acres and 39,000 people, Just a little less funding, or a project manager less driven than General Groves and the Bomb isn't ready.

Based on the described scenario, the USSR becomes the first country to test a nuclear weapon in the early 1950s, whereupon the US and UK governments demand an explanation for who filed the relevant reports in the wrong section back in 1940. In the case of the US, it's probably Lyman Briggs, who in OTL actually did lock away a key report in his safe without showing it to anyone else, which may have delayed the start of the Manhattan Project by several months. But even then, uranium fission was discovered in France in December 1938. The Einsten-Szilard letter warned the US government of the possibilities in August 1939. The Frisch-Peierls memorandum, the first description of a nuclear weapon, was written in March 1940 for the British government. By Frisch's own description, the work he and Peierls did was straightforward for any competent nuclear physicist. There might be a PoD wherein Frisch and Peierls are interned as enemy aliens and not allowed to work as physicists. Oliphant is focussed on the higher priority radar work, so Thomson's conclusion that it was not worth pursuing a chain reaction in uranium is accepted by the British government. There is therefore no MAUD committee, no report for Briggs to ignore, and no reason for Oliphant to kick things into gear. Instead, what is likely to happen is that eventually someone in the US does ask the questions that Frisch and Peierls asked, and they reach similar answers. Given OTL's trajectory, it's hard to see why that would happen any earlier than August 1941, given that US research was initially largely concerned with power plants rather than weapons. If we say it does, it might take the best part of a year for a US equivalent of the MAUD report to be carried out and an atomic weapons programme started. That puts a US weapons programme without the MAUD input as starting in mid-1942 - so about a six month delay. An arbitrarily longer delay is entirely plausible, but eventually - and probably sooner rather than later - someone is going to ask the right questions, and then things will start moving very quickly.

I do wonder if we don’t get the examples of nuclear destruction at the end of WW2 and if we delay the development of the bombs a bit so that by late 50s to mid 60s they are not quite as destructive as they were in real life if we don’t end up with a nuclear war. There are several reasons why WW3 was avoided. The example of how destructive the first generation bombers were, knowledge that the bombs were getting more powerful. Then the jump in power to the H bomb. Russia knowing that until the advent of ICBM they were behind the U.S. because their bombers sucked. The general aftermath of WW2 and no one really wanting to fight as a result. Russian back propaganda against nuclear weapons. Etc. All of this delay a possible WW3 until the combination of ICBM and drastically More powerful bombs made WW3 really unthinkable. But in a world we’re nuclear weapons are (somehow) drastically delayed we won’t see a lot of this, you are not seeing photos of nuked cities, you are getting 1st gen ICBMs with smaller nukes until h bombs get small enough to fit on ICBMs. Etc. So the taboo of a nuclear war is probably not built up soon enough to prevent a nuclear war. In fact they probably don’t segregate “conventional” war from “nuclear” as soon as we did otl. So we probably do see a WW3. Edited to add: BTW I think it is very unlikely to keep nuclear weapons from being developed by 1949. And almost impossible to keep nuclear weapons from being developed by 1955. And I thin it would be ASB to push them farther out then that. Physics simply allows for them so once you get the combination of the understanding of physics and the industrial/technical ability to make them you are getting them. And it is not exactly all that high tech to build a gun type nuke. So I just don’t see how you delay the development all that long. You would need the U.S. and the USSR to both come out of WW2 in much much worse shape to the point that they simply can’t afford to build nukes and I don’t see that happening.
items.original_question: What if No nuclear weapons? No Tubes Alloy or Los Alamos, and no German atomic research. Sadly, Japan is invaded - high causalities on both sides especially Japanese civilians much of it from starvation. No organised surrender, just quiet acceptance from district, to town, then the next. Japanese Americans were 'encouraged' to return to the homeland and rebuild - from the stone age! But what happens - with no nuclear umbrella - no ballistic missiles. WMD were confined to the Grandslams & Tallboys, with fuel air explosives via aircraft bombs or short range (V2) missiles. Research was more focused on better guidance for V1 type cruise missiles, and other ASM. Would the Berlin Blockade still happen, would it get hot? How would this affect Defence spending? Where would the focus on the difference between here and OTL?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Feasibility and Point of Divergence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer treats 'no nuclear weapons' as a constrained counterfactual requiring a plausible mechanism, rather than simply assuming physics or institutions change without explanation.
criteria.1-2: Assumes nuclear weapons never exist with no mechanism, or relies on impossible changes to physics without acknowledging them.
criteria.3-4: Gives a vague reason for nondevelopment but ignores known scientific discoveries and wartime incentives.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible delay mechanism, such as bureaucratic failure or reduced wartime mobilization, but leaves key feasibility issues underdeveloped.
criteria.7-8: Explains a credible point of divergence involving Manhattan Project, MAUD, Soviet espionage, funding, or personnel, while noting permanent nondevelopment is unlikely.
criteria.9-10: Precisely distinguishes permanent absence from delayed invention, grounds the divergence in real institutions and scientists, and clearly bounds what the premise can plausibly change.

criteria.name: Scientific and Industrial Causality
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer accounts for the physics, engineering, and industrial requirements that made nuclear weapons difficult but ultimately discoverable.
criteria.1-2: Ignores nuclear science and treats bombs as arbitrary political choices.
criteria.3-4: Mentions uranium or atomic science superficially but misses why discovery would likely recur.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that fission knowledge and industrial capacity matter, but gives only a partial account of enrichment, plutonium, reactors, or bomb design.
criteria.7-8: Connects fission discovery, critical mass reasoning, enrichment/reactor infrastructure, and state resources to likely development timelines.
criteria.9-10: Shows strong causal command of why gun-type and implosion weapons, wartime megaprojects, and postwar superpower capacity make indefinite prevention highly implausible.

criteria.name: World War II and Early Cold War Timeline Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer gives a coherent alternate timeline for WWII's end, the first successful nuclear program, and early US-UK-Soviet strategic behavior.
criteria.1-2: Produces a timeline that conflicts with basic WWII chronology or gives no sequence of events.
criteria.3-4: Mentions WWII or the Cold War but with major gaps or unsupported leaps.
criteria.5-6: Sketches plausible changes to Hiroshima/Nagasaki, Japan's surrender, or Soviet development, but lacks integration across actors.
criteria.7-8: Provides a coherent sequence linking delayed Manhattan work, Soviet/UK/US programs, espionage, Japan, and early Cold War military planning.
criteria.9-10: Builds a tightly reasoned timeline with actor-specific incentives, technological bottlenecks, and plausible dates for delayed or first nuclear tests.

criteria.name: Long-Range Downstream Effects and Strategic Mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of major downstream consequences, especially deterrence, nuclear taboo formation, conventional war incentives, arms races, alliances, and possible WWIII risk.
criteria.1-2: Stops at 'no Hiroshima' or gives simplistic utopian/apocalyptic outcomes.
criteria.3-4: Identifies one downstream effect but ignores deterrence, Cold War strategy, and military substitution.
criteria.5-6: Covers several effects, such as conventional warfare, superpower rivalry, or arms racing, but mechanisms are uneven.
criteria.7-8: Explains how absence or delay affects deterrence, taboo formation, bomber/ICBM strategy, NATO-Warsaw tensions, and risk of major war.
criteria.9-10: Offers a nuanced long-range chain showing how delayed weapons could either reduce early nuclear trauma or increase conventional/nuclear escalation risk, with multiple interacting mechanisms.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles uncertainty honestly, avoids overclaiming, and maintains internal consistency across the counterfactual chain.
criteria.1-2: Makes absolute claims, contradicts itself, or ignores the speculative nature of the scenario.
criteria.3-4: Uses some cautious language but contains major unsupported certainties or inconsistent assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges uncertainty and alternative paths, though some claims remain overconfident or loosely connected.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes likely, possible, and unlikely outcomes while keeping assumptions consistent over decades.
criteria.9-10: Maintains rigorous uncertainty calibration, explicitly flags branch points, avoids hidden contradictions, and explains why some outcomes are more plausible than others.

items.model_answer: If no nuclear weapons had ever been developed or deployed, the geopolitical landscape of the 20th and 21st centuries would likely have been significantly different. The Cold War might have escalated into direct large-scale conventional conflict between the United States and the Soviet Union, as the doctrine of Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD)—which relied on nuclear deterrence—would not have existed to prevent open warfare. Regional conflicts, such as those in Korea, Vietnam, or the Middle East, could have involved greater direct superpower military engagement without the restraining fear of nuclear escalation. Conversely, the absence of nuclear arsenals would eliminate the persistent risks of accidental launches, proliferation to non-state actors, or catastrophic humanitarian consequences from their use. International relations might have placed greater emphasis on conventional arms control, alliances, and diplomacy, though global security dynamics would remain complex and uncertain.

items.question: What If the USSR was leaked information about OB just before it happened and were thus better prepared and more competent in 1941? (No strike though)
human_answers: A couple days or weeks isn’t really enough if you’re going with the “Stalin finally makes a good decision” scenario. You need at least a couple months to have the Soviets dug in and prepared at more defensible spots further east than iotl, and considering the German initial manpower advantage (to say nothing of the purges creating widespread incompetence in the red army and said incompetence making their logistics horrible), they still probably lose pretty hard, although not quite as much as iotl. I think at least 6 or so (probably a bit more) months is needed to help close the manpower gap and create a Minsk-Kiev line that the Germans can’t penetrate if you don’t want Soviet losses to be seen as proportionally a lot bigger (though there’s a strong chance they still are in this scenario, just not enough to give the impression that all you need to do is kick in the rotten door enough and it’ll fall).

The Soviet Union possessed highly precise intelligence indicating that the German military's logistics were insufficient to sustain a protracted war and that its armaments factories had not yet shifted to a wartime footing. (This intelligence was derived from the infiltration of German industry by communist sympathizers.) Hitler also couldn't been so foolish as to believe that the mighty Soviet Union could be conquered within three months—at least, no analyst would have dared to venture such an insulting conjecture. Consequently, the less reliable intelligence from military and western country must have been false, and war is in next year. This chain of logic is remarkably robust; You cannot convince the Soviets that Germany is about to attack without introducing collateral changes—and different changes would inevitably lead to different outcomes in the war. Would they perceive their own military as weaker? Would they place their trust in Anglo-American intelligence while disregarding the Comintern’s own network? Or would they have managed to plant exceptionally reliable spies deep within the German military itself? Each of these scenarios would necessitate a distinct defensive strategy, thereby altering the very trajectory of the conflict. One thing, however, remains certain: if the Soviet Union were to lose the war while the United States remained an active belligerent, the Americans would undoubtedly drop the nuclear bomb.

I don't think there's an obvious way for the USSR to react to knowing war is coming. The Germans were much more ready for war. The USSR reaction will probably be a more planned withdrawal in the earliest days of the conflict, blowing some bridges behind their retreat, getting troops out of the pockets where they were surrounded and surrendered. Also less of the air force blown up on the ground in the opening days of the war. A better USSR reaction to Barbarossa might mean, 5,000 planes destroyed on the ground, 500,000 less troops taken as prisoners of war and a German advance that is stopped 100 miles from Moscow. That would probably look disasterous to the USSR and to historians looking backwards but would be a massive improvement over our time line. That said I've no idea how things would progress through the war. There's a lot of decisions to be made. I suspect the Germans might balance a stronger Soviet advance by putting more troops on that front which might make things easier on the Western front. No one really knows. Theres a long war and its all possibilities only.

As noted this ultimately may be worse for the USSR (but probably not) As Stalin had pretty well decimated his military command, So you have a lot of folks that either are no good at the job or have to little experience at the job or both. And if they know it is coming they may as noted by others be more forward deployed and more “aggressive” so they may not fall back as much. A good part of the beginning of the war for the USSR was the learning curve and while they were getting their butt kicked early on this did give them practice that they slowly implemented. In effect trading territory for “reduced” casualties. Compared to how bad they would have been clobbered if the tried to hold the liner harder the OTL. This is obviously exchanged for not getting surprised in this timeline. The question is which did more damage to the USSR the poor leadership needing time to find better officers or to at least get some learning in or the surprise? I tend to think it is a very minor advantage to the USSR to know ahead of time. But I think the poor leadership will mean that 90% of the advantages they get from not being surprised is tossed out the window by leadership that doesn’t know what it is doing. I suspect you will see more troops over run or surrender or otherwise forced to surrender as the order to not retreat will comedown and that there will be bigger battles sooner and closer to Germanies support system any anything that results in Germany have a shorter support line while still getting yo fight big battle vs the zuSSR is probably an improvement for Germany. Plus the war will be fought “faster” if the USSR is less inclined to pull back so the two don’t spend as much time traveling (retreating/advancing). So they are probably bigger battles sooner and more troops committed vs falling back so Germany by should able to kill more Russians faster. That being said it still ultimately sees Germany grind to a halt and it will see the USSR build enough troops and equipment and what have you to stop Germany so Germany will ultimately do better in terms of inflicting casualties on the USSR but they won’t get as far into the USSR. One thing I don’t know is if this fighting closer to the border will result in the German advance stoping before it gets so close that the USSR has to move its factories. Not moving a factory or two could make a big difference.

Again, as usual these scenarios entirely depend on one or both sides failing to react to changing circumstances. Firstly, USSR had information about possibility of German attack and was reacting. 'Stalin refused to believe the intelligence' is basically a myth. Soviet problem was not lack of the information or anyone's willingness or unwillingness 'to believe'. Soviet problem was lack of definitive information because everything that they had on Barbarossa was either utterly wrong, contaminated with enough false intelligence to make discerning what is true and what is not quite impossible or simply arrived too late for any sort of meaningful reaction. Secondly, USSR primary issue was that Germans at any point of preparation to Barbarossa were in position to speed these preparations up if they see an obvious Soviet reaction . And Germans were positioned to attack better than Soviets were positioned to defend. Let's say USSR starts mobilizing mid-April. Germany will not wait until June 22nd to attack because reality is not Hearts of Iron 4 game on a historical rails. Germans will simply attack in May before Soviet mobilization finishes. And yes, it could screw Mussolini by preventing Germany from bailing him out, but it was simple question of Germany already having mobilized army and having a better logistical infrastructure on their side of the border, so whatever obvious thing Soviets would do, Germans will have an opportunity to react. P.S. And no, Stalin will not give orders to pre-emptive attack against Germany for the very same reasons. Red Army was not in the position to attack anyone and everyone in Soviet leadership, including Stalin knew about that.

items.model_answer:
If the USSR had received credible intelligence about Operation Barbarossa (OB) shortly before its launch in June 1941—enabling better preparation without actually launching a preemptive strike—the course of the Eastern Front in World War II could have been significantly altered. Soviet forces might have avoided the catastrophic losses of men and materiel that resulted from Stalin’s initial disbelief and the Red Army’s disarray. With troops on higher alert, airfields dispersed, supply lines pre-positioned, and defensive lines reinforced, the Wehrmacht’s rapid advances during the summer and fall of 1941 could have been slowed or even halted earlier than historically occurred.

This improved readiness might have prevented the encirclement disasters at Minsk, Smolensk, and especially Kiev, preserving experienced personnel and equipment critical for later operations. Moscow might not have faced the existential threat it did in late 1941, potentially eliminating the need for desperate measures like throwing penal battalions into battle or relying on Siberian divisions rushed westward. A stronger early defense could have shortened the war by denying Germany the momentum it initially enjoyed, possibly altering strategic decisions such as Hitler’s diversion to Ukraine or the timing of the push toward Stalingrad.

However, structural weaknesses in the Red Army—such as poor leadership due to the purges, logistical inefficiencies, and doctrinal confusion—would still have limited Soviet effectiveness. Moreover, Germany might have adapted its plans if it sensed Soviet preparedness, perhaps delaying OB or altering its objectives. Still, even modest improvements in Soviet readiness could have shifted the balance enough to make the German invasion far costlier and less successful in its opening phase, with profound implications for the overall outcome of the war.

items.question: What If Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley.
human_answers: No Elvis will have minimal effect. Yes he was a popular Singer but he didn’t write anything. So the songs he is famous for will still exist. Will his lose have effects on music? Obviously. But it is not like music won’t more or less still evolve as it did. The lost of one singer is not going to have that drastic an effect there are simply to many of them. And as such someone else will slot in to become the “it” singer of that time. This is Not Like removing a given general from a given battle. In a battle the general has direct influence on the fighting. Swapping him out with someone else can have drastic effect. Who sings Hound Dog… not so much. Yes the song may or may not do worse at the charts and it may or may not have an impact on a company or a song writers career, But the removal of a singer is not effecting WW2. Singers and actors while obviously famous people in general are a dime a dozen! And pretty replaceable in most circumstances. Yes they have impact but is is hard to quantify. Yeah someone else singing a sang may mean that two people that loved that song and it formed the core of how they hooked up may not get it on in the back of a 1953 Chevy but… how the hell would anyone know that for certain? The impact of actors and singers and other people who are famous because they are famous has little impact if they are changed. You want an example of an impact from no Elvis? My uncle and his friend would not have had weekend gigs playing in the band of an Elvis impersonator. And I would have been able to stay home and avoid going to a really dull county fair that my folks dragged me to. And who knows I may have gotten farther with the pretty blonde next door sooner. But I doubt it. I know we have all heard of Elvis but he was simply not that important. I challenge you to tell me what he actually did that has a significance to history, or music. Yes a lot of folks imitated his style and his look and yes a lot of people bought his music. But if anything he had a negative knock on in music as his manager was an As$#@&*(. Of the first order and screwed many a song writers over big time. So there is a reasonable likelihood that some songwriters may have done better. Now the Beatles are a bit different. They wrote a LOT of music and some of that music had an impact on other writers. Once again the impact of them not being around has a knock on in pop culture in that you don’t get impersonator and it will effect in minor ways various individuals when they have to listen to different singers or whatever. But as with Elvis that has minimal influence on anything. And is almost impossible to document. But the lose of the songs that they wrote will have an effect on the evolution of music much more then not have an inspiration for singers shacking their hips. For example the Beach Boys will be effected as the album Pet Sounds was a direct response to some of the work the Beatles were doing. Writers have a more significant impact on music as they tend to influence each other a lot and it is simpler to replace the person singing any given song then the person that wrote it. Just look at how many people have success doing covers of songs. So the problem with this kind of post is twofold. One it is very very very hard to predict exactly what will change. For example will not having the song Dont Stop (thinking about tomorrow) influence the outcome one of the 1992 presidential election? Probably not. So you are dealing with things that are very nebulous. And if it just a singer that is even hard to say as it is possible that some unknown singer could get a break with the song instead. Elvis didn’t write his music so pretty much all his songs would be song by someone else if he disappeared. And the second problem with this kind of topic on this group is that there are a lot more people that know history and military stuff to a significant degree then know music. At least in the way that it will change. I probably know the words to 75% of the songs sung by Elvis and the Beatles but I don’t know who wrote most of Elvises songs nor who produced any songs for either of them. But I either know or have books that tell me who the major officers where at pretty much any major battle in the Civil War. And I know or can find out enough about most of them to have a good guess how swapping them will effect a given battle. But who can say what guy would have walked through the door and gotten the opportunity to perform if Elvis was gone. Frankly there are thousands of better singers in the world than Elvis that never got the chance. But the combination of his abilities and the opritunities he got made him a superstar. But it is impossible to know who would have gooten that chance if he was not there. But there are only a handful of people that may have been promoted if Montgomery got ran over by a tank.

I’m not saying that nothing would change. There absolutely would be changes from neither artist existing. It’s just that fundamentally: You still have popular music derived from Black American musical traditions. You still have a push away from large swing-style bands and towards smaller guitar-based bands - especially since before the digital era the guitar is the most accessible music instrument for young people wanting to make music. You still have the Baby Boom yielding a much larger youth cohort than before - thus yielding a significant generational divide by the early to mid 1960s as they’ve grown up having not known the struggles of their parents or older siblings - and have more room tackling lifestyle changes without worry for economic precarity. You still have big labels and radio stations wanting to play “different music” for “different races” so to speak. And with that you still have white singers becoming popular for their heavily sanitized covers of black R&B songs ( looks at Pat Boone ). You still have the post-WWII dominance and saturation of American pop culture - including music - in Europe and across the globe. And since the UK and the Commonwealth have virtually zero language barrier with the US - music that imitates American musical traditions (twice removed from Black American roots) has the potential to take off. You still have the advancements in recording technology that gave artists room to make more experimental and groundbreaking music than before. Plus the steady rise of FM radio later in the 1960s to provide a market for more ambitious music. You still have the Sexual Revolution to loosen norms around sex. On top of the various other drivers of the counterculture. You still have the payola scandal and the burnout of 1950s rock stars causing the 1959-64 dearth in the quality of pop music. But that’s just structurally speaking. Aesthetically speaking, things could be shifted around - with some new genre inspired by surf rock and garage rock (though realistically not actually either one of them) blowing up out of nowhere by 1964-65 - and Pat Boone is the King of Rock ‘n’ Roll all the artists of the 1960s are inspired by in terms of singing style and aura. While British rock bands are basically seen as a store brand that only gains later appreciation in the social media era decades later a la Japanese city pop. But it would still fundamentally fit the bigger variables that had been brewing years or even decades before the mid 1960s.

While the absence of the Beatles (and particularly Lennon and McCartney) would deprive us of some very good songs, there were vast numbers of competent bands in Britain that could have filled the niche if given the opportunity- whether together or singly. The bigger impact would probably have been on the penetration of British artists into the USA [1], but that's quite likely to happen eventually because there's money to be made from big crowds of relatively wealthy teenagers who happen to hit on a good enough band. The other impact might have been on the pressure to become singer-songwriters, rather than just singers/performers. Again, money is a big driver so it's likely to happen sooner or later. Otherwise, US innovation is likely to remain largely unchanged (Iggy and the Stooges will still form, and the drivers for hippy culture and rock bands is still there). Meanwhile, the Rolling Stones would still be experimenting with blues and quality musicians like Buddy Holly, Carl Perkins will be filling the niche that Elvis is no longer dominating. In short, different but still broadly recognisable. [1] The Monkees are unlikely to be formed, but songs like Day Dream Believer are too good not to end up being a success, even if it takes a few cover versions to become a real hit.

No Beatles or Elvis? Hmmm the amateur musicologist in me (that's what happens when you're a musician, who has also played in rock bands) says that rock 'n roll would still exist. The chances are also good that you would still have its superstar in the 50s - I read years ago that there were plans to push Carl Perkins (he of "Blue Suede Shoes" fame) towards superstardom by Sun Records. He might have actually become one if he hadn't suffered a major injury (he was in a car crash that kept him out of commission for a long time). Sam Phillips and even Elvis stated that Carl was doing rockabilly before Elvis, and unlike Elvis, Carl was also a songwriter. Most musicians will tell you that having that skill gives you much more staying power - you're not just a performer, you can make money off or songwriting royalties. By the time Carl recovered from the car crash it was too late, Elvis had overshadowed him. Jerry Lee Lewis, courtesy of his flamboyant personality might have become the 50s rock 'n roll superstar (how long he would have lasted would have depended upon whether or not he was still foolish enough to marry his underage cousin). The 60s? Hmmm that's not so certain - in the early 60s, rock 'n roll seemed to be on it's way out (or at least heading towards just being a niche genre of music). What rock 'n roll there was on Top 40 radio was mostly bland, and barely even qualified as rock 'n roll (Frankie Avalon anybody?). The Beach Boys were making songs with lame-o lyrics ("Be True to Your School", etc.). Even in Europe it was only doing so-so - I remember reading an interview of Jimmy Page (who along with playing guitar in Led Zeppelin, and the Yardbirds, was an in-demand session guitarist in the early and mid 60s), where he stated that in the early 60s, it was hard to even find rock 'n roll recording sessions to play on. Without the Beatles, rock'n roll might have just kept on being 50s-style teen hearthrob music performed by Cliff Richard, instrumental music played by bands like The Shadows (who also happened to be Cliff Richard's backing band), and possibly music played by 50s American rock 'n roll musicians, who were going nowhere in the USA with their careers (Bo Diddly, Eddie Cochran, etc. performed extensively in Europe in the early 60s when their careers fizzled out in the US). One of the big elements of the Beatles that helped to propel them to stardom IMO, was that for its time (the early 60s), the Beatles' music was considered HARD ROCK. As a result, it had more energy to it than your typical music of the period, and people liked it. The Stones? They were in their infancy, playing what is to me, watered down blues, that sounded nowhere near as intense. That hard rock edge the Beatles had is what kick started rock 'n roll again, and resulted in a million bands wanting to sound like them (even in the US, after they were on the Ed Sullivan Show). No Beatles and IMO, rock 'n roll continues its decline into a niche music genre, with the occasional Top 40 hit by bland groups like Gary Pucket and The Union Gap, Gary Lewis and The Playboys, etc. Not much in the way of edgy, interesting music. In the US, Link Wray never charts as high as he did with "Rumble" (which was actually banned by radio stations because it was "too threatening - it'll incite people to riot"), and Lonnie Mack at most has a few very modest hits like he had with "Wham".

Oh, for the love of Pete, not THIS again.... I just don't understand how some on this board can analyze military events down to the level of minutiae where they can argue that if a particular German general farted at a given moment in 1940, the entirety of World War II would come out differently, and yet at the same time assume that popular culture would remain essentially unaltered without the presence of two of its most important figures. Just as one example: before the Beatles, there was no such thing as a "British rock and roll group" in the eyes of Americans, and particularly American record companies, radio programmers, and concert promoters. Cliff Richard, who was Britain's biggest rock and roll superstar prior to the Beatles, went absolutely nowhere in America. Americans knew that rock and roll had originated in the U.S., and they were very parochial about it - the assumption, and it was not often wrong, before the Beatles was that anything coming from Britain would be a poor copy of records American teenagers already owned. (And it WAS teenagers almost exclusively who listened to rock and roll in 1963; projecting one's own current cultural dynamics into the past is part of the reason one gets lost). No British rock group - not one - had broken in the U.S. before 1964. The Beatles themselves at first were turned down by Capitol, the American division of EMI, who held their recording contract in the UK; Capitol refused to issue their first four singles in the U.S. It took the "Beatlemania" phenomenon to convince Capitol that it was worth giving the Beatles a shot, which enabled Beatlemania to cross the Atlantic. I'm sorry, but it's not as if "Holliemania" or "Dave Clark Fivemania" simply takes the place of that. There's a whole set of intangibles here. You can't just assume that you like the Rolling Stones better, so they automatically take the place of the Beatles. It would never have worked like that. What happens to the Rolling Stones becomes essentially undefinable. And that's just one example. I didn't even address the fact of no Elvis - which probably would have meant no Beatles AND virtually none of the other British Invasion acts either. Removing Elvis from the picture (which automatically would remove the Beatles as we know them) changes the ENTIRE trajectory of popular music from that day to this, in well-nigh unpredictable ways. Period.
items.original_question: What if Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley. American Singer and Actor Elvis Presley and British Rock Band The Beatles are the most Influential musicians in existence. With the former codifying Rockabilly and is credited for advancing the Feminist movement in America, and the Latter spearheaded the British Invasion, increased public interest in Psychedelic Drugs, Asian Spirituality and heralded the Album Era. Let's say both the musician and the Band never had any interest in music, preventing the codifying of Rockabilly and The British Invasion. How would this influence modern music?

items.model_answer:
Without The Beatles and Elvis Presley, modern music would be significantly different in both sound and structure. Elvis helped pioneer rock and roll by blending rhythm and blues with country and gospel, breaking racial and cultural barriers in popular music during the 1950s. His charisma and performance style set the template for the modern pop star. The Beatles, emerging a decade later, revolutionized songwriting, studio production, and the album format itself; they shifted popular music from singles-driven entertainment to artist-driven creative expression.

In their absence, rock and pop might have developed more slowly or along divergent lines—perhaps with greater influence from other early figures like Chuck Berry, Little Richard, or Buddy Holly, or with genres like soul, Motown, or folk taking center stage earlier. The British Invasion might not have occurred in the same way, delaying or altering the global dominance of Anglo-American pop. Additionally, innovations in recording techniques, concept albums, and the idea of bands writing their own material might have emerged later or differently. Overall, while music would still have evolved, the pace, direction, and cultural impact of that evolution would likely be markedly altered without these two foundational forces.

edus.text: Without The Beatles and Elvis Presley, modern music would be significantly different in both sound and structure.
Elvis helped pioneer rock and roll by blending rhythm and blues with country and gospel,
breaking racial and cultural barriers in popular music during the 1950s.
His charisma and performance style set the template for the modern pop star.
The Beatles, emerging a decade later, revolutionized songwriting, studio production, and the album format itself;
they shifted popular music from singles-driven entertainment to artist-driven creative expression.
In their absence, rock and pop might have developed more slowly or along divergent lines—
perhaps with greater influence from other early figures like Chuck Berry, Little Richard, or Buddy Holly,
or with genres like soul, Motown, or folk taking center stage earlier.
The British Invasion might not have occurred in the same way,
delaying or altering the global dominance of Anglo-American pop.
Additionally, innovations in recording techniques, concept albums, and the idea of bands writing their own material might have emerged later or differently.
Overall, while music would still have evolved,
the pace, direction, and cultural impact of that evolution would likely be markedly altered without these two foundational forces.

items.question: What If the Royal Navy had deployed carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward?
human_answers: Far too big Even with folding wings I don't think they would fit on the elevators and would take up too much room in the hanger even of they fit which again I suspect not Its landing on performance of he Beaufighter is about the same as an avenger (60 knots?) but its much heavier than the TBF so I am not sure the arrestor cables of the day could handle such a plane. Its a nice idea but its too much of a plane for the carriers of the day - might work on an Audacious class but not the carriers built in the late 30s. The Whispering Death is already doing sterling work as a land based anti shipping aircraft during the war and it has great range - not quite 'Rikko' (G3m and G4m Japanese bombers) range, but close too it, but still a scourge where ever it operated.

In the last thread on the subject I mentioned, given any wing-break would have to be somewhat outboard the engines*, that you could probably take one up and down on Implacable's forward lift but the hangar height would preclude you rolling it off. You could store one in Illustrious's hangar, if you made it from a kit of parts, as the lift is too narrow. So deck parks only. You could use some form of depressing oleos to lower the Beaufighter's resting angle. You might just scrape it into Implacable's hangar but clearances would be marginal. Any kind of seaway would make deck handling tricky to impossible. You could also only load a torpedo on the flight deck with the aircraft back up to full height. I also suggested an increased-chord rudder and handed props because the Beaufighter could be a handful with all the room in the world. Operating a Beau on/off of a carrier is an expensive way to give a pilot a coronary... ETA: The wing-breaks are going to be in the order of 25ft apart and Illustrious's elevators are only 22ft across. Folding the wings is also going to involve re-siting the cooling ducts from the outboard leading edge.
items.original_question: What if Sea Beaufort and Sea Beaufighters used on Royal Navy aircraft carriers? What if the Royal Navy used a possible Bristol Sea variant of both Beauforts and Beaufighters on their carriers starting in 1940 replacing Fairy Swordfish aircraft in the torpedo attack role for example? Would this be possible design wise? Would they be better than the bomb and torpedo attack aircraft available at the time? Would the aircraft actually be able to be used like this or would they be too large? How effective would they be if used on aircraft carriers? Regards

items.model_answer:
If the Royal Navy had deployed carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward, it would have significantly enhanced its naval strike and fighter capabilities during a critical phase of World War II. The Beaufort, adapted as a torpedo bomber for carriers, could have provided the Fleet Air Arm with a more effective and longer-range alternative to the outdated Swordfish and Albacore biplanes, particularly in anti-shipping and fleet attack roles. This might have improved outcomes in key operations such as the Battle of the Atlantic, Mediterranean convoy protection, and strikes against Axis naval forces—potentially altering the course of engagements like the hunt for the Bismarck or operations off Norway and North Africa.

Similarly, a carrier-based Sea Beaufighter—already a potent land-based night fighter and strike aircraft—would have offered the Royal Navy a fast, heavily armed multirole platform capable of fleet defense, anti-submarine patrols, and ground attack. Its introduction from 1940 could have mitigated the Royal Navy’s chronic shortage of modern monoplane fighters until the arrival of the Seafire and later American types like the Wildcat and Hellcat.

However, significant challenges would have arisen. Neither aircraft was originally designed for carrier operations; adapting them would have required structural reinforcement, arrestor hooks, folding wings, and other modifications that could delay deployment or reduce performance. Moreover, Britain’s limited industrial capacity in 1940–41 was already stretched thin producing aircraft for the RAF and meeting urgent wartime demands. Diverting resources to develop and produce naval variants might have strained production without guaranteed payoff.

In sum, while carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 could have strengthened the Royal Navy’s air power and potentially shifted tactical outcomes in several theaters, practical constraints of design, production, and timing would have tempered their impact.

edus.text: If the Royal Navy had deployed carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward,
it would have significantly enhanced its naval strike and fighter capabilities during a critical phase of World War II.
The Beaufort, adapted as a torpedo bomber for carriers, could have provided the Fleet Air Arm with a more effective and longer-range alternative to the outdated Swordfish and Albacore biplanes,
particularly in anti-shipping and fleet attack roles.
This might have improved outcomes in key operations such as the Battle of the Atlantic, Mediterranean convoy protection, and strikes against Axis naval forces—
potentially altering the course of engagements like the hunt for the Bismarck or operations off Norway and North Africa.

Similarly, a carrier-based Sea Beaufighter—already a potent land-based night fighter and strike aircraft—would have offered the Royal Navy a fast, heavily armed multirole platform capable of fleet defense, anti-submarine patrols, and ground attack.
Its introduction from 1940 could have mitigated the Royal Navy’s chronic shortage of modern monoplane fighters
until the arrival of the Seafire and later American types like the Wildcat and Hellcat.
However, significant challenges would have arisen.
Neither aircraft was originally designed for carrier operations;
adapting them would have required structural reinforcement, arrestor hooks, folding wings, and other modifications
that could delay deployment or reduce performance.
Moreover, Britain’s limited industrial capacity in 1940–41 was already stretched thin producing aircraft for the RAF and meeting urgent wartime demands.
Diverting resources to develop and produce naval variants might have strained production without guaranteed payoff.
In sum, while carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 could have strengthened the Royal Navy’s air power and potentially shifted tactical outcomes in several theaters,
practical constraints of design, production, and timing would have tempered their impact.

items.question: What If : FDR picks a Segregationist VP in 1944
human_answers: The only Southerner who got any serious support at the DNC in 1944 was Alabama Senator John H. Bankhead II, who came in a distant third with 98 votes (8.33%) on the first ballot. The only other (non Alben W. Barkley) Southerners who got even one vote were: J. Melville Broughton (Governor of North Carolina), Prentice Cooper (Governor of Tennessee), Robert S. Kerr (Senator from Oklahoma), Herbert O'Conor (Governor of Maryland), Claude Pepper (Senator from Florida), Sam Rayburn (Speaker of the House), and Bascom N. Timmons (D.C. based newspaperman who grew up in Texas). Of these, only Bankhead II, Barkley, Broughton, Cooper, Kerr, and O’Conor got double digits. So your best case scenario is Roosevelt and/or the convention see a need to nominate a Southerner, and go with Bankhead II who IOTL died on June 12, 1946 following a stroke on May 24, 1946, which means you end up with three Presidents in little over a year. Based on the 1886 Succession Act, Bankhead II’s successor would be none other than… James F. Byrnes. IOTL, Truman appointed him in July of 1945, and it’s pretty likely Bankhead II does similarly, wanting to support a follow Southerner. (Prior to the Succession Act of 1947, neither the Speaker of the House nor the President pro tempore of the Senate were in the line of succession.) So in a roundabout way, you do end up with Byrnes as President…

Right. Byrnes thought he was Roosevelt's choice. Truman went to the DNC planning to make a nominating speech for Byrnes. If Byrnes does get the nod... FDR wins in 1944 anyway. But things diverge after that. IMO the Republicans sweep in 1946 as OTL. Byrnes was a very capable man and won't make any big missteps, so IMO he will be renominated in 1948. There may be a feeling that the 1948 nomination is a poisoned chalice, what with the 1946 GOP sweep and general public fatigue with 16 years of Democrat Presidents. The "Humphreyite" liberals may still try to push a civil rights plank at the DNC, but against Byrnes' at least tacit opposition will fail. They won't bolt to support Wallace overtly. Instead they may sit back to watch Byrnes crash and burn in November, while they regroup for 1952. Byrnes will lose a fair number of voters to Wallace outside the South. Also, AIUI, Dewey chose to soft-pedal civil rights OTL in the vain hope of winning some Upper South states with the Democrats divided. TTL that ignis fatuus isn't around, so Dewey probably emphasizes civil rights to draw the increasingly important black vote in the North and also some white liberals. This should be enough for Dewey to win. The next question is whether he has enough "coat tails" for Republicans to hold Congress. Another question is how the civil rights issue shapes across the next decade. OTL, leadership on the issue was taken by liberal non-Southern Democrats, with the low-key support of Republicans. The first cracks in the "Solid South" came in the 1950s, as a few white Southerners who could no longer rely on the national Democratic party to protect Jim Crow found they could vote Republican. If under Dewey, Republicans claim the leading role, that's not going to happen. The "Humphreyites" will gain control of the Democrats by 1952; there may be a Dixiecrat ticket that year. Dewey will be re-elected, barring some debacle in Korea or whatever. Warren won't be Chief Justice, but the Court will still be making rulings like Brown .
items.original_question: What if : FDR picks a Segregationist VP in 1944 In 1944, after intense pressure, President Franklin Delano Roosevelt would drop Vice President Henry Asgard Wallace from the ticket but due to his initial choice of James F. Byrnes being rejected due to his conversion from Catholicism, he would ultimately be convinced to go with Missouri Senator Harry S. Truman. Truman, as President, proved to be a liberal on racial issues and on labor rights, seeing as his SCOTUS Appointments sealed the deal on Brown v Board of Education being unanimous. However, what if ultimately, FDR went with a strict segregationist who was in favor of the New Deal at least early in their career? What happens when he becomes President and any ideas who this could be (one idea is Russell and another is Connally but both might say no to the offer)? Who do they appoint to SCOTUS instead of Burton and Vinson in 1945 and 1946 and Clark and Minton if they won a full term in 1948? What would 1948 look like in this TL? I suspect the southern president would probably appoint segregationist justices or lawyers to the court who make it through thanks to the Conservative Coalition being aligned on this one issue, though I admit I am unsure how they would handle the post war time frame, especially with 1945-1949. Furthermore, I could see a case for Dewey not being nominated ittl as in 1948 iotl, his nomination wasn't guaranteed but his wing of the party was able to get things to align with him by the convention. Here, with a more conservative leaning court and administration, the Republicans may pick a Conservative who can bring stability to both the party and the nation as long as it isn't Taft Sr. Also, I imagine the effects this has on American politics, specifically the civil rights movement, especially if Brown v Board goes the other way, if this has happened with perhaps more radical actions being taken and maybe an earlier Black Panther Party if things get really bad, but that's up in the air for the first decade of this period in time.

items.model_answer: If Franklin D. Roosevelt had chosen a segregationist vice president in 1944—such as Harry F. Byrd or James F. Byrnes instead of Harry S. Truman—it would have significantly altered the trajectory of U.S. civil rights policy and Democratic Party politics after World War II. Upon FDR’s death in April 1945, a segregationist VP would have become president during a critical period of postwar reconstruction, decolonization, and rising demands for racial equality. Such a president likely would have resisted desegregation efforts, opposed anti-lynching legislation, and maintained or even reinforced Jim Crow policies at the federal level. This could have delayed or weakened landmark developments like Executive Order 9981 (which desegregated the military in 1948 under Truman) and undermined early momentum for the Civil Rights Movement. Domestically, it might have deepened divisions within the Democratic Party sooner, possibly accelerating the realignment that eventually saw Southern whites shift toward the Republican Party. Internationally, a segregationist U.S. leadership during the early Cold War would have damaged America’s moral standing, especially as it sought to position itself as a champion of democracy against Soviet critiques of American racism.
