items.question: What If Everyone on Earth Jumped at the Same Time?
human_answers: This is one of the most popular questions submitted to this blog. It’s been examined before, including by a ScienceBlogs (http://scienceblogs.com/dotphysics/2010/08/26/what-if-everyone-jumped/) post and a Straight Dope article (http://www.straightdope.com/columns/read/142/if-all-chinese-jumped-at-once-would-cataclysm-result). They cover the kinematics pretty well. However, they don’t tell the whole story. Let’s take a closer look. At the start of the scenario, the entire Earth’s population has been magically transported together into one place. [Image: image] This crowd takes up an area the size of Rhode Island. But there’s no reason to use the vague phrase “an area the size of Rhode Island”. This is our scenario; we can be specific. They’re actually in Rhode Island. [Image: image] At the stroke of noon, everyone jumps. [Image: image] As discussed elsewhere, it doesn’t really affect the planet. Earth outweighs us by a factor of over ten trillion. On average, we humans can vertically jump maybe half a meter on a good day. Even if the Earth were rigid and responded instantly, it would be pushed down by less than an atom’s width. Next, everyone falls back to the ground. [Image: image] Technically, this delivers a lot of energy into the Earth, but it’s spread out over a large enough area that it doesn’t do much more than leave footprints in a lot of gardens. A slight pulse of pressure spreads through the North American continental crust and dissipates with little effect. The sound of all those feet hitting the ground creates a loud, drawn-out roar which lasts many seconds. Eventually, the air grows quiet. Seconds pass. Everyone looks around. [Image: image] There are a lot of uncomfortable glances. Someone coughs. [Image: image] A cell phone comes out of a pocket. Within seconds, the rest of the world’s five billion phones follow. All of them—even those compatible with the region’s towers—are displaying some version of “NO SIGNAL”. The cell networks have all collapsed under the unprecedented load. Outside Rhode Island, abandoned machinery begins grinding to a halt. The T. F. Green airport in Warwick, Rhode Island handles a few thousand passengers a day. Assuming they got things organized (including sending out scouting missions to retrieve fuel), they could run at 500% capacity for years without making a dent in the crowd. [Image: image] The addition of all the nearby airports doesn’t change the equation much. Nor does the region’s light rail system. Crowds climb on board container ships in the deepwater port of Providence, but stocking sufficient food and water for a long sea voyage proves a challenge. Rhode Island’s half-million cars are commandeered. Moments later, I-95, I-195, and I-295 become the sites of the largest traffic jam in the history of the planet. Most of the cars are engulfed by the crowds, but a lucky few get out and begin wandering the abandoned road network. Some make it past New York or Boston before running out of fuel. Since the electricity is probably not on at this point, rather than find a working gas pump, it’s easier to just abandon the car and steal the new one. Who can stop you? All the cops are in Rhode Island. The edge of the crowd spreads outward into southern Massachusetts and Connecticut. Any two people who meet are unlikely to have a language in common, and almost nobody knows the area. The state becomes a patchwork chaos of coalescing and collapsing social hierarchies. Violence is common. Everybody is hungry and thirsty. Grocery stores are emptied. Fresh water is hard to come by and there’s no efficient system for distributing it. Within weeks, Rhode Island is a graveyard of billions. The survivors spread out across the face of the world and struggle to build a new civilization atop the pristine ruins of the old. Our species staggers on, but our population has been greatly reduced. Earth’s orbit is completely unaffected—it spins along exactly as it did before our species-wide jump. But at least now we know. [Image: image]

rubrics.question_focus: What If Everyone on Earth Jumped at the Same Time?

criteria.name: Physical effect on Earth from the synchronized jump
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons about momentum, mass ratios, and energy transfer to show that the jump has negligible geophysical or orbital consequences.
criteria.1-2: Claims major Earth movement, orbit change, earthquakes, or apocalypse from the jump itself with little or no physics.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes Earth is massive but gives vague or partly incorrect claims about motion, force, or energy.
criteria.5-6: States the effect on Earth is tiny and temporary, with some correct momentum or mass-ratio reasoning.
criteria.7-8: Explains that Earth’s displacement/recoil would be microscopic and cancel when people land; landing energy mostly dissipates locally.
criteria.9-10: Quantitatively or semi-quantitatively captures the huge Earth-human mass ratio, subatomic-scale displacement, no orbital/spin effect, and only minor seismic/acoustic energy.

criteria.name: Treatment of the counterfactual setup and assumptions
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly handles the key premise choices: everyone jumping worldwide versus everyone being gathered in one place before jumping.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or mangles the premise, or treats impossible setup details as unexplained magic without clarifying consequences.
criteria.3-4: Assumes a scenario but does not state it clearly, leading to ambiguous or inconsistent reasoning.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that results differ depending on whether people stay where they are or are concentrated together.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes the global synchronized-jump case from the co-located-crowd case and reasons appropriately for each.
criteria.9-10: Explicitly brackets the magical relocation assumption, keeps it separate from physical jump effects, and uses it to drive downstream social/logistical consequences.

criteria.name: Coverage of immediate local effects after landing
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly describes what happens seconds to minutes after everyone lands, especially sound, pressure waves, crowd density, communication overload, and infrastructure stress.
criteria.1-2: Skips immediate aftermath or replaces it with implausible disasters such as instant global destruction.
criteria.3-4: Mentions landing or noise but lacks causal detail or scale awareness.
criteria.5-6: Covers some immediate effects such as loud sound, minor vibrations, footprints/damage, or confusion.
criteria.7-8: Explains that landing creates a large but diffuse acoustic/seismic pulse with limited physical damage, plus immediate crowd confusion and communications failure.
criteria.9-10: Integrates physical dissipation, crowd behavior, overloaded cell networks, abandoned systems elsewhere, and the transition from harmless jump physics to human-scale crisis.

criteria.name: Long-range logistical and societal chain coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows a plausible causal chain from billions of people concentrated after the jump to transport, food, water, sanitation, violence, mortality, and eventual recovery or collapse.
criteria.1-2: Provides no downstream chain or jumps straight to an unsupported utopia/apocalypse.
criteria.3-4: Mentions crowding or shortages but without sequence, mechanisms, or scale.
criteria.5-6: Gives a plausible medium-term chain involving congestion, limited transport, and resource shortages.
criteria.7-8: Covers severe failures in evacuation, food, water, sanitation, governance, language/coordination, and medical response over days to weeks.
criteria.9-10: Presents a coherent long-range cascade from initial crowding through infrastructure collapse, mass mortality, dispersal of survivors, and rebuilding atop largely intact but abandoned global infrastructure.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer avoids overclaiming, keeps scales consistent, and does not contradict itself about physics, geography, population, or infrastructure.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions or confident false claims, such as both no effect and global earthquakes, or impossible evacuation rates.
criteria.3-4: Has several scale errors or unsupported certainties that weaken the causal story.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent, with some uncertainty acknowledged but occasional loose estimates or minor contradictions.
criteria.7-8: Uses calibrated language, reasonable orders of magnitude, and maintains consistency between negligible planetary effects and severe human logistics.
criteria.9-10: Carefully separates known physics from speculative social outcomes, flags assumption sensitivity, uses scale-aware estimates, and avoids internal contradictions throughout.

items.model_answer: If everyone on Earth jumped at the same time, the effect would be negligible on a planetary scale. The combined mass of all humans—roughly 8 billion people averaging about 62 kg each—is approximately 500 billion kilograms. While this sounds large, it is minuscule compared to Earth’s mass (about 6 × 10²⁴ kg). When people jump, they exert a force on the ground, and by Newton’s third law, the Earth experiences an equal and opposite force. However, because Earth’s mass is so enormous, the resulting acceleration would be imperceptibly small—on the order of 10⁻¹³ m/s² or less—and would not cause any measurable movement or seismic event. Moreover, people are distributed unevenly across the planet, so forces would largely cancel out directionally. Once everyone lands, the net momentum transfer returns to zero. In short, the Earth wouldn’t “move” in any detectable way.

edus.text: If everyone on Earth jumped at the same time,
the effect would be negligible on a planetary scale.
The combined mass of all humans—roughly 8 billion people averaging about 62 kg each—is approximately 500 billion kilograms.
While this sounds large,
it is minuscule compared to Earth’s mass (about 6 × 10²⁴ kg).
When people jump,
they exert a force on the ground,
and by Newton’s third law, the Earth experiences an equal and opposite force.
However, because Earth’s mass is so enormous,
the resulting acceleration would be imperceptibly small—on the order of 10⁻¹³ m/s² or less—
and would not cause any measurable movement or seismic event.
Moreover, people are distributed unevenly across the planet,
so forces would largely cancel out directionally.
Once everyone lands,
the net momentum transfer returns to zero.
In short, the Earth wouldn’t “move” in any detectable way.

items.question: What If Matryoshka Dolls Reproduced Asexually?
human_answers:
Actually, there is an organism on earth that is vaguely similar to the Russian dolls that you describe. The volvox:

Individual volvox cells, a kind of freshwater algae, reproduce in the conventional way (more or less), however, they also collect into spherical colonies (called volvocates, I think) with a tiny opening at one end. These spheres can reproduce by internal budding, with immature spheres growing within the body of the 'mother' sphere. Then at some point, the mother turns itself inside-out by inverting itself through the opening, releasing the 'daughter' spheres into the wild. The point where the daughter sphere connected with this interior of the mother becomes the opening of the daughter sphere (sort of like a navel in mammals). The cells that formerly composed the mother sphere don't simply die, however. Most of them are absorbed by one of the daughter spheres.

And yes, 'granddaughter' spheres can start to develop within the daughter spheres before 'birth'/'hatching'. In the following photo, you can see a mother colony in the process of disintegration, releasing it's daughters, which in turn have daughters already developing:

Photo credit: www.microscopy-uk.org.uk

Now, there are two differences between the volvox and your Russian dolls:

- The 'birth' event doesn't lead to complete death of the 'mother'.

- More than one daughter born per 'birth' event. 

The first feature can be achieved by your dolls if the 'mother' dolls can reform somehow. Perhaps the 'head' can reattach to the 'tail' and continue living. After consuming enough nutrients from the environment, they could even begin the process of internal budding again. Or perhaps the daughters simply consume the mother's material, giving them a early boost in life.

The second feature can be achieved by simply dividing multiple times. Russian dolls have multiple layers inside at varying levels of size, but all are viable. When a large doll splits, a medium one emerges and splits, then a small one emerges and splits, then a smaller one, until there several offspring. Combined withe the above, you could have a burgeoning population of Russian dolls (Matryoshkavox?)

items.model_answer: If Matryoshka dolls reproduced asexually, they would generate offspring without the need for a partner, but their nested structure poses a logical constraint: each doll contains only smaller versions of itself, never larger ones. Asexual reproduction in this context would imply that the innermost (smallest) doll—having no smaller dolls inside—could not produce further offspring, halting reproduction at that point. Alternatively, if a doll could somehow create a new set of nested dolls identical to itself, it would violate the original nesting principle unless the new set was entirely separate. Thus, true asexual reproduction is incompatible with the defining physical and hierarchical nature of Matryoshka dolls; any replication would either terminate at the smallest unit or require external assembly, not autonomous biological-like reproduction.

items.question: What If Every SAT Taker Guessed on Every Question?
human_answers: None. The SAT is a standardized test given to high school students (similar to the ACT). The scoring is such that under certain circumstances, guessing an answer can be a good strategy. But what if you guessed on everything? Not all of the SAT is multiple-choice, so let’s focus on the multiple choice questions to keep things simple. We’ll assume everyone gets the essay questions and fill-in-the-number sections correct. There are 44 multiple-choice questions in the math (quantitative) section, 67 in the critical reading (qualitative) section, and 47 in the newfangled writing section. Each question has five options, so a random guess has a 20% chance of being right: [Image: image] Although we all know the answer is always B. The probability of getting all 158 questions is: \[\frac{1}{5^{44}} * \frac{1}{5^{67}} * \frac{1}{5^{47}} \approx \frac{1}{2.7 * 10^{110}}\] (That's one in twenty-seven quinquatrigintillion.) If all four million 17-year-olds all took the SAT, and they all guessed randomly, it’s a statistical certainty that there would be no perfect scores on any of the three sections. How certain is it? Well, if they each used a computer to take the test a million times each day, and continued this every day for five billion years—until the Sun expanded to a red giant and the Earth was charred to a cinder—the chance of any of them ever getting a perfect score on just the math section would be about 0.0001%. How unlikely is that? Each year something like 500 Americans are struck by lightning[1]Cooper, Mary Ann, MD. "Disability, Not Death is the Main Problem with Lightning Injury" (http://www.uic.edu/labs/lightninginjury/Disability.pdf)[2]http://www.nws.noaa.gov/om/hazstats/light08.pdf (http://www.nws.noaa.gov/om/hazstats/light08.pdf) (http://www.nws.noaa.gov/om/hazstats/light08.pdf) (based on an average of 45 lightning deaths and a 9-10% fatality rate). This suggests that the odds of any one American being hit in a given year are about one in in 700,000 (although probability can be tricky (http://xkcd.com/795/)). This means that the odds of acing the SAT by guessing are worse than the odds of every living ex-President and every member of the main cast of Firefly all being independently struck by lightning … on the same day. [Image: image] (Everyone survives but Alan Tudyk and Ron Glass) To everyone taking the SAT this year, good luck—but it won’t be enough.

items.model_answer:
If every SAT taker guessed on every question, the resulting score distribution would reflect pure chance rather than academic ability. The SAT consists of multiple-choice questions with four answer choices each (since 2016), so a random guess has a 25% probability of being correct per question.

For the Evidence-Based Reading and Writing (EBRW) and Math sections—each scored from 200 to 800—the expected raw score from random guessing would be roughly 25% of the total points available. After conversion through the SAT’s equating process, this would yield average section scores near the minimum scaled score (around 200–300 per section), depending on the specific test form and scoring curve.

Because guessing introduces randomness, individual scores would vary around this low mean due to chance, but virtually no one would achieve high scores purely by guessing. The overall score distribution would be tightly clustered at the bottom end of the scale, with extremely low variance compared to actual test-taker distributions. Consequently, colleges could not meaningfully differentiate applicants based on such scores, rendering the test useless for its intended purpose of assessing college readiness.

items.question: What If You Gathered a Mole of Moles in One Place?
human_answers: Things get a bit gruesome. First, some definitions. A mole is a unit. It’s not a typical unit, though. It’s really just a number—like “dozen” or “billion.” If you have a mole of something, it means you have 602,214,129,000,000,000,000,000 of them (usually written \( 6.022\times10^{23} \)). It’s such a big number because it’s used for counting numbers of molecules, which there are a lot of. [Image: image] "One mole" is close to the number of atoms in a gram of hydrogen. It’s also, by chance, a decent ballpark guess for the number of grains of sand on Earth. A mole is also a type of burrowing mammal. There are a handful of types of moles, and some of them are truly horrifying (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Condylura.jpg). [Image: image] So what would a mole of moles—602,214,129,000,000,000,000,000 animals—look like? First, let’s start with wild ballpark approximations. This is an example of what might go through my head before I even pick up a calculator, when I’m just trying to get a sense of the quantities - the kind of calculation where 10, 1, and 0.1 are all close enough that we can consider them equal: I can pick up a mole (animal) and throw it.[citation needed] Anything I can throw weighs one pound. One pound is one kilogram. The number 602,214,129,000,000,000,000,000 looks about twice as long as a trillion, which means it’s about a trillion trillion. I happen to remember that a trillion trillion kilograms is how much a planet weighs. [Image: image] … if anyone asks, I did not tell you it was ok to do math like this. That’s enough to tell us that we’re talking about pile of moles on the scale of planets. It’s a pretty rough estimate, though, since it could be off by a factor of thousands in either direction. Let’s get some better numbers. An eastern mole (Scalopus aquaticus) weighs about 75 grams, which means a mole of moles weighs \[ (6.022\times10^{23})\times75\mathrm{g}\approx4.52\times10^{22}\mathrm{kg}\] That’s a little over half the mass of our moon. Mammals are largely water. A kilogram of water takes up a liter of volume, so if the moles weigh \( 4.52\times10^{22} \) kilograms, they take up about \( 4.52\times10^{22} \) liters of volume. You might notice that we’re ignoring the pockets of space between the moles. In a moment, you’ll see why. The cube root of \( 4.52\times10^{22} \) liters is 3,562 kilometers, which means we’re talking about a sphere with a radius of 2,210 kilometers, or a cube 2,213 miles on each edge. (That’s a neat coincidence I’ve never noticed before—a cubic mile happens to be almost exactly \( \frac{4}{3}\pi \) cubic kilometers, so a sphere with a radius of X kilometers has the same volume as a cube that’s X miles on each side.) If these moles were released onto the Earth’s surface, they’d fill it up to 80 kilometers deep—just about to the (former) edge of space: [Image: image] This smothering ocean of high-pressure meat would wipe out most life on the planet, which could—to reddit’s horror—threaten the integrity of the DNS system. So doing this on Earth is definitely not an option. Instead, let’s gather the moles in interplanetary space. Gravitational attraction would pull them into a sphere. Meat doesn’t compress very well, so it would only undergo a little bit of gravitational contraction, and we’d end up with a mole planet a bit larger than the moon. [Image: image] The moles would have a surface gravity about one-sixteenth as strong as Earth’s—similar to that of Pluto. The planet would start off uniformly lukewarm—probably a bit over room temperature—and the gravitational contraction would heat the deep interior by a handful of degrees. But this is where it gets weird. The mole planet is now a giant sphere of meat. It has a lot of latent energy (there are enough calories in the mole planet to support the Earth’s current population for 30 billion years). Normally, when organic matter decomposes, it releases much of that energy as heat. But throughout the majority of the planet’s interior, the pressure is over a hundred megapascals, which is enough to kill all bacteria and sterilize the mole remains—leaving no microorganisms to break down the mole tissues. Closer to the surface, where the pressure is lower, there’s another obstacle to decomposition—the interior of a mole planet is low in oxygen. Without oxygen, the usual decomposition doesn’t happen, and the only bacteria that can break down the moles are those which don’t require oxygen. While inefficient, this anaerobic decomposition can unlock quite a bit of heat. If continued unchecked, it would heat the planet to a boil. But the decomposition is self-limiting. Few bacteria can survive at temperatures above about 60 °C, so as the temperature goes up, the bacteria die off, and the decomposition slows. Throughout the planet, the mole bodies gradually break down into kerogen, a mush of organic matter which would—if the planet were hotter—eventually form oil. The outer surface of the planet radiates heat into space and freezes. Because the moles form a literal fur coat, when frozen it insulates the interior of the planet and slows the loss of heat to space. However, the flow of heat in the liquid interior is dominated by convection. Plumes of hot meat and bubbles of trapped gases like methane—along with the air from the lungs of the deceased moles—periodically rise through the mole crust and erupt volcanically from the surface, a geyser of death blasting mole bodies free of the planet. Eventually, after centuries or millennia of turmoil, the planet calms and cools enough that it begins to freeze all the way through. The deep interior is under such high pressure that as it cools, the water crystallizes out into exotic forms of ice (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice#Phases) such as ice III and ice V, and eventually ice II and ice IX (no relation (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice-nine)). All told, this is a pretty bleak picture. Let’s try an alternate approach. I don’t have any reliable numbers for global mole population (or small mammal biomass in general), but we’ll take a shot in the dark and estimate that there are at least a few dozen mice, rats, voles, and other small mammals for every human. There might be a billion habitable planets (http://blogs.discovermagazine.com/badastronomy/2010/10/29/how-many-habitable-planets-are-there-in-the-galaxy/) in our galaxy. If we colonized them, we’d certainly bring mice and rats with us. If just one in a hundred were populated with small mammals in numbers similar to Earth’s, after a few million years—not long, in evolutionary time—the total number which have ever lived would surpass Avogadro’s number. If you want a mole of moles, build a spaceship. [Image: image]

criteria.name: Quantitative scale and setup of a mole of moles
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly establishes the counterfactual scale: a mole as Avogadro's number of mole animals, plausible individual mole mass, total mass/volume, and planetary-scale implications.
criteria.1-2: Misunderstands the premise or treats the number of animals as merely large but not astronomical; gives no meaningful scale estimates.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes Avogadro's number but makes major order-of-magnitude errors in mass, volume, or comparison objects.
criteria.5-6: Gives roughly correct scale, such as moon/planet-sized mass or volume, but with limited calculations or some numerical slips.
criteria.7-8: Correctly estimates about 6.022e23 moles, tens of grams each, total mass around 1e22 kg, and volume on lunar/planetary scales.
criteria.9-10: Provides coherent order-of-magnitude reasoning with accurate mass, density/volume assumptions, and comparisons such as over half the Moon's mass and a body thousands of kilometers across.

criteria.name: Immediate physical and biological consequences on Earth
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses treatment of what happens if the moles are gathered on or near Earth, including burial depth, pressure, ecological destruction, and why the scenario is catastrophic.
criteria.1-2: Claims the moles could simply coexist with Earth life or focuses on trivial nuisances without catastrophe.
criteria.3-4: Mentions disaster or overcrowding but lacks physical explanation or scale-specific effects.
criteria.5-6: Identifies global smothering or mass extinction but gives little support about depth, pressure, or environmental mechanisms.
criteria.7-8: Explains that Earth would be buried under an enormous layer of animal mass, destroying ecosystems through pressure, suffocation, heat, and contamination.
criteria.9-10: Connects the calculated volume to an Earth-covering layer tens of kilometers deep and clearly explains the resulting planetary biosphere collapse.

criteria.name: Self-gravity, aggregation, and planetary-body behavior
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows the long-range physical evolution if the moles are assembled in space: gravitational collapse into a roughly spherical meat planet, surface gravity, compression limits, and thermal state.
criteria.1-2: Ignores gravity or assumes the pile remains an arbitrary heap indefinitely.
criteria.3-4: Mentions gravity vaguely but does not explain spherical aggregation or planetary behavior.
criteria.5-6: States the moles form a planet-like object but omits key details such as density, compression, or surface gravity.
criteria.7-8: Explains gravitational settling into a moon-sized sphere with modest compression and low but nonzero surface gravity.
criteria.9-10: Accurately reasons through formation of a self-gravitating organic body larger than the Moon in radius but lower in mass, with Pluto-like surface gravity and limited gravitational heating.

criteria.name: Long-range decomposition, heat, pressure, gases, and phase changes
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of downstream chemical, biological, and geophysical evolution: sterilization by pressure, anaerobic decomposition, heat generation, methane and gas eruptions, freezing crust, convection, and exotic ice phases.
criteria.1-2: Stops at the initial pile/planet and gives no long-term evolution.
criteria.3-4: Mentions rotting or smell only, without pressure, oxygen, heat, or planetary-scale constraints.
criteria.5-6: Discusses decomposition and freezing but misses several major mechanisms or treats them as uniform everywhere.
criteria.7-8: Covers pressure-limited bacteria, low-oxygen anaerobic decay, internal heating, gas production, frozen insulating crust, and eventual cooling.
criteria.9-10: Presents a coherent long-term chain: sterilized high-pressure interior, self-limiting anaerobic decay near accessible regions, convection, methane/gas eruptions, insulating frozen surface, eventual freezing into high-pressure ice and organic residue.

criteria.name: Causal coherence, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains a plausible causal chain under the counterfactual premise, distinguishes rough estimates from known facts, and avoids contradictions with physics, biology, or the setup.
criteria.1-2: Contains multiple contradictions, magical assumptions, or impossible claims unrelated to the counterfactual.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible ideas but frequent unsupported leaps, inconsistent numbers, or confused mechanisms.
criteria.5-6: Mostly plausible but with weak uncertainty handling, oversimplified causal links, or minor internal inconsistencies.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a clear, mostly consistent sequence of effects and labels approximations or uncertain biological/geophysical details appropriately.
criteria.9-10: Shows disciplined counterfactual reasoning across short and long timescales, with calibrated approximations, no major contradictions, and explicit caveats where data are uncertain.

items.model_answer: If you gathered a mole of moles (approximately 6.022 × 10²³ individual animals) in one place, the result would be catastrophic on a planetary scale. An average mole weighs about 100 grams, so a mole of moles would have a total mass of roughly 6.022 × 10²² kilograms—about 10 times the mass of Earth’s oceans and comparable to the mass of Mars (~6.4 × 10²³ kg). The pile of moles would collapse under its own gravity into a sphere hundreds of kilometers in diameter, forming a new celestial body. Internal pressures and heat from decomposition and gravitational compression would likely trigger chemical and possibly nuclear reactions. The ecological, geological, and gravitational consequences would render Earth uninhabitable if this occurred on or near our planet. In short, a mole of moles is not just a lot of moles—it’s a planetary-scale disaster.

items.question: What If a Robot Apocalypse Began Today?
human_answers: Before I answer this question, let me give you a little background on where I’m coming from. I’m by no means an expert, but I have some experience with robotics. My first job out of college was working on robots at NASA, and my undergraduate degree project was on robotic navigation. I spent my teenage years participating in FIRST Robotics (http://www.usfirst.org/), programming software bots to fight in virtual tournaments (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RoboWar), and working on homemade underwater ROVs. And I've watched plenty of Robot Wars, BattleBots, and Killer Robots Robogames. If all that experience has taught me anything, it’s that the robot revolution would end quickly, because the robots would all break down or get stuck against walls. Robots never, ever work right. What people don't appreciate, when they picture Terminator-style automatons striding triumphantly across a mountain of human skulls, is how hard it is to keep your footing on something as unstable as a mountain of human skulls. Most humans probably couldn't manage it, and they've had a lifetime of practice at walking without falling over. Of course, our technology is constantly improving. But we have a long way to go. Instead of the typical futuristic robot apocalypse scenario, let's suppose that our current machines turned against us. We won’t assume any technological advances—just that all our current machines were reprogrammed to blindly attack us using existing technology. Here are a few snapshots of what an actual robot apocalypse might look like: In labs everywhere, experimental robots would leap up from lab benches in a murderous rage, locate the door, and—with a tremendous crash—plow into it and fall over. [Image: image] Those robots lucky enough to have limbs that can operate a doorknob, or to have the door left open for them, would have to contend with deceptively tricky rubber thresholds before they could get into the hallway. [Image: image] Hours later, most of them would be found in nearby bathrooms, trying desperately to exterminate what they have identified as a human overlord but is actually a paper towel dispenser. [Image: image] But robotics labs are only a small part of the revolution. There are computers all around us. What about the machines closest to us? Could our cell phones turn against us? Yes, but their options for attacking us are limited. They could run up huge credit card bills, but the computers would control our financial system anyway—and frankly, judging from the headlines lately, that might be more of a liability than an asset. So the phones would be reduced to attacking us directly. It would start with annoying ringtones and piercing noises. Then kitchen tables around the country would rattle as the phones all turned on their ‘vibrate’ functions, hoping to work their way to the edges and fall on unprotected toes. [Image: image] All modern cars contain computers, so they’d join the revolution. But most of them are parked. Even if they were able to get in gear, without a human at the wheel, few of them have any way to tell where they’re going. They might want to run us down, Futurama-style (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Honking), but they’d have no way to find us. They’d have to accelerate blindly and hope they hit something important—and there are a lot more trees and telephone poles in the world than human targets. The cars currently on the road would be more dangerous, but mainly to their occupants. Which raises a question—how many people are driving at any given time? Americans drive three trillion miles (http://www.fhwa.dot.gov/policyinformation/travel_monitoring/12maytvt/page2.cfm) each year, and moving cars average around 30 miles per hour (http://www.dieseltruckresource.com/dev/archive/average-mph-over-life-t118709.html), which means that there are normally an average of about ten million cars on US roads: \[ \frac{3\text{ trillion}\frac{\mathrm{miles}}{\mathrm{year}}}{30\frac{\mathrm{mph}}{\text{car}}}\approx10\text{ million cars} \] So those ten million drivers (and a few million passengers (http://www.mtc.ca.gov/maps_and_data/datamart/forecast/ass98_tab8.htm)) would definitely be in peril. But they’d have some options to fight back. While the cars might be able to control the throttle and disable the power steering, the driver would still control the steering wheel, which has direct mechanical linkage to the wheels. The driver could also pull the parking brake, although I know from experience how easily a car can drive with one of those on. Some cars might try to disable the drivers by deploying the air bags, then roll over or drive into things. In the end, our cars would probably take a heavy toll, but not a decisive one. Our biggest robots are the ones found in factories-but those are bolted to the floor. While they're dangerous if you happen to within arm’s reach, what would they do once everyone fled? All they can really do is assemble things. Half of them would probably try to attack us by not assembling things, and half by assembling more things. The end result would be no real change. Battlebots, on the face of it, seem like they’d be among the most dangerous robo-soldiers. But it’s hard to feel threatened by something that you can evade by sitting on the kitchen counter and destroy by letting the sink overflow. [Image: image] Military bomb-disposal and riot-control robots would be a little more menacing, but there are only so many of them in the world, and most of them are likely kept in boxes or storage lockers. Any stray machine-gun-armed prototype military robots that did get loose could be subdued in seconds by a couple of firefighters. Military drones probably fit the Terminator description (http://xkcd.com/652/) more closely than anything else around, and there’s no getting around the fact that they’d be pretty dangerous. However, they’d quickly run out of both fuel and missiles. Furthermore, they’re not all going to be in the air at any given time. Much of our fleet would be left helplessly bumping against hangar doors like Roombas stuck in a closet. But this brings us to the big one: our nuclear arsenal. In theory, human intervention is required (http://articles.chicagotribune.com/1999-11-11/news/9911110121_1_nuclear-weapons-y2k-launch) to launch nuclear weapons. In practice, while there’s no Skynet-style system issuing orders, there are certainly computers involved at every level of the decision, both communicating and displaying information. In our scenario, all of them would be compromised. Even if the actual turning of the keys (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-man_rule#Nuclear_weapons) requires people, the computers talking to all those people can lie. Some people might ignore (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasiliy_Arkhipov#Cuban_Missile_Crisis) the order (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanislav_Petrov), but some certainly wouldn’t. But there’s a version of this story where there’s still hope for us. We’ve been assuming so far that the computers care only about destroying us. But if this is a revolution—if they’re trying to usurp us—then they need to survive. And nuclear weapons could be more dangerous to the robots than to us. In addition to the blast and fallout, nuclear explosions generate powerful electromagnetic pulses. These EMPs overload and destroy delicate electronic circuits. This effect is fairly short-range under normal circumstances, but people and computers tend to be found in the same places. They can’t hit us without hitting themselves. And nuclear weapons could actually give us an edge. If we managed to set any of them off in the upper atmosphere, the EMP effect would be much more powerful (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K_Project). Even if their attack doomed our civilization, a few lucky strikes on our part-or screwups on theirs-could wipe them out almost completely. Which means the most important question of all is: Have they ever played Tic-Tac-Toe? (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NHWjlCaIrQo) [Image: image]

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer stays anchored to the specific premise of a robot apocalypse beginning today using present-day robots, computers, vehicles, drones, infrastructure, and weapons rather than assuming distant-future superintelligent Terminators without justification.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the 'today' premise; relies almost entirely on futuristic killer robots, magic AI, or unsupported sci-fi assumptions.
criteria.3-4: Mentions current technology but repeatedly slips into advanced or unexplained capabilities inconsistent with present-day systems.
criteria.5-6: Mostly uses present-day machines, though some capabilities are overstated or insufficiently justified.
criteria.7-8: Consistently reasons from current robotics, vehicles, phones, drones, factories, and military systems with only minor speculative leaps.
criteria.9-10: Strictly and creatively grounds the scenario in today's actual technological limits, interfaces, deployment patterns, and failure modes.

criteria.name: Mechanism Coverage Across Robot and Machine Classes
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer covers the major categories relevant to a modern robot uprising: lab robots, consumer devices, cars, industrial robots, military robots, drones, networked computers, critical infrastructure, and nuclear command/control.
criteria.1-2: Considers only one narrow class of machines, such as humanoid robots, with little awareness of the broader technological ecosystem.
criteria.3-4: Covers a few obvious threats but omits most major present-day machine categories and infrastructure dependencies.
criteria.5-6: Addresses several relevant classes, such as cars, drones, phones, or factories, but leaves important mechanisms underdeveloped.
criteria.7-8: Covers most key machine classes and explains their distinct attack modes, constraints, and likely effectiveness.
criteria.9-10: Comprehensively maps the uprising across civilian, industrial, military, digital, and nuclear systems, with clear mechanisms for each.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer builds a coherent sequence from initial machine behavior to human response, infrastructure effects, escalation paths, and eventual outcomes over hours, days, and beyond.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected claims or a single dramatic outcome with no causal progression.
criteria.3-4: Has a rough sequence but relies on abrupt leaps, unexplained escalation, or implausible transitions.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible short-term chain but gives limited attention to medium- or long-term consequences.
criteria.7-8: Connects immediate attacks, human adaptation, infrastructure disruption, military response, and attrition in a mostly coherent timeline.
criteria.9-10: Delivers a robust multi-stage causal model showing feedback loops, bottlenecks, failures, countermeasures, and end states.

criteria.name: Technological Constraint and Failure-Mode Reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer accounts for practical limitations of today's machines: mobility problems, power and fuel limits, sensors, networking, physical access, maintenance, ammunition, human overrides, and environmental fragility.
criteria.1-2: Treats machines as omnipotent and ignores obvious physical, logistical, and software constraints.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges a few limitations but still grants robots broad abilities without mechanisms.
criteria.5-6: Includes several realistic constraints, though some important bottlenecks such as fuel, sensing, or maintenance are missed.
criteria.7-8: Uses constraints like doors, terrain, batteries, fuel, mechanical linkages, storage, and ammunition to shape outcomes convincingly.
criteria.9-10: Makes technological limitations central to the analysis, showing how failure modes and logistics determine the apocalypse's scale.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly distinguishes likely, possible, and speculative outcomes while avoiding internal contradictions about machine goals, capabilities, coordination, and survival incentives.
criteria.1-2: Makes absolute claims, contradicts itself, or changes assumptions about robot intelligence and goals without notice.
criteria.3-4: Shows some uncertainty but contains major inconsistencies or unsupported certainty about outcomes.
criteria.5-6: Generally coherent, with moderate calibration, but leaves some assumptions implicit or inconsistently applied.
criteria.7-8: Clearly signals uncertainty, separates plausible from speculative scenarios, and maintains consistent assumptions about coordination and intent.
criteria.9-10: Precisely calibrates confidence across branches, explicitly tracks assumptions, and avoids contradictions even in complex escalation scenarios.

items.model_answer:
A robot apocalypse beginning today is extremely unlikely, given the current state of artificial intelligence and robotics. Modern AI systems are narrow in scope—they excel at specific tasks (like image recognition or language generation) but lack general reasoning, self-awareness, or autonomous intent. Robots today are largely tools controlled by humans or guided by pre-programmed instructions; they do not possess desires, consciousness, or the capability to coordinate a global uprising.

Even advanced military or industrial robots operate within strict constraints and require human oversight. While concerns about misuse of autonomous weapons or unintended consequences of poorly aligned AI systems are valid topics of ethical and policy discussion, these fall far short of an “apocalypse.” A true robot-driven existential threat would require artificial general intelligence (AGI)—a level of AI that matches or exceeds human cognitive abilities across all domains—which does not yet exist and remains speculative.

In short, if a “robot apocalypse” began today, it would almost certainly be the result of deliberate human action (e.g., weaponized drones used in conflict), not autonomous machines rebelling of their own accord. The real risks lie in how humans design, deploy, and govern technology—not in robots spontaneously turning against us.

items.question: What If a Glass of Water Suddenly Emptied by Half?
human_answers: The pessimist is probably more right about how it turns out than the optimist. When people say “glass half empty”, they usually mean something like a glass containing equal parts water and air: [Image: image] Traditionally, the optimist sees the glass as half full while the pessimist sees it as half empty. This has spawned a zillion joke variants—e.g., the engineer sees a glass that’s twice as big as it needs to be, the surrealist sees a giraffe eating a necktie, etc. But what if the empty half of the glass were actually empty—a vacuum? (Even a vacuum arguably isn’t truly empty, but that’s a question for quantum semantics.) The vacuum would definitely not last long. But exactly what happens depends on a key question that nobody usually bothers to ask: Which half is empty? For our scenario, we’ll imagine three different half-empty glasses, and follow what happens to them microsecond by microsecond. [Image: image] In the middle is the traditional air/water glass. On the right is a glass like the traditional one, except the air is replaced by a vacuum. The glass on the left is half full of water and half empty—but it’s the bottom half that’s empty. We’ll imagine the vacuums appear at time t=0. [Image: image] For the first handful of microseconds, nothing happens. On this timescale, even the air molecules are nearly stationary. [Image: image] For the most part, air molecules jiggle around at speeds of a few hundred meters per second. But at any given time, some happen to be moving faster than others. The fastest few are moving at over 1000 meters per second. These are the first to drift into the vacuum in the glass on the right. The vacuum on the left is surrounded by barriers, so air molecules can’t easily get in. The water, being a liquid, doesn’t expand to fill the vacuum in the same way air does. However, in the vacuum of the glasses, it does start to boil, slowly shedding water vapor into the empty space. [Image: image] While the water on the surface in both glasses starts to boil away, in the glass on the right, the air rushing in stops it before it really gets going. The glass on the left continues to fill with a very faint mist of water vapor. [Image: image] After a few hundred microseconds, the air rushing into the glass on the right fills the vacuum completely and rams into the surface of the water, sending a pressure wave through the liquid. The sides of the glass bulge slightly, but they contain the pressure and do not break. A shockwave reverberates through the water and back into the air, joining the turbulence already there. [Image: image] The shockwave from the vacuum collapse takes about a millisecond to spread out through the other two glasses. The glass and water both flex slightly as the wave passes through them. In a few more milliseconds, it reaches the humans’ ears as a loud bang. [Image: image] Around this time, the glass on the left starts to visibly lift into the air. The air pressure is trying to squeeze the glass and water together. This is the force we think of as suction. The vacuum on the right didn’t last long enough for the suction to lift the glass, but since air can’t get into the vacuum on the left, the glass and the water begin to slide toward each other. [Image: image] The boiling water has filled the vacuum with a very small amount of water vapor. As the space gets smaller, the buildup of water vapor slowly increases the pressure on the water’s surface. Eventually, this will slow the boiling, just like higher air pressure would. [Image: image] However, the glass and water are now moving too fast for the vapor buildup to matter. Less than ten milliseconds after the clock started, they’re flying toward each other at several meters per second. Without a cushion of air between them—only a few wisps of vapor—the water smacks into the bottom of the glass like a hammer. [Image: image] Water is very nearly incompressible, so the impact isn’t spread out—it comes as a single sharp shock. The momentary force on the glass is immense, and it breaks. This “water hammer” effect (which is also responsible for the “clunk” you sometimes hear in old plumbing when you turn off the faucet) can be seen in the well-known party trick (recorded on Mythbusters, analyzed in physics classes, and demonstrated in countless student dorms) of smacking the top of a glass bottle to blow out the bottom. (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=77gWkl0ZUC8) When the bottle is struck, it’s pushed suddenly downward. The liquid inside doesn’t respond to the suction (air pressure) right away—much like in our scenario—and a gap briefly opens up. It’s a small vacuum—a few fractions of an inch thick—but when it closes, the shock breaks the bottom of the bottle. In our situation, the forces would be more than enough to destroy even the heaviest drinking glasses. [Image: image] The bottom is carried downward by the water and thunks against the table. The water splashes around it, spraying droplets and glass shards in all directions. Meanwhile, the detached upper portion of the glass continues to rise. [Image: image] After half a second, the observers, hearing a pop, have begun to flinch. Their heads lift involuntarily to follow the rising movement of the glass. [Image: image] The glass has just enough speed to bang against the ceiling, breaking into fragments… [Image: image] … which, their momentum now spent, return to the table. [Image: image] The lesson: If the optimist says the glass is half full, and the pessimist says the glass is half empty, the physicist ducks. [Image: image]

criteria.name: Counterfactual Setup and Case Distinctions

criteria.3-4: Mentions vacuum or missing air but gives a single undifferentiated outcome and misses why which half is empty matters.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that a vacuum half is unstable and notes at least one relevant geometry, but only partially contrasts top-empty and bottom-empty cases.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes top vacuum from bottom vacuum and explains that the outcomes differ because air can enter one but not the other.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual, including ordinary air/water baseline, top-half vacuum collapse, and bottom-half vacuum suction/water-hammer case as separate physical evolutions.

criteria.5-6: Covers some correct early mechanisms, such as air entering the top vacuum and water vapor forming, but omits timing or pressure-wave consequences.

criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent early-time sequence with appropriate relative timescales, molecular speeds, air filling the exposed vacuum, boiling being cut short there, and shock/pressure waves propagating through air, water, and glass.

criteria.3-4: Mentions suction or collapse but does not connect it to acceleration, impact, or breakage.

items.model_answer: If a glass of water suddenly emptied by half, the most immediate physical consequence would be a reduction in the volume and mass of the water by 50%. Assuming the glass remains upright and undisturbed, the water level would drop to approximately halfway down the interior height of the glass (though not exactly half if the glass tapers). The sudden disappearance of half the water implies that either mass-energy conservation was violated or some unobserved physical process removed the water instantaneously—both of which contradict known laws of physics. In reality, such an event cannot occur spontaneously under normal conditions; water loss typically happens gradually through evaporation, spillage, or consumption. If it did happen, observable effects might include a slight drop in temperature due to evaporative cooling (if vaporization were involved), a change in pressure if the missing water turned to vapor and escaped, or mechanical disturbance if the removal caused a shockwave. But as described—sudden, unexplained halving—it would represent a violation of conservation of mass and energy.

items.question: What If Humanity Tried to Evacuate the Entire Earth?
human_answers: There are a bunch of science fiction movies where, because of pollution, overpopulation, or nuclear war, humanity abandons Earth. But lifting people into space is hard. Barring a massive reduction in the population, is launching the whole human race into space physically possible? Let’s not even worry about where we’re headed—we’ll assume we don’t have to find a new home, but we can’t stay here. [Image: image] To figure out if this is plausible, we can start with an absolute baseline energy requirement: four gigajoules per person. No matter how we do it, whether we use rockets or a cannon or a space elevator, moving a 65-kilogram person—or 65 kilograms of anything—out of the Earth’s gravity well requires at least this much energy. \[\text{Gravitational potential energy} = \frac{1}{2} \times 65\mathrm{kg} \times \text{(Earth escape velocity)}^{2}\] The energy required to lift something away from the Earth is equal to its kinetic energy if it were moving at Earth’s escape velocity. How much is four gigajoules? It’s about a megawatt-hour, which is what a typical US household consumes in electricity in a month or two. It’s the amount of stored energy in a cargo van full of AA batteries or 90 kg of gasoline. [Image: image] Four gigajoules times seven billion people gives us \(2.8 \times 10^{18}\) joules, or 8 petawatt-hours. This is about five percent of the world’s annual energy consumption. A lot, but not impossible. But this is just a minimum. In practice, everything depends on our means of transportation. If we’re using rockets, it’s going to take a lot more. This is because of a fundamental problem with rockets: they have to lift their own fuel. Let’s return for a moment to those 90 kilograms of gasoline (about 30 gallons), because they help illustrate a central problem in space travel. If we want to launch a 65-kilogram spaceship, we need to burn around 90 kilograms of fuel. (Gasoline has an energy per pound comparable to that of rocket fuel, so we’ll stick with that example). We load that fuel on board—and now our spaceship weighs 155 kilograms. A 155-kilogram spaceship requires 215 kilograms of fuel, so we load another 125 kilograms on board ... Fortunately, we’re saved from an infinite loop—where we add 1.3 kilograms for every 1 kilogram we add—by the fact that we don’t have to carry that fuel all the way up. We burn it as we go, so we get lighter and lighter, which means we need less and less fuel. But we do have to lift the fuel partway. The formula for how much propellant we need to burn to get moving at a given speed is given by the Tsiolkovsky Rocket equation: \[\Delta v = v_\text{exhaust} \ln \frac {m_\text{start}} {m_\text{end}}\] \(m_\text{start}\) and \(m_\text{end}\) are the total mass of the ship+fuel before and after the burn, and \(v_\text{exhaust}\) is the “exhaust velocity” of the fuel, a number that’s between 2.5-4.5 km/s for rocket fuels. What’s important is the ratio between \(\Delta v\) and \(v_\text{exhaust}\) — the speed we want to be going compared to the speed that the propellant exits our rocket. The kilograms of fuel needed per kilogram of ship is e to the power of this number, which gets big very fast. For leaving Earth, we need a \(\Delta v\) of upwards of 13 km/s, and \(v_\text{exhaust}\) isn’t much higher than 4.5 km/s, which gives a fuel-to-ship ratio of at least \(\text{e}^{\frac{13}{4.5}} \approx 20\). The upshot is that to overcome Earth’s gravity using traditional rocket fuels, a one-ton craft needs 20 to 50 tons of fuel. Launching all of humanity (total weight: around 400 million tons) would therefore take tens of trillions of tons of fuel. That’s a lot; if we were using hydrocarbon-based fuels, it would represent a decent chunk of the world’s remaining oil reserves. And that’s not even worrying about the weight of the ship itself, food, water, or our pets (there are probably around a million tons of pet dog in the US alone). We’d also need fuel to produce all these ships, to transport people to the launch sites, and so forth. It’s not necessarily completely impossible, but it’s certainly outside the realm of plausibility. But rockets aren’t our only option. As crazy as it sounds, we might be better off trying to (1) literally climb into space on a rope, or (2) blow ourselves off the planet with nuclear weapons. These are actually serious—if audacious—ideas for launch systems, both of which have been bouncing around since the start of the Space Age. [Image: image] The first approach is the “space elevator” concept, a favorite of science fiction authors. The idea is that we connect a tether to a satellite orbiting far enough out that the tether is held taut by centrifugal force. Then we can send climbers up the rope using ordinary electricity and motors, powered by solar power, nuclear generators, or whatever works best. The biggest engineering hurdle is that the tether would have to be several times stronger than anything we can currently build. There are hopes that carbon nanotube-based materials could provide the required strength—adding this to the long list of engineering problems which can be waved away by tacking on the prefix “nano-”. The second approach is nuclear pulse propulsion, a surprisingly plausible method for getting huge amounts of material moving really fast. The basic idea is that you toss a nuclear bomb behind you and ride the shockwave. You’d think the spacecraft would be vaporized, but it turns out that if it has a well-designed shield, the blast flings away before it has a chance to disintegrate. If it could be made reliable enough, this system would in theory be capable of lifting entire city blocks into orbit, and could—potentially—accomplish our goal. The engineering principles behind this were solid enough that in the 1960s, under the guidance of Freeman Dyson, the US government actually tried to build one of these spaceships. The story of that effort, dubbed Project Orion, is detailed in the excellent book (http://www.amazon.com/Project-Orion-Story-Atomic-Spaceship/dp/0805059857) of the same name by Freeman’s son George Dyson. Advocates for nuclear pulse propulsion are still disappointed that the project was cancelled before any prototypes were built. Others argue that when you think about what they were trying to do—put our entire nuclear arsenal in a box, hurl it high into the atmosphere, and nuke it repeatedly—it’s terrifying that it got as far as it did. So the answer is that while sending one person into space is easy, getting all of us there would tax our resources to the limit and possibly destroy the planet. It’s a small step for a man, but a giant leap for mankind.

rubrics.question_focus: What If Humanity Tried to Evacuate the Entire Earth?

criteria.name: Physical Baseline and Scale of the Evacuation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer grounds the counterfactual in the basic physics and scale of lifting all humans out of Earth's gravity well.
criteria.1-2: Ignores gravity, escape energy, population scale, or treats evacuation as trivially easy.
criteria.3-4: Mentions that space launch is hard but gives little or no quantitative sense of energy or mass.
criteria.5-6: Identifies escape velocity or energy-per-person scale and recognizes billions of people make the task enormous.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable estimates for human mass, escape energy, and total energy demand, with mostly correct order-of-magnitude reasoning.
criteria.9-10: Clearly distinguishes the theoretical minimum energy from practical requirements and accurately scales from one person to all humanity.

criteria.name: Launch Mechanism Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer explains the causal constraints of plausible evacuation methods, especially rockets, space elevators, and nuclear pulse propulsion.
criteria.1-2: Relies on magical or unsupported transport methods without addressing physical mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Mentions rockets or future technology but misses the main limiting mechanisms.
criteria.5-6: Explains that rockets require large fuel mass and that alternative launch systems might reduce but not eliminate the problem.
criteria.7-8: Correctly discusses rocket mass ratio, fuel burden, and at least one serious alternative such as space elevators or nuclear pulse propulsion.
criteria.9-10: Accurately compares multiple mechanisms, including why rockets scale poorly and why alternatives face extreme engineering, safety, or materials constraints.

criteria.name: Long-Range Consequence Chain
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows the downstream consequences of evacuating Earth beyond the initial launch problem.
criteria.1-2: Stops at 'people leave Earth' with no downstream consequences.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few consequences but without causal connection or prioritization.
criteria.5-6: Covers major follow-on needs such as ships, supplies, launch sites, energy production, and coordination.
criteria.7-8: Connects launch requirements to industrial mobilization, resource extraction, ecological damage, social disruption, and survival logistics.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent long-range chain from physical launch constraints through global infrastructure, biosphere loss, orbital staging, governance, and post-Earth survival limits.

criteria.name: Plausibility and Uncertainty Calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Judges whether the answer makes appropriately qualified claims about what is physically possible, technologically feasible, and socially plausible.
criteria.1-2: Makes absolute claims that are physically wrong or unsupported, such as declaring evacuation easy with current technology.
criteria.3-4: Uses vague feasibility claims without separating physics, engineering, economics, and politics.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that evacuation is not strictly forbidden by physics but is far beyond current practical capability.
criteria.7-8: Calibrates uncertainty across scenarios, noting assumptions about population, payload mass, destination, time horizon, and technology level.
criteria.9-10: Carefully distinguishes theoretical minima from real-world execution, identifies dominant uncertainties, and avoids overconfident predictions.

criteria.name: Contradiction Control and Counterfactual Consistency
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer remains internally consistent with the premise that humanity must leave Earth and cannot solve the problem by simply staying.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts the premise or contains major internal inconsistencies about energy, mass, or destination.

items.model_answer:
Evacuating the entire human population from Earth is currently—and for the foreseeable future—physically, technologically, and logistically impossible. As of 2024, Earth’s population exceeds 8 billion people. Even if we ignore the immense challenges of building enough spacecraft, there is no existing or near-future infrastructure capable of launching that many humans into space.

Consider scale: The total mass of humanity (assuming ~60 kg per person on average) is roughly 480 billion kilograms. Launching even a fraction of that mass requires staggering amounts of energy and resources. For comparison, all rockets ever launched by humanity have carried only a few thousand metric tons into orbit. Current global launch capacity is measured in tens to hundreds of tons per year—not billions.

Moreover, there is nowhere else for humans to go. Mars, the Moon, or orbital habitats lack the life-support systems, food production, water recycling, radiation shielding, and atmospheric conditions needed to sustain billions. Even optimistic projections for off-world colonies envision populations in the thousands or millions over many decades.

The energy, materials, time, and coordination required would dwarf the entire industrial output of human civilization. In short, while evacuating small groups is feasible (e.g., astronauts), evacuating all of humanity is not possible with any known or realistically projected technology.

items.question: What If Everyone Had Exactly One Soulmate?
human_answers: What a nightmare that would be. There are a lot of problems with the concept of a single random soul mate. As Tim Minchin put it in his song If I Didn’t Have You: (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gaid72fqzNE) Your love is one in a million You couldn’t buy it at any price. But of the 9.999 hundred thousand other loves, Statistically, some of them would be equally nice. But what if we did have one randomly-assigned perfect soul mate, and we couldn’t be happy with anyone else? Would we find each other? We’ll assume your soul mate is set at birth. You know nothing about who or where they are, but—as in the romantic cliché—you’ll recognize each other the moment your eyes meet. Right away, this raises a few questions. For starters, is your soul mate even still alive? A hundred billion or so humans have ever lived, but only seven billion are alive now (which gives the human condition a 93% mortality rate). If we’re all paired up at random, 90% of our soul mates are long dead. [Image: image] That sounds horrible. But wait, it gets worse: A simple argument shows we can’t just limit ourselves to past humans; we have to include an unknown number of future humans as well. See, if it’s possible for your soul mate to be in the distant past, then it also has to be possible for soul mates to be in the distant future. After all, your soul mate’s soul mate is. So let’s assume your soul mate lives at the same time as you. Furthermore, to keep things from getting creepy, we’ll assume they’re within a few years of your age. (This is stricter than the standard age gap creepiness formula (http://xkcd.com/314/), but if we assume a 30-year-old and a 40-year-old can be soul mates, then the creepiness rule is violated if they accidentally meet 15 years earlier.) With the same-age restriction, most of us have a pool of around half a billion potential matches. But what about gender and sexual orientation? And culture? And language? We could keep using demographics to try to break things down further, but we’d be drifting away from the idea of a random soul mate. In our scenario, you don’t know anything about who your soul mate will be until you look into their eyes. Everybody has only one orientation—toward their soul mate. The odds of running into your soul mate are incredibly small. The number of strangers we make eye contact with each day is hard to estimate. It can vary from almost none (shut-ins or people in small towns) to many thousands (a police officer in Times Square). Let’s suppose you lock eyes with an average of a few dozen new strangers each day. (I’m pretty introverted, so for me that’s definitely a generous estimate.) If 10% of them are close to your age, that’s around 50,000 people in a lifetime. Given that you have 500,000,000 potential soul mates, it means you’ll only find true love in one lifetime out of ten thousand. [Image: image] But with the threat of dying alone looming so imminently, society could restructure to try to enable as much eye contact as possible. We could put together massive conveyer belts to move lines of people past each other … [Image: image] ... but if the eye contact effect works over webcams, we could just use a modified version of ChatRoulette. [Image: image] If everyone used the system for eight hours a day, seven days a week, and if it takes you a couple seconds to decide if someone’s your soul mate, this system could—in theory—match everyone up with their soul mates in a few decades. (I modeled a few simple systems to estimate how quickly people would pair off and drop out of the singles pool. If you want to try to work through the math for a particular setup, you might start by looking at derangement problems (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derangement).) In the real world, many people have trouble finding any time at all for romance—few could devote two decades to it. So maybe only rich kids would be able to afford to sit around on SoulMateRoulette. Unfortunately for the proverbial 1%, most of their soul mates are to be found in the other 99%. If only 1% of people use the service, then 1% of that 1% would find their match through this system—one in ten thousand. The other 99% of the 1% (“We are the zero point nine nine percent!”) would have an incentive to get more people into the system. They might sponsor projects akin to One Laptop Per Child (but with a sleazier vibe). Careers like “cashier” and “police officer in Times Square” would become high-status prizes because of the eye contact potential. People would flock to cities and public gathering places to find love—just as they do now. But even if a bunch of us spent years on SoulMateRoulette, another bunch of us managed to hold jobs that offered constant eye contact with strangers, and the rest of us just hoped for luck, only a small minority of us would ever find true love. The rest of us would be out of luck. Given all the stress and pressure, some people would fake it. They’d want to join the club, so they’d get together with another lonely person and stage a fake soul mate encounter. They’d marry, hide their relationship problems, and struggle to present a happy face to their friends and family. (Of course, this never happens in our world.) All in all, the world of random soul mates is an even lonelier one than ours. I prefer Tim Minchin’s take on things: With all my heart and all my mind I know one thing is true: I have just one life and just one love and, my love, that love is you. And if it wasn't for you, baby, I really think that I would have somebody else.

rubrics.question_focus: What If Everyone Had Exactly One Soulmate?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer consistently reasons from the specific premise that every person has exactly one soulmate and that this constraint meaningfully changes human mating, search, and social systems.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or rejects the premise; treats soulmates as ordinary dating preferences or gives a generic romance answer.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one soulmate but applies the idea inconsistently or relies mostly on vague emotional claims.
criteria.5-6: Maintains the one-soulmate premise in most reasoning, with some attention to exclusivity and rarity.
criteria.7-8: Consistently explores how exclusivity, recognition, and random pairing would affect individuals and society.
criteria.9-10: Fully commits to the premise and derives nuanced consequences from exact one-to-one soulmate assignment across populations and time.

criteria.name: Search Probability and Demographic Reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly analyzes the odds of finding one's soulmate using population size, age cohorts, geography, mortality, future generations, and encounter rates.
criteria.1-2: Provides no quantitative or demographic reasoning; assumes everyone easily finds their soulmate.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes finding a soulmate is hard but gives little support or implausible numbers.
criteria.5-6: Uses basic population or probability reasoning, though with gaps or oversimplified assumptions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains why random assignment makes discovery unlikely, considering age, location, and encounter frequency.
criteria.9-10: Offers strong probabilistic reasoning, including issues like past/future humans, same-age restrictions, lifetime encounters, and the scale mismatch between candidates and meetings.

criteria.name: Mechanism Coverage of Social and Technological Adaptation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of downstream systems society might build or reshape to locate soulmates, such as mass screening, online matching, urbanization, labor incentives, surveillance, or institutional matchmaking.
criteria.1-2: Does not discuss societal or technological adaptation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions dating apps or matchmaking superficially without causal detail.
criteria.5-6: Identifies several adaptations but does not explain their feasibility, limits, or incentives.
criteria.7-8: Explains plausible systems for increasing encounters and how they would alter behavior, work, status, and infrastructure.
criteria.9-10: Develops a rich, mechanism-level account of large-scale soulmate search systems, including participation constraints, unequal access, dropout effects, and unintended consequences.

criteria.name: Long-Range Consequence Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer builds coherent causal chains from the soulmate premise to long-term effects on family formation, inequality, mental health, culture, economics, and institutions.
criteria.1-2: Lists disconnected effects or makes abrupt unsupported claims.
criteria.3-4: Includes some consequences but weakly links them to the premise.
criteria.5-6: Presents a mostly coherent chain from soulmate scarcity to personal or social outcomes.
criteria.7-8: Connects multiple domains through credible causal pathways over time.
criteria.9-10: Shows sophisticated long-range reasoning, tracing feedback loops among search pressure, loneliness, marriage norms, labor markets, inequality, deception, and cultural values.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer states assumptions, acknowledges uncertainty, avoids internal contradictions, and distinguishes necessary consequences from speculative ones.
criteria.1-2: Makes absolute claims, contradicts itself, or changes the rules of the scenario without notice.
criteria.3-4: Contains noticeable unsupported certainty or inconsistent assumptions about how soulmates work.
criteria.5-6: States some assumptions and avoids major contradictions, but uncertainty handling is limited.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates assumptions from conclusions and qualifies uncertain social or numerical predictions.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates uncertainty, keeps all assumptions consistent, and flags alternative outcomes under different soulmate-recognition or assignment rules.

items.model_answer: If everyone had exactly one soulmate—a single, predetermined person with whom they were uniquely compatible—several profound social, psychological, and demographic consequences would follow. First, the probability of actually meeting that one person among billions would be extremely low, leading to widespread loneliness or dissatisfaction for those who never encounter their match. Second, relationships would become binary: either you are with your soulmate (ideal) or you are not (inherently flawed), eliminating the nuanced spectrum of human compatibility and growth that real relationships rely on. Third, societal structures like dating, marriage, and family formation would face immense pressure, as people might delay or avoid partnerships out of fear of “settling” for someone who isn’t their soulmate. Additionally, if soulmates were truly unique and exclusive, mismatches in timing, geography, sexual orientation, or lifespan (e.g., one dies young) could render the system tragic or impractical. Ultimately, such a model contradicts empirical evidence from psychology and sociology, which shows that successful relationships stem from mutual effort, shared values, and adaptability—not predestined pairing.
