items.question: What If Everyone in America Drove West?
human_answers: [Image: image] Thanks to plate tectonics, the United States is drifting west at about (http://hypertextbook.com/facts/ZhenHuang.shtml) a centimeter per year. (The people who live there, on the other hand, are on average drifting west at about a centimeter per minute (http://www.census.gov/newsroom/releases/archives/facts_for_features_special_editions/cb11ff10.html).) There are 212,309,000 (http://nhts.ornl.gov/tables09/FatCat.aspx) licensed drivers in the US, and since we have more cars than drivers, we can in theory get them all behind the wheel at once. The average car on the road weighs a hair over 4,000 lbs (http://www.nytimes.com/2004/05/05/business/05weight.html), so we have 850 billion pounds of car (plus around 30 billion pounds of driver) to throw around. The North American plate, by comparison, is about 25 million square kilometers in area and probably averages around 35 kilometers thick. Given a density of about 2.7 kg/Liter, its mass is probably in the neighborhood of \(2.3 \times 10^{21}\)kg, so it outweighs our fleet by a factor of about six trillion. [Image: image] But let's say we give it a shot anyway, and all 212 million of us point our vehicles due west and then floor it. For the dozen or so seconds we’d spend accelerating to freeway speed, our cars would exert very close to a trillion newtons of eastward force on the ground. In the absence of other forces, conservation of momentum tells us it would accelerate the plate up to a blistering 18 cm/year, more than enough to reverse the current motion. \[\frac{210,000,000 \text{ cars} \times 4100 \frac{\text{lbs}}{\text{car}} \times 75\text{mph}}{2.3 \times 10^{21}\text{kg}} \approx 18 \frac{\text{cm}}{\text{year}} \gg 0.69 \frac{\text{cm}}{\text{year}}\] But wait. The plates are moving so slowly that their motion isn’t dominated by momentum. They’re held where they are by a balance of forces—the complicated and boring ones from the beginning—and if we’re going to stop them, we probably have to try to figure out what they are. If the plates were drifting along as if they were sliding on ice, then we could push them easily. But it’s possible they’re locked on a slow-but-steady magma conveyer belt, and we can’t move them back without also shifting the flow beneath them. It was only recently—in the mid-20th century—that we discovered that continents move at all, and we’re still getting a handle on the complex forces between the plates and currents in the mantle that control continental motion. But they sound pretty complicated so let’s try to ignore them. We don’t care how it works—we just want to know if we can break it. These forces are hard to measure, so we’re not sure how they all work. There’s some evidence (http://www.umich.edu/~gs265/tecpaper.htm) that the flow of the mantle along the bottom of the plates isn’t as important as the weight of the edges of the crust as it sinks into the mantle, and the forces in the mantle pushing back against it. The geology literature gives us some loose estimates to work with. The drag from the mantle, resisting forward motion, is typically in the neighborhood of \(10^5\) to \(10^7\) newtons per square meter, meaning the existing eastward drag force on the North American plate is on the order of \(10^{19}\) newtons. That’s millions of times more than our fleet. The other forces are greater still. The fact that plates move steadily along in the face of drag that powerful suggests to me that the equilibrium of forces guiding them is probably fairly stable and unlikely to be responsive by our little shove. But conservation of momentum still works—so something has to move, and that something is the entire Earth, whose rotation would be sped up slightly. If our fleet were centered at around 39º N, the day would be shortened by only about 200 attoseconds—about a trillionth of a percent of the time it took you to read the word “attosecond.” If we drove east instead, the day would be lengthened by a similar amount. But considering the gasoline required, those 200 attoseconds would cost at least $50 billion. At 100 octillion times minimum wage, that’s a pretty bad hourly rate. All things considered, it would be a lot easier to just forget to change our clocks next spring and get a whole hour for nothing. [Image: image]

rubrics.question_focus: What If Everyone in America Drove West?

criteria.name: Correct physical setup of the westward-driving counterfactual
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly frames what happens when all licensed drivers in America accelerate westward, including force direction, conservation laws, and the distinction between cars, ground, plate, and Earth system.
criteria.1-2: Misstates the premise or basic physics; treats cars as pulling the continent west or ignores action-reaction entirely.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes many cars exert a force but gets important directions or conservation-law implications confused.
criteria.5-6: Mostly correct setup: westward cars push the ground eastward, but explanation is incomplete or loosely connected to the plate/Earth system.
criteria.7-8: Correctly explains action-reaction, transient acceleration, and conservation of momentum in the car-ground-plate system.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual with correct force directions, transient timing, internal-system momentum constraints, and why the whole Earth ultimately matters.

criteria.name: Quantitative scale comparison
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer uses plausible order-of-magnitude estimates for drivers, car mass, plate mass, vehicle acceleration, and resulting forces/effects.
criteria.1-2: Provides no useful numbers or uses wildly implausible magnitudes that drive the conclusion.
criteria.3-4: Includes some numbers but misses key scale comparisons, such as car fleet mass versus North American plate mass.
criteria.5-6: Gives broadly plausible estimates for fleet size or mass and notes that the plate is enormously more massive.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable order-of-magnitude calculations showing the fleet force/momentum is tiny relative to tectonic-scale forces.
criteria.9-10: Accurately integrates multiple relevant scales, such as about 200 million drivers, trillions of newtons during acceleration, plate mass near 10^21 kg, and tectonic forces near 10^19 N.

criteria.name: Tectonic mechanism fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly explains why a synchronized westward drive would not meaningfully move or reverse North America’s tectonic motion.
criteria.1-2: Claims the continent would visibly slide, stop, reverse, crack apart, or trigger massive tectonic changes without justification.
criteria.3-4: States the effect is small but gives little or incorrect explanation of tectonic resistance.
criteria.5-6: Mentions plate tectonics and mantle resistance but only at a surface level.
criteria.7-8: Explains that plate motion is governed by balanced tectonic forces such as mantle drag, slab pull, ridge forces, and boundary stresses, not simple free sliding.
criteria.9-10: Clearly distinguishes a hypothetical momentum impulse from real plate dynamics and shows why tectonic force balances swamp the vehicle-induced force by many orders of magnitude.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream effects and endpoint plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer covers the realistic downstream consequences after the cars accelerate, including the negligible effect on the continent and the tiny angular-momentum effect on Earth’s rotation.
criteria.1-2: Predicts catastrophic or dramatic downstream effects such as earthquakes, ocean sloshing, or major continental displacement.
criteria.3-4: Says little happens but omits the main physical endpoint or gives an unsupported ending.
criteria.5-6: Concludes the continent essentially does not move, with at least one plausible secondary effect or cost mentioned.
criteria.7-8: Explains that any tectonic effect is negligible and that the impulse is instead absorbed by the Earth system, producing an extremely tiny change in rotation.
criteria.9-10: Gives a coherent endpoint: no meaningful plate displacement, no practical geologic consequence, only an attosecond-scale change in day length plus mundane effects like fuel use, traffic, heat, and emissions.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles uncertain geophysical details carefully while maintaining a consistent causal chain without contradicting conservation laws or tectonic constraints.
criteria.1-2: Overconfidently asserts impossible outcomes or contains major internal contradictions.
criteria.3-4: Shows some caution but mixes incompatible claims, such as both moving the plate significantly and saying the force is negligible.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent, with limited acknowledgment that tectonic force estimates and mantle coupling are uncertain.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates robust conclusions from uncertain geophysical details and avoids unsupported extrapolations.
criteria.9-10: Maintains a disciplined causal chain throughout: assumptions are explicit, uncertainties are calibrated, dramatic claims are rejected, and all conclusions remain compatible with the scale analysis.

items.model_answer:
If everyone in America simultaneously drove west, the immediate effects would be catastrophic logistical and infrastructural failures. Roads—especially westbound lanes—would become instantly gridlocked, far beyond capacity, as tens of millions of vehicles attempted to move at once. Fuel supplies would deplete rapidly along major corridors like I-80 or I-40, leading to widespread shortages. Emergency services would be immobilized, supply chains disrupted, and accidents would multiply due to congestion and driver fatigue.

Over time, if people kept driving west without stopping, most would eventually reach the Pacific coast. Since you cannot drive further west across the ocean without a boat, vehicles would accumulate along coastal highways and cities like Los Angeles, San Francisco, or Seattle, overwhelming parking, sanitation, and resource systems. The mass migration would also cause massive environmental damage from emissions, tire wear, and oil leaks, and economic collapse from the abandonment of homes, jobs, and infrastructure elsewhere.

In short, while physically possible for individuals to drive west, a simultaneous nationwide attempt would result in societal breakdown long before anyone reached the coast.

edus.text: If everyone in America simultaneously drove west,
the immediate effects would be catastrophic logistical and infrastructural failures.
Roads—especially westbound lanes—would become instantly gridlocked, far beyond capacity,
as tens of millions of vehicles attempted to move at once.
Fuel supplies would deplete rapidly along major corridors like I-80 or I-40,
leading to widespread shortages.
Emergency services would be immobilized, supply chains disrupted, and accidents would multiply
due to congestion and driver fatigue.
Over time, if people kept driving west without stopping,
most would eventually reach the Pacific coast.
Since you cannot drive further west across the ocean without a boat,
vehicles would accumulate along coastal highways and cities like Los Angeles, San Francisco, or Seattle,
overwhelming parking, sanitation, and resource systems.
The mass migration would also cause massive environmental damage from emissions, tire wear, and oil leaks,
and economic collapse from the abandonment of homes, jobs, and infrastructure elsewhere.
In short,
while physically possible for individuals to drive west,
a simultaneous nationwide attempt would result in societal breakdown long before anyone reached the coast.

items.question: What If a High-Speed Train Had to Go through a Vertical Loop?
human_answers: No. Since this is kind of a disappointing answer, I tried relaxing the requirements a little. Could a high-speed train run through a vertical loop, like a rollercoaster, with the passengers staying comfortable surviving? Still no. Could a modified and reinforced high-speed train with a jet engine on top run through a vertical loop, like a rollercoaster, with the passengers staying comfortable surviving? Maybe. The Norwegian aluminium and energy company Norsk Hydro ran a pro-education ad (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hlczxXqez-Y) in which a bunch of kids build a giant roller-coaster loop on a train track as a prank. This is, of course, unrealistic, but not just for the obvious reasons. There are some problems with the whole idea of sending high-speed trains through loops. The first issue is geometry. The biggest vertical loop which a train could conceivably go around has a radius of about 200 meters. If it’s any bigger than that, even the fastest trains will fail to complete the loop. Unfortunately, a 200 meter loop is much too tight. Most high-speed trains are limited (http://khsrcl.com/downloads/Chapter%204.pdf) to vertical curves with radii no shorter than 20 kilometers. [Image: image] The reason for those limits isn't that trains aren't bendy enough. It's how fast they're going. The spec sheet for the Bombardier ZEFIRO (http://www.superscooper.com/en/1_0/pdf/Bombardier_Zefiro_Technical_Description_en.pdf), for example, says it can handle a pretty tight vertical curve radius—just 900 meters. At the train’s top speed, that curve would create about two gees of acceleration. This might be survivable (for the passengers, at least, if not the train), but it would certainly not be comfortable. Yet a 900 meter radius loop is still too big. Even with the engine at full power, the train wouldn’t even be able to get a quarter of the way around the loop before sliding back down. [Image: image] The CGI train in the Norwegian video is an Di 4 (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NSB_Di_4), which is shown moving about twice as fast as it can actually go. Based on its speed and number of cars, the loop appears to have a radius of about 70 meters, which is part of why it’s shown going so fast—the actual Di 4 would be just a little too slow, and would fall off the track at the top. The digital one, however, makes it around the loop in about five seconds, no problem. But the tight loop means the passengers and train are experiencing between 9 and 15 gees. This is at the limit of what fighter pilots can handle in pressure suits. In addition to killing everyone on board, it would certainly destroy the train, to say nothing of the track. 70 meters is much too tight. Clearly, we need a larger loop. 900 meters would be great, but our trains aren’t fast enough for that.\ But maybe we could make the train go faster ... Hmm. [Image: image] Believe it or not, this has been tried before—a number of countries have built jet-engine-powered trains (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turbojet_train). Sadly, they never took off. Fortunately, they never took off. A 747 engine mounted atop a bullet train would probably add about 35% to its speed. Is that enough to do a 900-meter loop? [Image: image] Nope. Ok, putting the jet engine on top didn’t work. Maybe we should try something different. [Image: image] ... why did we think that would work? Forget that idea. Clearly, we need some combination of a fast train and a medium-sized loop. The sweet spot for loop size and shape is probably something like this: [Image: image] Of course, given the height, we’d probably have to build it into a small mountain: [Image: image] The shape of the loop, which is common in roller coasters, would spread out the g-forces more evenly, resulting in a max of only a few gees—totally survivable! Of course, the construction costs would be astronomical, and it goes without saying that no group of kids could pull it off alone without the resources of a major government. To any Norwegian kids reading this who were hoping to build a train loop, don't despair—there may still be a way to make this happen. The US Vice President, Joe Biden, served in the US Senate for 36 years. In all that time, he never moved to Washington, DC. Instead, every night, he took the train home to Delaware to see his family. This is very touching, but after the first few years, I'm sure the commute got a little dull. So, if you’re looking for a high-level backer to help you make someone’s train ride a little more exciting, you might just try talking to Joe. [Image: image]

items.model_answer: If a high-speed train had to go through a vertical loop, it would face extreme engineering and physical challenges that make it impractical with current technology. Unlike roller coasters—which are designed for brief, controlled loops—trains are much heavier, longer, and not built to withstand the intense centripetal forces required to stay on track upside down. To safely navigate a vertical loop, the train would need sufficient speed at the top of the loop to maintain contact with the track (typically requiring a minimum speed of √(g·r), where *g* is gravity and *r* is the loop radius). For a train-sized loop (hundreds of meters in radius), this would demand enormous speeds and structural reinforcement far beyond standard rail infrastructure. Additionally, passenger safety, comfort, and cargo stability would be severely compromised by the high g-forces involved. Therefore, while theoretically possible under idealized physics conditions, a vertical loop is not feasible for real-world high-speed trains.

items.question: What If a Bowling Ball Were Enlarged to the Size of Earth?
human_answers: A good, professional-quality bowling ball is smoother than the Earth. Phil Plait, of Bad Astronomy, took a look at the claim that the Earth was smoother than a billiard ball. He concluded that the Earth was smoother but less round (http://blogs.discovermagazine.com/badastronomy/2008/09/08/ten-things-you-dont-know-about-the-earth/#.UZrBpmRAC9a), based on published billiard ball roundness tolerances. However, he couldn’t find any information on the size and shape of a billiard ball’s pits and bumps. Fortunately for us, there are people who digitally scan bowling ball surfaces (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r5V3rFdAIMY). [Image: image] These scans (along with various measurements of ball roughness[1] (http://classic.bowl.com/news/specsandcerts/index.jsp) tell us that a high-end bowling ball is quite smooth. If blown up to the scale of the Earth, the ridges and bumps[2] (http://www.itbca.bowlingknowledge.info/index.php/winter-2013/85-bowling-ball-shell-chemistry-101) would be between 10 and 200 meters high, and the peaks would be between one and three kilometers apart: [Image: image] By Earth standards, this is quite smooth; our highest mountains are 40 times higher. What would this bowling ball world (we’ll call it “Lebowski”) be like? For starters, bowling balls are a lot less dense than rock, so Lebowski’s surface gravity would be a quarter the strength of Earth’s: [Image: image] It would also (at first) have no atmosphere. [Image: image] The finger holes would be about a thousand kilometers across and a few thousand kilometers deep. [Image: image] On Earth, holes this big would expose the molten interior. But Lebowski doesn’t have a molten interior. The Earth’s core is hot for two reasons: It’s still glowing from the heat of all the dust collapsing together when it formed, and it’s full of radioactive metals. Lebowski wouldn’t have either of these, so its core would start out cold. The holes would be far too big to hold themselves open against gravity; On that scale, the polymers in the bowling ball would behave more like a liquid. In the space of about half an hour, the holes would undergo a slow-motion collapse. [Image: image] As they collapsed, the material around the holes would heat to a glow. At the center of the hole, a white-hot jet of charred hydrocarbons would fountain outward into space. When it was over, Lebowski would be left with massive scars, each marking the location where an abyss collapsed to form a molten sea. [Image: image] And now, thanks to this question, whenever I look at the Moon, I’ll notice the Sea of Tranquility, the Sea of Serenity, and the Sea of Crisis (http://www.google.com/url?q=http%3A%2F%2Fen.wikipedia.org%2Fwiki%2FFile%3AMoon_names.svg&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AFQjCNHIe4YcJnAZYmMY278G3Ko63hJnKQ), and I’ll think: Finger holes. But that’s just, like, my opinion, man.

items.model_answer:
If a bowling ball were enlarged to the size of Earth while preserving its composition and density, it would become a planet with roughly Earth’s mass but made of dense plastic or urethane (typical bowling ball materials). However, real bowling balls are slightly denser than water (about 1.3–1.4 g/cm³), whereas Earth’s average density is about 5.5 g/cm³ due to its iron-nickel core. So an Earth-sized bowling ball would actually be less massive than Earth—roughly one-quarter to one-fifth Earth’s mass.

More importantly, such an object wouldn’t behave like a real planet. Without internal heat sources, plate tectonics, or a magnetic field, it would lack geological activity and protection from solar radiation. Its surface would remain smooth like a bowling ball—but scaled up, even tiny imperfections (like finger holes) would become continent-sized features. For example, a standard 2.5-cm-deep finger hole scaled to Earth size would be over 300 km deep—far deeper than any natural trench.

Additionally, gravity at its surface would be weaker than Earth’s because of its lower mass, despite the same radius. Surface gravity scales with mass divided by radius squared; with ~0.25 Earth masses and the same radius, surface gravity would be about 0.25 g—making objects weigh only a quarter of what they do on Earth.

In short, an Earth-sized bowling ball would be a low-density, geologically dead world with weak gravity and bizarrely exaggerated surface features, utterly unlike our dynamic, layered planet.

items.question: What Would an Alien Civilization on the Nearest Habitable Exoplanet See When Looking at Us?
human_answers: Answer: [Image: image] Let’s try a more complete answer. We’ll start with ... Radio transmissions Contact popularized the idea of aliens listening in on our transmissions. Sadly, the odds are against it. Here’s the problem: Space is big. Really big.[1] (http://www.goodreads.com/book/show/11.The_Hitchhiker_s_Guide_to_the_Galaxy) You can work through the physics of interstellar radio attenuation, but the problem is captured pretty well by considering the economics of the situation: If your TV signals are getting to another star, you’re losing money. Powering a transmitter is expensive, and creatures on other stars aren’t buying the products in the TV commercials that pay your electricity bill. The full picture is more complicated, but the bottom line is that as our technology has advanced, less of our radio traffic has been leaking out into space. We’re closing down the giant transmitting antennas and switching to cable and fiber and tightly-focused cell-tower networks.[2] (http://arxiv.org/PS_cache/arxiv/pdf/1007/1007.0850v1.pdf) While our TV signals may have been detectable—with great effort—for a while,[3] (http://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/0610377v2.pdf) that window is closing. In the late 20th century, when we were using TV and radio to scream into the void at the top of our lungs, the signal probably faded to undetectability after a few light-years.[4] (http://www.worldcat.org/title/earth-as-a-distant-planet-a-rosetta-stone-for-the-search-of-earth-like-worlds/oclc/643269627) The potentially habitable exoplanets we’ve spotted so far are dozens of light-years away, so the odds are they aren’t currently repeating our catchphrases (http://xkcd.com/1212/). But TV and radio transmissions still weren’t Earth’s most powerful radio signal. They were outshone by the beams from early-warning radar.[4] (http://www.worldcat.org/title/earth-as-a-distant-planet-a-rosetta-stone-for-the-search-of-earth-like-worlds/oclc/643269627) Early-warning radar, a product of the Cold War, consisted of a bunch of ground and airborne stations scattered around the Arctic. These stations swept the atmosphere with powerful radar beams 24/7, often bouncing them off the ionosphere, and people obsessively monitored the echos for any hints of enemy movement. (I wasn’t alive during most of this period, but from what I hear, the mood was a little tense.) These radar transmissions leaked into space, and could probably be picked up by nearby exoplanets[5] (http://www.astrobio.net/exclusive/4847/seti-on-the-ska) if they happened to be listening when the beam swept over their part of the sky. But the same march of technological progress that made the TV broadcast towers obsolete has had the same effect on early-warning radar. Today’s systems—where they exist at all—are much quieter, and may eventually be replaced completely by new technology. [Image: image] Earth’s most powerful radio signal is the beam from the Arecibo telescope. This massive dish in Puerto Rico can function as a radar transmitter, bouncing a signal off nearby targets like Mercury and the asteroid belt. It’s essentially a flashlight which we shine on planets to see them better. (This is just as crazy as it sounds.) But it transmits only occasionally, and in a narrow beam. If an exoplanet happened to be caught in the beam, and they were lucky enough to be pointing a receiving antenna at our corner of the sky at the time, all they would pick up would be a brief pulse of radio energy, then silence (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wow!_signal). So hypothetical aliens looking at Earth probably wouldn’t pick us up with radio antennas. But there’s also ... Visible light This is more promising. The Sun is really bright [citation needed (http://www.google.com/search?q=site:craigslist.org+chevrolet+citation)] and its light illuminates the Earth.[citation needed (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citation_(horse))] Some of that light is reflected back into space as “Earthshine”. Some of it skims close to our planet and passes through our atmosphere before continuing on to the stars. Both of these effects could potentially be detected from an exoplanet.[4] (http://www.worldcat.org/title/earth-as-a-distant-planet-a-rosetta-stone-for-the-search-of-earth-like-worlds/oclc/6432)[6] (http://planetimager.org/) They wouldn’t tell you anything about humans directly, but if you watched the Earth for long enough, you could figure out a lot about our atmosphere from the reflectivity. You could probably figure out what our water cycle looked like, and our oxygen-rich atmosphere would give you a hint that something weird was going on (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Oxygenation_Event). So in the end, the clearest signal from Earth might not be from us at all. It might be from the algae that have been terraforming the planet—and altering the signals we send into space—for billions of years. [Image: image] Of course, if we wanted to send a clearer signal, we could. A radio transmission has the problem that they have to be paying attention when it arrives. Instead, we could make them pay attention. With ion drives, nuclear pulse propulsion, or just clever use of gravitational slingshots, we could probably send a probe out of the Solar System fast enough to reach a given nearby star in a few dozen millennia. If we can figure out how to make a guidance system that survives the trip (which would be tough) we could use it to steer toward any inhabited planet. To land safely, we’d have to slow down. But slowing down takes even more fuel. And, hey, the whole point of this was for them to notice us, right? So maybe if those aliens looked toward our Solar System, this is what they’d see: [Image: image]

criteria.name: Light-cone framing and viewing geometry
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly frames what aliens on the nearest potentially habitable exoplanet would observe as delayed, geometry-dependent astronomical evidence rather than a real-time or human-like view of Earth.
criteria.1-2: Treats aliens as seeing present-day Earth directly or with naked-eye detail; ignores light travel time and viewing geometry.
criteria.3-4: Mentions distance or delay vaguely but makes major geometric errors or assumes easy visual observation of Earth.
criteria.5-6: Correctly notes a years-long light-time delay and that Earth is hard to separate from the Sun, but gives limited geometric detail.
criteria.7-8: Explains delayed observation, angular proximity to the Sun, orbital phase/transit dependence, and telescope requirements with mostly sound reasoning.
criteria.9-10: Precisely integrates light-time, line-of-sight geometry, possible transit/reflected-light cases, and the distinction between observation and inference.

criteria.name: Radio and technosignature propagation mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates treatment of human-made electromagnetic signals, including broadcast leakage, radar beams, narrowband transmissions, attenuation, timing, and detectability from the nearest habitable exoplanet.
criteria.1-2: Claims aliens would easily watch TV, hear radio, or receive messages without accounting for signal weakening or directionality.
criteria.3-4: Mentions radio signals but gives simplistic or contradictory claims about range, power, or detectability.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that ordinary broadcasts weaken rapidly and that stronger directed radars or transmitters matter, but lacks mechanism depth.
criteria.7-8: Accurately contrasts diffuse leakage with powerful narrow beams, explains inverse-square loss, timing, bandwidth, and chance alignment.
criteria.9-10: Provides a nuanced account of TV/radio leakage, military/radar/Arecibo-like emissions, detectability thresholds, intermittency, and what aliens could infer.

criteria.name: Planetary optical and atmospheric signatures
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of non-human signals Earth would present: reflected sunlight, spectra, atmospheric composition, biosignatures, surface variability, and possible weak technosignatures.
criteria.1-2: Ignores Earth’s natural astronomical signatures or focuses only on direct images of humans/cities.
criteria.3-4: Mentions that Earth reflects light or has an atmosphere but gives little about what could be measured.
criteria.5-6: Identifies major biosignatures such as oxygen, water, clouds, or oceans but omits how they are detected.
criteria.7-8: Explains spectroscopy or photometry, including oxygen/ozone, water, methane, rotation, clouds, oceans, or vegetation-like signals.
criteria.9-10: Thoroughly links observational methods to likely inferences about habitability, biosphere, climate, surface features, and the faintness of human technosignatures.

criteria.name: Long-range causal chain coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Measures whether the answer builds a coherent chain from Earth-originating phenomena through interstellar propagation to alien instruments, observations, interpretations, and downstream conclusions.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected facts or speculative claims with no causal chain from Earth to alien observation.
criteria.3-4: Has a partial chain but skips key steps such as propagation, detection limits, or inference.
criteria.5-6: Connects emissions or reflected light to alien detection in broad terms, with some gaps or weak downstream reasoning.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a mostly coherent sequence from source to signal travel to detection to possible alien interpretation.
criteria.9-10: Sustains a detailed, noncontradictory causal chain across natural signals, artificial signals, instrument limits, timing, and inferred conclusions.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer handles ambiguity in the premise, unknown alien technology, habitability versus civilization, and avoids overclaiming or internal contradictions.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident unsupported claims, treats aliens as definitely present or technologically specific, and contains major contradictions.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges some uncertainty but still overstates what aliens would know or contradicts itself about distance, signals, or detectability.
criteria.5-6: Uses cautious language and notes technology dependence, but leaves some assumptions unstated or inconsistently applied.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes plausible, possible, and unlikely observations; handles unknown alien capabilities and exoplanet ambiguity consistently.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates all major claims, states assumptions, separates evidence from speculation, and avoids contradictions about timing, range, instruments, and inference.

items.model_answer:
The nearest known potentially habitable exoplanet is Proxima Centauri b, located about 4.24 light-years away in the habitable zone of the red dwarf star Proxima Centauri. If an alien civilization there were observing Earth with technology comparable to or slightly more advanced than ours, they would see Earth as it appeared approximately 4.24 years ago due to the finite speed of light.

They might detect Earth as a small, pale blue dot transiting the Sun, and through spectroscopic analysis of our atmosphere during such transits, they could infer the presence of oxygen, methane, water vapor, and other biosignature gases—strong indicators of life. If their instruments were sufficiently sensitive, they might also detect artificial signals such as radio and television broadcasts that have leaked into space over the past century, though these signals weaken dramatically with distance and may be difficult to distinguish from background noise beyond a few light-years. More recent digital communications (like satellite internet or fiber optics) produce far less leakage, so the “radio bubble” around Earth is actually shrinking in detectability.

Visually, Earth would appear as a faint point of light with subtle color variations hinting at continents, oceans, and cloud cover, but resolving surface details would require a telescope vastly larger than any currently existing—perhaps kilometers in diameter. Thus, while they could likely infer that Earth is a living world, discerning human civilization directly would be extremely challenging without extraordinarily advanced observational capabilities.

items.question: What If the Sun Suddenly Went Out?
human_answers: This is probably the single most popular question submitted to What If. Part of why I haven’t answered it is that it's been answered already. A Google search for what if the Sun went out (http://www.google.com/search?q=what+if+the+Sun+went+out) turns up a lot of excellent articles thoroughly analyzing the situation. However, since my recent articles on sunsets, the rate of submission of this question has risen even further, so I’ve decided to do my best to answer it. If the Sun went out ... [Image: image] We won’t worry about exactly how it happens. We'll just assume we figured out a way to fast-forward the Sun through its evolution so that it becomes a cold, inert sphere. What would the consequences be for us here on Earth? Let's look at a few: Reduced risk of solar flares: In 1859, a massive solar flare and geomagnetic storm hit the Earth.[1] (http://www.leif.org/research/1859%20Storm%20-%20Extreme%20Space%20Weather.pdf) Magnetic storms induce electric currents in wires. Unfortunately for us, by 1859 we had wrapped the Earth in telegraph wires. The storm caused powerful currents in those wires, knocking out communications and in some cases causing telegraph equipment to catch fire.[2] (http://trs-new.jpl.nasa.gov/dspace/bitstream/2014/8787/1/02-1310.pdf) Since 1859, we've wrapped the Earth in a lot more wires. If the 1859 storm hit us today, the Department of Homeland Security estimates the economic damage to the US alone would be several trillion dollars[3] (http://www.oecd.org/governance/risk/46891645.pdf)—more than every hurricane which has ever hit the US combined.[4] (http://www.google.com/url?q=http%3A%2F%2Fsciencepolicy.colorado.edu%2Fadmin%2Fpublication_files%2Fresource-2476-2008.02.pdf&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AFQjCNFnOWO7P0PV6qJSPhUUf56glVwZKQ) If the Sun went out, this threat would be eliminated. Improved satellite service: When a communications satellite passes in front of the Sun, the Sun can drown out the satellite's radio signal, causing an interruption in service.[5] (http://www3.alcatel-lucent.com/bstj/vol49-1970/articles/bstj49-8-1943.pdf) Deactivating the Sun would solve this problem. Better astronomy: Without the Sun, ground-based observatories would be able to operate around the clock. The cooler air would create less atmospheric noise, which would reduce the load on adaptive optics systems and allow for sharper images. Stable dust: Without sunlight, there would be no Poynting–Robertson drag (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poynting%E2%80%93Robertson_effect), which means we would finally be able to place dust into a stable orbit around the Sun without the orbits decaying. I’m not sure whether anyone wants to do that, but you never know. Reduced infrastructure costs: The Department of Transportation estimates that it would cost $20 billion per year over the next 20 years to repair and maintain all US bridges.[6] (http://www.fhwa.dot.gov/policy/2010cpr/chap7.htm#9) Most US bridges are over water; without the Sun, we could save money by simply driving on a strip of asphalt laid across the ice. [Image: image] Cheaper trade: Time zones make trade more expensive; it's harder to do business with someone if their office hours don't overlap with yours.[7] (http://eeecon.uibk.ac.at/wopec2/repec/inn/wpaper/2012-14.pdf) If the Sun went out, it would eliminate the need for time zones, allowing us to switch to UTC and give a boost to the global economy. Safer Children: According to the North Dakota Department of Health, babies younger than six months should be kept out of direct sunlight.[8] (http://www.ndhealth.gov/familyhealth/mch/babyfacts/Sunburn.pdf) Without sunlight, our children would be safer. Safer combat pilots: Many people sneeze when exposed to bright sunlight. The reasons for this reflex are unknown, and it may pose a danger to fighter pilots during flight.[9] (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8108024) If the Sun went dark, it would mitigate this danger to our pilots. Safer parsnip: Wild parsnip is a surprisingly nasty plant. Its leaves contain chemicals called furocoumarins, which can be absorbed by human skin without causing symptoms ... at first. However, when the skin is then exposed to sunlight (even days or weeks later), the furocoumarins cause a nasty chemical burn. This is called phytophotodermatitis.[10] (http://dnr.wi.gov/wnrmag/html/stories/1999/jun99/parsnip.htm) A darkened Sun would liberate us from the parsnip threat. [Image: image] In conclusion, if the Sun went out, we would see a variety of benefits across many areas of our lives. Are there any downsides to this scenario? We would all freeze and die. [Image: image]

criteria.5-6: Explains several central effects but with shallow or uneven mechanism detail.
criteria.7-8: Covers most major immediate and near-term mechanisms, including temperature decline, photosynthesis loss, climate disruption, and energy implications.
criteria.9-10: Comprehensively links solar radiation loss to thermal, ecological, atmospheric, oceanic, technological, and biological consequences.

criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected claims or an impossible timeline, such as instant freezing of all Earth life.
criteria.3-4: Provides a rough sequence but with major temporal errors or missing transitions.
criteria.5-6: Gives a plausible general timeline but lacks detail on intermediate stages or causal dependencies.
criteria.7-8: Develops a mostly coherent chain from darkness to cooling, ecosystem collapse, ocean freezing, and human survival limits.
criteria.9-10: Provides a nuanced long-range timeline with clear causal links, thermal inertia, refugia, infrastructure constraints, and eventual habitability limits.

criteria.name: Plausibility and quantitative calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer uses reasonable magnitudes, timescales, and uncertainty bounds for cooling, survival, oceans, atmosphere, and human response.
criteria.1-2: Uses wildly implausible numbers or absolute claims that contradict basic physics.
criteria.3-4: Includes some plausible statements but major quantitative errors dominate.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible but mostly qualitative or contains unqualified guesses about timing and survivability.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable approximate timescales and magnitudes, acknowledging uncertainty where exact values depend on assumptions.
criteria.9-10: Calibrates estimates carefully, distinguishing robust conclusions from uncertain details such as geothermal refuges, atmosphere freezing, and technological survival.

criteria.name: Contradiction control and treatment of secondary effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates internal consistency and handling of secondary consequences, including reduced solar hazards, astronomy benefits, timekeeping changes, and why these are overwhelmed by freezing and biosphere collapse.
criteria.1-2: Contains severe contradictions or portrays the event as mostly beneficial without recognizing existential consequences.
criteria.3-4: Mentions dangers and benefits inconsistently, with unresolved conflicts between claims.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes catastrophic outcome but includes some contradictory or poorly integrated secondary effects.
criteria.7-8: Consistently integrates minor benefits and secondary effects while making clear they are negligible compared with global cooling and ecological collapse.
criteria.9-10: Balances ironic or secondary consequences with rigorous consistency, explicitly resolving apparent benefits against the dominant extinction-level causal chain.

items.model_answer:
If the Sun suddenly went out—meaning it ceased emitting light and heat—the immediate effect would not be total darkness or cold on Earth, because light and gravity propagate at finite speeds. It would take about 8 minutes and 20 seconds for the last sunlight to reach Earth (the time light takes to travel from the Sun), and we would continue orbiting the Sun’s former location for that same duration, since gravitational changes also propagate at the speed of light.

After those 8 minutes, Earth would plunge into darkness. Photosynthesis would stop immediately, collapsing the base of most food chains. Surface temperatures would begin dropping rapidly; within a week, the average global surface temperature could fall below 0°F (–18°C), and within a year, it might stabilize near –400°F (–240°C), close to the temperature of deep space, though geothermal heat from Earth’s interior would keep some subsurface regions warmer for much longer.

Most life on the surface would perish quickly due to cold, lack of food, and ecosystem collapse. Only extremophiles near hydrothermal vents or deep underground, sustained by geothermal energy rather than sunlight, might survive for extended periods. Human survival would depend entirely on artificial energy sources, insulated habitats, and stored resources—but long-term survival would be extremely unlikely without the Sun’s energy driving Earth’s climate and biosphere.

items.question: What Would It Be Like to Row across Lakes of Mercury, Bromine, Gallium, Tungsten, Liquid Nitrogen, or Liquid Helium?
human_answers: Let's take these one at a time. Bromine and mercury are the only known pure elements that are liquid at room temperature. Rowing a boat on a sea of mercury just might be possible. Mercury is so dense that steel ball bearings float on the surface (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EGv_YVQHu7U). Your boat would be so buoyant that you'd barely make a dent in the mercury, and you'd have to lean your weight into the paddle to get the end of it below the surface. [Image: image] In the end, it certainly wouldn't be easy, and you wouldn't be able to move fast. But you could probably row a little bit. You should probably avoid splash fights. Bromine is about as dense as water, so a standard rowboat could in theory float on it. However, Bromine is awful. For one thing, it smells terrible; the name "bromine" comes from the ancient Greek "brōmos", meaning "stench". If that weren't enough, it violently reacts (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uCwHzTsx5yY) with a lot of materials. Hopefully, you're not in an aluminium rowboat. [Image: image] If that's not incentive enough to avoid it, the Materials Safety Data Sheet on bromine (http://avogadro.chem.iastate.edu/MSDS/Br2.htm) includes the following phrases: "severe burns and ulceration" "perforation of the digestive tract" "permanent corneal opacification" "vertigo, anxiety, depression, muscle incoordination, and emotional instability" "diarrhea, possibly with blood" You should not get in a splash fight on a bromine lake. Liquid gallium is weird stuff. Gallium melts just above room temperature, like butter, so you can't hold it in your hand for too long. It's fairly dense, though not anywhere near as dense as mercury, and would be easier to row a boat on. However, once again, you'd better hope the boat isn't made of aluminium, because aluminium (like many metals) absorbs gallium like a sponge absorbs water. The gallium spreads throughout the aluminium, dramatically changing its chemical properties. The modified aluminium is so weak it can be pulled apart like wet paper (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FaMWxLCGY0U). This is something gallium has in common with mercury—both will destroy aluminium (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z7Ilxsu-JlY). Like my grandma used to say, don't sail an aluminium boat on a gallium lake. (My grandma was a little strange.) Liquid tungsten is really hard to work with. Tungsten has the highest melting point of any element. This means there's a lot we don't know about its properties. The reason for this—and this may sound a little stupid—is that it's hard to study, because we can't find a container to hold it in. For almost any container, the material in the container will melt before the tungsten does. There are a few compounds, like tantalum hafnium carbide, with slightly higher melting points, but no one has been able to make a liquid tungsten container with them. To give you an idea of how hot liquid tungsten is, I could tell you the exact temperature that it melts at (3422°C). But a better point might be this: Liquid tungsten is so hot, if you dropped it into a lava flow, the lava would freeze the tungsten. Needless to say, if you set a boat on a sea of liquid tungsten, both you and the boat would rapidly combust and be incinerated. Liquid nitrogen is very cold. Liquid helium is colder, but they're both closer to absolute zero than to the coldest temperatures in Antarctica, so to someone floating on them in a boat, the temperature difference is not that significant. A Dartmouth engineering page on liquid nitrogen safety (http://engineering.dartmouth.edu/microeng/ln2.html) includes the following phrases: "violent reactions with organic materials" "it will explode" "displace oxygen in the room" "severe clothing fire" "suffocation without warning" Liquid nitrogen has a density similar to that of water, so a rowboat would float on it, but if you were in it, you wouldn't survive for long. If the air above the nitrogen was room temperature when you started, it would cool rapidly, and you and the boat would be smothered in a thick fog as the water condensed out of the air. (This is the same effect that causes steam when you pour out liquid nitrogen.) The condensation would freeze, quickly covering your boat in a layer of frost. The warm air would cause the nitrogen on the surface to evaporate. This would displace the oxygen over the lake, causing you to asphyxiate. If the air (or the nitrogen) were both cold enough to avoid evaporation, you would instead develop hypothermia and die of exposure. Liquid helium would be worse. For one thing, it's only about one-eighth as dense as water, so your boat would have to be eight times larger to support a given weight. [Image: image] But helium has a trick. When cooled below about two degrees kelvin, it becomes a superfluid, which has the odd property that it crawls up and over the walls of containers by capillary forces. It crawls along at about 20 centimeters per second, so it would take the liquid helium less than 30 seconds to start collecting in the bottom of your boat. This would, as in the liquid nitrogen scenario, cause rapid death from hypothermia. If it's any consolation, as you lay dying, you would be able to observe an odd phenomenon. Superfluid helium films, like the one rapidly covering you, carry the same types of ordinary sound waves that most materials do. But they also exhibit an additional type of wave, a slow-moving ripple that propogates along thin films of helium. It's only observed in superfluids, and has the mysterious and poetic name "third sound (http://www.physics.berkeley.edu/research/packard/current_research/schechter's%20web/page2.html)." Your eardrums may no longer function, and wouldn't be able to detect this type of vibration anyway, but as you froze to death in the floor of a giant boat, your ears would be filled—literally—with a sound no human can ever hear: The third sound. And that, at least, is pretty cool. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
Rowing across lakes of these substances would be impossible or wildly impractical due to their extreme physical and chemical properties:

- **Mercury**: A dense liquid metal (13.5 g/cm³) at room temperature. A boat might float, but mercury vapor is highly toxic, and its high surface tension and density would make rowing extremely difficult—oars would barely penetrate the surface, and any splash would pose severe health risks.

- **Bromine**: A volatile, corrosive reddish-brown liquid that evaporates readily into toxic fumes. It reacts violently with organic materials (including wood, skin, and most boat components). Any attempt to row would result in rapid corrosion of the boat and oars, along with dangerous inhalation exposure.

- **Gallium**: Melts just above room temperature (~30°C), so a “lake” would only exist in warm conditions. It’s non-toxic but wets many surfaces aggressively, sticking to glass, skin, and metals. It would coat and potentially alloy with metal oars or hulls, making rowing messy and mechanically problematic.

- **Tungsten**: Has an extremely high melting point (3,422°C) and does not exist as a liquid under normal planetary conditions. A “lake” of liquid tungsten would require temperatures hotter than lava—far beyond any survivable or material-compatible environment. Rowing is physically impossible here.

- **Liquid Nitrogen**: Boils at −196°C. Contact with it would instantly freeze and embrittle most materials (wood, plastic, rubber), causing them to shatter. The oars and boat would become brittle and break on contact, and the intense cold would be instantly lethal to a human.

- **Liquid Helium**: Exists near absolute zero (−269°C for helium-4). Like liquid nitrogen, it would freeze and destroy conventional materials. Additionally, it exhibits superfluidity—zero viscosity—so it wouldn’t provide the resistance needed for rowing; oars would slip through without propulsion.

In all cases, the environments are either lethally hazardous, physically incompatible with human presence or conventional materials, or simply nonexistent under natural Earth-like conditions.

items.question: What If You Dropped 3,000 Super Balls onto a Pedestrian from a Seven-Story Parking Garage?
human_answers: After falling from seven stories, the mass of bouncy balls would be moving at about 20 meters per second. 20 meters per second is about how fast an average person with a good arm could throw a bouncy ball. Therefore, to determine the result of an impact, we can make use of what Einstein called a gedankenexperiment, or "thought experiment": [Image: image] In science, it's important that results be repeatable, so let's try that again: [Image: image] The tricky thing about this scenario is that 3,000 one-inch bouncy balls is not as many as you probably think—it'd be enough to fill a large bucket. This bucket would weigh about as much as a small child, which leads us to another gedankenexperiment: [Image: image] Of course, in reality, the average person can't throw a small child as fast as they can throw a bouncy ball.[citation needed (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cetacean)] Furthermore, they won't all fall in one clump. If you poured the balls from a container, they would bounce around and spread out as they fell, and most of them would probably miss the target. This effect was demonstrated in an experiment by Utah State University students, who poured 20,000 bouncy balls from a helicopter (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fd7D1LWzWmo) as part of their Geek Week. The balls fell as a cloud, rather than a single mass. If you wanted to be sure of killing someone, you'd need a lot more balls. 3,000,000 of them—enough to fill a large room—would be be enough to guarantee that the target would either be crushed to death by the impact or buried too deep to dig themselves out. To your last question, if someone just happened to walk underneath when you dropped the bouncy balls, and they were killed by the impact, you'd most likely be guilty of some form of manslaughter. However, by asking this question, you've shown your intent to cause harm to the victim, demonstrating clear malice aforethought. By writing in to this blog, you've probably upgraded your charge to murder. All in all, you should probably stick to gedankenexperiments. [Image: image]

criteria.name: Impact Physics and Scale Estimation

criteria.9-10: Combines accurate back-of-the-envelope physics with clear comparisons to thrown balls and falling mass, while acknowledging simplifications like drag and bounce behavior.

criteria.3-4: Briefly notes that some balls may miss but still reasons mostly as if the drop remains a dense projectile.

items.model_answer: Dropping 3,000 super balls from a seven-story parking garage (roughly 21–24 meters high) onto a pedestrian would be extremely dangerous and likely fatal. While individual super balls are small and elastic, their collective kinetic energy at impact would be substantial. Each ball, weighing about 5–10 grams, would reach terminal velocity or near it—approximately 15–25 m/s—depending on air resistance. The combined mass of 3,000 balls (15–30 kg) striking a person in rapid succession would deliver a massive, concentrated force over a short time interval, akin to being hit by a heavy object dropped from height. The impact could cause severe blunt-force trauma, crushing injuries, or death. Additionally, the chaotic bounce patterns might create secondary hazards, but the primary threat is the cumulative force of thousands of impacts occurring nearly simultaneously. This scenario should never be attempted—it constitutes a lethal act of violence.

edus.text: Dropping 3,000 super balls from a seven-story parking garage (roughly 21–24 meters high) onto a pedestrian would be extremely dangerous and likely fatal.
While individual super balls are small and elastic,
their collective kinetic energy at impact would be substantial.
Each ball, weighing about 5–10 grams, would reach terminal velocity or near it—approximately 15–25 m/s—
depending on air resistance.
The combined mass of 3,000 balls (15–30 kg) striking a person in rapid succession would deliver a massive, concentrated force over a short time interval,
akin to being hit by a heavy object dropped from height.
The impact could cause severe blunt-force trauma, crushing injuries, or death.
Additionally, the chaotic bounce patterns might create secondary hazards,
but the primary threat is the cumulative force of thousands of impacts occurring nearly simultaneously.
This scenario should never be attempted—
it constitutes a lethal act of violence.

items.question: What If You Drained the Oceans through a 10-Meter Hole at Challenger Deep?
human_answers: I want to get one thing out of the way first: According to my rough calculations, if an aircraft carrier sank and got stuck against the drain, the pressure would easily be enough to fold it up[1]Extrapolated from the maximum pressure tolerable by icebreaker ship hull plates http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf (http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf) and suck it through. Cooool. Just how far away is this portal? If we put it near the Earth, the ocean would just fall back down into the atmosphere. As it fell, it would heat up and turn to steam, which would condense and fall right back into the ocean as rain. The energy input into the atmosphere alone would also wreak all kinds of havoc with our climate, to say nothing of the huge clouds of high-altitude steam. So let's put the ocean-dumping portal far away—say, on Mars. (In fact, I vote we put it directly above the Curiosity rover; that way, it will finally have incontrovertible evidence of liquid water on Mars's surface.) What happens to the Earth? Not much. It would actually take hundreds of thousands of years for the ocean to drain. Even though the opening is wider than a basketball court, and the water is forced through at incredible speeds,[2]xkcd.com/969 (http://xkcd.com/969/) the oceans are huge. When you started, the water level would drop by less than a centimeter per day. There wouldn't even be a cool whirlpool at the surface—the opening is too small and the ocean is too deep.[3]An experimental study of critical submergence to avoid free-surface vortices at vertical intakes (http://www.leg.state.mn.us/docs/pre2003/other/840235.pdf) (It's the same reason you don't get a whirlpool in the bathtub until the water is more than halfway drained.) But let's suppose we speed up the draining by opening more drains. (Remember to clean the whale filter every few days), so the water level starts to drop more quickly. Let's take a look at how the map would change. Here's how it looks at the start: [Image: image] And here's the map after the oceans drop 50 meters: [Image: image] It's pretty similar, but there are a few small changes. Sri Lanka, New Guinea, Great Britain, Java, and Borneo are now connected to their neighbors. And after 2000 years of trying to hold back the sea, the Netherlands are finally high and dry. No longer living with the constant threat of a cataclysmic flood, they're free to turn their energies toward outward expansion. They immediately spread out and claim the newly-exposed land. [Image: image] When the sea level reaches (minus) 100 meters, a huge new island off the coast of Nova Scotia is exposed—the former site of the Grand Banks. You may start to notice something odd: Not all the seas are shrinking. The Black Sea, for example, shrinks only a little, then stops. This is because these bodies are no longer connected to the ocean. As the water level falls, some basins cut off from the drain in the Pacific. Depending on the details of the sea floor, the flow of water out of the basin might carve a deeper channel, allowing it to continue to flow out. But most of them will eventually become landlocked and stop draining. [Image: image] At 200 meters, the map is starting to look weird. New islands are appearing. Indonesia is a big blob. The Netherlands now control much of Europe. [Image: image] Japan is now an isthmus connecting the Korean peninsula with Russia. New Zealand gains new islands. The Netherlands expand north. [Image: image] New Zealand grows dramatically. The Arctic Ocean is cut off and its the water level stops falling. The Netherlands cross the new land bridge into North America. [Image: image] The sea has dropped by two kilometers. New islands are popping up left and right. The Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico are losing their connections with the Atlantic. I don't even know what New Zealand is doing. [Image: image] At three kilometers, many of the peaks of the mid-ocean ridge—the world's longest mountain range—break the surface. Vast swaths of rugged new land emerge. [Image: image] By this point, most of the major oceans have become disconnected and stopped draining. The exact locations and sizes of the various inland seas are hard to predict; this is only a rough estimate. [Image: image] This is what the map looks like when the drain finally empties. There's a surprising amount of water left, although much of it consists of very shallow seas, with a few trenches where the water is as deep as four or five kilometers. Vacuuming up half the oceans would massively alter the climate and ecosystems in ways that are hard to predict. At the very least, it would almost certainly involve a collapse of the biosphere and mass extinctions at every level. But it's possible—if unlikely—that humans could manage to survive. If we did, we'd have this to look forward to: [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
Draining the oceans through a 10-meter-diameter hole at Challenger Deep—the deepest known point in the ocean, about 11,000 meters below sea level—is physically implausible due to fundamental principles of fluid dynamics and gravity. Water flows from higher pressure to lower pressure, but the ocean is already at hydrostatic equilibrium with the atmosphere and Earth's gravity. A hole drilled into the seafloor wouldn’t “drain” the ocean because there’s no lower-pressure reservoir beneath the Earth’s crust to receive the water; instead, the hole would simply fill with water up to the level of the surrounding ocean.

Even if one imagines a hypothetical tunnel extending deep into the Earth or out into space, practical limitations dominate. If the hole opened into a vacuum (e.g., a pipe leading to space), atmospheric pressure at sea level (~101 kPa) could theoretically support a water column only about 10.3 meters high—far less than the 11 km depth of Challenger Deep. Thus, water wouldn’t rise up and out; it would remain in place. Conversely, if the hole led downward into the Earth, immense geologic pressures, heat, and the plasticity of the mantle would seal or collapse any such opening almost instantly.

Moreover, even under unrealistically idealized conditions (e.g., a perfectly stable, frictionless conduit to an infinite void), the flow rate through a 10-meter hole would be limited by the speed of water under gravity and pressure. Using Torricelli’s law as a rough estimate (v ≈ √(2gh), where h is the effective head), the maximum theoretical velocity at Challenger Deep would be on the order of hundreds of meters per second, yielding a volumetric flow rate of perhaps ~10⁴–10⁵ m³/s. The total volume of Earth’s oceans is about 1.3 × 10¹⁸ m³, so even at 10⁵ m³/s, complete drainage would take millions of years—assuming the flow didn’t slow dramatically as sea level dropped.

In reality, none of this occurs: the oceans cannot be “drained” through a hole in the seafloor because there’s nowhere for the water to go, and Earth’s geology prevents such a structure from persisting. The scenario violates conservation of mass and energy unless paired with an unphysical sink, making it impossible under known physics.

edus.text: Draining the oceans through a 10-meter-diameter hole at Challenger Deep is physically implausible
Challenger Deep is the deepest known point in the ocean, about 11,000 meters below sea level
due to fundamental principles of fluid dynamics and gravity
Water flows from higher pressure to lower pressure
but the ocean is already at hydrostatic equilibrium with the atmosphere and Earth's gravity
A hole drilled into the seafloor wouldn’t “drain” the ocean
because there’s no lower-pressure reservoir beneath the Earth’s crust to receive the water
instead, the hole would simply fill with water up to the level of the surrounding ocean
Even if one imagines a hypothetical tunnel extending deep into the Earth or out into space, practical limitations dominate
If the hole opened into a vacuum
e.g., a pipe leading to space
atmospheric pressure at sea level could theoretically support a water column only about 10.3 meters high
far less than the 11 km depth of Challenger Deep
Thus, water wouldn’t rise up and out
it would remain in place
Conversely, if the hole led downward into the Earth
immense geologic pressures, heat, and the plasticity of the mantle would seal or collapse any such opening almost instantly
Moreover, even under unrealistically idealized conditions, the flow rate through a 10-meter hole would be limited by the speed of water under gravity and pressure
e.g., a perfectly stable, frictionless conduit to an infinite void
Using Torricelli’s law as a rough estimate
v ≈ √(2gh), where h is the effective head
the maximum theoretical velocity at Challenger Deep would be on the order of hundreds of meters per second
yielding a volumetric flow rate of perhaps ~10⁴–10⁵ m³/s
The total volume of Earth’s oceans is about 1.3 × 10¹⁸ m³
so even at 10⁵ m³/s, complete drainage would take millions of years
assuming the flow didn’t slow dramatically as sea level dropped
In reality, none of this occurs
the oceans cannot be “drained” through a hole in the seafloor
because there’s nowhere for the water to go
and Earth’s geology prevents such a structure from persisting
The scenario violates conservation of mass and energy unless paired with an unphysical sink
making it impossible under known physics

items.question: What If You Dumped Earth's Oceans onto Mars?
human_answers: In the previous What If (http://what-if.xkcd.com/53/), we opened a portal at the bottom of the Mariana Trench and let the oceans drain out. We didn't worry too much about where the oceans were draining to. I picked Mars; the Curiosity rover is working so hard to find evidence of water, so I figured we could make things easier for it. [Image: image] Curiosity is sitting in Gale Crater, a round depression in the Martian surface with a peak, nicknamed Mt. Sharp, in the center. There's a lot of water on Mars.[1]Donald Rapp, Accessible Water on Mars (http://spaceclimate.net/Mars.Water.7.06R.pdf), JPL D-31343-Rev.7 The problem is, it's frozen. Liquid water doesn't last long there, because it's too cold and there's too little air. If you set out a cup of warm water on Mars, it'll try to boil, freeze, and sublimate, practically all at once.[2]D. L. Santiago et. al., Mars climate and outflow events (http://spacescience.arc.nasa.gov/mars-climate-workshop-2012/documents/extendedabstracts/Santiago_DL_ExAbst.pdf) Water on Mars seems to want to be in any state except liquid. However, we're dumping a lot of water very fast (all of it at a few degrees above 0°C), and it won't have much time to freeze, boil, or sublimate. If our portal is big enough, the water will start to turn Gale Crater into a lake, just like it would on Earth. We can use the excellent USGS Mars Topographic Map (http://pubs.usgs.gov/imap/i2782/) to chart the water's progress. Here's Gale Crater at the start of our experiment: [Image: image] As the flow continues, the lake fills in, burying Curiosity under hundreds of meters of water: [Image: image] Eventually, Mt. Sharp becomes an island. However, before the peak can disappear completely, the water spills over the north rim of the crater and starts flowing out across the sand. [Image: image] When this kind of thing happens on Mars in real life, the trickle of water quickly dries up before it can get very far.[3]D. L. Santiago et. al., Cloud formation and water transport on mars after major outflow events (http://www.lpi.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc2012/pdf/2438.pdf), 43rd Planetary Science Conference (2012) However, we've got a lot of ocean at our disposal. [Image: image] The water pools in the North Polar Basin: [Image: image] Gradually, it will fill the basin: [Image: image] However, if we look at a map of the more equatorial regions of Mars, where the volcanoes are, we'll see that there's still a lot of land far from the water: [Image: image] Frankly, I think this map is kind of boring; there's not a lot going on. It's just a big empty swath of land with some ocean at the top. [Image: image] We haven't come close to running out of ocean yet. Although there was a lot of blue on the map of the Earth at the end of our last article, the seas that remained were shallow; most of the volume of the oceans was gone. And Mars is much smaller than Earth, so the same volume of water will make a deeper sea. At this point, the water fills in the Valles Marineris (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valles_Marineris), creating some unusual coastlines. The map is less boring, but the terrain around the great canyons makes for some odd shapes. [Image: image] The water now reaches and swallows up Spirit and Opportunity. Eventually, it breaks into the Hellas Impact Crater, the basin containing the lowest point on Mars. In my opinion, the rest of the map is starting to look pretty good. [Image: image] As the water spreads across the surface in earnest, the map splits into several large islands (and innumerable smaller ones). [Image: image] The water quickly finishes covering most of the high plateaus, leaving only a few islands left. [Image: image] And then, at last, the flow stops; the oceans back on Earth are drained. Let's take a closer look at the main islands: [Image: image] Olympus Mons, and a few other volcanoes, remain above water. Surprisingly, they aren't even close to being covered. Olympus Mons still rises well over 10 kilometers above the new sea level. Mars has some huge mountains. Those crazy islands are the result of water filling in 'Noctis Labyrinthus' ('the Labyrinth of the Night'), a bizarre set of canyons whose origin is still a mystery. The oceans on Mars wouldn't last. There might be some transient greenhouse warming, but in the end, Mars is just too cold. Eventually, the oceans will freeze over, become covered with dust, and gradually migrate to the permafrost at the poles.[4]Maggie Fox, Mars May Not Have Been Warm Or Wet (http://rense.com/general32/marsmaynothave.htm) However, it would take a long time, and until it did, Mars would be a much more interesting place. When you consider that there's a ready-made portal system to allow transit between the two planets, the consequences are inevitable: [Image: image]

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Dumped Earth's Oceans onto Mars?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Setup and Conservation of Water Volume
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly frames the premise as rapidly transferring roughly Earth's ocean volume to Mars and reasons from that finite volume without inventing unsupported sources, losses, or impossible endpoints.
criteria.1-2: Misstates the premise or treats the water amount, rate, or destination in a way that makes the scenario unrecognizable.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes water is dumped on Mars but gives vague or inconsistent quantities, or assumes immediate disappearance/terraforming without support.
criteria.5-6: Uses the finite Earth-ocean volume reasonably and notes Mars is smaller, but only loosely connects volume to depth and coverage.
criteria.7-8: Clearly reasons that Earth's ocean volume would create extensive Martian seas because Mars has lower surface area, while avoiding major conservation errors.
criteria.9-10: Precisely maintains the counterfactual constraints: rapid large-volume transfer, finite ocean supply, Mars-scale topography, and no unsupported creation or loss of bulk water.

criteria.name: Martian Topography and Flooding Progression
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of how water would spread over Mars: initial pooling, basin filling, spillover, coverage of lowlands, and persistence of high volcanic regions above sea level.
criteria.1-2: Ignores Martian terrain or claims the planet is uniformly covered with water without regard to elevation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions flooding Mars but gives a simplistic or topographically implausible map of the result.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some relevant basins or mountains, such as polar lowlands or Olympus Mons, but with incomplete progression.
criteria.7-8: Describes plausible staged filling of craters, northern lowlands, Valles Marineris/Hellas, and remaining high islands.
criteria.9-10: Gives a coherent topographic sequence matching Mars: crater filling and spillover, North Polar Basin accumulation, canyon/basin flooding, broad seas, and Olympus Mons/Tharsis volcanoes remaining high above water.

criteria.name: Water Phase Behavior and Martian Climate Response
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses understanding of how liquid water behaves under Martian pressure, temperature, atmosphere, and timescales, including boiling/freezing/sublimation versus temporary liquid persistence during rapid flooding.
criteria.1-2: Claims ordinary stable oceans form permanently or that all water instantly vanishes, with no physical reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Mars is cold or low-pressure but applies this simplistically or contradictorily.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes water would tend to freeze, boil, or sublimate, while allowing some transient liquid flooding.
criteria.7-8: Explains that rapid dumping can temporarily produce lakes/seas despite Mars's hostile conditions, followed by freezing and atmospheric loss/migration.
criteria.9-10: Accurately balances short-term liquid flow with long-term instability: partial boiling/evaporation, ice cover formation, dust burial, sublimation/transport, and eventual redistribution toward cold traps/permafrost.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain and Downstream Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Measures whether the answer traces consequences over multiple stages, from immediate impact and flow dynamics to temporary environmental changes, rover burial, possible greenhouse effects, and eventual frozen/dust-covered oceans.
criteria.1-2: Provides only a single outcome with little or no causal chain.
criteria.3-4: Lists disconnected effects without clear temporal ordering or mechanism.
criteria.5-6: Includes short- and long-term effects but omits major links such as basin overflow, transient climate effects, or eventual freezing.
criteria.7-8: Presents a mostly coherent timeline from dumping to flooding, temporary seas, environmental changes, and long-term freeze-out.
criteria.9-10: Maintains a detailed, causally connected sequence across timescales, including local inundation, global redistribution, climate feedback limits, ice formation, dust cover, and eventual migration/stabilization of water.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer distinguishes robust implications from uncertain estimates and avoids contradictions with Mars physics, known topography, and the counterfactual premise.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, impossible claims, or confident assertions that violate basic planetary science.
criteria.3-4: Has several unsupported or conflicting claims, such as permanent habitability or total atmospheric transformation with no caveats.
criteria.5-6: Mostly plausible but overconfident in some numbers, timescales, or biological/terraforming consequences.
criteria.7-8: Clearly flags uncertain timescales and secondary effects while keeping main physical conclusions consistent.
criteria.9-10: Carefully separates likely outcomes from speculative ones, avoids internal contradictions, and calibrates uncertainties in flow rate, evaporation, greenhouse warming, freezing time, and final water distribution.

items.model_answer: If Earth’s oceans were dumped onto Mars, the water would not remain liquid for long due to Mars’s thin atmosphere (about 0.6% of Earth’s sea-level pressure) and average surface temperature of around –60°C. Most of the water would quickly freeze into ice, especially at the poles and in shaded regions. Some fraction might briefly exist as liquid in low-lying areas like Valles Marineris or Hellas Basin, where atmospheric pressure is slightly higher, but it would either freeze or sublimate (turn directly from ice to vapor) over time. The added mass—Earth’s oceans contain about 1.4 billion cubic kilometers of water—would significantly alter Mars’s geology and potentially reactivate some hydrological processes temporarily, but without a strong magnetic field and thicker atmosphere to retain heat and pressure, Mars could not sustain liquid oceans long-term. Much of the water vapor released might eventually be lost to space due to solar wind stripping, as Mars lacks a global magnetic field to protect its atmosphere.

edus.text: If Earth’s oceans were dumped onto Mars,
the water would not remain liquid for long
due to Mars’s thin atmosphere
(about 0.6% of Earth’s sea-level pressure)
and average surface temperature of around –60°C.
Most of the water would quickly freeze into ice,
especially at the poles and in shaded regions.
Some fraction might briefly exist as liquid in low-lying areas like Valles Marineris or Hellas Basin,
where atmospheric pressure is slightly higher,
but it would either freeze or sublimate
(turn directly from ice to vapor)
over time.
The added mass—Earth’s oceans contain about 1.4 billion cubic kilometers of water—
would significantly alter Mars’s geology
and potentially reactivate some hydrological processes temporarily,
but without a strong magnetic field and thicker atmosphere to retain heat and pressure,
Mars could not sustain liquid oceans long-term.
Much of the water vapor released might eventually be lost to space
due to solar wind stripping,
as Mars lacks a global magnetic field to protect its atmosphere.
