items.question: What If You Tried to Hold an Airplane to the Ground with a Rope?
human_answers: Ah, the Just Cause 2 scenario (http://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=just+cause+2+plane+grapple). At takeoff, a 747's four engines can each generate 281.57 kN of thrust. I have no real sense for what that number means, so let's put it in different terms: [Image: image] A 747 with all engines at full could roughly balance the weight of a dangling blue whale. With all that weight, how thick would the cable need to be? Surprisingly, not all that thick! A cable a little over an inch in diameter would do it.[1]Bethlehem Wire Rope General Purpose Catalog (http://www.wwwrope.com/product_pdfs/GP_CAT.pdf) Let's suppose you don't have a cable lying around. What else could you use? If you're into fishing, you might have some fishing line. A typical line for saltwater fishing might have a 50-100 lb strength,[2]West Marine: Selecting Fishing Line (http://www.wwwrope.com/product_pdfs/GP_CAT.pdf) so it would take a brigade of several thousand people armed with fishing rods to restrain the plane. [Image: image] If you don't have fishing line, there's one thing you probably do have: Hair. While hair isn't as strong as steel, it's just about the strongest material in your body,[3]Examples of the Tensile Strength of Materials (http://web2.clarkson.edu/class/me380/materials_tenstrength.pdf) with a tensile strength rivaling or exceeding that of bone.[4]Properties of Textile Fibers (http://www.academia.edu/2179355/Properties_of_Textile_Fibers) This tensile strength is why performers are able to hang by their hair at the circus. In fact, from a materials standpoint, it's actually more impressive that performers are able to hang by their arms. Based on these hair strength figures, a piece of hair three inches in diameter would be strong enough to restrain a 747.[5]If you wanted to measure the strength of a strand of hair, you could use the device described by US Patent #4628742A (http://www.google.com/patents/US4628742), "Tensile strength tester for hair" Hairs that big around are hard to come by.[6]... I hope. Since most of us have many small hairs, instead of one big hair ... [Image: image] ... we'd need to get a lot of hairs and bundle them together. Given that individual hairs can support about 50 grams of weight, we'd need roughly 20 heads of hair to restrain the aircraft. [Image: image] Conclusion: Restraining a plane with a cable would be pretty easy. Further conclusion: Blue whales are not typically covered in hair,[8]Although they are mammals, most whales do not have coats of hair like land mammals typically do (http://bioweb.uwlax.edu/bio203/s2012/olson_rile/adaptation.htm) but if we transplanted the hair from at least 20 human heads onto a blue whale ... [Image: image] ... it would have enough hair to perform acrobatics at a circus.

criteria.name: 747 thrust-to-rope load quantification
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer grounds the counterfactual in the relevant forces: a large jet's takeoff thrust, how that translates into rope tension, and the approximate scale of the load being resisted.
criteria.1-2: Gives only vague claims such as 'the plane would pull hard' with no meaningful force scale or confuses thrust with aircraft weight/lift.
criteria.3-4: Mentions large engine thrust or rope tension but uses implausible magnitudes, omits units, or treats the rope as resisting the entire aircraft weight without explanation.
criteria.5-6: Provides a roughly plausible force estimate for a 747-class aircraft and recognizes the rope mainly resists engine thrust during takeoff, though with limited precision or caveats.
criteria.7-8: Correctly estimates total thrust on the order of 1 MN, relates it to an intuitive equivalent load, and distinguishes thrust, weight, lift, and tension reasonably well.
criteria.9-10: Accurately and clearly quantifies the thrust/load scale, explains why the rope tension is set primarily by engine thrust and dynamics, and uses comparisons without introducing misleading physics.

criteria.name: Material strength and required rope size reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly reasons from tensile strength or rated breaking strength to the required rope/cable size, including safety and failure considerations.
criteria.1-2: Does not address rope strength, or asserts that any ordinary rope/cable would or would not work with no basis.
criteria.3-4: Mentions strong rope or steel cable but gives unsupported or physically inconsistent size requirements.
criteria.5-6: Uses breaking strength or tensile strength in a plausible way and concludes that a robust steel cable of inch-scale diameter could restrain the thrust, though details may be rough.
criteria.7-8: Connects material strength, cross-sectional area, and total thrust; notes that cable ratings, knots, attachments, and safety factors can dominate real-world failure.
criteria.9-10: Gives a well-calibrated estimate for cable diameter/strength, distinguishes ideal tensile capacity from real rigging limits, and explains likely failure points such as anchors, knots, or connectors.

criteria.name: Takeoff dynamics, anchoring, and causal outcome
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the causal chain of what actually happens when the airplane attempts to take off while tied down: acceleration, tension buildup, possible breakage, anchor failure, aircraft damage, or successful restraint.
criteria.1-2: Offers a cartoon outcome with no causal mechanism, such as the plane simply stops or instantly crashes.
criteria.3-4: Identifies one possible outcome, like the rope snaps, but does not explain how tension develops or what determines the result.
criteria.5-6: Explains that the result depends on rope/anchor strength versus thrust and that a sufficiently strong setup can hold the aircraft while a weak one fails.
criteria.7-8: Traces the sequence from engine spool-up to increasing tension, limited acceleration, load transfer to anchor, and likely failure modes if any component is undersized.
criteria.9-10: Presents a coherent dynamic scenario including transient loads, runway friction/braking or chocks if relevant, anchor-ground interaction, aircraft structural attachment limits, and the difference between static restraint and a moving snag.

criteria.name: Coverage of alternative restraining materials and scale comparisons
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer explores the counterfactual's downstream implications using plausible comparisons such as steel cable, fishing line, hair bundles, or biological analogies, without losing physical consistency.
criteria.1-2: Provides no meaningful scale comparisons or uses fanciful comparisons that contradict the force estimates.
criteria.3-4: Includes one comparison, but it is numerically unsupported or wildly inconsistent with material strengths.
criteria.5-6: Includes at least one plausible alternative-material comparison, such as many fishing lines or many hairs, with order-of-magnitude reasoning.
criteria.7-8: Covers several alternatives and explains how many strands/people/hairs would be needed based on breaking strength, while keeping estimates within plausible ranges.
criteria.9-10: Uses comparisons to deepen understanding of the force scale, accurately translating thrust into quantities of cable, fishing line, hair, or equivalent weight, and avoids overclaiming precision.

criteria.name: Long-range coherence, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer maintains a consistent causal model across the entire explanation, flags assumptions, and avoids contradictions about engines, lift, rope behavior, and material limits.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions or impossible claims, such as the rope preventing lift by canceling gravity or the aircraft pulling with unlimited force.
criteria.3-4: Has some correct ideas but mixes incompatible assumptions, ignores uncertainty, or changes the scenario mid-answer without notice.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent and plausible, with stated or implied assumptions, though some estimates or causal links are underdeveloped.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a consistent premise and causal chain, acknowledges uncertainty in aircraft model, rope material, attachment, and loading, and separates rough estimates from firm conclusions.
criteria.9-10: Delivers a tightly controlled long-range explanation with explicit assumptions, calibrated uncertainty, no internal contradictions, and conclusions that follow directly from the physics and material limits.

items.model_answer: If you tried to hold an airplane to the ground with a rope, the outcome would depend on the size and power of the airplane, the strength of the rope, and how securely it was anchored. For a typical commercial jet preparing for takeoff, the thrust generated by its engines (often exceeding 100,000 pounds-force per engine) vastly exceeds the tensile strength of any practical rope or cable. Even heavy-duty steel cables used in industrial applications typically fail well below that threshold. As the engines spool up, the force would quickly snap the rope or rip its anchor point from the ground. The airplane would then accelerate normally and take off, possibly with minor damage if the rope caused entanglement. In short, a rope cannot meaningfully restrain a powered aircraft attempting to take off—it would break almost instantly under the load.

edus.text: If you tried to hold an airplane to the ground with a rope,
the outcome would depend on the size and power of the airplane, the strength of the rope, and how securely it was anchored.
For a typical commercial jet preparing for takeoff,
the thrust generated by its engines vastly exceeds the tensile strength of any practical rope or cable.
often exceeding 100,000 pounds-force per engine
Even heavy-duty steel cables used in industrial applications typically fail well below that threshold.
As the engines spool up,
the force would quickly snap the rope or rip its anchor point from the ground.
The airplane would then accelerate normally and take off,
possibly with minor damage if the rope caused entanglement.
In short,
a rope cannot meaningfully restrain a powered aircraft attempting to take off—
it would break almost instantly under the load.

items.question: What If the Bottom Inch of a Massive Mountain Vanished?
human_answers: The one-inch gap would take about 70 milliseconds to close. Don't stick your hand in. [Image: image] The impact could trigger an earthquake. Denali (also known as Mount McKinley) is a mountain in Alaska that sits just to the south of a major fault line.[1]Roger A. Hansen, Earthquake and Seismic Monitoring in Denali National Park (http://www.nps.gov/akso/nature/science/ak_park_science/PDF/2006Vol5-1/Earthquake-Monitoring.pdf), National Park Service This fault is active,[2]Alaska Earthquake Information Center, M 7.9 Denali Fault earthquake of November 3, 2002 (http://www.aeic.alaska.edu/Denali_Fault_2002/) and we know that drilling can trigger earthquakes.[3]Van der elst NJ, Savage HM, Keranen KM, Abers GA. Enhanced remote earthquake triggering at fluid-injection sites in the midwestern United States (http://www.sciencemag.org/content/341/6142/164.abstract). Science. 2013;341(6142):164-7. Earthquakes can happen at any time, so there's always a chance that dropping a mountain any distance could trigger one. So could kicking a tree. The only way to find out for sure would be to try it.[4]This article has an awful lot of citations. Assuming it didn't trigger an earthquake, the impact wouldn't be all that dramatic. If you were standing on the mountain when it happened, you'd definitely feel a jolt, but it probably wouldn't even be enough to knock you down. [Image: image] When the mountain hit the ground, the rock under it would be damaged, but only a little. The granite base is strong enough to hold up under the tremendous resting weight of a mountain;[5]Citation: The rock was holding up a mountain when you got there. the shockwave from dropping it an inch doesn't add too much pressure on top of that, and the rock would survive with a little minor cracking. People nearby would definitely feel the impact, and probably hear it; the sound would likely resemble the crack of a lightning strike (if you were standing near the mountain) fading into a long, deep rumble.[6]Citation: A dream I had once. The vibration would be equivalent to that of a 3.5-magnitude earthquake[7]For more on the specific seismic details, see Stein, Seth, and Michael Wysession. "Earthquakes." An Introduction to Seismology, Earthquakes, and Earth Structure. Malden, MA: Blackwell Pub., 2003. 241 (http://books.google.com/books?id=-z80yrwFsqoC&lpg=PA241&ots=nrVTZ77_mJ&pg=PA241#v=onepage&q&f=false). Print.; at worst, it would knock a few pictures off the wall if you happened to be living next to the mountain. Frankly, I'd be more worried about debris flying out of the gap.[8]If your magical mountain-cutter put air in the space where the rock used to be, you should avoid standing near the crack when it falls. The air will come jetting out from the closing crack, spraying rocks and dust at speeds approaching, or even—thanks to some fun heat-related effects—exceeding, Mach 1. [Image: image] Oh. You again. Ok. Dropping from a height of one foot wouldn't be all that different. [Image: image] The mountain would hit the ground at 2.5 m/s, or roughly walking speed. The shockwave from that impact would be in the range of 50 megapascals of pressure,[9]You can calculate the peak pressure of the compressive strain wave in the rock using the Joukowsky equation, which says that the peak pressure of the compressive wave in a material is (material's density)x(speed at impact)x(the speed of sound in the material). This equation is is normally used in fluid mechanics, but it works fine here, too! (http://www.win.tue.nl/analysis/reports/rana06-08.pdf) which granite can handle without too much trouble.[10]Bhat HS, Sammis CG, Rosakis AJ. The Micromechanics of Westerley Granite at Large Compressive Loads (http://www.rosakis.caltech.edu/downloads/pubs/2011/181%20The%20Micromechanics%20of%20Westerley.pdf). Pure Appl. Geophys. 2011;168(12):2181-2198. [11]"... for a plane shock wave ... granite will stand a compressive stress of 3000-4000 MPa elastically before failing." Persson, Per-Anders, Roger Holmberg, and Jaimin Lee. Rock Blasting and Explosives Engineering (http://books.google.com/books?id=sdLO5HESJwgC&lpg=PA5&ots=-SJy8Yx-ea&pg=PA5#v=onepage&q&f=false). Boca Raton, FL: CRC, 1994. 5-6. Print. [Image: image] Ok. Let's jump straight to the end of John-Clark's question: [Image: image] After falling from summit height to base height—about 5 kilometers—the mountain would be moving at roughly the speed of sound. The last two impacts were pretty minor. This one wouldn't be. The jolt to the ground would be as violent as in a magnitude 7 earthquake.[12]In addition, there's a good chance that a shock this large will release some existing seismic energy; see: U.S. Congress, Office of Technology Assessment, Seismic Verification of Nuclear Testing Treaties (http://www.princeton.edu/~ota/disk2/1988/8838/883809.PDF), P. 715, OTA-ISC-361 (Washington, DC: U.S. Government Printing Office, May 1988). There wouldn't exactly be a crater, but the mountain would definitely not be shaped like it used to be. The pressure from the impact would be high enough to produce some unusual geologic strutures. If you put a lump of coal under the meteor, the impact would be enough to convert it to diamond (and, unfortunately, smash it to bits).[13]French B. M. (1998) Traces of Catastrophe: A Handbook of Shock-Metamorphic Effects in Terrestrial Meteorite Impact Structures., Chapter 4 (http://www.lpi.usra.edu/publications/books/CB-954/chapter4.pdf), LPI Contribution No. 954,Lunar and Planetary Institute, Houston. 120 pp The good news is that, the last time a magnitude 7+ earthquake hit Denali, no one was killed.[2]Alaska Earthquake Information Center, M 7.9 Denali Fault earthquake of November 3, 2002 (http://www.aeic.alaska.edu/Denali_Fault_2002/) Let's just hope nobody is on the mountain itself when we do this. [Image: image] It would hit Alaska at 10 kilometers per second. The Last Frontier would not fare well. A 50-mile-wide crater would have obliterated Denali National Park. Anchorage would be buried under three meters of gravel.[14]Purdue University ImpactEarth asteroid impact simulator (http://www.purdue.edu/impactearth/) The shaking, combined with the debris falling into the ocean, would cause tsunamis across the Pacific. Across North America, the ground would tremble. A wind would sweep in from the northwest. The sky would darken. In 1815, Mount Tambora erupted in the largest volcanic event in recorded history. The resulting global veil of aerosols made 1816 the "year without a summer". Snow fell in Massachusetts in June, ice formed on rivers in Pennsylvania in August, and frost killed most of the spring crops. The cooling effects lingered for several years. The Alaska impact would be far worse. Over the next few months, the skies around the globe fill with dust. Summer is canceled and winter arrives. This debris fell back to Earth around the world, heating the atmosphere and igniting global firestorms. These may have played a role in the mass extinctions.[16]I don't have a citation for this. But, c'mon, it's a 'global firestorm'. Can you really imagine that every species made it through unscathed? However, our mountain would carry only about 10% of the energy of the Chicxulub impactor, which means that it wouldn't be capable of igniting global firestorms.[17]Osinski, G. R., and E. Pierazzo. "Environmental Effects of Impact Events." In Impact Cratering Processes and Products. (http://books.google.com/books?id=3Vzky11ZR3UC&lpg=PA149&ots=8kqLGZFB1g&pg=PA151#v=onepage&q&f=false). Chicester: Wiley, 2012. 151. The firestorms would, in fact, only cover some of North America. So that's a relief. The northern hemisphere would be covered in ice, but our species would probably manage to limp through. Civilization, on the other hand, might well collapse. A total collapse of modern civilization would be a serious blow to the already sluggish economy, and the economic damage could amount to $80 trillion per year (the total value of all human goods and services). All in all, it would have serious implications for the upcoming elections. And that's that. We've dropped the mountain from as high as it can be dropped, and I hope John-Clark is proud of the resulting devastation. criteria.7-8: Gives plausible estimates for closure time and impact speed, e.g. tens of milliseconds and under 1 m/s, with mostly sound reasoning.

criteria.name: Impact, Stress, and Seismic Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly analyzes the mechanical impact of the mountain landing after a one-inch fall, including stress waves, rock strength, seismic shaking, and earthquake-triggering uncertainty.
criteria.1-2: Claims inevitable continent-scale destruction, no effect at all, or other outcomes incompatible with the small drop and huge mass.
criteria.3-4: Mentions impact or earthquake effects but with vague, exaggerated, or physically inconsistent claims.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that the impact would create noticeable shaking and stress but likely not catastrophic damage by itself.
criteria.7-8: Explains that rock can generally withstand the added stress, with local cracking and shaking comparable to a small earthquake, while noting possible triggered seismicity.
criteria.9-10: Balances the modest direct impact with the nonzero chance of triggering an existing fault, distinguishing induced seismic release from impact energy itself.

criteria.name: Local Hazards and Material Response
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of near-field effects specific to a one-inch mountain-wide gap, including air expulsion, dust and rock jets, cracking, sound, vibration, and danger to people at or near the base.
criteria.1-2: Ignores local hazards or invents unrelated effects such as lava, nuclear fireballs, or universal liquefaction.
criteria.3-4: Mentions danger nearby but gives little mechanism or focuses only on generic earthquake damage.
criteria.5-6: Covers some local effects such as a jolt, noise, dust, or rock fracture, but misses key gap-closure hazards.
criteria.7-8: Explains that compressed/expelled air, debris, dust, and cracking near the gap may be more dangerous locally than the fall itself.
criteria.9-10: Provides a vivid but physically grounded account of local hazards, including high-speed air/debris expulsion, lightning-like crack/rumble sounds, minor cracking, and risk to nearby observers.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Measures whether the answer traces downstream consequences from the initial vanishing inch through immediate impact, local damage, possible seismic triggering, and broader human/geological effects without skipping causal links.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected conclusions with no causal chain or jumps directly to apocalyptic/global outcomes from the one-inch event.
criteria.3-4: Has a partial chain but relies on unsupported leaps, such as assuming total mountain collapse or global climate effects.
criteria.5-6: Gives a reasonable immediate-to-local sequence but treats longer-range effects shallowly or inconsistently.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a coherent sequence from gap creation to fall, impact, vibrations, local hazards, and conditional earthquake effects.
criteria.9-10: Builds a clear, conditional, multi-stage causal narrative that separates likely local outcomes from rarer long-range seismic consequences.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control

criteria.3-4: Shows some awareness of uncertainty but makes confident unsupported claims or conflates one-inch, one-foot, summit-height, and space-drop scenarios.
criteria.5-6: Mostly stays with the premise and uses cautious language, though some estimates or distinctions are muddled.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates direct expected effects from low-probability triggered events and flags assumptions such as air filling the gap.
criteria.9-10: Precisely calibrates confidence, states assumptions, avoids scenario drift, and keeps all consequences consistent with the one-inch removal premise.

items.model_answer:
If the bottom inch of a massive mountain vanished instantaneously, the immediate physical consequences would be negligible on a human or even geological timescale. Mountains are composed of solid rock and can be tens of thousands of feet tall; removing just one inch from the base would reduce the total height by an imperceptible amount—far less than natural erosion or tectonic uplift over a single day.

However, if we interpret the scenario more precisely—meaning that a one-inch-thick horizontal slice of material at the very base of the mountain is removed, creating a gap—the structural implications depend on how the removal occurs. In reality, rock behaves as a brittle solid under such loads. If a void were suddenly introduced at the base, the overlying mass (which could weigh billions of tons) would immediately begin to settle into the gap due to gravity. This would likely cause fracturing, localized collapse, or seismic activity as stress redistributes through the mountain’s foundation.

In practice, though, the Earth’s crust is not perfectly rigid, and the lithostatic pressure beneath a mountain is immense. A one-inch void would almost instantly close due to compression and plastic deformation of the surrounding rock, especially at depth where temperatures and pressures are high. Thus, while the thought experiment highlights interesting aspects of geomechanics, the actual observable effect would be minimal—perhaps detectable only by sensitive instruments as a tiny seismic tremor or subsidence.

edus.text: If the bottom inch of a massive mountain vanished instantaneously,
the immediate physical consequences would be negligible on a human or even geological timescale.
Mountains are composed of solid rock
and can be tens of thousands of feet tall;
removing just one inch from the base would reduce the total height by an imperceptible amount
far less than natural erosion or tectonic uplift over a single day.
However, if we interpret the scenario more precisely
meaning that a one-inch-thick horizontal slice of material at the very base of the mountain is removed, creating a gap
the structural implications depend on how the removal occurs.
In reality, rock behaves as a brittle solid under such loads.
If a void were suddenly introduced at the base,
the overlying mass (which could weigh billions of tons) would immediately begin to settle into the gap due to gravity.
This would likely cause fracturing, localized collapse, or seismic activity
as stress redistributes through the mountain’s foundation.
In practice, though, the Earth’s crust is not perfectly rigid,
and the lithostatic pressure beneath a mountain is immense.
A one-inch void would almost instantly close due to compression and plastic deformation of the surrounding rock,
especially at depth where temperatures and pressures are high.
Thus, while the thought experiment highlights interesting aspects of geomechanics,
the actual observable effect would be minimal
perhaps detectable only by sensitive instruments as a tiny seismic tremor or subsidence.

items.question: What If a Spacecraft Used Rockets to Slow to a Few Miles per Hour during Reentry?
human_answers: The answers to these questions all hinge on the same idea. It's an idea I've touched on in other articles, but today I want to focus on it specifically: The reason it's hard to get to orbit isn't that space is high up. It's hard to get to orbit because you have to go so fast. Space isn't like this: [Image: image] Space is like this: [Image: image] Space is about 100 kilometers away. That's far away—I wouldn't want to climb a ladder to get there—but it isn't that far away. If you're in Sacramento, Seattle, Canberra, Kolkata, Hyderabad, Phnom Penh, Cairo, Beijing, central Japan, central Sri Lanka, or Portland, space is closer than the sea. Getting to space[1]Specifically, low Earth orbit, which is where the International Space Station is and where the shuttles could go. is easy. It's not, like, something you could do in your car, but it's not a huge challenge. You could get a person to space with a small sounding rocket the size of a telephone pole. The X-15 aircraft reached space[2]The X-15 reached 100 km on two occasions, both when flown by Joe Walker. just by going fast and then steering up.[3]Make sure to remember to steer up and not down, or you will have a bad time. [Image: image] But getting to space is easy. The problem is staying there. Gravity in low Earth orbit is almost as strong as gravity on the surface. The Space Station hasn't escaped Earth's gravity at all; it's experiencing about 90% the pull that we feel on the surface. To avoid falling back into the atmosphere, you have to go sideways really, really fast. The speed you need to stay in orbit is about 8 kilometers per second.[4]It's a little less if you're in the higher region of low Earth orbit. Only a fraction of a rocket's energy is used to lift up out of the atmosphere; the vast majority of it is used to gain orbital (sideways) speed. This leads us to the central problem of getting into orbit: Reaching orbital speed takes much more fuel than reaching orbital height. Getting a ship up to 8 km/s takes a lot of booster rockets. Reaching orbital speed is hard enough; reaching to orbital speed while carrying enough fuel to slow back down would be completely impractical.[5]This exponential increase is the central problem of rocketry: The fuel required to increase your speed by one km/s multiplies your weight by about 1.4. To get into orbit, you need to increase your speed to 8 km/s, which means you'll need a lot of fuel: $ 1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\approx 15$ times the original weight of your ship. Using a rocket to slow down carries the same problem: Every 1 km/s decrease in speed multiplies your starting mass by that same factor of 1.4. If you want to slow all the way down to zero—and drop gently into the atmosphere—the fuel requirements multiply your weight by 15 again. These outrageous fuel requirements are why every spacecraft entering an atmosphere has braked using a heat shield instead of rockets—slamming into the air is the most practical way to slow down. (And to answer Brian's question, the Curiosity rover was no exception to this; although it used small rockets to hover when it was near the surface, it first used air-braking to shed the majority of its speed.) How fast is 8 km/s, anyway? I think the reason for a lot of confusion about these issues is that when astronauts are in orbit, it doesn't seem like they're moving that fast; they look like they're drifting slowly over a blue marble. But 8 km/s is blisteringly fast. When you look at the sky near sunset, you can sometimes see the ISS go past ... and then, 90 minutes later, see it go past again.[6]There are some good apps and online tools to help you spot the station, along with other neat satellites. My favorite is ISS Detector (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.runar.issdetector), but if you Google you can find lots of others. In those 90 minutes, it's circled the entire world. The ISS moves so quickly that if you fired a rifle bullet from one end of a football field,[7]Either kind. the International Space Station could cross the length of the field before the bullet traveled 10 yards.[8]This type of play is legal in Australian rules football. Let's imagine what it would look like if you were speed-walking across the Earth's surface at 8 km/s. To get a better sense of the pace at which you're traveling, let's use the beat of a song to mark the passage of time.[9]Using song beats to help measure the passage of time is a technique also used in CPR training, where the song "Stayin' Alive" is used to . suppose you started playing the 1988 song by The Proclaimers, I'm Gonna Be (500 Miles). That song is about 131.9 beats per minute, so imagine that with every beat of the song, you move forward more than two miles. In the time it took to sing the first line of the chorus, you could walk from the Statue of Liberty all the way to the Bronx: [Image: image] It would take you about two lines of the chorus (16 beats of the song) to cross the English Channel between London and France. The song's length leads to an odd coincidence. The interval between the start and the end of I'm Gonna Be is 3 minutes and 30 seconds,[10]Based on timing from the official Youtube video (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tbNlMtqrYS0) and the ISS is moving at 7.66 km/s. This means that if an astronaut on the ISS listens to I'm Gonna Be, in the time between the first beat of the song and the final lines ... [Image: image] ... they will have traveled just about exactly 1,000 miles.

criteria.name: Core counterfactual framing: reentry speed is orbital speed, not falling-from-height speed
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly identifies that the spacecraft must shed roughly orbital horizontal velocity before it can descend gently, and that altitude alone is not the main difficulty.
criteria.1-2: Treats reentry mainly as falling from high altitude; misses orbital sideways speed or implies only small braking is needed.
criteria.3-4: Mentions high speed but only vaguely; does not clearly distinguish orbital velocity from vertical descent speed.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that orbital spacecraft move around 7-8 km/s and must lose that speed, but explanation is partial or imprecise.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains that staying in orbit requires large sideways velocity and that rocket-braking to a few mph means removing most of it.
criteria.9-10: Uses the orbital-speed insight as the central causal premise, explicitly correcting the intuition that space is hard mainly because it is high up.

criteria.name: Rocket-equation and fuel-mass consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer captures why carrying enough propellant to slow from orbital speed to a few mph is impractical, including compounding mass penalties.
criteria.1-2: Claims rockets could simply slow the craft without addressing fuel mass, or gives physically impossible fuel assumptions.
criteria.3-4: Says it would need 'a lot of fuel' but gives no mechanism for why this becomes prohibitive.
criteria.5-6: Explains that propellant requirements are very large and reduce payload, but lacks rocket-equation-style compounding.
criteria.7-8: Accurately describes exponential or multiplicative mass growth from needing propellant to brake, plus propellant to carry that propellant.
criteria.9-10: Connects the full mission penalty: reaching orbit while carrying deorbit/braking fuel is vastly harder, making near-zero-speed reentry impractical compared with aerobraking.

criteria.name: Atmospheric entry, heat shield, and aerobraking mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains how normal reentry uses the atmosphere to dissipate kinetic energy and how rocket braking would change heating, trajectory, and landing dynamics.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the atmosphere or incorrectly says heat shields are unnecessary simply because rockets exist.
criteria.3-4: Mentions heat or air resistance but does not explain their role in removing orbital energy.
criteria.5-6: Correctly states that heat shields/aerobraking normally shed most speed, with rockets only possibly used near landing.
criteria.7-8: Explains that slowing before dense atmosphere would greatly reduce heating but requires enormous propellant; also notes remaining descent/terminal landing issues.
criteria.9-10: Gives a coherent entry sequence comparing normal aerobraking with powered braking, including energy dissipation, heating reduction, trajectory control, and final low-speed descent.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream effects on spacecraft design and mission feasibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows consequences beyond the immediate maneuver, including launch mass, payload, staging, cost, safety, and practical alternatives.
criteria.1-2: Stops at a yes/no claim with little discussion of broader mission impacts.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few impacts such as cost or weight but without causal connection to the counterfactual.
criteria.5-6: Connects extra propellant to reduced payload and larger launch vehicles, with some discussion of operational tradeoffs.
criteria.7-8: Traces a plausible chain from braking requirement to bigger boosters, staging/tankage, lower payload fraction, cost, reliability, and landing architecture.
criteria.9-10: Integrates system-level consequences and alternatives, explaining why spacecraft use heat shields, parachutes, lift, or small terminal rockets rather than full powered orbital deceleration.

criteria.name: Quantitative plausibility, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer uses reasonable scales and avoids internal contradictions while being appropriately cautious about edge cases.
criteria.1-2: Contains major numerical errors or contradictions, such as confusing mph with km/s or saying orbit requires escape velocity.
criteria.3-4: Has some correct ideas but includes misleading numbers, overconfident claims, or inconsistent statements about gravity, speed, or fuel.
criteria.5-6: Uses broadly reasonable figures and caveats but may be approximate or omit important limitations.
criteria.7-8: Provides consistent order-of-magnitude reasoning, e.g. orbital speed near 8 km/s and huge delta-v/fuel needs, with sensible caveats.
criteria.9-10: Maintains precise, internally consistent reasoning throughout, distinguishes idealized from practical cases, and handles exceptions such as suborbital flights or propulsive landers without undermining the main conclusion.

items.model_answer:
If a spacecraft used rockets to slow to just a few miles per hour during reentry, it would drastically reduce or eliminate the need for aerodynamic heating and deceleration forces typically experienced during atmospheric entry. Conventional reentry relies on atmospheric drag to shed orbital velocity (about 17,500 mph for low Earth orbit), which generates intense heat due to compression of air in front of the vehicle—hence the need for heat shields. By using rockets to cancel nearly all of that speed before encountering dense atmosphere, the spacecraft would avoid extreme temperatures and g-forces, making reentry gentler and potentially allowing simpler thermal protection or even none at all.

However, this approach is highly impractical with current technology because it requires an enormous amount of propellant. Carrying enough fuel to decelerate from orbital velocity using rockets alone would demand a massive increase in launch mass due to the rocket equation—making missions prohibitively expensive and inefficient. This is why most spacecraft use aerobraking (atmospheric drag) as a "free" way to slow down, reserving rockets only for final landing maneuvers (as seen in SpaceX’s Falcon 9 boosters or Blue Origin’s New Shepard). In theory, though, such a rocket-assisted slow reentry would be feasible—it’s just not mass- or cost-effective with today’s propulsion systems.

edus.text: If a spacecraft used rockets to slow to just a few miles per hour during reentry,
it would drastically reduce or eliminate the need for aerodynamic heating and deceleration forces typically experienced during atmospheric entry.
Conventional reentry relies on atmospheric drag to shed orbital velocity (about 17,500 mph for low Earth orbit),
which generates intense heat due to compression of air in front of the vehicle—
hence the need for heat shields.
By using rockets to cancel nearly all of that speed before encountering dense atmosphere,
the spacecraft would avoid extreme temperatures and g-forces,
making reentry gentler and potentially allowing simpler thermal protection or even none at all.
However, this approach is highly impractical with current technology
because it requires an enormous amount of propellant.
Carrying enough fuel to decelerate from orbital velocity using rockets alone would demand a massive increase in launch mass due to the rocket equation—
making missions prohibitively expensive and inefficient.
This is why most spacecraft use aerobraking (atmospheric drag) as a "free" way to slow down,
reserving rockets only for final landing maneuvers
(as seen in SpaceX’s Falcon 9 boosters or Blue Origin’s New Shepard).
In theory, though, such a rocket-assisted slow reentry would be feasible—
it’s just not mass- or cost-effective with today’s propulsion systems.

items.question: What If You Tried to Print the Entire English Wikipedia in Real Time?
human_answers: This many: [Image: image] That's surprisingly few printers! But before you try to create a live-updating paper Wikipedia, let's look at what those printers would be doing ... and how much they'd cost. Printing Wikipedia People have considered printing out Wikipedia before. A few years ago, student Rob Matthews printed every Wikipedia featured article (http://www.brandnew.uk.com/wikipedia-as-a-printed-book/), creating a book several feet thick. Of course, that's just a small slice of the best of Wikipedia; the entire encyclopedia would be a lot bigger. Wikipedia user Tompw (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User:Tompw) has set up a page (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Size_in_volumes) for calculating the size of the whole English Wikipedia in printed volumes. It would currently fill a lot of bookshelves. Keeping up with the edits would be harder. Keeping up The English Wikipedia currently receives about 125,000 to 150,000 edits each day, or 90-100 per minute.[1]ToolServer: Edit rate (http://toolserver.org/~emijrp/wmcharts/wmchart0001.php) We could try to define a way to measure the "word count" of the average edit, but that's hard bordering on impossible. Fortunately, we don't need to—we can just estimate that each change is going to require us to reprint a page somewhere. Many edits will actually change multiple pages—but many other edits are reverts, which would let us put back pages we've already printed.[2]The filing system for this would be staggering (http://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IBM_card_storage.NARA.jpg). One page per edit seems like a reasonable middle ground. For a mix of photos, tables, and text typical of Wikipedia, a good inkjet printer might put out 15 pages per minute. That means you'd only need about six printers running at any given time to keep pace with the edits. The paper would stack up quickly. Using Rob Matthews' book as a starting point, I did my own back-of-the-envelope estimate for the size of the current English Wikipedia. Based on the average length of featured articles vs. all articles, I came up with an estimate of 300 cubic meters for a printout of the whole thing.[3]That's a little larger than Tompw's estimate, but I'm assuming they're printed straight from the browser, which is less compact and includes images. By comparison, if you were trying to keep up with the edits, you'd print out 300 cubic meters every month. $500,000 per month Six printers isn't that many, but they'd be running all the time. And that gets expensive. The electricity to run them would be cheap—a few dollars a day. The paper would be about one cent per sheet, which means you'll be spending about a thousand dollars a day. You'd want to hire people to manage the printers 24/7, but that would actually cost less than the paper. Even the printers themselves wouldn't be too expensive, despite the terrifying replacement cycle. But the ink cartridges would be a nightmare. Ink A study by QualityLogic[4]QualityLogic: Cost of Ink Per Page Analysis (http://www.qualitylogic.com/tuneup/uploads/docfiles/QualityLogic-Cost-of-Ink-Per-Page-Analysis_US_1-Jun-2012.pdf), June 2012 found that for a typical inkjet printer, the real-life cost of ink ran from 5 cents per page for black-and-white to around 30 cents per page for photos. That means you'd be spending four to five figures per day on ink cartridges. You definitely want to invest in a laser printer. Otherwise, in just a month or two, this project could end up costing you half a million dollars: [Image: image] But that's not even the worst part. If, someday, Wikipedia decides to go dark (http://sys01-public.msnbc.msn.com/technology/wikipedia-goes-dark-piracy-bill-protest-day-117714) again, and you want to join the protest ... [Image: image] You'll have to get a crate of markers and color every page solid black yourself. I would definitely stick to digital.

criteria.name: Counterfactual setup and core throughput estimate
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly frames the task as continuously printing Wikipedia updates in real time, estimates edit rate and page output needs, and derives a plausible number of printers needed.
criteria.1-2: Misunderstands the premise, e.g. treats it only as printing Wikipedia once or gives no usable throughput reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes real-time printing but uses implausible or unsupported numbers for edits, pages, or printer speed.
criteria.5-6: Provides a rough edit-rate-to-pages-to-printers calculation, but with weak assumptions or missing caveats.
criteria.7-8: Gives a plausible calculation, such as about 100 edits per minute and roughly several printers, with clear assumptions.
criteria.9-10: Accurately explains the one-page-per-edit approximation, printer pages-per-minute limits, and why only a surprisingly small number of printers could keep pace.

criteria.name: Mechanism coverage for updating a paper Wikipedia
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains the practical mechanism of maintaining a live paper encyclopedia: reprinting changed pages, handling reverts, multi-page edits, version replacement, and organization.
criteria.1-2: Ignores how edits would translate into printed pages or assumes the whole encyclopedia must be reprinted after every edit.
criteria.3-4: Mentions updates but gives a simplistic or inconsistent replacement process.
criteria.5-6: Explains that edits require printing replacement pages, but only partially addresses reverts, multi-page changes, or filing.
criteria.7-8: Covers page replacement, edit variability, reverts, and the organizational burden in a mostly coherent way.
criteria.9-10: Clearly models the live-update workflow, including why one page per edit is a reasonable approximation and why the filing/version-control system becomes a major hidden difficulty.

criteria.name: Downstream physical scale and storage consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer tracks the long-range physical consequences: paper volume, accumulating monthly output, storage space, handling, and waste.
criteria.1-2: Omits physical accumulation or gives impossible claims such as negligible paper use.
criteria.3-4: Mentions lots of paper but gives no scale or conflates one-time size with ongoing update volume.
criteria.5-6: Provides a rough sense of large storage needs, but with limited quantification or unclear time scale.
criteria.7-8: Distinguishes the one-time printout from continuous update output and gives plausible magnitudes for paper stacks or volume.
criteria.9-10: Coherently explains that the full encyclopedia is hundreds of cubic meters and that update printing can generate comparable volumes over time, creating major storage and disposal problems.

criteria.name: Cost, consumables, and operational feasibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer identifies the dominant costs and operational constraints, including paper, ink or toner, printer wear, staffing, electricity, and the inkjet-versus-laser distinction.
criteria.1-2: Provides no cost analysis or focuses on irrelevant costs while missing consumables.
criteria.3-4: Mentions expense generally but misidentifies electricity or printers as the dominant cost without justification.
criteria.5-6: Includes paper and ink or toner costs with rough numbers, but misses staffing, maintenance, or printer-type effects.
criteria.7-8: Explains that electricity and printer purchase are minor compared with paper and especially ink, with plausible daily or monthly costs.
criteria.9-10: Gives a well-supported cost chain showing why inkjet printing could reach very high monthly costs, why laser printing would be preferable, and how 24/7 staffing and replacement cycles affect feasibility.

criteria.name: Causal coherence, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains a consistent causal chain under uncertain assumptions, avoids contradictions, and communicates estimates as approximations rather than false precision.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, impossible arithmetic, or unsupported definitive claims that break the scenario.
criteria.3-4: Has some coherent points but mixes incompatible assumptions or overstates uncertain quantities.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent, with approximate reasoning, but contains minor inconsistencies or poorly calibrated confidence.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a clear causal chain from edits to pages to printers to costs and storage, while flagging uncertainty in edit size and page layout.
criteria.9-10: Shows strong long-range reasoning, explicitly separates assumptions from conclusions, avoids double-counting, and keeps all downstream effects mutually consistent.

items.model_answer:
Printing the entire English Wikipedia in real time is effectively impossible due to the site’s constant, rapid growth and the physical limitations of printing technology. As of 2024, the English Wikipedia contains over 6.7 million articles and grows by tens of thousands of edits per day—roughly 1.5 to 2 edits every second. Even if you had a printer capable of producing pages instantly, the content would change faster than any physical printer could output it.  

For context, a static snapshot of Wikipedia (excluding talk pages, user pages, and edit histories) has been estimated to fill around 1,000–2,000 volumes of 1,000 pages each—roughly 1–2 million printed pages. At a typical high-speed commercial printing rate of 100 pages per minute, just printing that static version would take about 7–14 days nonstop. But because Wikipedia is continuously edited—adding new articles, updating facts, correcting errors—the “real-time” target is always moving. By the time you finish printing even a single article, it may already be outdated or expanded.  

Thus, attempting to print the entire English Wikipedia in real time would result in an ever-incomplete, perpetually obsolete physical copy, forever lagging behind the live digital version. The endeavor is fundamentally unfeasible due to the mismatch between dynamic digital content and the fixed, sequential nature of physical printing.

edus.text: Printing the entire English Wikipedia in real time is effectively impossible
due to the site’s constant, rapid growth
and the physical limitations of printing technology.
As of 2024, the English Wikipedia contains over 6.7 million articles
and grows by tens of thousands of edits per day
roughly 1.5 to 2 edits every second.
Even if you had a printer capable of producing pages instantly,
the content would change faster than any physical printer could output it.
For context, a static snapshot of Wikipedia
excluding talk pages, user pages, and edit histories
has been estimated to fill around 1,000–2,000 volumes of 1,000 pages each
roughly 1–2 million printed pages.
At a typical high-speed commercial printing rate of 100 pages per minute,
just printing that static version would take about 7–14 days nonstop.
But because Wikipedia is continuously edited
adding new articles, updating facts, correcting errors
the “real-time” target is always moving.
By the time you finish printing even a single article,
it may already be outdated or expanded.
Thus, attempting to print the entire English Wikipedia in real time would result in an ever-incomplete, perpetually obsolete physical copy
forever lagging behind the live digital version.
The endeavor is fundamentally unfeasible
due to the mismatch between dynamic digital content and the fixed, sequential nature of physical printing.

items.question: What If You Jumped from a Plane with Helium Tanks and a Giant Balloon?
human_answers: As ridiculous as it sounds, this is—sort of—possible. Falling from great heights is dangerous.[citation needed (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Republic_Presidential_Unit_Citation)] A balloon could actually help save you, although a regular helium one from a party obviously won't do the trick. [Image: image] If the balloon is large enough, you don't even need the helium. A balloon will act as a parachute, slowing your fall to non-fatal speeds. Avoiding a high-speed landing is, unsurprisingly, the key to survival. As one medical paper[1]De Haven H. Mechanical analysis of survival in falls from heights of fifty to one hundred and fifty feet (http://injuryprevention.bmj.com/content/6/1/62.3.long). Injury Prevention. 6(1):62-b-68. put it, It is, of course, obvious that speed, or height of fall, is not in itself injurious ... but a high rate of change of velocity, such as occurs after a 10 story fall onto concrete, is another matter. ... which is just a wordy version of the old saying, "It's not the fall that kills you, it's the sudden stop at the end." To act as a parachute, a balloon filled with air, rather than helium, would have to be 10 to 20 meters across—far too big to be inflated with portable tanks. A powerful fan could be used to fill it with ambient air, but at that point, you may as well just use a parachute. Helium The helium makes things easier. It doesn't take too many helium balloons to lift a person. In 1982, Larry Walters (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Walters) flew across Los Angeles in a lawn chair lifted by weather balloons, eventually reaching several miles in altitude. After passing through LAX airspace, he descended by shooting some of the balloons with a pellet gun. On landing, Walters was arrested, although the authorities had some trouble figuring out what to charge him with. At the time, an FAA safety inspector told the New York Times, "We know he broke some part of the Federal Aviation Act, and as soon as we decide which part it is, some type of charge will be filed."[2]ARMCHAIR AIRMAN SAYS FLIGHT FULFILLED HIS LIFELONG DREAM (http://www.nytimes.com/1982/07/04/us/armchair-airman-says-flight-fulfilled-his-lifelong-dream.html?pagewanted=all), New York Times, July 4, 1982 A relatively small helium balloon—certainly smaller than a parachute—will suffice slow your fall, but it still has to be huge by party balloon standards. The biggest consumer rental helium tanks are about 250 cubic feet, and you'd need to empty at least 10 of them to put enough air in the balloon to support your weight. You'd have to do it quickly. The compressed helium cylinders are smooth and often quite heavy, which means they have a high terminal velocity. You'll only have a few minutes to use up all the cylinders. (As soon as you emptied one, you could drop it.) You can't get around this problem by moving your starting point higher. Since the upper atmosphere is pretty thin, anything dropped from the stratosphere up will accelerate to very high speeds until it hits the lower atmosphere, then fall slowly the rest of the way. This is true of everything from small meteors[3]By the time meteors hit the Earth, they have slowed down (http://www.geology.wisc.edu/~museum/meteorite.html) to a few hundred miles per hour. to Felix Baumgartner.[4]Jason Martinez, Falling Faster than the Speed of Sound (http://blog.wolfram.com/2012/10/24/falling-faster-than-the-speed-of-sound/), Wolfram Blog, October 24, 2012 [Image: image] But if you inflated the balloons quickly, possibly by connecting many canisters to it at once, you'd be able to slow your fall. Just don't use too much helium, or you'll end up floating at 16,000 feet like Larry Walters.http://xkcd.com/1110 [Image: image] While researching this article,[5]Additionally, while researching impact speeds for this article, I came across a discussion (http://boards.straightdope.com/sdmb/showthread.php?t=361878) on the Straight Dope Message Boards about survivable fall heights. One poster compared a fall from height to being hit by a bus. Another user, a medical examiner, replied (http://boards.straightdope.com/sdmb/showpost.php?p=7180162&postcount=40) that this was a bad comparison: "When hit by a car, the vast majority of people are not run over; they are run under. The lower legs break, sending them into the air. They usually strike the hood of the car, often with the back of the head impacting the windshield, "starring" the windshield, possibly leaving a few hairs in the glass. They then go over the top of the car. They are still alive, although with broken legs, and maybe with head pain from the nonfatal windshield impact. They die when they hit the ground. They die from head injury." The lesson: Don't mess with medical examiners. They're apparently pretty hardcore. I managed to lock up my copy of Mathematica several times on balloon-related differential equations, and subsequently got my IP address banned from Wolfram|Alpha (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=how+many+days+have+i+been+alive) for making too many requests. The ban-appeal form asked me to explain what task I was performing that necessitated so many queries, so this is what I put: [Image: image] I hope they understand.

criteria.9-10: Clearly distinguishes theoretical possibility from practical near-impossibility, tying survival to reduced landing speed, adequate balloon volume, deployment timing, and manageable descent.

criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly explains the relevant mechanisms: helium lift, air-filled balloon drag, parachute-like behavior, and the very large volume needed to affect a human fall.
criteria.1-2: Misstates basic physics, such as implying a small party balloon or single tank can meaningfully lift or stop a person.
criteria.3-4: Mentions helium or drag but confuses lift with parachute effects or gives highly unrealistic scale estimates.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that the balloon must be very large and can act like a parachute, but gives limited or vague mechanism detail.
criteria.7-8: Accurately explains both buoyant lift and aerodynamic drag, including why party-scale balloons are inadequate.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent quantitative or semi-quantitative account of needed balloon volume, helium lift, drag area, and why an air-filled balloon could slow descent even without helium.

criteria.name: Deployment sequence and long-range causal chain
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses the answer's treatment of the full chain of events after the jump: initial acceleration, tank handling, inflation, descent stabilization, possible overshoot into floating, and landing.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the sequence of events and treats the setup as if the balloon is instantly and safely usable.
criteria.3-4: Mentions falling or inflation but omits major timing or sequencing problems during free fall.
criteria.5-6: Covers several stages, such as falling, inflating, and landing, but leaves gaps in how one stage affects the next.
criteria.7-8: Builds a mostly coherent causal chain from exit to landing, including rapid inflation, tank disposal, slowing descent, and landing risks.
criteria.9-10: Tracks the full long-range scenario with strong causal continuity, including acceleration before deployment, limited time to empty tanks, changing descent rate, possible excessive lift, and final impact dynamics.

criteria.name: Treatment of altitude, atmosphere, and terminal velocity
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly handles how starting altitude and atmospheric density affect falling speed, balloon behavior, and the usefulness of going higher.
criteria.1-2: Makes incorrect claims such as higher altitude always giving more time and therefore making the plan easy.
criteria.3-4: Mentions altitude but misses how thin air, acceleration, or terminal velocity change during descent.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that altitude affects fall speed and available time, but gives incomplete treatment of atmospheric density.
criteria.7-8: Explains that very high starts can cause high speeds in thin air before slowing in denser air, limiting the benefit of extra altitude.
criteria.9-10: Accurately connects altitude, air density, terminal velocity, balloon expansion/drag, and descent timing, avoiding simplistic 'start higher' reasoning.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer appropriately qualifies uncertain details, avoids internal contradictions, and keeps speculative extensions consistent with the physics of the scenario.
criteria.1-2: Presents confident but inconsistent claims, such as saying the balloon both cannot help and can safely land the person without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Includes some caveats but also contains contradictions or unjustified certainty about survival, tank counts, or balloon dimensions.
criteria.5-6: Generally avoids contradictions and acknowledges some uncertainty, though estimates or assumptions may be underexplained.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable caveats about equipment, human control, inflation rate, and landing conditions while maintaining a consistent conclusion.
criteria.9-10: Carefully separates known physics from rough estimates, states assumptions, flags practical unknowns, and keeps all claims mutually consistent throughout the counterfactual analysis.

items.model_answer:
If you jumped from a plane with helium tanks and a giant balloon, your survival would depend on whether you could inflate the balloon quickly enough to slow your descent before hitting the ground. Helium is lighter than air, so a sufficiently large balloon filled with it would generate buoyant lift, potentially allowing you to float or descend slowly like a hot-air balloon.

However, several critical challenges make this extremely dangerous and likely fatal in practice:

1. **Inflation Time**: At typical skydiving altitudes (around 10,000–15,000 feet), you have only about 30–60 seconds of freefall before reaching the ground. Inflating a balloon large enough to support your weight (which would need to be tens of thousands of cubic feet in volume) from compressed helium tanks in that time is practically impossible with current portable technology.

2. **Balloon Deployment**: A giant uninflated balloon would create massive drag and instability during freefall, possibly tangling you or causing uncontrolled spinning. Deploying it safely while falling at terminal velocity (~120 mph) is highly unlikely.

3. **Helium Volume Requirements**: To lift a 70 kg (154 lb) person, you’d need roughly 60–70 cubic meters (over 2,000 cubic feet) of helium just to achieve neutral buoyancy—more to actually ascend. Compressing that much helium into portable tanks is not feasible; standard scuba-sized tanks hold far less.

4. **Altitude and Oxygen**: Above 15,000 feet, hypoxia becomes a risk without supplemental oxygen, impairing judgment and coordination needed for such a complex maneuver.

In theory, if you had a pre-inflated, properly sized balloon and released it at altitude, you could float down safely—but carrying and deploying it mid-fall from a plane makes the scenario unrealistic and almost certainly lethal. Real-world alternatives like parachutes are reliable precisely because they deploy quickly and create drag, not lift.

edus.text: If you jumped from a plane with helium tanks and a giant balloon,
your survival would depend on whether you could inflate the balloon quickly enough to slow your descent before hitting the ground.
Helium is lighter than air,
so a sufficiently large balloon filled with it would generate buoyant lift,
potentially allowing you to float or descend slowly like a hot-air balloon.
However, several critical challenges make this extremely dangerous and likely fatal in practice:
At typical skydiving altitudes (around 10,000–15,000 feet), you have only about 30–60 seconds of freefall before reaching the ground.

Inflating a balloon large enough to support your weight (which would need to be tens of thousands of cubic feet in volume) from compressed helium tanks in that time is practically impossible with current portable technology.
A giant uninflated balloon would create massive drag and instability during freefall,
possibly tangling you or causing uncontrolled spinning.
Deploying it safely while falling at terminal velocity (~120 mph) is highly unlikely.
To lift a 70 kg (154 lb) person, you’d need roughly 60–70 cubic meters (over 2,000 cubic feet) of helium just to achieve neutral buoyancy
more to actually ascend.
Compressing that much helium into portable tanks is not feasible;
standard scuba-sized tanks hold far less.
Above 15,000 feet, hypoxia becomes a risk without supplemental oxygen,
impairing judgment and coordination needed for such a complex maneuver.
In theory, if you had a pre-inflated, properly sized balloon and released it at altitude,
you could float down safely
but carrying and deploying it mid-fall from a plane makes the scenario unrealistic and almost certainly lethal.
Real-world alternatives like parachutes are reliable
precisely because they deploy quickly and create drag, not lift.

items.question: What If All Digital Data Were Stored on Punch Cards?
human_answers: [Image: image] Google almost certainly has more data storage capacity than any other organization on Earth. Google is very secretive about its operations, so it's hard to say for sure. There are only a handful of organizations who might plausibly have more storage capacity or a larger server infrastructure. Here's my short list of the top contenders: NSA (http://www.nsa.gov/) NRO (http://www.nro.gov/) NGIP (https://www1.nga.mil/Pages/default.aspx) CIA (https://www.cia.gov/index.html) Schlumberger (http://www.slb.com/) Tencent (http://www.tencent.com/en-us/index.shtml) Chevron (http://www.chevron.com/) Honorable mentions: Amazon (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River) (They're huge, but probably not as big as Google.) Facebook (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Face_book) (They're on the right scale and growing fast, but still playing catch-up.) Microsoft (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Bob) (They have a million servers,[1]Data Center Knowledge: [Ballmer: Microsoft has 1 Million Servers although no one seems sure why.) Let's take a closer look at Google's computing platform. Follow the money We'll start by following the money. Google's aggregate capital expenditures–spending on building stuff[2]I'm excluding the cost of an extremely expensive building they bought in New York.—adds up to somewhere over $12 billion dollars.[3]Data Center Knowledge: Google’s Data Center Building Boom Continues: $1.6 Billion Investment in 3 Months (http://www.datacenterknowledge.com/archives/2013/07/19/google-data-center-spending-continues-to-soar-1-6-billion-in-3-months/) Their biggest data centers cost half a billion to a billion dollars, so they can't have more than 20 or so of those. On their website,[4]Data center locations (http://www.google.com/about/datacenters/inside/locations/index.html) Google acknowledges that they have datacenters in the following locations: Berkeley County, South Carolina Council Bluffs, Iowa Atlanta, Georgia Mayes County, Oklahoma Lenoir, North Carolina The Dalles, Oregon Hong Kong Singapore Taiwan Hamina, Finland St Ghislain, Belgium Dublin, Ireland Quilicura, Chile In addition, they appear to operate a number of other large datacenters (sometimes through subsidiary corporations), including: Eemshaven, Netherlands Groningen, Netherlands Budapest, Hungary Wrocław, Poland Reston, Virginia Additional sites near Atlanta, Georgia They also operate equipment at dozens to hundreds of smaller locations around the world. Follow the power To figure out how many servers Google is running, we can look at their electricity consumption. Unfortunately, we can't just sneak up to a datacenter and read the meter.[5]Actually, wait, can we? Somebody should try that. Instead, we have to do some digging. The company disclosed that in 2010 they consumed an average of 258 megawatts of power.[6]Google used 2,259,998 MWh of electricity in 2010 (http://www.environmentalleader.com/2011/09/09/google-reveals-electricity-use-breaking-its-silence/), which translates to an average of 258 megawatts. How many computers can they run with that? We know that their datacenters are quite efficient, only spending 10-20% of their power on cooling and other overhead.[7]Google: Efficiency: How we do it (http://www.google.com/about/datacenters/efficiency/internal/) To get an idea of how much power each server uses, we can look at their "container data center" concept from 2005. It's not clear whether they actually use these containers in practice—it may just have been a now-outdated experiment—but it gives an idea of what they consider(ed) reasonable power consumption. The answer: 215 watts per server. Judging from that number, in 2010, they were operating around a million servers. They've grown a lot since then. By the end of 2013, the total amount of money they've pumped into their datacenters will be three or four times what it was as of 2010. They've contracted to buy over three hundred megawatts of power at just three sites,[8]Google: Purchasing clean energy (http://www.google.com/green/energy/use/#purchasing) which is more than they used for all their operations in 2010. Based on datacenter power usage and spending estimates, my guess would be that Google is currently running—or will soon be running—between 1.8 and 2.4 million servers. But what do these "servers" actually represent? Google could be experimenting in all kinds of wild ways, running boards with 100 cores or 100 attached disks. If we assume that each server has a couple[9]Anywhere from 2 to 5 (http://xkcd.com/1070/) of 2 TB disks attached, we come up with close to 10 exabytes[10]As a refresher, the order is: kilo, mega, giga, tera, peta, exa, zetta, yotta. An exabyte is a million terabytes. of active storage attached to running clusters. 10 Exabytes The commercial hard disk industry ships about 8 exabytes worth of drives annually.[12]IDC: Worldwide External Disk Storage Systems Factory Revenue Declines for the Second Consecutive Quarter (http://www.idc.com/getdoc.jsp?containerId=prUS24302513) Those numbers don't necessarily include companies like Google, but in any case, it seems likely that Google is a large piece of the global hard drive market. To make things worse, given the huge number of drives they manage, Google has a hard drive die every few minutes.[11]Eduardo Pinheiro, Wolf-Dietrich Weber and Luiz Andre Barroso, [Failure Trends in a Large Disk Drive Population This isn't actually all that expensive a problem, in the grand scheme of things—they just get good at replacing drives—but it's weird to think that when a Googler runs a piece of code, they know that by the time it finishes executing, one of the machines it was running on will probably have suffered a drive failure. Google tape storage Of course, that only covers storage attached to running servers. What about "cold" storage? Who knows how much data Google—or anyone else—has stored in basement archives? In a 2011 phone interview with Paul Mah of SMB Tech, Simon Anderson of Tandberg Data let slip[13]SMB Tech: Is Tape Still Relevant for SMBs? (http://www.itbusinessedge.com/cm/blogs/mah/is-tape-still-relevant-for-smbs/?cs=45557) that Google is the world's biggest single consumer of magnetic tape cartridges, purchasing 200,000 per year. Assuming they've stepped up their purchasing since then as they've expanded, this could add up to another few exabytes of tape archives. Putting it all together Let's assume Google has a storage capacity of 15 exabytes, or 15,000,000,000,000,000,000 bytes. A punch card can hold about 80 characters, and a box of cards holds 2000 cards: [Image: image] 15 exabytes of punch cards would be enough to cover my home region, New England, to a depth of about 4.5 kilometers. That's three times deeper than the ice sheets that covered the region during the last advance of the glaciers: [Image: image] That seems like a lot. However, it's nothing compared to the ridiculous claims by some news reports about the NSA datacenter in Utah. NSA datacenter The NSA is building a datacenter in Utah. Media reports claimed that it could hold up to a yottabyte of data,[14]CNET: NSA to store yottabytes in Utah data centre (http://crave.cnet.co.uk/gadgets/nsa-to-store-yottabytes-in-utah-data-centre-49304118/) which is patently absurd. Later reports changed their minds, suggesting that the facility could only hold on the order of 3-12 exabytes.[15]Forbes: Blueprints Of NSA's Ridiculously Expensive Data Center In Utah Suggest It Holds Less Info Than Thought (http://www.forbes.com/sites/kashmirhill/2013/07/24/blueprints-of-nsa-data-center-in-utah-suggest-its-storage-capacity-is-less-impressive-than-thought/) We also know the facility uses about 65 megawatts of power,[16]Salt-Lake City Tribune: NSA Bluffdale Center won’t gobble up Utah’s power supply (http://www.sltrib.com/sltrib/news/56493868-78/power-center-electricity-utah.html.csp) which is about what a large Google datacenter consumes. A few headlines, rather than going with one estimate or the other, announced that the facility could hold "between an exabyte and a yottabyte" of data[17]Dailykos: Utah Data Center stores data between 1 exabyte and 1 yottabyte (http://www.dailykos.com/story/2013/08/05/1228923/-Utah-Data-Center-stores-data-between-1-exabyte-and-1-yottabyte) ... which is a little like saying "eyewitnesses report that the snake was between 1 millimeter and 1 kilometer long." Uncovering further Google secrets There are a lot of tricks for digging up information about Google's operations. Ironically, many of them involve using Google itself—from Googling for job postings in strange cities to using image search to find leaked cell camera photos of datacenter visits. However, the best trick for locating secret Google facilities might be the one revealed by ex-Googler talentlessclown (http://www.reddit.com/user/talentlessclown) on reddit:[18]reddit: Can r/Australia help find Google's Sydney data center? Seems like a bit of a mystery... (http://www.reddit.com/r/australia/comments/1hctj4/can_raustralia_help_find_googles_sydney_data/catef4f) The easiest way to find manned Google data centres is to ask taxi drivers and pizza delivery people. There's something pleasing about that. Google has created what might be the most sophisticated information-gathering apparatus in the history of the Earth ... and the only people with information about them are the pizza delivery drivers. Who watches the watchers? [Image: image] Apparently, Domino's.

rubrics.question_focus: What If All Digital Data Were Stored on Punch Cards?

criteria.name: Quantitative grounding of punch-card storage scale
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer estimates the physical magnitude of storing modern digital data on punch cards using defensible orders of magnitude, especially bytes per card, number of cards, volume/mass/area, and comparison to real-world geographic or industrial scales.
criteria.1-2: Gives no meaningful quantitative estimate or uses wildly impossible units without recognizing scale.
criteria.3-4: Mentions that the card volume would be enormous but provides little or incorrect arithmetic.
criteria.5-6: Uses plausible card capacity and data-size assumptions but has limited or rough physical-scale calculations.
criteria.7-8: Computes credible orders of magnitude for cards, boxes, volume, mass, land area, or depth with clear assumptions.
criteria.9-10: Provides robust, internally checked scale estimates and vivid comparisons while noting sensitivity to data-size assumptions.

criteria.name: Fidelity to the counterfactual premise
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer consistently reasons from the premise that all digital data must be stored on punch cards, rather than slipping back into magnetic, optical, semiconductor, or cloud storage for primary storage.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the premise or continues to rely on ordinary digital storage as if unchanged.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges punch cards but repeatedly contradicts the premise with modern storage assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Mostly follows the premise, with some ambiguous or minor lapses about backups, caches, or transmission.
criteria.7-8: Maintains the punch-card constraint across storage, backup, indexing, and retrieval scenarios.
criteria.9-10: Applies the premise rigorously, including edge cases such as metadata, redundancy, logs, encryption keys, and temporary data.

criteria.name: Mechanism coverage for storage, retrieval, and computation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains the concrete mechanisms by which punch-card-only data storage would affect writing, reading, sorting, searching, updating, backing up, and computing over data.
criteria.1-2: Only says the system would be slow or impossible, with no mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Covers one or two mechanisms, such as storage space or read speed, superficially.
criteria.5-6: Explains several mechanisms, including read/write throughput, mechanical handling, and indexing.
criteria.7-8: Connects storage density, card readers, sorting systems, error rates, duplication, and update costs into a coherent operating model.
criteria.9-10: Deeply analyzes the full data lifecycle, including random access, distributed processing, versioning, checksums, failures, and archival workflows.

items.model_answer: If all digital data were stored on punch cards, the physical scale, cost, and inefficiency would be staggering. A single IBM 80-column punch card holds about 80 bytes of data. As of 2023, global digital data is estimated at around 100 zettabytes (10²³ bytes). Storing that amount on punch cards would require roughly 1.25 × 10²¹ cards. Each card weighs about 1 gram, so the total mass would exceed 1.25 trillion metric tons—more than twice the mass of all humans combined. The volume would fill millions of large warehouses, and accessing or processing data would be impossibly slow compared to modern electronic storage. Moreover, punch cards are fragile, prone to damage, and not rewritable, making them wholly impractical for today’s data needs.
