items.question: What If You Began Rising Upward at One Foot per Second?
human_answers: Did you bring a coat? A foot per second isn't that fast—it's substantially slower than a typical elevator.[1]Otis: About Elevators (http://www.otisworldwide.com/pdf/AboutElevators.pdf) It would take you 5-7 seconds to rise out of arms' reach, depending how tall your friends are. [Image: image] After 30 seconds, you'd be 30 feet—9 meters—off the ground. Judging from What-If #44 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/44/), this is getting close to your last chance for a friend to throw you a sandwich or water bottle or something.[2]Not that it will help, ultimately. [Image: image] After a minute or two you would be above the trees. You'd still be about as comfortable as you were on the ground. If it's a breezy day, it will probably get chillier thanks to the steadier wind above the treeline.[3]For this article, I'm going to assume a typical atmosphere temperature profile. It can, of course, vary quite a bit. After 10 minutes you would be above all but the tallest skyscrapers, and after 25 minutes you'd pass the spire of the Empire State Building. [Image: image] The air at these heights is about 3% thinner than it is at the surface. Fortunately, your body handles air pressure changes like that all the time. Your ears may pop, but you wouldn't really notice anything else. Air pressure changes quickly with height. Surprisingly, when you're standing on the ground, air pressure is even measurably lower at your head than at your feet. If your phone has a barometer in it, as a lot of new Android phones do, you can download an app and actually see the pressure difference between your head and your feet. A foot per second is pretty close to a kilometer per hour, so after an hour, you'll be about a kilometer off the ground. At this point, you definitely start to get chilly. If you have a coat, you'll still be ok, though you might also notice the wind picking up. At about two hours and two kilometers, the temperature would drop below freezing. The wind would also, most likely, be picking up. If you have any exposed skin, this is where frostbite starts to become a concern.[4]National Weather Service: Wind Chill Temperature Index (http://www.nws.noaa.gov/om/windchill/images/wind-chill-brochure.pdf) Starting at this point, the air pressure would drop below what you'd experience in an airliner cabin,[5]... which are typically kept pressurized at about 70%-80% of sea level pressure, judging from the barometer in my phone. and the effects would start to become more significant, but unless you had a warm coat, the temperature would be a bigger problem. Over the next two hours, the air would drop to below-zero[6]Either unit.​[7]Not Kelvin, though. temperatures. Assuming for a moment that you survived the oxygen deprivation, at some point you'd freeze to death. But when? The scholarly authorities on freezing to death seem to be, unsurprisingly, Canadians. The most widely-used model for human survival in cold air was developed by Peter Tikuisis and John Frim for the Defence and Civil Institute of Environmental Medicine in Ontario.[8]Prediction of Survival Time in Cold Air (http://cradpdf.drdc-rddc.gc.ca/PDFS/zba6/p144967.pdf)—see page 24 for the relevant tables. According to their model, the main factor in the cause of death would be your clothes. If you were nude, you'd probably succumb to hypothermia somewhere around the five hour mark, before your oxygen ran out.[9]And frankly, this really raises more questions than it answers. If you were bundled up, you may be frostbitten, but you would probably survive ... ... long enough to reach the Death Zone. [Image: image] Above 8,000 meters—above the tops of all but the highest mountains—the oxygen content in the air is too low to support human life. Near this zone, you would experience a range of symptoms, possibly including confusion, dizziness, clumsiness, impaired vision, and nausea. As you approach the Death Zone, your blood oxygen content would plummet. Your veins are supposed to bring low-oxygen blood back to your lungs to be refilled with oxygen. But in the Death Zone, there's so little oxygen in the air that your veins lose oxygen to the air instead of gaining it.[10]Linda D. Pendleton, When Humans Fly High: What Pilots Should Know About High-Altitude Physiology, Hypoxia, and Rapid Decompression (http://www.avweb.com/news/aeromed/181893-1.html) The result would be a rapid loss of consciousness and death. This would happen around the seven hour mark; the chances are very slim that you would make it to eight. [Image: image] And two million years later, your frozen body, still moving along steadily at a foot per second, would pass through the heliopause into interstellar space—the same boundary that Voyager just crossed.[11]Again. Clyde Tombaugh, the astronomer who discovered Pluto, died in 1997. A portion of his remains were placed on New Horizons spacecraft, which will fly past Pluto and then continue out of the Solar System. It's true that your hypothetical foot-per-second trip would be cold, unpleasant, and rapidly fatal. But when the Sun becomes a red giant in four billion years and consumes the Earth, you and Clyde would be the only ones to escape. So there's that. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If you began rising upward at a constant speed of one foot per second (≈0.305 m/s), you would ascend slowly but steadily. After 1 minute, you’d be 60 feet (≈18.3 m) above your starting point; after 1 hour, about 3,600 feet (≈1.097 km); and after 24 hours, roughly 86,400 feet (≈26.3 km)—well into the stratosphere.

However, several physical realities would intervene long before then:

- **Breathable air runs out**: Above ~18,000 feet (5.5 km), oxygen levels become dangerously low without supplemental oxygen.
- **Temperature drops**: In the troposphere, temperature decreases by about 6.5°C per kilometer; at 26 km, it’s around –50°C or colder.
- **Atmospheric pressure plummets**: At 86,400 feet, pressure is less than 1% of sea level, requiring a pressurized suit to avoid ebullism (body fluids boiling).
- **No propulsion or support**: Sustaining upward motion without a vehicle or lift mechanism isn’t physically possible for a human under normal conditions—this scenario assumes an external force continuously lifting you.

So while mathematically you’d keep rising at 1 ft/s indefinitely, biologically and physically, you’d face life-threatening conditions within minutes to hours unless protected.

edus.text: If you began rising upward at a constant speed of one foot per second (≈0.305 m/s),
you would ascend slowly but steadily.
After 1 minute, you’d be 60 feet (≈18.3 m) above your starting point;
after 1 hour, about 3,600 feet (≈1.097 km);
and after 24 hours, roughly 86,400 feet (≈26.3 km)—well into the stratosphere.
However, several physical realities would intervene long before then:
Breathable air runs out:
Above ~18,000 feet (5.5 km), oxygen levels become dangerously low without supplemental oxygen.
Temperature drops:
In the troposphere, temperature decreases by about 6.5°C per kilometer;
at 26 km, it’s around –50°C or colder.
Atmospheric pressure plummets:
At 86,400 feet, pressure is less than 1% of sea level,
requiring a pressurized suit to avoid ebullism (body fluids boiling).
No propulsion or support:
Sustaining upward motion without a vehicle or lift mechanism isn’t physically possible for a human under normal conditions—
this scenario assumes an external force continuously lifting you.
So while mathematically you’d keep rising at 1 ft/s indefinitely,
biologically and physically, you’d face life-threatening conditions within minutes to hours unless protected.

items.question: What If the Wind Reached 500 Miles per Hour?
human_answers: Absolutely! [Image: image] Some things don't work like they do in the movies. Getting shot doesn't really make someone fly backward. The vacuum of space doesn't make your skin explode. But high wind can definitely pick up a person. In fact, if you were standing in the parking lot, the wind wouldn't just pick you up—it would also peel the pavement from the ground! [Image: image] It wouldn't be strong enough to peel your skin off. Humans can survive blasts of 500 mph wind, which is important because pilots sometimes need to eject from airplanes at those speeds. In the 1940s, the US government put pilots in wind tunnels to learn how they reacted to high winds. Have you ever been curious what happens to a person's face in 457 mph winds? Well, you can watch a video of one of those wind tunnel tests here (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IU4SDDNXuUA). (That test was conducted at NASA Langley Research Center, where I worked before I started drawing internet comics for a living.) It doesn't look very comfortable—I didn't know cheeks could flap like that—but the pilot appears to stay alive. Luckily, he's strapped into that chair. He wouldn't be able to stand up in those winds! If he tried, he would go flying backward down the tunnel. High wind is really powerful. In a paper in the journal Weather, J. F. R. McIlveen showed how to calculate the force of wind on the human body.[1]McIlveen, J. F. R.. "The Everyday Effects Of Wind Drag On People. (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1256/wea.29.02/pdf)" Weather 57, no. 11 (2002): 410-413. The calculations on page 2 show how far you'd have to lean to stay upright in wind of various speeds. [Image: image] When wind speed rises above about 120 mph, it's no longer possible to stay upright no matter how far you lean; you'll start to slide backward across the ground,[2]When Hurricane Isabel hit Virginia in 2003, I had the bright idea of standing on a skateboard with a poncho held up like a sail, so the wind would blow me down the street. But the moment I got the sail up, the wind fell quiet. Later, I learned that people die from doing that (http://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-1327705/Kite-surfer-28-dies-gale-drags-100mph-beach-drops-50ft.html). Oops. then quickly go head over heels and start to tumble. You wouldn't necessarily be thrown very high. If the wind were perfectly level, you'd tumble along the surface, bouncing against the ground. However, if there were any updrafts, you could easily be lifted up and carried away. The good news is that 500 mph winds are rare. The strongest hurricanes have wind speeds around 200 mph with gusts up to 250.[3]Courtney, J.; Buchan, S.; Cerveny, R.S.; Bessemoulin, P.; Peterson, T.C.; Rubiera Torres, J.M.; Beven, J.; King, J.; Trerwin, B.; Rancourt, K.. 2012 "Documentation and verification of the world extreme wind gust record: 113.3 m s–1 on Barrow Island, Australia, during passage of tropical cyclone Olivia. (http://www.bom.gov.au/amoj/docs/2012/courtney_hres.pdf)" Australian Meterological and Oceanographic Journal, 62 (1). 1-9. Tornadoes can reach 300 mph.[4]It's difficult to get accurate measurements of surface winds since those tornadoes destroy most measuring equipment (http://www.spc.noaa.gov/faq/tornado/#History)! 300 is a far cry from 500; the force from a 500 mph wind is several times stronger than the force from a 300 mph wind. There are a few ways you could experience wind speeds faster than 500 mph. One is to stand on top of a volcano when it erupts. When Mount St. Helens exploded in 1980, the column of ash was blasted outward at 700 mph, which is close to the speed of sound.[5]Kieffer, S. W., 1981, Fluid dynamics of the May 18 blast at Mount St. Helens, in Lipman, P.W., and Mullineux, D.R., eds., The 1980 Eruptions of Mount St. Helens, Washington: U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 1250, p. 379-400. Another way to experience 500 mph winds is to trigger a hypercane.[6]Limits on Hurricane Intensity (http://wind.mit.edu/~emanuel/holem/holem.html) A hypercane is an exotic type of hurricane with 500 mph winds spinning in a very tight vortex just a few miles across. Hypercanes can't exist on Earth right now. To form, they require ocean temperatures of about 50°C. No matter how much we warm the planet, we're not going to get the temperature that high any time soon. However, there's one way these storms might happen. When an asteroid or comet—coincidentally, one about the size of the recently-named 4942 Munroe (http://blog.xkcd.com/2013/09/30/asteroid-4942-munroe/)—hit Mexico 65 million years ago, it punched a hole in the crust and left behind a sea of lava.[7]Christeson, Gail L., Gareth S. Collins, Joanna V. Morgan, Sean P.S. Gulick, Penny J. Barton, and Michael R. Warner. "Mantle Deformation Beneath The Chicxulub Impact Crater (https://spiral.imperial.ac.uk/bitstream/10044/1/4214/1/icpub.pdf)." Earth and Planetary Science Letters 284, no. 1-2 (2009): 249-257. When water flowed back in to fill the hole, it would have been heated by contact with the molten rock. This might have created the conditions for hypercanes to form, and one paper suggests that these storms could have lifted a large amount of dust and debris into the upper atmosphere—thus contributing to a global winter and extinction of the dinosaurs.[8]Emanuel, Kerry A., Kevin Speer, Richard Rotunno, Ramesh Srivastava, and Mario Molina. "Hypercanes: A Possible Link In Global Extinction Scenarios (ftp://texmex.mit.edu/pub/emanuel/PAPERS/hypercane95.pdf)." Journal of Geophysical Research 100, no. D7 (1995): 13755-13765. [Image: image] In short, the answer to Grey's question is yes—500 mph winds would send you flying through the air. But don't worry about that. Instead, worry about is the thing that created the 500 mph winds. Odds are, that's what's going to kill you. [Image: image]

rubrics.question_focus: What If the Wind Reached 500 Miles per Hour?

criteria.name: Physical plausibility of 500 mph wind effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons from the 500 mph wind premise using appropriate physics, especially drag force scaling, human survivability, and object/material response.
criteria.1-2: Treats 500 mph wind like ordinary storm wind or makes cinematic claims such as skin being stripped off without support.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes extreme danger but gives mostly vague or exaggerated effects with little physical basis.
criteria.5-6: Correctly states that a person would be knocked down or carried away, with some mention of force or debris hazards.
criteria.7-8: Explains that drag rises roughly with wind speed squared and distinguishes being blown/tumbled from instant bodily destruction.
criteria.9-10: Accurately applies the physics to humans, pavement, debris, structures, and survivability, avoiding both understatement and sensationalism.

criteria.name: Coverage of immediate and downstream consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer traces the cascading effects of 500 mph winds from direct human impacts to environmental, infrastructural, and societal consequences.
criteria.1-2: Mentions only one isolated effect, such as people flying, with no downstream reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Lists several damages but without causal sequencing or scale.
criteria.5-6: Covers humans, buildings, vehicles, and debris, but misses broader environmental or systemic consequences.
criteria.7-8: Connects immediate destruction to power failure, transport collapse, flooding or erosion, casualties, and emergency response breakdown.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent chain from aerodynamic forces through structural failure, debris missiles, infrastructure collapse, ecological damage, and long-term recovery.

criteria.name: Mechanism coverage for how such winds could occur
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer addresses the rarity and possible origins of 500 mph winds, such as volcanic blasts, asteroid impacts, hypercanes, or other extreme atmospheric scenarios.
criteria.1-2: Assumes 500 mph winds are normal hurricane or tornado conditions.
criteria.3-4: Notes that such winds are rare but gives inaccurate or unsupported causes.
criteria.5-6: Correctly says they exceed normal hurricanes and most tornadoes, with at least one plausible extreme source.
criteria.7-8: Compares hurricanes, tornadoes, volcanic blasts, and/or hypercanes with approximate speed ranges and formation limits.
criteria.9-10: Clearly explains that the cause of the 500 mph wind is likely more catastrophic than the wind itself, with scientifically plausible formation pathways and constraints.

criteria.name: Long-range causal coherence under the counterfactual
criteria.criteria_description: Judges whether the answer maintains a consistent timeline and scale when reasoning from the premise rather than jumping between incompatible scenarios.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts the premise or mixes unrelated disasters without causal links.
criteria.3-4: Has some logical sequence but frequently changes scale, duration, or setting inconsistently.
criteria.5-6: Maintains a mostly consistent scenario but leaves important transitions unexplained.
criteria.7-8: Uses a clear causal chain and distinguishes local gusts, sustained winds, vortices, and blast fronts.
criteria.9-10: Sustains a well-scoped counterfactual from initial wind exposure through regional/global aftermath, with no major causal gaps or scale errors.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer appropriately qualifies uncertain claims, avoids overprecision, and prevents contradictions with known wind records and biological limits.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident false claims, such as guaranteed instant death, global destruction, or common 500 mph storms.
criteria.3-4: Includes some correct statements but also major contradictions or unjustified certainty.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible, with modest caveats, but contains minor overclaims or imprecise comparisons.
criteria.7-8: Calibrates uncertainty about survival, lofting, structural damage, and storm formation while staying consistent with known extremes.
criteria.9-10: Carefully separates known evidence from speculation, uses appropriate caveats, and avoids contradictions about hurricanes, tornadoes, ejection survival, and hypercane feasibility.

items.model_answer:
If the wind reached 500 miles per hour (mph), it would far exceed the strongest winds ever recorded on Earth—such as those in the most intense tornadoes (around 300 mph) or Category 5 hurricanes (sustained winds up to about 180 mph). At 500 mph, the wind would be supersonic at sea level (since the speed of sound is roughly 767 mph), though still subsonic, but approaching extreme dynamic pressures.

Structures not specifically engineered for such forces would be obliterated. Most buildings, bridges, and infrastructure would suffer catastrophic failure due to the immense aerodynamic loads. The wind pressure scales with the square of velocity, so 500 mph wind exerts over seven times the force of a 190 mph hurricane wind. Even reinforced concrete structures could collapse.

Outdoors, unsecured objects would become deadly projectiles. Human survival would be nearly impossible without shelter deep underground or in specially designed bunkers. Vegetation would be stripped from the ground, and topsoil scoured away. Aircraft could not operate safely, and vehicles would be tossed like toys.

Such wind speeds do not occur naturally in Earth’s atmosphere under current climatic conditions. They are more typical of severe storms on gas giants like Jupiter or Neptune. If Earth somehow experienced 500 mph surface winds—perhaps due to an extreme extraterrestrial event or atmospheric instability—it would constitute a global catastrophe with unprecedented destruction.

items.question: What If You Lived on a Tiny but Ultra-Massive Asteroid?
human_answers: Last week, we looked at at life on a giant world (http://what-if.xkcd.com/67/). This week, let's look at a small one. [Image: image] The Little Prince, by Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, is a story about a traveler from a distant asteroid. It's simple and sad and poignant and memorable.[1]For another take on the Petit Prince, scroll down to the last section of this wonderful piece (http://the-toast.net/2013/08/02/texts-from-peter-pan-et-al/) by Mallory Ortberg. It's ostensibly a children's book, but it's hard to pin down who the intended audience is. In any case, it certainly has found an audience; it's among the best-selling books in history. [Image: image] It was written in 1942. That's an interesting time to write about asteroids, because in 1942 we didn't actually know what asteroids looked like. Even in our best telescopes, the largest asteroids were only visible as points of light. In fact, that's where their name comes from—the word asteroid means "star-like." We got our first confirmation of what asteroids looked like in 1971, when Mariner 9 visited Mars and snapped pictures of Phobos and Deimos.[2]Here's (http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/imgcat/html/object_page/m09_mtvs4109_09.html) a picture of Phobos looking like the archetypical asteroid. The archived images from the mission are at the NASA Space Science Data Center (http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/masterCatalog.do?ds=PSPG-00235), but strangely, the NSSDC refers readers to someone's personal Tripod page (http://petermasek.tripod.com/mariner9.html) to browse the actual images. These moons, believed to be captured asteroids,[3]Ironically, while Phobos and Deimos look like asteroids, new research suggests they're not. See Craddock, Robert A.. "Are Phobos And Deimos The Result Of A Giant Impact? (http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0019103510004100)". Icarus (2010) solidified the modern image of asteroids as cratered potatoes. [Image: image] Before the 1970s, it was common for science fiction to assume small asteroids would be round, like planets.[4]Not always; plenty of people had a good idea of what they would look like. And there were stranger ideas (http://pencilink.blogspot.com/2010/08/uncle-scrooge-29-carl-barks-art-cover.html) ... The Little Prince took this a step further, imagining an asteroid as a tiny planet with gravity, air, and a rose. There's no point in trying to critique the science here, because (1) it's not a story about asteroids, and (2) it opens with a parable about how foolish adults are for looking at everything too literally. So rather than trying to take things away from the story, let's see what strange new pieces science can add. If there really were a superdense asteroid with enough surface gravity to walk around on, it would have some pretty surprising properties. If the asteroid has a radius of 1.75 meters, then in order to have Earth-like gravity at the surface, it would need to have a mass of about 500 million tons. This is roughly equal to the combined mass of every human on Earth. If you stood on the surface, you'd experience tidal forces. Your feet would feel heavier than your head, which you'd feel as a gentle stretching sensation. It would feel like you were stretched out on a curved rubber ball, or were lying on a merry-go-round with your head near the center. [Image: image] The escape velocity at the surface would be about 5 meters per second. That's slower than a sprint, but still pretty fast. As a rule of thumb, if you can't dunk a basketball, you wouldn't be able to escape by jumping straight up. [Image: image] However, the weird thing about escape velocity is that it doesn't matter which direction you're going.[5]... which is why it should really be called "escape speed"—the fact that it has no direction (which is the distinction between "speed" and "velocity") is actually very significant here. If you go faster than the escape speed, as long as you don't actually go toward the planet, you'll escape. That means you might be able to leave our asteroid by running horizontally and jumping off the end of a ramp. [Image: image] If you didn't go fast enough to escape the planet, you'd go into orbit around it. Your orbital speed would be roughly 3 meters per second, which is a typical jogging speed. [Image: image] But this would be a weird orbit. Tidal forces would act on you in several ways. If you reach your arm down toward the planet, it would be pulled much harder than the rest of you. And if you reach down with one arm, the rest of you gets pushed upward, which means other parts of your body feel even less gravity. Effectively, every part of your body would be trying to go in a different orbit. A large orbiting object under these kinds of tidal forces—say, a moon—will generally break apart into rings. This wouldn't happen to you. However, your orbit would become chaotic and unstable. These types of orbits were investigated in an interesting paper by Radu D. Rugescu and Daniele Mortari.[6]Rugescu, Radu D., Mortari, Daniele, "Ultra Long Orbital Tethers Behave Highly Non-Keplerian and Unstable (http://www.academia.edu/3453325/Ultra_Long_Orbital_Tethers_Behave_Highly_Non-Keplerian_and_Unstable)", WSEAS Transactions on Mathematics, Vol. 7, No. 3, March 2008, pp. 87-94. Their simulations showed that large, elongated objects follow strange patterns around their central bodies. Even their centers of mass don't move in the traditional ellipses; some adopt pentagonal orbits, while others spin chaotically and crash into the planet. [Image: image] This type of analysis could actually have practical applications. There have been various proposals over the years to use long, whirling tethers to move cargo in and out of gravity wells—a sort of free-floating space elevator (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_elevator). Such tethers could transport cargo to and from the surface of the Moon, or to pick up spacecraft from the edge of the Earth's atmosphere. The inherent instability of many tether orbits poses an interesting challenge for this kind of project. As for the residents of our superdense asteroid, they'd have to be careful; if they ran too fast, they'd be in serious danger of going into a tumble and losing their lunch. Fortunately, vertical jumps would be fine. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If you lived on a tiny but ultra-massive asteroid—meaning it has a very small radius but an extremely high density, giving it a large mass—you would experience intense surface gravity despite its small size. Surface gravity depends on both mass and radius (g = GM/R²), so if the mass is huge while the radius is tiny, gravity could be far stronger than Earth’s. For example, if the asteroid were only 100 meters across but had the mass of Earth, surface gravity would be about 400,000 times Earth’s—crushing you instantly.

Moreover, such an object would likely be a neutron star fragment or something similarly exotic, as ordinary matter cannot be compressed to that degree without collapsing under its own gravity. In reality, a stable, solid body with those properties probably couldn’t exist outside extreme astrophysical contexts. If it somehow did, tidal forces near its surface would be enormous, potentially spaghettifying anything approaching it. You also wouldn’t have a breathable atmosphere, protection from radiation, or a day-night cycle like on Earth. In short, survival would be impossible under known physics.

edus.text: If you lived on a tiny but ultra-massive asteroid
meaning it has a very small radius but an extremely high density, giving it a large mass
you would experience intense surface gravity despite its small size.
Surface gravity depends on both mass and radius (g = GM/R²)
so if the mass is huge while the radius is tiny, gravity could be far stronger than Earth’s.
For example, if the asteroid were only 100 meters across but had the mass of Earth
surface gravity would be about 400,000 times Earth’s
crushing you instantly.
Moreover, such an object would likely be a neutron star fragment or something similarly exotic
as ordinary matter cannot be compressed to that degree without collapsing under its own gravity.
In reality, a stable, solid body with those properties probably couldn’t exist outside extreme astrophysical contexts.
If it somehow did
tidal forces near its surface would be enormous
potentially spaghettifying anything approaching it.
You also wouldn’t have a breathable atmosphere, protection from radiation, or a day-night cycle like on Earth.
In short, survival would be impossible under known physics.

items.question: Could You Boil Water by Stirring It?
human_answers: No. The basic idea makes sense. Temperature is just kinetic energy. When you stir tea, you're adding kinetic energy to it, and that energy goes somewhere. Since the tea doesn't do anything dramatic like rise into the air or emit light, the energy must be turning to heat. [Image: image] The reason you don't notice the heat is that you're not adding very much of it. It takes a huge amount of energy to heat water; by volume, it has a greater heat capacity than any other common substance.[1]Hydrogen and helium have a higher heat capacity by mass, but they're diffuse gasses. The only other common substance with a higher heat capacity by mass is ammonia. All three of these lose to water when measured by volume. If you want to heat water from room temperature to nearly boiling in two minutes, you'll need a lot of power: \[1\text{ cup}\times\text{Water heat capacity}\times\tfrac{100^\circ\rm{C}-20^\circ\rm{C}}{2\text{ minutes}}=700\text{ watts}\] (Note: Pushing almost-boiling water to boiling takes a large burst of extra energy on top of what's required to heat it to the boiling point—this is called the enthalpy of vaporization (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enthalpy_of_vaporization).) Our formula tells us that if we want to make a cup of hot water in two minutes, we'll need a 700-watt power source. A typical microwave uses 700 to 1100 watts, and it takes about two minutes to heat a mug of water to make tea. It's nice when things work out![2]If they didn't, we'd just blame "inefficiency" or "vortices". 700 watts for two minutes is an awful lot of energy. When water falls from the top of Niagara Falls, it gains kinetic energy, which is converted to heat at the bottom. But even after falling that great distance, the water only heats up by a fraction of a degree.[3]\(\text{Height of Niagra Falls}\times\frac{\text{Acceleration of gravity}}{\text{Specific heat of water}}=0.12^\circ\text{C}\) To boil a cup of water, you'd have to drop it from higher than the top of the atmosphere. [Image: image] How does stirring compare to microwaving? Based on figures from industrial mixer engineering reports,[4]Brawn Mixer, Inc., Principles of Fluid Mixing (http://www.craneengineering.net/products/mixers/documents/craneEngineeringPrinciplesOfFluidMixing.pdf) (2003) I estimate that vigorously stirring a cup of tea adds heat at a rate of about a ten-millionth of a watt. That's completely negligible.[5]Tea loses heat a much higher rate than this. See: Ben Harden, Tea temperature vs. Time graph (http://www.whoi.edu/vanishingarctic/page.do?pid=48597&tid=441&cid=120786&ct=61&article=82910) The physical effect of stirring is actually a little complicated.[6]In some situations, mixing liquids can actually help keep them warm. Hot water rises, and when a body of water is large and still enough (like the ocean) a warm layer forms on the surface. This warm layer radiates heat much more quickly than a cold layer would. If you disrupt this hot layer by mixing the water, the rate of heat loss decreases. This is why hurricanes tend to lose strength if they stop moving forward—their waves churn up cold water from the depths, cutting them off from the thin layer of hot surface water that was their main source of energy. Most of the heat is carried away from teacups by the air convecting over them, and so they cool from the top down. Stirring brings fresh hot water from the depths, so it can help this process. But there are other things going on—stirring disturbs the air, and it heats the walls of the mug. It's hard to be sure what's really going on without data. Fortunately, we have the internet. StackExchange user drhodes measured the rate of teacup cooling (http://physics.stackexchange.com/a/5510) from stirring vs. not stirring vs. repeatedly dipping a spoon into the cup vs. lifting it. Helpfully, drhodes posted both high-resolution graphs and the raw data itself, which is more than you can say for a lot of journal articles. The conclusion: It doesn't really matter whether you stir, dip, or do nothing; the tea cools at about the same rate (although dipping the spoon in and out of the tea cooled it slightly faster). Which brings us back to the original question: Could you boil tea if you just stirred it hard enough? No. The first problem is power. 700 watts is about a horsepower, so if you want to boil tea in two minutes, you'll need at least one horse to stir it hard enough. [Image: image] You can reduce the power requirement by heating the tea over a longer period of time, but if you reduce it too far the tea will be cooling as fast as you're heating it. Even if you could churn the spoon hard enough—tens of thousands of stirs per second—fluid dynamics would get in the way. At those high speeds, the tea would cavitate; a vacuum would form along the path of the spoon and stirring would become ineffective. And if you stir hard enough that your tea cavitates, its surface area will increase very rapidly, and it will cool to room temperature in seconds: [Image: image] No matter how hard you stir your tea, it's not going to get any warmer.

items.model_answer: Yes, in principle, you could boil water by stirring it, but it is extremely impractical. Boiling water requires adding enough energy to raise its temperature to 100°C (at standard atmospheric pressure) and then supply the latent heat of vaporization. Stirring transfers mechanical energy into the water, which is converted into thermal energy through viscous dissipation. However, the amount of energy needed is enormous: heating 1 liter of water from room temperature (20°C) to boiling requires about 334,000 joules, plus an additional 2.26 million joules to actually boil it. Even with vigorous stirring, the power input from human effort is only on the order of tens of watts, meaning it would take days of continuous, intense stirring to reach boiling—assuming no heat loss to the environment, which is unrealistic. In practice, heat loss would far exceed the energy added by stirring, making it effectively impossible under normal conditions.

edus.text: Yes, in principle, you could boil water by stirring it,
but it is extremely impractical.
Boiling water requires adding enough energy to raise its temperature to 100°C (at standard atmospheric pressure)
and then supply the latent heat of vaporization.
Stirring transfers mechanical energy into the water,
which is converted into thermal energy through viscous dissipation.
However, the amount of energy needed is enormous:
heating 1 liter of water from room temperature (20°C) to boiling requires about 334,000 joules,
plus an additional 2.26 million joules to actually boil it.
Even with vigorous stirring, the power input from human effort is only on the order of tens of watts,
meaning it would take days of continuous, intense stirring to reach boiling—
assuming no heat loss to the environment,
which is unrealistic.
In practice, heat loss would far exceed the energy added by stirring,
making it effectively impossible under normal conditions.

items.question: What If a Nearby Supernova Hit Earth with Lethal Neutrino Radiation?
human_answers: The phrase "lethal dose of neutrino radiation" is a weird one. I had to turn it over in my head a few times after I heard it. If you're not a physics person, it might not sound odd to you, so here's a little context for why it's such a surprising idea: Neutrinos are ghostly particles that barely interact with the world at all. Look at your hand—there are about a trillion neutrinos from the Sun passing through it every second. [Image: image] The reason you don't notice the neutrino flood is that neutrinos hardly interact with ordinary matter at all. On average, out of that massive flood, only one neutrino will "hit" an atom in your body every few years.[1]Less often if you're a child, since you have fewer atoms to be hit. Statistically, my first neutrino interaction probably happened somewhere around age 10. In fact, neutrinos are so shadowy that the entire Earth is transparent to them; nearly all of the Sun's neutrino flood goes straight through it unaffected. To detect neutrinos, people build giant tanks filled with hundreds of tons of material in the hopes that they'll register the impact of a single solar neutrino. This means that when a particle accelerator (which produces neutrinos) wants to send a neutrino beam to a detector somewhere else in the world, all it has to do is point the beam at the detector—even if it's on the other side of the Earth! [Image: image] That's why the phrase "lethal dose of neutrino radiation" sounds weird—it mixes scales in an incongruous way. It's like the idiom "knock me over with a feather" or the phrase "football stadium filled to the brim with ants".[2]Which would still be less than 1% of the ants in the world. If you have a math background, it's sort of like seeing the expression "ln(x)e"—it's not that, taken literally, it doesn't make sense, but it's hard to imagine a situation where it would apply.[3]If you want to be mean to first-year calculus students, you can ask them to take the derivative of ln(x)e dx. It looks like it should be "1" or something, but it's not. Similarly, it's so hard to get enough neutrinos to compel even a single one of them to interact with matter, making it hard to picture a scenario in which there'd be enough of them to affect you. Supernovae[4]"Supernovas" is also fine. "Supernovii" is discouraged. provide that scenario. The physicist who mentioned this problem to me told me his rule of thumb for estimating supernova-related numbers: However big you think supernovae are, they're bigger than that. Here's a question to give you a sense of scale: Which of the following would be brighter, in terms of the amount of energy delivered to your retina: A supernova, seen from as far away as the Sun is from the Earth, or The detonation of a hydrogen bomb pressed against your eyeball? [Image: image] Applying the physicist rule of thumb suggests that the supernova is brighter. And indeed, it is ... by nine orders of magnitude. That's why this is a neat question; supernovae are unimaginably huge and neutrinos are unimaginably insubstantial. At what point do these two unimaginable things cancel out to produce an effect on a human scale? A paper by radiation expert Andrew Karam provides an answer.[5]Karam, P. Andrew. "Gamma And Neutrino Radiation Dose From Gamma Ray Bursts And Nearby Supernovae. (http://wayback.archive.org/web/20120313045458/http://www.andrewkaram.com/andy/pdf/HPJ.pdf)" Health Physics 82, no. 4 (2002): 491-499. It explains that during certain supernovae, the collapse of a stellar core into a neutron star, 1057 neutrinos can be released (one for every proton in the star that collapses to become a neutron). Karam calculates that the neutrino radiation dose at a distance of one parsec[6]3.262 light-years, or a little less than the distance from here to Alpha Centauri. would be around half a nanosievert, or 1/500th the dose from eating a banana.[7]xkcd.com/radiation (http://xkcd.com/radiation/) A fatal radiation dose is about 4 sieverts. Using the inverse-square law, we can calculate the radiation dose: \[ 0.5\text{ nanosieverts} \times\left ( \frac{1\text{ parsec}}{x}\right )^2 = 5\text{ sieverts} \] \[ x=0.00001118\text{ parsecs}=2.3\text{ AU} \] 2.3 AU is a little more than the distance between the Sun and Mars. Core collapse supernovae happen to giant stars, so if you observed a supernova from that distance, you'd probably be inside the outer layers of the star that created it. [Image: image] The idea of neutrino radiation damage reinforces just how big supernovae are. If you observed a supernova from 1 AU away—and you somehow avoided being being incinerated, vaporized, and converted to some type of exotic plasma—even the flood of ghostly neutrinos would be dense enough to kill you. If it's going fast enough, a feather can absolutely knock you over. [Image: image]

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise and Physical Scale Handling
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly frames the unusual premise: neutrinos are normally weakly interacting, but a core-collapse supernova can produce an enormous enough flux that lethal dose becomes meaningful only at extremely close astronomical distances.
criteria.1-2: Treats neutrinos like ordinary radiation or ignores why the premise is unusual; gives no credible scale.
criteria.3-4: Mentions neutrinos are weakly interacting or supernovae are energetic, but does not connect the two quantitatively or causally.
criteria.5-6: Explains the weak interaction of neutrinos and the huge supernova output, with rough but incomplete scale reasoning.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains the tension between ghostly neutrinos and supernova scale, including inverse-square dilution or comparable scaling.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual with correct physical intuition, emphasizing that only an extreme nearby core-collapse event makes lethal neutrino radiation plausible.

criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer reaches or respects the key quantitative endpoint: a lethal neutrino dose requires being roughly a few AU from the supernova, about 2.3 AU using the cited assumptions, not light-years away.
criteria.1-2: Claims lethal neutrino effects at ordinary stellar distances or gives wildly incorrect distances without caveat.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes lethal neutrino exposure needs closeness but places it at an implausible scale, such as many light-years or inside Earth-like ranges without reasoning.
criteria.5-6: Gives a roughly close-in astronomical distance but lacks calculation, units, or connection to dose.
criteria.7-8: Uses a plausible dose comparison and inverse-square scaling to locate lethality at a few AU.
criteria.9-10: Correctly identifies the approximate lethal radius near 2.3 AU, explains assumptions such as dose threshold and parsec-to-AU scaling, and avoids overstating precision.

criteria.name: Mechanism Coverage: Neutrino Interaction and Biological Dose
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses depth and correctness of the causal mechanism by which neutrinos, despite rarely interacting, could deposit a harmful radiation dose in tissue under an extreme supernova flux.
criteria.1-2: Provides no mechanism or invents nonphysical effects such as neutrinos heating matter efficiently at normal fluxes.
criteria.3-4: Says neutrinos can damage cells but gives little explanation of interaction rarity or radiation dose.
criteria.5-6: Connects rare neutrino interactions to ionizing radiation dose, but with limited biological or particle-physics detail.
criteria.7-8: Explains that enormous flux compensates for tiny cross sections, producing enough interactions in body tissue to create a lethal sievert-scale dose.
criteria.9-10: Accurately links neutrino production, weak interaction probability, energy deposition, ionization, and fatal whole-body dose while distinguishing this from ordinary solar neutrino exposure.

criteria.name: Long-Range Consequence Chain and Competing Hazards
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer coherently follows downstream effects of being close enough for lethal neutrino radiation, including the fact that other supernova-related hazards and stellar structure would likely dominate.
criteria.1-2: Considers only neutrinos and ignores the broader consequences of being within a few AU of a supernova.
criteria.3-4: Mentions other dangers vaguely, such as heat or blast, without integrating them into the scenario.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that light, gamma rays, ejecta, or stellar material would also be catastrophic, but the causal ordering is incomplete.
criteria.7-8: Coherently explains that at a few AU Earth would likely be incinerated, engulfed, stripped, or otherwise destroyed apart from the neutrino dose.
criteria.9-10: Integrates neutrino lethality with the full counterfactual chain: progenitor size, radiation flash, plasma/ejecta, orbital context, and why neutrino death is a theoretical threshold rather than the practical main danger.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer avoids internal contradictions and calibrates uncertainty around supernova type, neutrino energies, dose models, biological thresholds, and geometric assumptions.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident false claims or contradicts itself about neutrino harmlessness versus lethality.
criteria.3-4: Shows some awareness of uncertainty but mixes incompatible assumptions or overgeneralizes across all supernovae.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent, with basic caveats about supernova type or dose thresholds, but some imprecision remains.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a consistent model and notes key dependencies such as core-collapse neutrino yield, distance, shielding irrelevance, and fatal-dose approximation.
criteria.9-10: Carefully distinguishes robust conclusions from model-dependent numbers, avoids contradictions, and clearly states that the result is an order-of-magnitude counterfactual estimate.

items.model_answer: A nearby supernova would not harm Earth with “lethal neutrino radiation,” because neutrinos interact so weakly with matter that even the immense burst from a supernova passes through the planet—and living organisms—almost entirely without effect. During a core-collapse supernova, about 99% of the energy is emitted as neutrinos, and if such an event occurred within tens of light-years, trillions of neutrinos would pass through every square centimeter of Earth (including human bodies) in a few seconds. However, due to their extremely low interaction cross-section, only a handful might actually collide with atoms in a person’s body—far too few to cause biological damage. The real threats from a nearby supernova are high-energy electromagnetic radiation (like gamma rays and X-rays) and cosmic rays, which could strip ozone from the atmosphere and trigger climate and ecological disruptions. But neutrinos themselves pose no lethal risk.

items.question: What If Humans Kept Growing at the Rate of a One-Month-Old Baby?
human_answers: Tall. According to the National Center for Health Statistics, the average newborn's height (length) is approximately 0.5 meters,[1]or 0.56 meters in heels. or a quarter of the diameter of the Death Star thermal exhaust port. [Image: image] From this initial height of 0.5 meters, they grow to about 1.5 or 2.0 meters: [Image: image] Babies grow fastest right after they're born. During their first month, infants grow about 4.4 centimeters, ten times their growth rate during their early teenage years. [Image: image] In Maria's scenario, this growth rate continues until about age 20: [Image: image] Let's follow that child's growth over the years. By its first birthday, the baby would be a meter long: [Image: image] At 2 years and 3 months, the kid would reach 169 centimeters (5'7"), the average adult height in the US. [Image: image] By age 3, we'd have a 2.08 meter (6'10") toddler, taller than Darth Vader ... [Image: image] ... and much taller than Yoda: [Image: image] By age 4, the child would be nearly nine feet tall, able to dunk a basketball without jumping.[2]A 7'8" Harlem Globetrotters player can almost dunk without jumping (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HTnC0RBXwws), so the threshold for a clear no-jump dunk is probably around 8 feet. [Image: image] A few months later, the kid would surpass Robert Wadlow (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Wadlow) to become the tallest human in history. At age 5, the child would be π meters tall (10'4"): [Image: image] At age 7, the child would be 4.2 meters tall, able to stare down a T-rex: [Image: image] By age 10, the child would be 5.8 meters tall (19 feet). If we assume these giants are proportioned like adult humans, this kid would weigh over a metric ton. [Image: image] Actual humans wouldn't be able to grow to such heights. Thanks to the square-cube law (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square-cube_law), our bones would be too thin to support our weight and our hearts would be unable to pump blood around our bodies. Even breathing would be difficult; we might be able to position ourselves to keep our airways opened, but to breathe in a lungful of air would require very high airflow rates; we'd experience tornado winds all the way down our airways. Our giant would reach a final height of between 10 and 12 meters, assuming growth tapered off around age 20. At that height, they'd be able to comfortably dunk a basketball while keeping one hand on the court outside the three-point line.[3]A creative NBA 2K3 mod shows us what that player might look like (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vGt10eu4XB8). [Image: image] In addition to the insurmountable health problems, someone with this rapid growth rate would face another hardship. To ride roller coasters, you have to be above a certain minimum height. However, they generally also have a maximum height. [Image: image] Bizarro, a coaster at Six Flags New England, has a minimum height of 137 cm (4'6") and a maximum height of 193 cm (6'4"). Our child would be tall enough to ride Bizarro at age 2 ... and too tall by age 3. Their coaster-riding window would last only 387 days. It's a sad truth: Roller coasters just aren't for everyone. [Image: image]

items.model_answer: If humans continued growing at the rate of a one-month-old baby—roughly 2.5 cm (1 inch) per month in length and gaining about 0.7 kg (1.5 lbs) per week—their size and mass would quickly become biologically and physically unsustainable. By age 10, a person would be over 3 meters (10 feet) tall and weigh several hundred kilograms; by adulthood, they would exceed tens of meters in height and weigh many tons. Such growth would violate biomechanical constraints (e.g., bone strength scaling with cross-sectional area while weight scales with volume), overwhelm metabolic demands, and exceed the limits of circulatory and respiratory systems. In reality, human growth slows dramatically after infancy and stops in late adolescence due to hormonal regulation and evolutionary adaptations that balance size, energy use, and reproductive fitness.

items.question: What If a Tyrannosaurus Rex Were Released in New York City?
human_answers: About half of an adult, or one ten-year old child: [Image: image] Tyrannosaurus rex weighed about as much as an elephant.[1]This always seemed a little off to me; my mental image of elephants is that they're in the same size range as cars or trucks, whereas T-rex, as Jurassic Park showed, is big enough to stomp on cars. But a Google image search for car+elephant (https://www.google.com/search?tbm=isch&q=elephant+car) shows elephants looming over cars just like the T-rex in Jurassic Park. So, great, now I'm also afraid of elephants. [Image: image] No one is totally sure what dinosaur metabolism looked like, but the best guesses for how much food T-rex ate seem to cluster around 40,000 calories per day.[2]Food calories (kcal). Sources: This (http://www.pnas.org/content/106/29/12184.full) and this (http://palaeo-electronica.org/1999_2/gigan/issue2_99.htm), and this (http://www.jstor.org/discover/10.2307/2666002) with some notes from this (http://www.plosone.org/article/info%3Adoi%2F10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0026037) and distraction from this (http://regex.alf.nu/). If we assume dinosaurs had metabolisms similar to today's mammals, they'd eat a lot more than 40,000 calories each day. But the current thinking is that while dinosaurs were more active (loosely speaking, "warm-blooded") than modern snakes and lizards, very large dinosaurs probably had metabolisms that more closely resembled komodo dragons than elephants and tigers.[3]For big sauropods, we know this must be the case, because otherwise they would overheat. However, there's a lot of uncertainty surrounding T-rex-sized dinosaurs. Next, we need to know how many calories are in a human. This number is helpfully provided, by Dinosaur Comics author Ryan North, on this wonderful t-shirt (http://www.topatoco.com/merchant.mvc?Screen=PROD&Store_Code=TO&Product_Code=QW-PERSON&Category_Code=QW). Ryan's shirt tells us that an 80-kg human contains about 110,000 calories of energy. Therefore, a T-rex would need to consume a human every two days or so.[4]Although a T-rex would likely be willing to eat several days to weeks worth of food in one meal, so if it has the option, it might eat a bunch of people at a time, then go for a while without eating. The city of New York had 239,736 births in 2011, which could support a population of about 1,000 tyrannosaurs. However, this ignores immigration—and, more importantly, emigration, which would probably increase substantially in this scenario. [Image: image] Ands if you live in New York, and you see a T-rex, don't worry. You don't have to choose a friend to sacrifice; just order 80 burgers instead. rubrics.question_focus: What If a Tyrannosaurus Rex Were Released in New York City?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Fidelity and Biological Plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer reasons from the specific premise of a Tyrannosaurus rex suddenly released in modern New York City while maintaining plausible T. rex biology, scale, metabolism, sensory abilities, locomotion, and behavioral constraints.
criteria.1-2: Treats the T. rex as a fantasy monster or ignores the NYC premise; major biological claims are implausible.
criteria.3-4: Uses the premise but relies on cinematic assumptions; includes several inaccurate claims about size, speed, diet, or behavior.
criteria.5-6: Mostly plausible biology and setting; some oversimplifications or unsupported assumptions remain.
criteria.7-8: Grounds the scenario in reasonable estimates of mass, food needs, movement, predation, and stress responses.
criteria.9-10: Carefully applies uncertain but evidence-based T. rex biology to the exact NYC release scenario without sensationalism.

criteria.name: Mechanism Coverage of Immediate Urban Interactions
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of the direct mechanisms by which a T. rex would interact with New York City: streets, crowds, vehicles, buildings, transit systems, noise, barriers, police response, and animal-control logistics.
criteria.1-2: Gives only vague destruction or panic with no concrete urban mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a few effects such as traffic or panic but lacks causal detail.
criteria.5-6: Covers several immediate interactions, including people, vehicles, and emergency services, with moderate detail.
criteria.7-8: Explains how NYC infrastructure, congestion, visibility, barriers, and responders would shape the event.
criteria.9-10: Provides a rich, mechanically coherent account of the first minutes to hours across crowds, transport, buildings, and containment.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces coherent downstream effects beyond the initial release, including containment, casualties, public behavior, institutional response, media, legal consequences, scientific interest, and city recovery.
criteria.1-2: Stops at the initial encounter or gives disconnected consequences.
criteria.3-4: Includes some later effects but with weak sequencing or missing causes.
criteria.5-6: Presents a plausible short-to-medium-term chain but omits major downstream domains.
criteria.7-8: Links immediate events to longer-term emergency, political, economic, scientific, and social consequences.
criteria.9-10: Builds a well-sequenced long-range scenario from release through containment and aftermath with minimal causal gaps.

criteria.name: Food, Energy, and Survival Reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly estimates or qualitatively reasons about the T. rex's caloric needs, feeding opportunities, prey availability, scavenging, zoo/livestock/human food sources, and whether it could survive in NYC.
criteria.1-2: Ignores food needs or makes absurd claims about constant mass killing or starvation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions eating people or animals but gives little metabolic or availability reasoning.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes large but finite food requirements and identifies plausible food sources.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable quantitative or comparative estimates and connects them to NYC food systems and human behavior.
criteria.9-10: Carefully analyzes survival using calibrated caloric needs, feeding intervals, available food, and containment timescale.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes knowns from uncertainties, avoids internal contradictions, and resists overconfident claims about extinct-animal behavior, emergency outcomes, or exact casualty counts.
criteria.1-2: Highly overconfident, contradictory, or internally inconsistent.
criteria.3-4: Some uncertainty is acknowledged, but key claims conflict or are asserted without support.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent; notes a few uncertainties but still overstates some outcomes.
criteria.7-8: Clearly flags uncertain areas such as T. rex behavior, response time, and casualties while keeping the scenario consistent.
criteria.9-10: Maintains tight internal consistency and well-calibrated uncertainty across biological, logistical, and social consequences.

items.model_answer:
If a Tyrannosaurus rex were released in New York City, it would cause catastrophic disruption due to its immense size, strength, and predatory nature. An adult T. rex weighed up to 9 tons, stood about 12–20 feet tall at the hips, and could reach speeds of 10–25 mph over short distances. Its powerful jaws—capable of exerting over 8,000 pounds of bite force—could crush vehicles, concrete barriers, or building facades with ease.

In Manhattan’s dense urban environment, the dinosaur would quickly destroy infrastructure: overturning cars, collapsing storefronts, damaging subway entrances, and potentially toppling weaker structures. Emergency services would be overwhelmed; conventional police weapons would be ineffective, and military intervention would likely be required. Evacuations would be chaotic, especially in crowded areas like Times Square or Midtown.

Ecologically, the T. rex would struggle long-term—it needs vast amounts of food (estimates suggest hundreds of pounds of meat daily) and space—but in the short term, it would pose an extreme danger to human life and property. Ultimately, such an event would result in mass panic, significant casualties, and extensive damage until the animal was subdued or killed.

items.question: What If You Dumped All the World's Tea into the Great Lakes?
human_answers: Weak, bordering on homeopathic. The standard cup of tea, as described by the International Organization for Standardization in ISO 3103 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=8250), contains two grams of tea per 100 mL of water.[1]Further ISO standards concerning tea include ISO 3720 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=51541) (black tea), ISO 11287 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=51540) (green tea), and ISO 14502-2 (http://www.iso.org/iso/iso_catalogue/catalogue_tc/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=31357) (the difference between black tea and green tea). The Great Lakes have a volume of about 22,600 cubic kilometers, which means we would need about 450 billion tons of tea to reach proper strength. According to the Tea Board of India, one year's global tea harvest totals only about 4.8 million tons,[2]Using figures from this report (http://www.teaboard.gov.in/pdf/Tea%20Statistics%20Global%20Scenario.pdf) extrapolated forward to 2014. only 1/100,000th of what we'd require to make Great Lake Tea. If we dumped those 4.8 million tons into the lakes, the resulting tea would be about as strong as if we'd dripped two drops of tea in a bathtub.[3]Technically, calling this kind of tea "homeopathic" is an exaggeration, since substances in homeopathy are diluted way more than this. Proper bathtub tea, of course, requires one 3-kg bag. [Image: image] For better lake tea, we should find a lake with a volume of 240 million cubic meters (0.24 cubic kilometers). Wular Lake in Kashmir is one candidate. Its volume varies with the seasons, but during the winter it's just about exactly the right size.[4]Unfortunately, it's shrinking (http://www.ramsar.org/pdf/wurc/wurc_mgtplan_india_wular.pdf). (For winter volume, see the chart on page 18 of that report.) India is the world's second-largest tea producer, so it's also conveniently located. Ullswater, in the UK's Lake District, is another great candidate. With a relatively stable year-round volume of about 0.23 cubic kilometers, it would be an excellent site for brewing a global cup of tea. Of course, while neither Wular Lake or Ullswater has ever been used as a giant teakettle, something like this was—famously—attempted in my own backyard in Boston. In 1773, a group of colonists disguised as American Indians[5]They dressed up as American Indians to align themselves politically with the Americas—against Britain—invoking the popular European stereotype of the free and noble savage. The Mohawk people, the actual Indians who the protesters were mimicking, mistrusted the settlers encroaching on their land, sided with the British during the subsequent war, and afterward were driven from their homes by the Americans and fled to Canada. boarded three British ships and threw the cargo of tea—around 44 tons of it—into Boston Harbor to protest British-run tax policy. Boston Harbor has a volume of about 0.44 cubic kilometers, which means that the "tea" brewed in 1773 would have been even more dilute than our Great Lakes tea. criteria.name: Dilution and Scale Quantification
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly estimates how dilute the Great Lakes tea would be by comparing world tea production to the volume of the Great Lakes and to normal tea-brewing concentrations.
criteria.1-2: Gives no meaningful quantitative comparison or falsely implies the lakes would become strong drinkable tea.
criteria.3-4: Mentions dilution but with missing, vague, or severely incorrect scale estimates.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes extreme dilution and gives some plausible numbers, but omits either lake volume, tea mass, or normal tea concentration.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable estimates for Great Lakes volume, global tea production, and tea strength to show the result is extremely weak.
criteria.9-10: Accurately connects all key scales, including about 22,600 km³ of water, millions of tons of annual tea versus hundreds of billions of tons needed, and a near-homeopathic-strength conclusion.

criteria.name: Physical and Chemical Mechanism Coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains the physical processes involved in dumping tea into the Great Lakes, including extraction, mixing, temperature, solubility, and particulate behavior.
criteria.1-2: Treats the event as magical or instantaneous without relevant physical mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one mechanism such as mixing or weak flavor but ignores most physical constraints.
criteria.5-6: Covers dilution and some mixing or extraction issues, but gives limited treatment of heat, steeping efficiency, or solids.
criteria.7-8: Explains that cold lake water would extract poorly, tea would disperse unevenly at first, and solids would float, sink, or wash ashore.
criteria.9-10: Integrates dilution, cold extraction limits, lake circulation timescales, suspended organic matter, tannins/caffeine release, sedimentation, and shoreline accumulation into a coherent mechanism.

criteria.name: Ecological and Environmental Downstream Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly reasons through biological and environmental consequences of adding all global tea to the Great Lakes.
criteria.1-2: Ignores environmental consequences or makes unsupported catastrophic claims.
criteria.3-4: Mentions pollution or harm in generic terms without connecting to tea composition or lake ecology.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some plausible impacts, such as organic loading or caffeine, but lacks depth or scale calibration.
criteria.7-8: Discusses likely localized or temporary effects from organic matter, decomposition, oxygen demand, tannins, nutrients, and cleanup burden while noting dilution limits.
criteria.9-10: Carefully distinguishes chemical dilution from solid biomass impacts, addresses oxygen depletion risks, microbial decomposition, shoreline smothering, invasive/pathogen concerns, water treatment effects, and spatial heterogeneity.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows consequences over time from the initial dump through mixing, ecological response, human response, and eventual dissipation without skipping or reversing causal steps.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected claims with no temporal or causal structure.
criteria.3-4: Has a basic sequence but includes major causal gaps or implausible jumps.
criteria.5-6: Provides a mostly sensible short-term chain but weakly handles medium- or long-term consequences.
criteria.7-8: Tracks immediate dumping, partial extraction, dispersal, environmental response, cleanup, water-use disruptions, and gradual degradation/flushing.
criteria.9-10: Builds a robust multi-timescale chain from hours to years, including uneven initial concentrations, basin circulation, biological decay, sediment burial, outflow through the St. Lawrence, monitoring, and policy/public health responses.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer states assumptions, handles uncertainty in estimates, and avoids contradictions with the counterfactual premise and known facts.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, impossible claims, or overconfident unsupported assertions.
criteria.3-4: Shows some awareness of uncertainty but relies on inconsistent numbers or conflicting conclusions.
criteria.5-6: States a few assumptions and avoids obvious contradictions, but confidence and estimates are uneven.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes annual world tea production versus all existing tea if relevant, notes estimate sensitivity, and keeps conclusions consistent with extreme dilution.
criteria.9-10: Explicitly calibrates uncertainties in tea mass, lake volume, extraction temperature, mixing, and ecological thresholds while maintaining internally consistent quantitative and causal reasoning throughout.

items.model_answer:
If you dumped all the world’s tea into the Great Lakes, the lakes would become very slightly tinted—perhaps a faint amber or brown—but not enough to look like a cup of brewed tea. Here’s why:

The total annual global production of tea is roughly 6 billion kilograms (including both green and black tea). Even if we assume all of it were brewed (which it isn’t—it’s mostly consumed as dry leaves that are steeped), the volume of liquid tea would still be minuscule compared to the volume of the Great Lakes.

The Great Lakes hold about **22,671 cubic kilometers** of water—that’s **22.7 trillion cubic meters**, or **22.7 quadrillion liters**. Even if you magically converted all 6 billion kg of dry tea into fully brewed tea (say, using a standard ratio of 2 grams of tea per 200 mL of water), you’d end up with roughly **600 billion liters** of brewed tea. That sounds like a lot, but when mixed into the Great Lakes, it would dilute to a concentration of about **0.000026%**—far too low to significantly affect color, taste, or chemistry.

Moreover, tea is mostly water already, and its organic compounds (like tannins) would quickly degrade or disperse. Any minor change in water quality would be negligible on a lake-wide scale and likely undetectable without sensitive instruments.

So, while the image of turning the Great Lakes into a giant cup of tea is whimsical, in reality, the effect would be imperceptible.

items.question: What If All the World's Viruses Were Gathered in One Place?
human_answers: It would be a huge pile, but human viruses would make up only a tiny fraction of it. HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, has killed tens of millions of people worldwide, and over 30 million people are currently living with HIV. The number of copies of the virus carried in someone's blood can vary dramatically,[1]Data on viral load—the number of copies of the virus per mL of blood—can be found in this paper (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23196933). but across all the people in the world, there probably exists about a spoonful worth of HIV. [Image: image] The typical healthy human body contains about \(3 \times 10^{12}\) viruses. This is actually not as many as you might expect; by volume, humans are apparently a less friendly environment for viruses than, say, soil.[2]An area of wetlands in Delaware (http://www.rcn.montana.edu/pubs/pdf/2008/Srinivasiah%20Res%20%20Micro%202008.pdf) contains something like four billion viruses per mL of soil, in case you were looking for a fun vacation destination. If you gathered together all the viruses in all the humans in the world, they would fill about ten oil drums: [Image: image] These 10 barrels only represent a tiny portion of the global virus community. Most of the world's viruses aren't found in humans. They're found in the sea. Seawater is full of microorganisms, and we've recently learned that those microorganisms are preyed on by viruses in a big way. Every day, about one in five living cells in the ocean is killed by a virus.[3]Marine viruses—major players in the global ecosystem (https://www.uni-due.de/imperia/md/content/water-science/ws0910/2031b_02z_ws0910_suttle_marine_viruses.pdf) These viruses are found from the surface of the ocean down to the depths.[4]Oddly, as you go further offshore and further down, the concentration of viruses doesn't decrease as much as the concentration of bacteria, so the virus-to-bacteria ratio is higher in the deep oceans than near the shore. Because the sea is so big,[5]Citation: Go and look at the sea. It's big. it contains a staggering number of viruses. If you piled up all these viruses—more than 1030 of them—in one place, they would be the size of a small mountain. [Image: image] It's hard to say exactly what the virus mountain would look like, but it would probably resemble something in between pus and meat slurry.[6]Blame Dave—he's the one who asked. Regardless of its exact appearance, it would almost certainly be disgusting. [Image: image] The pile wouldn't stay mountain-shaped for long, any more than a mountain of any organic secretion would.[7]If you don't believe me, try building a mountain of earwax or snot. You'll find you can't make it higher than a few inches before your friends and family show up and sit you down for a talk. To avoid a gigantic flood, it might be better to collect them into some kind of container. MetLife Stadium, host of Super Bowl XLVIII, has a volume of about 1.5 million cubic meters. rubrics.question_focus: What If All the World's Viruses Were Gathered in One Place?

criteria.name: Scale and Source Attribution of the Virus Pile
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly reasons about the quantity, volume, and dominant sources of all viruses on Earth under the gathering premise.
criteria.1-2: Gives wildly incorrect scale claims, such as saying the pile is microscopic, planet-sized, or mostly human viruses.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes viruses are numerous but gives vague or materially wrong estimates and misses that humans contribute only a tiny fraction.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that most viruses are environmental, especially marine, and gives a broadly large but imprecise pile size.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable order-of-magnitude reasoning, noting around 10^30 viruses and a pile comparable to a small mountain or many stadium volumes.
criteria.9-10: Clearly distinguishes human, soil, and ocean contributions, keeps estimates order-of-magnitude plausible, and avoids false precision.

criteria.name: Physical Consequences of Gathering Viruses in One Place
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly models what the gathered viruses would physically be like and how the mass would behave.
criteria.1-2: Treats viruses as magical, gaseous, glowing, or self-organizing matter with no physical constraints.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a pile but gives implausible physical behavior, such as a stable sharp mountain or a solid block without justification.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes the gathered material would be a large biological slurry and would not retain a tall pile shape for long.
criteria.7-8: Explains that water, organic material, capsids, and host-associated residues would form a disgusting fluid or paste needing containment.
criteria.9-10: Connects volume, density, fluid collapse, containment needs, decomposition, and environmental exposure in a physically coherent way.

criteria.name: Virology and Infectious-Risk Mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer accurately reasons about infectivity, host specificity, and disease risk from concentrating all viruses.
criteria.1-2: Claims all viruses would instantly merge, become one supervirus, or infect every organism indiscriminately.
criteria.3-4: Overstates pandemic risk while ignoring host specificity, viability limits, and the need for susceptible hosts.
criteria.5-6: Notes that many viruses would not infect humans, though some concentrated pathogens would pose local hazards.
criteria.7-8: Explains host range, environmental decay, dose, exposure routes, and the difference between virions being present and causing infection.
criteria.9-10: Balances severe local biosafety danger with rejection of universal-contagion claims, including bacteriophages, plant viruses, animal viruses, and human pathogens.

criteria.name: Long-Range Ecological and Biological Downstream Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer traces plausible longer-term consequences of removing and relocating Earth's viruses.
criteria.1-2: Ignores downstream effects or gives unrelated apocalyptic claims with no mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Mentions ecosystem disruption but only in generic terms and without linking to viral ecological roles.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that removing viruses would affect oceans, microbes, and disease dynamics, but with limited causal detail.
criteria.7-8: Connects viral removal to microbial population changes, nutrient cycling, marine food webs, phage control of bacteria, and microbiome disruption.
criteria.9-10: Develops a coherent multi-step chain from viral disappearance to microbial blooms/crashes, altered carbon and nutrient fluxes, ecosystem instability, and possible recovery or replacement dynamics.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Consistency, Uncertainty, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer maintains a clear interpretation of the counterfactual and calibrates uncertainty without contradicting itself.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts the premise, shifts scenarios repeatedly, or presents impossible outcomes as certain.
criteria.3-4: Uses an unclear version of the premise and mixes incompatible assumptions, such as viruses both remaining everywhere and being fully gathered.
criteria.5-6: Mostly follows the gathering premise but leaves key assumptions ambiguous and makes some overconfident claims.
criteria.7-8: States reasonable assumptions, distinguishes immediate from long-term effects, and flags uncertain estimates or biological responses.
criteria.9-10: Maintains one consistent counterfactual, separates physical aggregation from ecological removal effects, and uses uncertainty ranges without undermining causal reasoning.

items.model_answer: If all the world's viruses were gathered in one place, they would occupy an astonishingly small volume—estimates suggest that despite their astronomical numbers (on the order of 10³¹ individual virus particles globally), their total physical mass would be roughly equivalent to that of a few hundred adult humans, and if packed tightly, they might fit inside a single soda can or a large shipping container. However, this hypothetical collection would be extraordinarily diverse, containing countless species—most of which infect bacteria, plants, or animals—and the vast majority would be harmless or even beneficial to humans. Only a tiny fraction would include known human pathogens like influenza, HIV, or SARS-CoV-2. Crucially, without their host cells, viruses are inert; they cannot replicate or cause disease outside a living host. So while the concentration of all viruses in one location sounds alarming, it would pose little immediate danger unless viable hosts were also present. The real significance lies in what such a collection would reveal about viral diversity, evolution, and ecological roles—particularly in regulating microbial populations and driving genetic exchange across ecosystems.
